title: Steel-intensive press-hardened safety cell instead of an aluminium-intensive monocoque
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Swaps €4.8-5.5/kg aluminium semi-finished products for €1.1-1.6/kg AHSS and press-hardened steel. Replaces rivet, adhesive and flow-drill-screw consumables with resistance spot welds. The extra mass is charged back explicitly as CO2-compliance cost (MHEV) and added battery capacity (BEV), so the net figure is honest. Baseline: an aluminium-intensive monocoque of the MLA-Flex type – roughly 330 kg of 5182/6016 sheet, 6082-T6 extrusions and AlSi10MnMg HPDC nodes, held together by about 3,200 self-piercing rivets, 110 m of structural adhesive and flow-drill screws. Proposal: a steel-intensive body of about 395 kg. The ring structure (A/B-pillars, roof rails, sill inners, tunnel, seat cross-members – about 38% of BIW mass) is 22MnB5 AS150 press-hardened steel at 1,500 MPa. Rails and floor are CR780T/420Y-DP and CR980Y700T-CP to EN 10338, and body-side skins DX54D+Z. Aluminium stays only where it is cheapest per kilogram saved: the bonnet, AlSi10MnMg HPDC front shock towers, and a BEV-only 6082-T6 multi-cell sill insert. About 4,600 resistance spot welds replace the SPR and FDS. Why it works: landed aluminium sheet and extrusion cost €4.8-5.5/kg against €1.1-1.6/kg for AHSS. At 50,000/yr the aluminium premium of about €1,000 per body buys only 60-70 kg. That mass is priced honestly: about +4 g/km WLTP CO2 for MHEV at a €60/g compliance shadow price, and about +1.6 kWh for BEV to hold WLTP range. Benchmark: Volvo's SPA family (XC90/EX90) puts over 40% hot-formed steel in its safety structure and reaches top crash ratings with a steel-intensive cell.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Body shop moves from an SPR/adhesive/FDS line to a conventional RSW line, which is cheaper per joint and has a shorter cycle. Press shop needs about 14 hot-stamp die sets from a supplier with 2-3 roller-hearth furnace lines. Laser trimming of the PHS ring is bought in. The aluminium HPDC shock towers are carried over.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Ring parts are designed as laser-welded PHS blanks with tailored soft zones, so the part count stays close to the aluminium body's. Spot-weld flanges are 16 mm wide on PHS. The 3-2-1 RPS scheme carries over from the aluminium body so the framing concept changes little.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High – architecture-level material switch; largest lever in the body, but it is a next-platform decision
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Body material: aluminium body €1,650 vs steel body €700 (to be confirmed as including the retained aluminium bonnet, HPDC towers and BEV sill insert) + PHS conversion premium 150 kg × €1.8 = €970 → €680. Joining: SPR/FDS/adhesive €210 vs RSW €70 → €140. Mass compensation for +65 kg (fleet average 60/40 MHEV/BEV: 4 g/km × €60 = €240 MHEV; 1.6 kWh × €90 + chassis = €210 BEV) ≈ −€230. Zinc coating/cavity-wax uplift −€40. Mid = 680 + 140 − 230 − 40 = €550. Low €420 (aluminium price −15%, mass value +25%); high €600. Net €420-€600 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €21M-€30M per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: About 65 kg more mass raises crash energy and suspension loads. Full re-validation is needed: UN R94/R95/R135/R137, FMVSS 208/214/216/301, Euro NCAP 2026, IIHS small overlap, plus CAE on 6 prototype crash bodies and WLTP CO2/range re-homologation. Brand risk if aluminium construction is marketed. Steel corrosion needs zinc-coated skins and cavity-wax cover. Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: Investment is far too small for a whole-body material change: €4M tooling, €0 capex and €3M validation cover only the hot-stamp dies. Converting the body shop from SPR/FDS/adhesive to RSW, plus all the new cold-stamping dies and framing fixtures for a 395 kg steel body, is a much larger capex. The 3.3-month payback does not hold, even as an increment at next-platform level.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Volvo XC90 (2025, SPA) — Steel-intensive safety cage with over 40% hot-formed steel in the structure, against the 7% of the first XC90. How this differs: We apply that steel-intensive logic to a dual MHEV/800V BEV luxury SUV in place of an aluminium-intensive body, and price the mass penalty separately for each powertrain.

title: Cold-stamped QP1180 steel takes eight simple cabin reinforcements off the hot-stamp line
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes furnace energy, the in-die quench cycle and 5-axis laser trimming from 38 kg of parts. Cold stamping with trimming in the die costs about €0.7/kg against €2.0/kg for hot-stamp conversion. The partly offsetting coil premium and the +4.5 kg mass are charged in the bridge. Baseline: eight cabin reinforcements with simple, open geometry are hot-stamped in 22MnB5 AS150 at 1.2-1.6 mm, 38 kg in all: front and rear seat cross-members, LH/RH tunnel-side reinforcements, front and rear roof bows, the heel-kick reinforcement and the dash-lower cross-member. Each carries furnace, in-die quench and 5-axis laser-trim cost of about €2.0/kg. Proposal: cold-stamp them in third-generation quenched-and-partitioned steel QP1180 (UTS ≥1,180 MPa, A80 ≥14%), coated with GI, on a 2,500 t servo transfer press with springback-compensated dies and trimming in the die. To recover strength, strength-limited parts go up about 12% in gauge (for example 1.2 → 1.35 mm), adding about 4.5 kg. Hot stamping stays on the intrusion-critical ring (A/B-pillars, sill, roof rail). Why it works: these eight parts are bending- or stiffness-loaded cross-members with shallow draws. They do not need 1,500 MPa, and they pay the full hot-stamp conversion premium only because of grade habit. Q&P keeps enough elongation for flanged hat sections. Context: Kia puts hot-stamped parts in the EV9 safety cage and Hyundai/Kia's hot-stamped share is rising (about 15% in combustion cars to 20% in EVs), so this idea runs against the trend and must be justified part by part. ideaData.riskNotes: Springback and edge cracking at pierced holes. Hydrogen-induced delayed fracture in Q&P is tested to SEP 1970. Joining of mixed PHS/Q&P stacks is checked for weld-lobe width.

title: Three bought-in mid-size rear castings instead of an owned 9,000 t megacast cell
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Turns an under-used €25M owned casting cell into a variable piece price on a shared supplier cell. Scrap and straightening fall because the flow paths are shorter. The megacast die is never bought. The added cost of the stamped infill panel and node joining is charged in the bridge. Baseline: one rear megacast of about 60 kg AlSi10MnMg, vacuum HPDC, on an OEM-owned 9,000 t cell (≈€25M including trim press, X-ray and straightening). At a 150 s cycle the cell could make about 150,000 a year, so at 50,000 vehicles/yr it runs at about 35% utilisation. Scrap is 5-8% during the long ramp-up and the die costs about €4M. Proposal: split the rear underbody into three mid-size vacuum castings – LH and RH rear-rail nodes (damper, subframe and towbar mounts) and one rear cross-member node, 54 kg in total. A tier-1 makes them on 4,400 t cells that it shares with other customers, and the piece price includes its press, die and margin. A stamped CR340LA rear floor infill panel closes the structure. Why it works: megacasting pays back on press utilisation. A 50,000 a year luxury SUV cannot load a 9,000 t cell, but a supplier's 4,400 t cell running several programmes can. Mid-size castings also have shorter flow lengths, so they reach lower porosity and scrap. They can be repaired one node at a time, and they avoid the ~€25M up-front capex. Benchmark: Rivian's R2 uses three large HPDC castings for its rear structure, replacing about 50 stampings and over 300 joints, which shows that three medium castings can do the job of one megacast.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium – make-or-buy and capex avoidance tuned to 50,000/yr volume
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Megacast metal + conversion €244 vs bought nodes €286 → −€42. Owned cell capex €25M ÷ 350,000 = €71 avoided. Megacast die €4M ÷ 350,000 = €11.4 avoided. Scrap and straightening €18 → €6 = €12. Infill panel + node joining −€34. Mid = −42 + 71 + 11.4 + 12 − 34 = €18.4. Low €12 (supplier margin +5%), high €24. Net €12-€24 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €600K-€1.2M per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: Node joints add compliance, so torsional stiffness and damper-mount stiffness must be confirmed (target ≥95% of the megacast). Rear impact UN R34 / FMVSS 301 for the MHEV fuel tank and UN R100 for BEV pack integrity, 3,500 kg towing fatigue, CT porosity to ASTM E505 level 2. Depends on supplier capacity. The CR340LA steel infill joins aluminium nodes, so it needs cold joining (SPR/FDS + adhesive) with galvanic isolation and sealing that is compatible with e-coat.

title: 800V high-voltage components packaged inside CAE no-deformation zones, deleting guard castings
description: [800V BEV] Deletes two HPDC guard castings, a radiator-cross-member doubler and 1.1 m of HV armour. Cuts 0.9 m of 800V harness by moving the OBC and PDU out of the crush zone into zones that CAE shows do not deform. Baseline: on the 800V BEV, the front power-distribution unit, 22 kW on-board charger and DC/DC converter sit ahead of the front axle line, inside the frontal crush zone. Each needs crash protection: two AlSi10MnMg HPDC guard brackets (3.2 kg in total), a 1.5 mm CR420LA doubler on the radiator lower cross-member, and 1.8 m of corrugated PA12 HV cable armour. These satisfy UN R94/R137 and FMVSS 305 post-crash electrical isolation. Proposal: a packaging rule set from CAE. Every HV component goes inside a 'no-deformation envelope' taken from the 2026 Euro NCAP MPDB/FW, IIHS small overlap and pole load cases: behind the front subframe front cross-member line, and above the pack front flange. The OBC moves to the rear under-floor bay above the rear EDU, and the PDU moves onto the dash-lower cross-member. The two guard castings, the doubler and 1.1 m of armour are deleted, and the HV harness is 0.9 m shorter. Why it works: protecting a component sitting in the crush zone costs mass and parts. Moving it to a zone that does not deform costs nothing per vehicle once it is designed in. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 crush cans and reinforced mounts steer impact forces away from the battery and cabin, the same principle applied here to every HV box.

title: Zinc-magnesium ZM coating at half the coating mass replaces Z140 on body steels
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Halves zinc mass on about 260 kg of body coil at a small mill premium for the Mg-Al alloy bath, and reduces weld-electrode wear. Corrosion protection is equal or better, so no cavity-wax increase is needed. Baseline: about 260 kg per body of non-press-hardened steel – DX54D/DX56D skins and inners, CR340LA/CR420LA HSLA and CR590/CR780 DP grades – is bought hot-dip galvanised Z140 (140 g/m² total, about 10 µm per side), or electro-galvanised on exposed skins. Proposal: re-specify these coils to a zinc-aluminium-magnesium coating (ZM, Zn with about 1.5% Al and 1.5% Mg, to EN 10346) at about 70 g/m² total. Exposed outer skins keep their surface-quality class. ZM's Mg-rich corrosion products seal scratches and cut edges, so published cyclic-corrosion results put ZM at half the coating mass level with or better than Z140. Zinc consumption per body roughly halves. Why it works: a thinner, more corrosion-efficient coating costs less zinc. It also builds up less zinc on spot-weld electrodes (longer tip-dressing intervals) and less zinc vapour in laser joints. Context (not a ZM precedent): Volvo discloses seven different metal alloys in the EX90 body, showing how many material specifications a luxury body carries. The coating system on the non-PHS steels is one of the few specifications that applies to almost all of them.

title: Stochastic crash simulation releases gauge margins on forty-five crash-relevant stampings
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes about 4.5 kg of steel and four late reinforcement patches from the crash structure by replacing blanket gauge margins with measured 3σ robustness. A mass credit is included at a conservative €2.5/kg. Baseline: gauges of about 45 crash-relevant stampings (about 190 kg) are set from deterministic, nominal CAE. Each team then adds 0.1-0.2 mm of 'engineering margin' and, late in the programme, adds four reinforcement patches after prototype scatter. Proposal: a stochastic robustness loop in LS-DYNA with LS-OPT, about 60 runs per load case. Input distributions come from mill certificates for yield and thickness (for example CR780T/420Y-DP yield 420-560 MPa, thickness ±0.05 mm) and from spot-weld failure scatter. Load cases are Euro NCAP 2026 MPDB/FW/side/pole, IIHS small overlap and FMVSS 216. A gauge is reduced only where the 3σ response still passes. The expected outcome is an average 0.1 mm off on about 70 kg of parts (4.5 kg) and the four late patches designed out. Why it works: margins stacked on margins exist because scatter is unknown. Measuring scatter lets margin go only where it is needed. Benchmark: Xiaomi developed the YU7's 2,200 MPa steel by computationally screening millions of alloy formulations. We apply the same compute-first approach to gauge decisions instead of materials.

title: MHEV rails run thinner blanks in the BEV-sized dies, scaled to kerb mass
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The lighter MHEV no longer carries BEV-sized rail gauges: 3.6 kg less steel per fleet-average vehicle, plus MHEV CO2 compliance value. One die set is kept, so the only added cost is blank part-number complexity and one tryout loop. Baseline: front and rear longitudinal rails (eight stampings: inner and outer, LH/RH, front and rear) are shared by the MHEV (about 2,350 kg kerb) and the 800V BEV (about 2,780 kg). Gauges are sized for the heavier BEV: front rail outer 1.8 mm CR780T/420Y-DP, rear rail 1.6 mm Ductibor 1000-type PHS. Frontal and rear crash energy scales with mass, so the MHEV carries about 15% surplus capacity. Proposal: keep one die set and one geometry, but give the MHEV its own blanks 0.15-0.2 mm thinner (front outer 1.8 → 1.6 mm, front inner 1.6 → 1.45 mm, rear rails 1.6 → 1.45 mm), with a die recipe change (cushion pressure, draw-bead height) stored per part number. MHEV body mass falls by about 4.2 kg. Why it works: the MHEV's engine block adds crush stack-up but less mass, and CAE shows its rail force plateau needs about 12-14% less section. One die tolerates a 0.2 mm gauge window with recipe tuning. Benchmark: JLR's aluminium-intensive MLA-Flex is designed to carry mild-hybrid, PHEV and BEV on one body. We keep the one body and let blank gauge follow powertrain mass.

title: One nested-crash-can front module serves road and off-road packs, raising approach angle
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the second crash-module variant (dies, part numbers, CAE, MPDB and RCAR test series) and the off-road lower closure. The only added cost is a small premium for the nested can extrusion and its machined collar. Baseline: two front crash modules. The road version has a 7003-T6 bumper beam at 455 mm centre height on 170 mm crash cans. The off-road pack (about 30% take) has the beam raised 45 mm on shorter 120 mm cans plus a 1.5 mm CR420LA lower closure to recover lower-leg and MPDB compatibility. Each needs its own part numbers, dies, CAE, MPDB and RCAR 15 km/h tests. Proposal: one module for every car. A nested crash can in 6008-T7 has 150 mm of stroke, of which 60 mm telescopes into the rail tip through a machined guide collar, so the front overhang shortens by about 25 mm while the stroke is kept. The beam sits at 475 mm for all cars. The off-road lower closure is deleted because the nested can keeps the beam engaged with the MPDB face at all suspension heights. Approach angle rises by about 2° at off-road height, and the road car loses nothing measurable. Why it works: a crash can only needs stroke, not overhang. Nesting it inside the rail tip recovers overhang that the off-road geometry needs. Benchmark: listed 2024 Defender 110 trims quote about 30-31° approach and about 37.7° departure, which shows that off-road geometry is a headline specification in this segment.

title: Hot-gas-formed 1,900 MPa tube runs from A-pillar to roof rail, replacing four stampings
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four hot stamps, their laser trimming and about 60 spot welds per side become one hot-gas-formed tube per side that is 1.8 kg lighter. The tube's forming conversion costs more per kilogram, but less material and the deleted joining make the total lower. Baseline: per side, the A-pillar upper and front roof rail are reinforced by four hot-stamped 22MnB5 parts – A-pillar outer reinforcement 1.6 mm, inner 1.2 mm, front roof-rail reinforcement 1.4 mm and a B-pillar-top gusset – 9.6 kg per side with about 60 spot welds and 5-axis laser trimming. Proposal: one closed-section tube per side, formed by hot gas forming and quenched in the die (Hot Metal Gas Forming). A 34MnB5 HF-welded tube blank of 1.5 mm wall is heated, formed by 70 bar nitrogen and quenched to about 1,900 MPa. It runs from the A-pillar base through the header corner along the roof rail to the B-pillar top, 7.8 kg per side. The A-pillar section narrows by about 12 mm, giving a measurable obscuration gain. Why it works: a closed tube has far more torsion and buckling resistance per kilogram than two welded open hats. Forming in one shot removes the weld flanges, laser trim and three part numbers. Benchmark: Xiaomi's YU7 embeds 2,200 MPa steel in its A- and B-pillars using hot gas expansion of tubes, so the route is already in production on a 2025 SUV.

title: Correlated subsystem crash rigs replace twelve full prototype crash bodies
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes 12 hand-built prototype crash bodies (€4.2M) from the development plan by answering local questions on correlated subsystem rigs. Rig build and correlation engineering are charged against the saving. Baseline: the dual-powertrain programme plans about 38 hand-built prototype bodies for crash development (MHEV and BEV) at about €350,000 each including build, instrumentation and test. Many are used only to confirm one subsystem, for example sill-and-pack pole behaviour, front-rail crush sequence or roof strength. Proposal: 14 correlated subsystem rigs – a sill-plus-pack-section pole rig on a 1,500 kg sled, a front-rail drop tower (to 60 kJ), a roof-crush platen rig to FMVSS 216 and a B-pillar quasi-static intrusion rig – each correlated to LS-DYNA within ±7% force and ±10 mm intrusion before it is trusted. Twelve full bodies are removed from the plan, while every regulatory and Euro NCAP confirmation test stays on full vehicles. Why it works: most development loops ask a local question. A €60,000 rig answers it in days, and repeated subsystem tests narrow scatter better than a few full crashes. Benchmark: Xiaomi says it ran over 50 passive-safety tests on the YU7, showing how large full-vehicle programmes now are. We keep the confirmation tests and move the development loops to rigs.

title: Aluminium-silicon-coated boron offal returned to the steel mill in a closed loop
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 55 kg of coated boron offal per body is valued at mill-remelt price instead of merchant price, and the uplift is returned through the coil price. The segregation and logistics cost is charged. Baseline: about 95 kg of hot-stamped 22MnB5 AS150 parts per body come from about 150 kg of coil. Blanking offal (about 35 kg) and laser-trim and pierce scrap (about 20 kg) go into the hot-stamp suppliers' general steel-scrap bins. Merchants pay below clean new-production bushelling for it (about €0.06-0.10/kg lower), because the Al-Si coating and boron are contaminants for many melt chemistries. Proposal: a closed-loop contract. Coated boron offal is collected in dedicated chutes and bins at each blanking line and laser cell, and the PHS-producing mill buys it back at its own internal scrap value for remelting into the same grade family, where the Al and B are already in the specification. The scrap credit is passed into the coil price under an index clause. Why it works: the same scrap is worth more to the mill that makes 22MnB5 than to a general merchant, because its aluminium and boron are part of the target chemistry rather than a dilution cost. Segregation costs little because blanking and laser cells already have separate scrap conveyors. Benchmark: Volvo's SPA structures carry over 40% hot-formed steel. A body with that much press-hardened mass produces a large, steady stream of offal that is worth managing as a material loop.

title: Two body-extrusion alloys instead of five: 6082-T6 for strength, 6008-T7 for crush
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Pools 38 kg of extrusion billet into two contracts, raises scrap buy-back on segregated single-alloy streams, and allows lower-cost high-recycled-content 6082 billet. The 7003 → 6082 bumper-beam mass penalty is charged. Baseline: about 38 kg of body extrusions per vehicle are spread across five alloy/temper combinations: 6063-T6 (BEV sill insert), 6082-T6 (rear cross-members), 6008-T7 (crash cans), 7003-T6 (bumper beams) and 6061-T6 (seat cross-member ends). Each has its own billet contract, extrusion press set-up, scrap stream and qualification. Proposal: two families only. 6082-T6 (EN 573-3 allows Fe ≤0.50%; tightened to ≤0.35% by OEM spec) covers strength members – sill insert, cross-members, and the bumper beams re-sectioned from 7003 (wall +0.4 mm). 6008-T7 (EN 15088) covers every energy-absorbing profile. Billet is specified with up to 75% post-consumer content on 6082 within its Fe limit. Machining and offcut scrap returns as two clean, segregated streams. Why it works: alloy count drives billet premiums, die-change losses and scrap downgrading. Mixed 6xxx/7xxx swarf is sold as low-grade scrap, while single-alloy streams are bought back near primary price. Benchmark: Volvo says the EX90 body uses seven different metal alloys, showing how many grades a modern luxury body carries. We cap the extrusion part of the body at two.

title: Thin AS080 aluminium-silicon coating on every press-hardened blank instead of AS150
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts coating cost per tonne, shortens furnace dwell by about 15% on 95 kg of blanks, and reduces die build-up and electrode wear. A small corrosion allowance (cavity wax in three zones) is charged. Baseline: about 95 kg of 22MnB5 blanks per body are bought with the standard AS150 aluminium-silicon coating (150 g/m² total, EN 10346 designation AS150). The thicker coating needs a longer furnace dwell (about 4.5 min at 930°C) to fully alloy into Fe-Al-Si, builds up on die surfaces, and widens spot-weld electrode wear. Proposal: specify AS080 (80 g/m² total, EN 10346) on all PHS parts that sit inside the cabin and are e-coated, keeping AS150 only on the sill outer reinforcement and wheel-house-adjacent parts exposed to stone-chip and salt. Furnace dwell drops to about 3.8 min, and electrode tip-dressing intervals lengthen. Why it works: the coating's job in hot stamping is to prevent scale and decarburisation, and 80 g/m² does that fully. Corrosion protection inside the cabin comes from the e-coat. A thinner coating diffuses faster, so furnace throughput rises about 15%, and it leaves less soft interdiffusion layer at the weld. Benchmark: Volvo's SPA structures use over 40% hot-formed steel, so on a body like this the coating specification is spread across a large share of the BIW mass.

title: Powertrain-specific €/kg exchange rate gates every body lightweighting proposal
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Stops paying more for kilograms than they are worth. Five lightweighting items costing €11-22 per kg are reverted to steel or deleted, and their 7 kg is priced back in at the fleet exchange rate. Baseline: body lightweighting proposals are judged against one generic target of €8 per kg saved for both powertrains. Even so, legacy and brand-driven exceptions have left the plan carrying items such as a 6016-T4 aluminium roof panel (€11/kg saved), a magnesium AM60B rear-seat back frame bracket (€14/kg) and a CFRP tunnel cover (€22/kg) that cost more than the mass is worth. Proposal: two exchange rates derived from first principles and re-issued every six months. MHEV: WLTP CO2 sensitivity about 0.06 g/km per kg × €60/g shadow price ≈ €3.6/kg. 800V BEV: about 0.022 kWh per kg to hold WLTP range × €90/kWh at pack level ≈ €2.0/kg, plus brake and tyre knock-on ≈ €2.8/kg. Each proposal is priced at the fleet mix and rejected if it costs more. Applied to the current plan, it reverts five items that add 7 kg but cost €58 per vehicle. Why it works: lightweighting has a real but limited value that differs by powertrain. A single target over-pays on BEV and is unrelated to CO2 regulation on MHEV. Benchmark: Tesla's Model Y uses its structural pack as the floor, so mass and cost are traded at system level. We formalise that trade into an explicit exchange rate.

ideaData.title: Powertrain-specific €/kg exchange rate gates every body lightweighting proposal
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: body lightweighting proposals are judged against one generic target of €8 per kg saved for both powertrains. Even so, legacy and brand-driven exceptions have left the plan carrying items such as a 6016-T4 aluminium roof panel (€11/kg saved), a magnesium AM60B rear-seat back frame bracket (€14/kg) and a CFRP tunnel cover (€22/kg) that cost more than the mass is worth. Proposal: two exchange rates derived from first principles and re-issued every six months. MHEV: WLTP CO2 sensitivity about 0.06 g/km per kg × €60/g shadow price ≈ €3.6/kg. 800V BEV: about 0.022 kWh per kg to hold WLTP range × €90/kWh at pack level ≈ €2.0/kg, plus brake and tyre knock-on ≈ €2.8/kg. Each proposal is priced at the fleet mix and rejected if it costs more. Applied to the current plan, it reverts five items that add 7 kg but cost €58 per vehicle. Why it works: lightweighting has a real but limited value that differs by powertrain. A single target over-pays on BEV and is unrelated to CO2 regulation on MHEV. Benchmark: Tesla's Model Y uses its structural pack as the floor, so mass and cost are traded at system level. We formalise that trade into an explicit exchange rate.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Stops paying more for kilograms than they are worth. Five lightweighting items costing €11-22 per kg are reverted to steel or deleted, and their 7 kg is priced back in at the fleet exchange rate.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: No new tooling. The reverted parts go back to conventional steel stampings already in the supplier base (roof panel DX56D+Z 0.7 mm, steel brackets). The magnesium and CFRP supply chains are removed from the body BOM.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Each lightweighting proposal must arrive with a one-line €/kg figure and the powertrain mix it was priced at. Steel fall-back geometries are kept in the CAD so a later reversal is fast.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium – governance that prevents uneconomic content
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Roof panel 6016-T4 → DX56D+Z saves €22 (+4.2 kg). Mg bracket integrated into the steel cross-member saves €12 (+0.8 kg). CFRP tunnel cover → PP-GF30 saves €16 (+1.1 kg). Two aluminium brackets → steel save €8 (+0.9 kg). Gross €58. Mass priced back 7.0 kg × fleet €3.3/kg (60% × €3.6 + 40% × €2.8) = −€23.2. Governance −€0.5. Mid = 58 − 23.2 − 0.5 = €34.3. Low €24 (only three items reverted), high €40. Net €24-€40 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €1.2M-€2M per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

title: Press-hardened sill skid lip with replaceable wear strip replaces bolt-on rock sliders
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the 18 kg bolt-on slider kit on off-road-pack cars, and the weld nuts and doublers that every body carries to accept it. A 1.4 kg PHS skid lip on all bodies and a wear strip on off-road cars are charged. Baseline: the off-road pack (about 30% take) adds bolt-on rock sliders: 2 × 9 kg S355J2H tubes (Ø 50 × 3) on six forged brackets per side, which need M12 weld nuts and 1.5 mm doublers in every sill inner so all bodies can take them. The sliders hang 35 mm below the sill and cost about 12 mm of effective breakover clearance. Proposal: integrate the slider into the body. The sill lower closing panel becomes 2.0 mm 22MnB5 AS150 press-hardened steel with a 30 mm downturned skid lip running between the wheel arches, backed by the existing sill multi-cell section. Off-road-pack cars receive a clip-in PA6-GF30 wear strip (0.6 kg per side) that can be replaced after rock contact. The lip is rated to carry 50% of the static vehicle weight resting on one sill at mid-span without permanent set. On the BEV, the same lip sits outboard of the pack-side extrusion. Why it works: the sill is already the stiffest longitudinal member in the body, so making its bottom face the sliding surface adds 1.4 kg of PHS instead of 18 kg of tube and brackets, and clearance is kept. Benchmark: Mercedes' G 580 EQ underbody plate doubles as a skid plate on rocky terrain, so structural protection and off-road contact surfaces can be the same part.

title: MHEV sills drop the BEV pack-protection extrusion insert, keeping two bulkheads
description: [MHEV] The 2 × 6.1 kg 6082 extrusion insert is deleted on MHEV bodies and replaced by four small hot-stamped bulkheads. Variant control in sill build is charged. Per-MHEV figure. Baseline: to keep one body build, every sill (MHEV and 800V BEV) carries the BEV's 6082-T6 multi-cell extrusion insert, about 6.1 kg per side, whose job is to stop side-pole intrusion reaching the battery cells. The MHEV has no pack in that space, only the fuel tank under the rear seat behind the cross-member line and the exhaust in the tunnel. Its side-impact requirement is occupant intrusion (UN R95, UN R135, FMVSS 214, Euro NCAP 2026), which the PHS sill inner and B-pillar ring already meet with a smaller margin. Proposal: MHEV sills omit the insert. Two 1.5 mm 22MnB5 hot-stamped bulkheads (0.35 kg each) are placed inside each sill at the front and rear seat cross-member stations to keep the section from collapsing where cross-members load it. The insert positioning clips stay in the sill so a body can still be built as BEV. Why it works: the insert's crush capacity is sized for zero cell intrusion, a much tighter requirement than occupant survival space. The MHEV needs only local section stability at the cross-member joints. Benchmark: Porsche reports that its aluminium sill extrusions cut the Taycan's sill from 15 parts to three per side because the extrusion carries battery protection. Without a battery, the MHEV does not need that extrusion.

Net €55-€75 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €2.75M-€3.75M per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated). title: Bumper-beam outboard wedge induces small-overlap glance-off, slimming hinge-pillar reinforcement
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Swaps cabin-side reinforcement (sill-front insert, two bulkheads, 0.3 mm of hinge-pillar PHS per side) for a pair of compact beam-end wedges that reduce the load reaching the cabin. Baseline: to pass the IIHS small overlap test on both sides at 2.4-2.8 t, the cabin is reinforced so it survives the barrier's direct hit. Per side: the hinge-pillar inner reinforcement is 2.0 mm 22MnB5 (4.1 kg), two internal hinge-pillar bulkheads are fitted, and a 0.9 kg 6082-T6 small-overlap insert sits in the sill front. Proposal: make the car glance off the barrier instead. The front bumper beam is extended 70 mm outboard on each side with a 6082-T6 extruded wedge end-cap (0.45 kg) angled at 25°, tied to the front rail outer by a 1.5 mm CR780T/420Y-DP bracket. The wedge engages the barrier edge early and pushes the vehicle sideways, so less energy goes into the wheel and hinge pillar. The cabin reinforcement can then shed load: the sill-front insert and hinge-pillar bulkheads are deleted, and the hinge-pillar reinforcement drops from 2.0 to 1.7 mm. Why it works: lateral translation lowers delta-V and wheel-to-pillar loading. A compact engagement structure is cheaper than stiffening the occupant compartment against the full impact. Benchmark: Volvo's SPA cabin uses over 40% hot-formed steel, the stiff-cage route. IIHS's own analysis of small-overlap redesigns found that engagement structures produced more glance-off and lower delta-V than compartment reinforcement alone.

title: One press-hardened rear impact beam also serves as the towbar cross-tube
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the 8.5 kg towbar cross-tube and its brackets on tow-pack cars by upgrading the standard bumper beam to a tow-rated press-hardened section. The upgrade cost and +1.6 kg on all cars are charged. Baseline: every car has a rear impact beam (roll-formed CR1220Y1500T-MS 1.4 mm, 4.6 kg) for RCAR and FMVSS 301 rear impact. About 50% of cars (MHEV rated to 3,500 kg, BEV to 2,500 kg) add a separate S420MC cross-tube (Ø 80 × 4, 8.5 kg) bolted to the rails 60 mm further forward, with its own brackets. Proposal: one 1.6 mm 22MnB5 hot-stamped closed B-section (6.2 kg) on every car, bolted to the rear rails through the crash-can flanges with M12 10.9 bolts, with a pierced and nutted centre receiver plate. Cars with the tow option bolt on only the detachable neck and electrics. Why it works: the rear impact member already carries crash loads into the rails. Sized for 140 kg static nose weight and UN R55 D-values of about 17-21 kN, the same section does both jobs, so the second cross-member is redundant. Benchmark: Toyota's Land Cruiser 250 frame places tailor-welded blanks of different thicknesses and ultra-high-tensile steel where loads need them. We apply that load-placed logic by merging two rear cross-members into one.

title: Twelve-corner crush section in the front-rail tip raises crush force per kilogram
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Section shape, not more material, provides the crush force: 0.45 kg less 780 MPa steel per side for the same force plateau. Die complexity rises slightly and that is charged. Baseline: the front 350 mm of each front rail, the zone that crushes progressively behind the crash can in Euro NCAP full-width and MPDB, is a rectangular hat-plus-closing-plate section (about 110 × 130 mm) in 1.8 mm CR780T/420Y-DP, 2.6 kg per side. A four-corner tube folds with long, lightly loaded flat walls between corners, so most of the force comes from the corners and the flat walls add mass without matching force. Proposal: keep the same two-stamping construction, but form the crush zone as a twelve-cornered section. Each stamping has three inward re-entrant notches along its walls, giving short wall segments between twelve corners. Mean crush force per kilogram rises by about 20-25% in CAE and drop-tower tests, so the gauge drops to 1.5 mm for the same force plateau (about 2.15 kg per side). The section stays inside the existing rail envelope, and the crash-can flange and the rail behind the crush zone are unchanged. Why it works: progressive folding concentrates plastic work at corners. More, shorter walls fold in shorter, more stable lobes, so the same energy is absorbed with less material. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 front structure uses crush cans and reinforced mounts to manage frontal energy away from the battery. We raise the specific energy of the rail crush zone itself through section shape.

title: Flexible 3D roll-formed martensitic front beam with tapered ends replaces 7003 extrusion
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces €5.5/kg aluminium extrusion with €1.6/kg martensitic coil, and folds stretch bending and machining into one inline roll-forming pass. The +0.6 kg is charged at €3/kg. Baseline: the front bumper beam is a 7003-T6 double-chamber extrusion, stretch-bent to the fascia sweep, with machined crash-can seats: 6.5 kg, about €44 including bending and machining. Proposal: flexible (3D) roll forming of CR1220Y1500T-MS martensitic steel, 1.2 mm, closed B-section laser-welded inline. The rolls follow a variable sweep and a section depth that tapers from 110 mm at the centre to 70 mm at the ends, so the fascia packaging and the outboard compatibility profile are formed in line with no separate bending. That gives 7.1 kg at about €27. Crash-can seats are pierced inline, and the beam ends are crimped, not machined. Why it works: martensitic steel at 1,500 MPa is about four times as strong as 7003-T6 per unit thickness at a quarter of the price per kilogram. Flexible roll forming makes the variable section that previously forced the choice of extrusion and stretch-bending. Benchmark: Xiaomi's YU7 uses 2,200 MPa steel for door crash beams, which shows how far steel beams are pushed in 2025 SUVs. We apply the variable-section capability to the front bumper beam.

title: Closed-section cowl cross-member doubles as strut-tower brace, deleting the bolt-on brace
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The bolt-on strut brace and its fitting operation are deleted. The cowl gains a closing panel and a gauge step, so the stiffness is provided by structure that is already there. Baseline: the front strut towers are tied across by a bolt-on brace – a 6082-T6 tube with two HPDC end-caps, 3.1 kg, €29 plus €2 of fitting – fitted after the front damper on all cars because CAE torsion and steering-response targets need tower-to-tower stiffness. Beneath it the cowl (plenum) upper panel is an open 0.8 mm DX54D channel that adds little stiffness. Proposal: make the cowl a closed box section. The upper panel goes to 1.0 mm CR340LA, a 1.2 mm CR590Y980T-DP closing panel is spot-welded beneath it to form a 90 × 70 mm box, and the box ends are welded directly to the tower tops through gussets formed in the tower inner. Tower-to-tower lateral stiffness reaches the brace's level, and the bolt-on brace is deleted. Why it works: the cowl already spans tower to tower. Closing its section gives the moment of inertia the brace provided, with 0.9 kg extra steel instead of 3.1 kg of aluminium and castings. Benchmark: BMW's iX makes the cowl panel a structural member of its Carbon Cage, in continuous-fibre thermoplastic. We make the same structural use of the cowl in steel.

title: Downward skirt on the hot-stamped sill inner hides the battery side seam and bolts
description: [800V BEV] Deletes two PP-T20 side covers, 16 clips and their fitting by extending the hot-stamped sill inner downward as a skirt over the battery side seam. The extra 0.6 kg of press-hardened steel is charged. Baseline: on the 800V BEV, the line where the battery side frame meets the body sill (with its perimeter seal and side bolts) is exposed to stones and spray from the front wheels. Two clip-on PP-T20 covers (1.6 m each, 16 clips in total) protect it. Proposal: the sill inner gets a skirt 25 mm deeper and 10 mm further inboard, formed in the existing hot-stamp die by moving the trim line. The skirt overlaps the battery frame's lower edge with a 6 mm gap, so the seam and bolt heads sit behind press-hardened steel. Covers and clips are deleted, and a 10 mm drain gap at each end lets water out. Why it works: the sill inner already runs the full length directly outboard of the seam. A 25 mm skirt adds about 0.3 kg of steel per side and puts 1,500 MPa steel where a plastic cover used to be. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 battery is through-bolted directly into the unibody, so its seam and bolts sit in this exposed zone. We guard them with the sill's own skirt.

title: Hot-form-quench AA7075 B-pillar reinforcement replaces three-piece cold-formed 6082
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three parts and 24 rivets per side become one HFQ part 0.9 kg lighter. The higher conversion cost of HFQ (heating, cooled die, ageing) is charged against the deleted doublers, rivets and mass. Architecture assumed: aluminium-intensive body. Baseline: the B-pillar inner reinforcement is a three-piece assembly of cold-formed 6082 sheet (formed in T4 and aged to T6 at 3.5 mm) – a main reinforcement plus two doublers at the belt-line and at the foot. That is 3.8 kg per side joined by 24 self-piercing rivets, because 6082-T6 cannot be cold-drawn deep enough to make the section in one piece. Proposal: one HFQ (hot form quench) part per side in AA7075. The blank is solution-heated to about 480°C, formed and quenched in a cooled die in a 5-10 s cycle, then artificially aged to T6 (≥500 MPa). It is 3.0 mm and 2.9 kg per side, a single deep section including the belt-line and foot geometry. Why it works: hot forming gives aluminium the ductility to draw the full section in one shot, with almost no springback. The 7xxx T6 strength lets one part do what three 6082 parts did. Benchmark: HFQ panels are in production in Aston Martin's DB11 bonded aluminium architecture and have been used by Lotus since 2016. BMW's iX makes its pillar structures part of a CFRP Carbon Cage. We use HFQ as a cheaper non-steel route for the same pillar job.

title: MHEV transmission cross-member bolts across the tunnel, deleting the separate tunnel brace
description: [MHEV] Deletes the 1.8 kg bolt-on tunnel brace, its four bolts and one fitting operation on MHEV bodies. The transmission cross-member's upgrade to a closed hat section is charged. Baseline: the MHEV underbody has two transverse parts under the transmission tunnel. A bolt-on 2.5 mm S355MC tunnel brace (1.8 kg, four M10 bolts) ties the tunnel flanges together for torsional stiffness and to stop the tunnel opening under side impact. About 250 mm rearward, a pressed-steel transmission cross-member (3.5 kg) carries the 8-speed gearbox's rear mount and bolts to the tunnel side rails. Proposal: move the transmission cross-member 60 mm forward to the brace position (gearbox mount bracket re-angled accordingly) and re-section it as a 2.5 mm closed hat that bolts flange to flange across the tunnel at four points. It carries the gearbox mount and does the brace's job. The brace and its four bolts are deleted. Why it works: both parts are cross-tunnel ties within 250 mm of each other. One closed section sized for the higher of the two loads does both. Benchmark: JLR's MLA-Flex is designed to carry mild-hybrid, PHEV and BEV on one aluminium-intensive body, so MHEV-only underbody content like this brace is exactly what a dual-powertrain platform should minimise.

title: Rear roof header carries the tailgate hinges, deleting two hinge reinforcement plates
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two hinge reinforcement plates, their welded nut-plates and a harness bracket are deleted. The header inner's gauge and grade go up so it carries hinge loads directly, and that small material increase is charged. Baseline: the rear roof header is a two-piece open channel (DX54D outer 0.8 mm + CR420LA inner 1.2 mm). Tailgate hinge and gas-strut loads go into it through two separate 2.0 mm CR420LA hinge reinforcement plates with welded M8 nut-plates (0.6 kg each), plus a third bracket for the high-mount stop-lamp harness. Proposal: deepen the rear-header inner into a 1.4 mm CR590Y980T-DP closed box with the outer. Hinge mounting faces are coined flat in the inner during forming, and floating cage-nut strips are clipped into embossed pockets, giving ±1.5 mm hinge adjustment. Strut ball-stud bosses are extruded (flow-drilled) collars in the same inner. The two hinge plates, their nut-plates and the harness bracket are deleted. Why it works: a closed header at 1.4 mm DP has more than enough local stiffness for the hinge moment of a 30 kg powered tailgate. The separate plates only existed to stiffen an open, thin header. Benchmark: BMW's iX includes the rear window frame in its Carbon Cage, so the tailgate aperture frame is treated as primary structure. We give the steel header the same job.

title: BEV front subframe rear bushings mount into the pack-front body cross-member
description: [800V BEV] Two HPDC tower brackets, eight bolts and a stamping are removed by moving the front subframe rear mounts onto the existing pack-front cross-member. The sleeve nuts and local patch are charged. Baseline: on the 800V BEV, the front subframe's rear bushings attach to the body through two AlSi10MnMg HPDC tower brackets (1.4 kg each, €9) bolted under the front floor ahead of the pack, each with four M10 bolts. Directly behind them the body's dash-lower (pack-front) cross-member, a 1.6 mm 22MnB5 closed section, takes the pack front flange. Two adjacent load paths carry related loads. Proposal: the cross-member takes both jobs. Two M14 weld-through sleeve nuts and a 1.8 mm CR780T/420Y-DP local patch are added in the cross-member, so the subframe rear bushings bolt straight to it. The pack front flange bolts to the same member. Both cast tower brackets, eight bolts and one tunnel-side stamping are deleted. Why it works: the closed press-hardened cross-member is already the stiffest transverse member at that station, and putting the bushing load there shortens the load path into the sills. Benchmark: Tesla's Model Y treats the structural pack and body as one integrated floor system. We integrate the front subframe mount into the pack-front body member in the same spirit.

title: Tailored-tempered press-hardened upper load-path rail: soft crush front, hard rear
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Five parts and 22 spot welds per side become two, saving 0.7 kg per side. The hot-stamp conversion premium on the hat is charged against the deleted parts. Tailored tempering, not extra parts, now gives the rail its crush-then-stabilise behaviour. Baseline: per side, the upper load-path rail (the 'shotgun' running from the A-pillar to the headlamp and bumper) is built from three CR590Y980T-DP stampings at 1.4 mm (outer, inner, front extension) plus two brackets, 3.6 kg with about 40 spot welds. It carries part of the frontal and small-overlap load and the fender and lamp mounts. Proposal: one 22MnB5 AS150 hot-stamped hat section at 1.2 mm, with a tailored-tempered soft front third (about 700 MPa, so it crushes progressively) and a 1,500 MPa rear section that feeds the A-pillar, closed by a 1.0 mm CR420LA plate. Lamp and fender mount features are pierced in the hat. That is 2.9 kg per side and 18 welds. Why it works: the shotgun has two different jobs – crush at the front and stability at the rear – which the three-piece design achieved by overlapping parts. Tailored tempering gives both properties in one continuous part. Benchmark: Volvo's SPA safety structure uses over 40% hot-formed steel. Porsche's Taycan uses hot-formed steel in its A-pillar structure, so this rail joins the same hot-formed load path.

title: Two internal bulkheads at the front-rail S-bend replace the external bending doubler
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces a 1.6 kg doubler and 14 welds per side with two small internal bulkheads and 8 welds, saving 1.1 kg per side. No change to rail dies other than bead positions. Baseline: the front rail's kick-down (S-bend) under the dash tends to fold early in a frontal crash, before the crush zone ahead of it has been used. To stop this, a 2.0 mm CR780T/420Y-DP outer doubler (1.6 kg per side, 14 spot welds) is welded over the bend. Proposal: two internal stamped bulkheads (1.5 mm CR420LA, 0.25 kg each) are placed inside the rail section at the two plastic-hinge lines of the S-bend. They hold the section shape so it does not collapse at the hinges. The crush-initiator beads in the front rail are moved 20 mm forward so the forward crush still completes first. The external doubler is deleted. Why it works: S-bends fail by the section flattening at the hinge lines, not by lack of material, and stopping the section distorting restores its bending capacity. A doubler adds thickness everywhere to fix a local shape problem. Bulkheads fix the shape with about 30% of the mass. Benchmark: Toyota describes placing ultra-high-tensile steel 'in the right places' with tailor-welded blanks on the Land Cruiser 250 frame for +50% frame rigidity. The same principle of local reinforcement only where needed is applied here to the rail S-bend.

title: Four pack-to-sill lateral shear keys let pack mounting drop from 28 to 16 bolts
description: [800V BEV] Twelve M10 bolts, their nut inserts and their pack-frame boss machining are removed. Four forged shear keys and their slots are added, and nut-running time falls by 12 operations. Baseline: the 800V BEV pack is held to the body by 28 M10 10.9 bolts (18 vertical bolts in the sill flanges and 10 in the cross-members). The count is set by lateral load in a side-pole impact (UN R135), carried by clamp friction (μ ≈ 0.15) – far more bolts than vertical retention needs. Each bolt needs a pack-frame boss machined and a rivet-nut or weld-nut on the body. Proposal: four shear keys take the lateral load in direct bearing: forged 6082-T6 key blocks (0.35 kg each) bolted to the pack frame at the B-pillar and rear-door stations, engaging 22MnB5 stamped key slots in the sill-inner brackets with 0.5 mm clearance. Bolts are then sized for vertical clamp and fatigue only: 16 M10. Why it works: shear in bearing is several times stiffer and stronger per part than shear by friction, so a few keys replace the bolts that only existed for lateral friction. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 pack is through-bolted directly into the unibody. Our proposal keeps direct body mounting but lets keys carry the lateral load, so the bolt count falls.

title: Front and rear crash cans cut from one 6008-T7 extrusion profile
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Second extrusion die, second machining fixture and second qualification are removed. Longer runs lower the profile price per kilogram. Billet volume for the front and rear cans is pooled. Baseline: front crash cans are a 6008-T7 double-chamber extrusion (90 × 110 mm, 2.2 mm wall, 170 mm long), and rear crash cans a separate 6063-T6 single-chamber profile (80 × 100 mm, 2.5 mm, 140 mm long). They need two extrusion dies, two machining fixtures, two crush-trigger patterns and two material qualifications. Proposal: one 6008-T7 double-chamber profile for both. The rear can is the same section cut to 140 mm, with the trigger notch pattern changed by the CNC program only. The double-chamber section has about 20% more wall area than the old rear can, so rear-can crush force is expected to rise; the rear rail tip must be shown to stay stronger than the can (RCAR repairability), and its flange is re-drilled to the front bolt pattern. Why it works: front and rear cans do the same job – a repeatable, bolt-replaceable crush at RCAR 15 km/h – and differ mainly in length. One profile doubles the extrusion run length and halves set-up and qualification. Benchmark: Volvo discloses seven metal alloys in the EX90 body, and this idea removes one alloy-and-profile combination from that kind of mix.

title: 1.2 mm martensitic MS1500 pack underbody shield replaces 3 mm 5754 aluminium plate
description: [800V BEV] Swaps €6/kg aluminium plate for €1.5/kg martensitic steel of equal puncture resistance. Corrosion coating and the +2.9 kg are charged honestly against the saving. Baseline: the 800V BEV pack is protected by a full-length 3.0 mm 5754-H22 aluminium underbody shield, 2.2 m² at 8.1 kg/m² (17.8 kg), at about €6/kg landed plus €5 of forming – roughly €112 per car. Proposal: a 1.2 mm CR1220Y1500T-MS martensitic steel shield (9.4 kg/m², 20.7 kg), press-formed with shallow 4 mm stiffening beads and flanged edges in a cold die. It is zinc-nickel electroplated and given a 300 µm PVC underbody coat for stone-chip. Puncture resistance from a pointed object scales roughly with UTS × t². That gives 1,500 MPa × 1.44 mm² ≈ 2,160 for the steel against about 240 MPa × 9 mm² ≈ 2,160 for the aluminium, so penetration resistance is about equal at +2.9 kg. The fastener pattern is unchanged. title: Front belt height-adjuster rail bolts straight into the B-pillar inner soft zone
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the welded adjuster bracket on each side with its four welds. Two nuts weld directly to a tempered soft pad in the B-pillar inner. The slightly larger heated die segment is charged. Baseline: the front seat-belt upper anchorage (D-loop) height adjuster is mounted on a separate 2.5 mm CR420LA bracket (0.42 kg) welded inside each B-pillar inner with four spot welds and two projection-welded M10 nuts. The bracket exists because the hot-stamped 22MnB5 B-pillar inner is too hard (1,500 MPa) to pierce cleanly or weld nuts onto. Proposal: extend the B-pillar inner's in-die tailored-tempered soft zone (about 600 MPa, already used at its foot) to a 120 × 60 mm pad at the adjuster position. The two M10 nuts are projection-welded directly to the pad, and the adjuster rail is bolted to the pillar. The anchorage load (UN R14: 13.5 kN on the shoulder belt) goes straight into the pillar section, which is far stiffer than the bracket. Why it works: the bracket was only an interface fix for hard steel. A local soft zone is free in the hot-stamping die once heated segments exist, and it makes the pillar weldable and pierceable where needed. Benchmark: ArcelorMittal's Usibor/Ductibor laser-welded blanks put lower-strength, ductile zones exactly where pillars need them. We use in-die tempering to put a soft zone at the belt anchorage.

title: Roof-rail inner with four nut-strip hard points rated for 300 kg static roof load
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Eight reinforcement plates and 16 spot welds are replaced by two nut strips on tempered soft zones in the roof-rail inner, keeping a 300 kg static roof rating on every body. Baseline: to accept accessory racks and rooftop tents, every body carries eight separate 2.0 mm CR420LA plates (four per side) with welded M8 nuts. These are spot-welded inside the hot-stamped 22MnB5 side-rail inner, each sealed through the skin, adding 16 spot welds and a sealing operation. Proposal: one projection-welded nut strip per side (1.5 mm CR420LA, four M8 nuts at the foot stations) on four tempered soft zones (about 600 MPa) created in the hot-stamped rail inner during quenching. The closed rail section carries the load and is sized for 300 kg static (a tent with occupants) and 100 kg dynamic. The plates and their welds are deleted, and sealing points drop from eight to four per side. Why it works: the closed side-rail section is already the strongest member at that height. The plates existed only so nuts could be welded to hard steel and to spread load, and soft zones plus a strip do both. Benchmark: Land Rover quotes up to 300 kg static load on the Defender's top, with much lower dynamic ratings, so a static camping load is a real design case in this segment.

title: Cold-formed uncoated 22MnB5 rear-rail kick-up with laser-hardened tracks along fold lines
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Furnace, die quench and the AlSi coating premium are removed from 8.4 kg of rear-rail steel. They are replaced by cold stamping and a short laser-hardening pass, and the extra cavity wax is charged. Baseline: the rear-rail kick-up over the rear axle (the section that must not fold in an FMVSS 301 / UN R34 rear impact and carries towing loads) is hot-stamped 22MnB5 AS150 at 1.8 mm, 4.2 kg per side, at about €2.0/kg conversion plus the AlSi coating premium. Proposal: cold-stamp the same part in uncoated 22MnB5 in its as-delivered ferrite-pearlite state (about 600 MPa, easy to form). Then, in a robot cell, a 4 kW diode laser hardens six 12 mm-wide tracks along the predicted fold lines and section corners (3.6 m of track per side) to about 1,400 MPa martensite. The rest of the part stays ductile at about 600 MPa. Corrosion protection is the normal e-coat plus cavity wax. Why it works: kick-up stability is decided by local folding at a few hinge lines. Full-part hardening is not needed – hardened tracks at the hinges raise the folding load where it matters, while the ductile remainder absorbs energy. Benchmark: Volvo's SPA structure carries over 40% hot-formed steel, which is the full-hardening approach. We get the strength in this rear rail only where the folds are, using a laser.

title: BEV cabin floor panels down-gauged to 0.65 mm with hexagonal bead pattern
description: [800V BEV] The BEV floor uses 2.2 kg less steel through a 0.15 mm gauge reduction in the same dies. Beads replace lost stiffness, so the only costs are a die recipe and an extra bead re-strike. Baseline: the front and rear seat floor panels are 0.8 mm DX54D+Z (1.9 m², 11.9 kg) on both powertrains. Their gauge is set by the MHEV, whose floor spans between tunnel and sill carry seat loads, foot loads and jacking without support from below. On the 800V BEV the same panels sit 8-12 mm above a bolted structural pack whose lid and cross-members support the floor spans, while seat loads go into body seat cross-members. Proposal: BEV floor panels in 0.65 mm DX54D+Z from the same dies (draw recipe stored per part number), with a 3 mm-deep hexagonal bead pattern in the open spans to restore panel stiffness and keep the first panel mode above 80 Hz. Four PU foam stand-off pads (already used for rattle) rest on the pack lid. That is 9.7 kg, 2.2 kg lighter. Why it works: floor-panel gauge only has to resist foot load (1,000 N on a 100 mm pad) and panel vibration once spans are supported. Beads give the bending stiffness that the extra 0.15 mm gave on the MHEV. Benchmark: Tesla's Model Y makes the pack lid the cabin floor outright. We keep a body floor for sealing and the dual-powertrain build, but credit the pack's support so the floor can be thinner.

title: Embossed stand-off dimples in the pack shield replace twenty-two bonded foam pads
description: [800V BEV] Twenty-two bonded foam pads and their manual application are deleted by forming the spacing into the shield. A thin anti-chafe coating on the dimple tops is applied inline and charged. Baseline: the underbody shield beneath the 800V BEV pack keeps a 12 mm crush gap below the pack bottom using 22 bonded PU foam spacer pads (40 × 80 × 12 mm, about €0.35 each). These also stop rattle. Each is hand-applied with a pressure-sensitive adhesive after a cleaning wipe, about 4 s per pad. Proposal: form 22 stand-off dimples, 10 mm high with a 30 mm flat top, into the shield in the existing forming die. Each dimple top carries a 2 mm sprayed-on wax-based anti-chafe coating applied inline by the same robot that applies the underbody PVC. The dimples hold the gap under static load and collapse progressively in a ground strike, but each dimple is a stiff bridge across the 12 mm gap, so its collapse load must be tuned below the local dent load of the pack bottom and cooling plate. Pads and their application are deleted. Why it works: the pads' only jobs are spacing and silence. A formed dimple gives the spacing for free, and the anti-chafe film stops metal-on-metal squeak at 2 mm of relative motion. Benchmark: Mercedes fixes the G 580 EQ's underbody plate with about 50 bolts directly to the structure, which shows the shield-to-pack interface is designed as a structural joint rather than a loose cover.

title: 2,000 MPa press-hardened B-pillar outer reinforcement at 1.55 mm instead of 1.8 mm
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 2,000 MPa grade carries a coil premium, but 0.8 kg less steel per side and the mass credit outweigh it. Die, process and part count are unchanged. The saving is small, but it recurs on every body. Baseline: the B-pillar outer reinforcement is a laser-welded blank of 22MnB5 AS150 (1,500 MPa) at 1.8 mm over the upper and middle zones, with a ductile 1.6 mm foot, 6.1 kg per side. Its gauge is set by side-impact intrusion (UN R95 MDB, FMVSS 214, Euro NCAP 2026 side). Proposal: change the upper and middle strip to a 2,000 MPa press-hardening grade (34MnB5 / Usibor 2000 class, AS coated) at 1.55 mm. The ductile foot stays as a Ductibor 1000-type strip, and the same die and process window are used (furnace 930°C, quench to < 200°C). Bending strength scales with UTS × t²: 2,000 × 1.55² ≈ 4,800 against 1,500 × 1.8² ≈ 4,860, so equivalent within 1%. Mass falls to about 5.3 kg per side. Why it works: intrusion resistance of a bending-loaded pillar follows strength × thickness², so the 33% strength step allows a 14% gauge cut. Benchmark: Xiaomi uses 2,200 MPa hot-formed steel in the YU7's A/B-pillars and door beams. ArcelorMittal positions Usibor 2000 for pillars and rockers combined with Ductibor 1000 in laser-welded blanks.

title: Rear megacast CT inspection moved from 100% to statistical sampling plus inline X-ray
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] CT time per part falls by about 95%. An inline zone X-ray and shot-data monitoring take over the routine screening. The second CT cell otherwise needed for capacity is avoided. Baseline: every rear megacast (AlSi10MnMg vacuum HPDC, about 60 kg) gets a full computed-tomography (CT) scan for porosity at about 3 min per part and €6 per part including the €3M CT cell's amortisation, operators and data handling. That is about 2,500 h of CT time a year at 50,000 parts. Proposal: once the process is proven stable, 100% CT moves to a statistical scheme. Every part gets an inline 2D X-ray of three defined critical zones (damper mounts, subframe bosses and the towbar node) in a 25 s station. Full CT stays on one part in 20 plus all parts after a die change or alarm. Shot parameters (vacuum level < 50 mbar, intensification pressure, die temperatures) are monitored on every shot and must stay inside their control limits for a part to be released. The switch is only made after six months of porosity Cpk ≥ 1.67. Why it works: porosity in a stable vacuum HPDC process correlates with monitored shot data, and critical zones are known from the first 10,000 CT scans. 100% CT measures what the process data already guarantees. Benchmark: Volvo's rear-floor megacasting replaces 60-100 welded parts with one HPDC structure, so its quality assurance carries the weight of all those parts. ideaData.title: Rear megacast CT inspection moved from 100% to statistical sampling plus inline X-ray
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: every rear megacast (AlSi10MnMg vacuum HPDC, about 60 kg) gets a full computed-tomography (CT) scan for porosity at about 3 min per part and €6 per part including the €3M CT cell's amortisation, operators and data handling. That is about 2,500 h of CT time a year at 50,000 parts. Proposal: once the process is proven stable, 100% CT moves to a statistical scheme. Every part gets an inline 2D X-ray of three defined critical zones (damper mounts, subframe bosses and the towbar node) in a 25 s station. Full CT stays on one part in 20 plus all parts after a die change or alarm. Shot parameters (vacuum level < 50 mbar, intensification pressure, die temperatures) are monitored on every shot and must stay inside their control limits for a part to be released. The switch is only made after six months of porosity Cpk ≥ 1.67. Why it works: porosity in a stable vacuum HPDC process correlates with monitored shot data, and critical zones are known from the first 10,000 CT scans. 100% CT measures what the process data already guarantees. Benchmark: Volvo's rear-floor megacasting replaces 60-100 welded parts with one HPDC structure, so its quality assurance carries the weight of all those parts. We keep that assurance with data and sampling.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One CT cell instead of two at full rate. A 25 s 2D X-ray station is added inline after trim. Shot-data release logic in the MES blocks parts outside limits. Quality lab handles 2,500 CT scans a year instead of 50,000.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Critical zones are defined at design release with X-ray-friendly wall orientation. Cast-in part ID (dot-peen data matrix) links each part to its shot record. Critical zones are flagged on the drawing.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-Medium – quality-cost saving after process maturity

Mid = 5.7 − 1.2 − 0.2 + 0.4 = €4.7. Low €3 (1-in-10 sampling and X-ray maintenance), high €6 (part of a second CT cell avoided). Net €3-€6 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €150K-€300K per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

title: Stiffness-driven closing plates and floor inners relaxed from DP590 to HSLA grades
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes the DP590 coil premium from 9 kg of stiffness-limited panels and improves weldability and forming yield. Gauge and geometry are unchanged, so tooling is unchanged. Baseline: six panels totalling 9 kg per body – front-rail closing plates LH/RH, rear-rail closing plates LH/RH, the heel-board inner and the rear-seat pan inner – are specified in CR330Y590T-DP at 1.2-1.5 mm. These grades were carried over from a previous programme where these parts sat in a crash load path. CAE plastic-strain and stress maps on the current structure show they are stiffness-limited: peak stress in all crash cases is below 320 MPa. Proposal: re-specify the six panels in CR340LA HSLA (EN 10268) at the same gauge. Stiffness is unchanged (same modulus and gauge), the strength margin stays at least 1.06× peak, spot-weld lobes widen, and forming splits drop. Why it works: Young's modulus is the same for every steel, so on a stiffness-limited part the extra strength of DP590 is paid for and not used. HSLA costs less per kilogram and welds better. Benchmark: Toyota's description of the Land Cruiser 250 frame – ultra-high-tensile steel used 'in the right places' with tailor-welded blanks – is the same principle: high-strength grades only where strength is the limit.

title: Bake-hardening HX220BD roof skin at 0.65 mm keeps dent resistance, saves roof mass
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Roof skin gauge drops 0.1 mm using a bake-hardening grade at a small coil premium. Roof-level mass (worth more because of centre-of-gravity height) falls by 0.75-1.5 kg. Baseline: the steel roof skin is 0.75 mm DX56D+Z (about 1.9 m² on steel-roof bodies, about 35% take). Glass-roof bodies keep a 0.9 m² roof ring skin in the same grade. Its gauge is set by dent resistance (hail, car-wash brushes, and leaning on the roof during loading), not by structure. Proposal: a 0.65 mm HX220BD+Z bake-hardening grade (EN 10346), which gains about 40 MPa yield in the e-coat and paint ovens. Dent resistance scales with yield × t², so 260 × 0.65² ≈ 110 against about 160 × 0.75² ≈ 90 for the baseline, which is better after bake. The roof skin is 0.75 kg lighter on glass-roof bodies and 1.5 kg on steel-roof bodies, all at the highest point of the car. Why it works: dent resistance needs yield strength at final state, which bake-hardening provides after paint at no forming penalty. Roof mass high up costs centre-of-gravity height on a tall SUV. Benchmark: BMW makes the iX roof frame part of its CFRP Carbon Cage. We take a low-cost route to less mass at roof level.

title: Front long-range radar mounts on pierced bosses in the bumper-beam face, deleting its bracket
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the steel radar support, the plastic bracket and four fasteners by giving the bumper beam three pierced bosses and a snap-in carrier. The carrier clip is charged. Baseline: the front long-range radar is held by a PA6-GF30 bracket (about €3) screwed to a stamped steel support (about €2) that bolts to the front bumper beam with two M8 bolts. That is three parts and five fasteners, with aim adjusted through the plastic bracket. Proposal: the 3D roll-formed or extruded front bumper beam carries the radar directly. Three pierced and coined bosses in the beam's front face (positioned to ±0.3 mm from the beam datum) take a snap-in PA66 radar carrier clip (about €1) that holds the sensor at its nominal elevation. The steel support and bracket are deleted, and aim is corrected by the radar's own software calibration in the end-of-line ADAS station (already required). Why it works: the beam is the stiffest and most dimensionally stable part at that height. Mounting to it shortens the tolerance chain to the body datum, so a separate adjustable bracket is no longer needed. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 front structure uses crush cans and reinforced mounts to manage frontal loads. Our idea uses the same structure as the sensor's datum.

title: MHEV engine mounts bolt to a drawn front-rail pad, deleting cast brackets
description: [MHEV] Two die-cast brackets and eight bolts are deleted on MHEV bodies. Taller mount housings and a local pad in the rail are charged. A bolted joint also leaves the mount load path, which improves mount stiffness consistency. Baseline: the 3.0 L I6 MHEV's LH/RH hydraulic engine mounts sit on two AlSi9Cu3 die-cast mount brackets (1.1 kg each, about €6.5) bolted to the top of each front rail with four M10 bolts into weld nuts. Beneath each bracket is a 2.0 mm CR420LA rail reinforcement. The brackets mainly provide height, putting the mount at the engine's elastic axis. Proposal: form a raised 30 mm mounting pad into the front-rail inner during drawing (1.8 mm CR780T/420Y-DP rail, local pad 150 × 110 mm), and weld three M12 projection nuts into it. The hydromount bolts directly to the rail. Its own cast housing is lengthened by 28 mm to recover the height, about €2 extra per mount. The cast brackets and eight M10 bolts are deleted, and the reinforcement plate is retained but shortened. Why it works: the cast bracket was a height spacer between two strong parts. Putting the height into the mount housing removes a bolted joint from the load path and a part from the BOM. Benchmark: Kia uses reinforced mounts as part of the EV9's crash-energy management, steering forces away from cabin and battery. We make the engine mount part of the rail section in the same way. The BEV front drive unit mounts on its subframe and is not affected.

title: Front roof header inner takes visors and overhead console directly, deleting four brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four brackets and two welds are deleted by forming mounting bosses and clinch nuts into a slightly thicker header inner. The header's gauge step and nuts are charged. Baseline: the front roof header inner (CR420LA 1.0 mm) carries the sun visors, the overhead console and the interior-mirror harness through four separate stamped brackets (two spot-welded, two clipped), 0.6 kg in all. The windscreen camera and rain-sensor bracket are bonded to the glass. Proposal: the header inner goes to 1.2 mm CR420LA, with formed and pierced bosses at the visor and console positions and pressed-in clinch nuts (M6) on the bosses, positioned from the windscreen-aperture RPS. Visor pivots and the console bolt directly to the header. The four brackets are deleted, and the camera bracket stays on the glass. Why it works: the brackets only offset the visor and console from a thin, flat header. Bosses formed in the header do the same, and the extra 0.2 mm gives the local stiffness for visor rattle and console loads (UN R21 head impact through the headliner is unchanged because the bosses sit behind the same headliner energy absorbers). Benchmark: BMW's iX includes the roof frame in its Carbon Cage as primary structure. We make the steel header the direct mounting structure as well.

title: Rear-seat heel cross-member becomes the pack's rear-impact load stopper
description: [800V BEV] The pack's rear crush extrusion becomes a light single-wall profile, because the body heel cross-member, upgraded to a closed press-hardened box, stops the rail kick-ups intruding. The upgrade is charged. Baseline: for FMVSS 301 (80 km/h, 70% overlap MDB) and UN R34-type rear impact, the 800V BEV traction pack carries its own rear crush extrusion (6082-T6, 1.2 m at 3.4 kg/m, 4.1 kg). It is there because the longitudinals' kick-ups can rotate forward into the enclosure's rear face. The body's heel member under the second-row seat is an open CR780T/420Y-DP hat with little fore-aft stiffness. Proposal: close the heel member into a 22MnB5 AS150 hot-stamped box at 1.4 mm, tied at both ends to the kick-up roots by gussets formed in the longitudinal inners. It becomes a stopper that holds the roots in place and stops them rotating forward. The enclosure's rear profile becomes a single-wall 6063-T6 mounting member (2.2 kg/m). Why it works: rear-impact intrusion into the traction pack comes from kick-ups rotating at their roots. Stopping that rotation in the body removes the reason for crush capacity in the enclosure. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 enclosure is through-bolted directly into the unibody, so the body already surrounds it. Here the body takes the rear-impact role.

title: MHEV 48 V battery sits in a cradle formed into the rear cross-member flange
description: [MHEV] The battery tray, four brackets and the rear guard U-bar are deleted on MHEV bodies by seating the 48 V battery directly in a cradle formed into the existing rear cross-member. The nuts and form are charged. Baseline: the MHEV's 48 V lithium-ion battery (about 8 kg) sits under the rear load floor in a separate stamped DC04 steel tray (1.1 kg) on four bolted brackets to the rear floor cross-member. A 1.5 mm steel U-bar guards it against rear-impact intrusion (FMVSS 301 / UN R34 – 48 V is below HV thresholds, but the battery must not be crushed or short). Proposal: the rear floor cross-member (CR590Y980T-DP 1.4 mm, already the strongest transverse member in that zone) is re-drawn so its rear flange forms a 30 mm-deep cradle seat. Four M8 projection nuts are welded in. The battery bolts directly to the cross-member through its own case lugs. The cross-member's closed section sits between the battery and the rear crush zone, so it provides the guard function. Tray, brackets and U-bar are deleted. Why it works: the cross-member already exists in the same place and is stiffer than the tray-plus-bracket stack. Using its flange as the seat removes three parts and a joint layer. Benchmark: JLR's MLA-Flex is designed to carry mild-hybrid, PHEV and BEV powertrains on one aluminium-intensive body. We use a cross-member every body has to carry the MHEV-only 48 V battery.

title: Formed channel in the sill inner protects the 800V cable, replacing armoured conduit
description: [800V BEV] Stainless-steel armour overbraid and six clips are deleted because the sill inner channel and a simple cover strip protect the cable. Cover and channel forming are charged. Baseline: the 800V BEV's high-voltage cable from the front PDU to the rear drive unit and charger runs under the floor alongside the pack. It is protected by 2.0 m of corrugated PA12 conduit with a stainless-steel armour overbraid (about €12) and fixed with eight clips, because it sits in a stone-strike and jacking zone and must remain intact after side impact (UN R94/R95/R137 post-crash isolation). Proposal: the sill inner (already a deep hot-stamped section) is formed with a 40 × 30 mm open channel along its lower inboard edge, between the pack and the sill's crush cells. The cable runs in the channel in plain PA12 conduit, closed by a clipped 0.8 mm DX54D+Z cover strip. Side-pole crush stays outboard of the channel, and the steel sill-and-cover protects against stone-strike. The stainless armour is deleted and the clip count drops from eight to two. Why it works: the sill is the stiffest member beside the pack and the cable is shielded on three sides by steel; but the sill is the side-pole crush member, so CAE must show the channel stays clear of inboard intrusion. Benchmark: Kia's EV9 places crush cans and reinforced mounts to steer impact forces away from HV systems. We place the HV cable in a sill channel that must be shown by pole CAE to stay clear of intrusion.

title: Inline 3D vision closes the loop on adhesive beads, cutting over-dosing and peel coupons
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Adhesive dosing margin falls from about 20% to 8% on structural beads, gauge checks and peel coupons are largely replaced by per-body camera records, and repairs of missed beads found downstream fall; camera upkeep is added. Baseline: structural and hem adhesive beads in the body shop are dosed with a ≈20% volume margin because bead position and size are checked only by operators with gauges twice a shift and by peel coupons; a missed or broken bead is found at teardown or after paint, so several bodies need repair or scrap. Proposal: put a 3D laser-line bead camera behind each of 12 critical dispense nozzles, measuring bead width, height and position on every body at nozzle speed (≤600 mm/s), with closed-loop correction of pump flow and robot path offset; dosing margin falls to ≈8%, gauge checks and most peel coupons are replaced by the camera record, and a gap triggers an immediate in-cell re-dose. Why it works: the margin exists to cover unseen variation; once every bead is measured, the margin can be cut to the measured spread and defects are fixed in the cell. Benchmark: in the Range Rover L460 mixed aluminium-steel body, the bonding process is reportedly camera-monitored so steel never touches aluminium – camera supervision of bonding is already used where bond quality is critical.

title: 800V BEV service-only bonnet deletes cabin release, gas struts and handle
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the cabin release handle and Bowden cable, both gas struts with ball studs and the user secondary-catch lever on BEV bodies, replacing them with a clip-on prop rod and a dealer-tool latch release; strut and cable fitting labour also disappears from the BEV build. Baseline: the shared aluminium bonnet (6016-T4 1.0 mm outer, 6016 0.9 mm inner) carries the same opening hardware on both powertrains: cabin release handle and 1.9 m Bowden cable, two 450 N gas struts with ball studs, a user secondary-catch lever and the washer filler neck under the bonnet. On the 800V BEV there is nothing under the bonnet the owner services – the frunk opens separately and coolant/brake fluid are dealer items. Proposal: on the BEV variant only, the bonnet becomes a service-only panel. The primary latch stays (FMVSS 113 two-position latch retained) but is released by a dealer tool at the latch; the cabin handle, cable, struts and user catch lever are deleted and replaced by a 6 mm steel prop rod clipped to the inner; the washer filler moves to a flip-up flap in the bonnet badge or the left wing. MHEV keeps the full kit, so the bonnet panels and hinges stay common. Why it works: user-opening hardware exists only for user servicing; with no user tasks the hardware is pure content, and a prop rod is enough for the few dealer openings in life.
