title: Vision-guided robot hangs and gaps doors, deleting hand-fit shims and re-fit loops
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Manual hanging labour drops from about 4 min to 1 min of supervision per body, closure re-fits after paint fall from 8% to about 2% of bodies, and hinge shims plus their logistics are deleted. Baseline: doors, bonnet and tailgate are hung on the body-in-white by two operators per side using hard gap gauges, with hinge shims for flush; about 8% of bodies need a closure re-fit after paint or at final audit (25 min each), and every shim is a part number. Proposal: a closure-fitting cell where a robot presents each closure on a compliant gripper, a pair of 3D laser line sensors measure gap and flush at 12 points around the aperture, and the robot best-fits the closure (least-squares on gap/flush targets weighted for the visible lines) before two nut-runners torque the hinges. The fit result is stored per body; a model predicts paint-shop and trim sag (door +0.6 mm drop with dressed mass) and biases the BIW set point. Hinge shims are deleted. Why it works: manual fitting tunes to the worst point the operator sees; a measured best-fit uses the whole tolerance band and compensates for known downstream sag, so re-fits fall to a residual. Benchmark: general practice in premium body shops. Lucid Gravity uses frameless doors with flush side glass – the most gap-and-flush-sensitive closure layout, where fitting by measurement rather than by hand pays most.

title: Body-shop adhesive catalogue cut from seven chemistries to two
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Volume concentrated on two adhesive grades earns about 6% better pricing; pump stations go from 14 to 6, cutting purge, drum-end waste and maintenance; mis-application errors from look-alike materials disappear. A small premium is paid for CTE in hem joints. Baseline: the mixed aluminium/steel body uses seven pumped materials – crash-toughened 1K epoxy (structural), a separate hem-flange epoxy, a semi-structural rubber, an anti-flutter expanding rubber, a body-shop PVC seam sealer, a mastic for damping pads and a 2K epoxy at two repair-sensitive joints – fed from 14 pump stations with drum-end waste, purge losses and seven qualification files. Proposal: two chemistries. (1) One crash-toughened 1K epoxy (≈30 MPa lap shear, ≥25 N/mm impact peel to ISO 11343, e-coat wash-off resistant after induction pre-gel) used for structural and hem joints; (2) one heat-expanding 1K rubber (100-150% expansion) for anti-flutter and semi-structural damping. PVC seam sealing moves wholly to the paint shop; the 2K repair epoxy becomes a service item only. Why it works: modern CTE grades meet hem-flange viscosity and squeeze-out needs, so the separate hem epoxy is no longer justified; consolidating volume to two grades earns a better price, halves pump stations and removes purge and drum-end waste. Benchmark: the aluminium Range Rover body line at Solihull is described as glued, bonded and riveted with very little welding – adhesive is the main joining medium, so adhesive logistics and qualification are a first-order body-shop cost.

title: Robot phased-array ultrasonic weld checks replace weekly destructive body teardowns
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Destructive teardowns fall from 48 to 4 bodies a year, daily chisel checks shrink, and repairs from late-detected weld drift fall because drift is seen within a shift. Probe wear and calibration are added. Baseline: spot-weld and joint quality on the steel content (doors' steel reinforcements, steel tailgate inner, closure-mounting flanges) is policed by one destructive body teardown per week (≈€1,800 body plus 40 h of chisel and peel work) and a daily chisel check of 60 welds, with late detection meaning repairs on several days of bodies. Proposal: a robot-mounted phased-array ultrasonic probe (e.g. 64-element, water-film coupled) inspects 300 critical welds per shift at the end of each closure and framing line, measuring nugget diameter and stick welds; results go to SPC and to the adaptive weld controllers. Destructive teardown drops to one body per quarter as an audit of the UT method. Why it works: PAUT measures nugget size non-destructively with ±0.3 mm repeatability, so the sample size goes up while bodies stop being scrapped; drift is caught within a shift rather than a week. Benchmark: in the Audi Q6 e-tron paint shop an automated measuring system scans each body and drives robot finishing instead of manual inspection – the same shift from sampled manual checks to automated measurement.

title: Joint-sensitivity CAE audit deletes surplus spot welds and rivets on closure assemblies
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 80 self-piercing rivets (≈€0.07 each with rivet and cycle) and 60 spot welds (≈€0.035 each) leave every vehicle, freeing robot cycle time on closure lines; a short adhesive extension is added where joint pitch grows. Baseline: the four doors, bonnet and tailgate carry about 1,400 joints (≈880 in doors, 120 in the bonnet, 250 in the tailgate, plus hinge and check mountings) – SPR in aluminium, resistance spot welds in steel reinforcements – laid out by pitch rules (25-35 mm) plus "insurance" joints added during prototype issues that were never removed. Proposal: a joint-sensitivity study removes joints whose deletion changes no load case by more than 2%: each joint is scored by its strain energy in the closure load cases (door sag 900 N, over-opening, slam fatigue 100k cycles, side intrusion, bonnet torsion and pedestrian), and joints in adhesive-bonded flanges with low scores are removed in groups and confirmed by test. Target −10% (≈140 joints: ≈80 SPR, ≈60 RSW), with a small adhesive extension where pitch rises above 45 mm. Why it works: bonded flanges carry most shear through the adhesive, so many mechanical joints only resist peel at flange ends; pitch rules treat every flange the same. Benchmark: Rivian removed about 65 body parts from the R2 and cut its body joint count by about 1,500 – evidence that joint count is a direct cost lever once it is engineered rather than inherited.

title: Low-bake 160 °C cathodic e-coat avoids extending the oven for cast-intensive bodies
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The e-coat oven extension planned for cast-intensive bodies is never built, oven gas per body falls about a quarter, and the tin catalyst is removed; the low-bake paint carries a small price premium and the skin bake-hardening loss is compensated. Baseline: the cathodic e-coat cures at 180 °C object temperature for 20 min. On the BEV variant, thick HPDC castings (5-8 mm walls) lag the panels by 8-10 min, so the plan was to lengthen the e-coat oven by ≈12 m to get every point to temperature, and the oven burns ≈120 kWh of gas per body. Proposal: switch to a bismuth-catalysed low-bake epoxy e-coat curing at 160 °C object temperature for 15 min (tin-free), re-zone the existing oven (higher first-zone convection, lower soak) and keep the current oven length. Why it works: the lower cure temperature narrows the gap the castings must close, so the existing oven reaches full cure on castings without extension, and oven gas demand falls ≈25%. 6016 closure skins still gain bake-hardening from the 140-150 °C topcoat/clearcoat ovens; dent targets are re-verified. Benchmark: for the Q6 e-tron, Audi extended the dryer after the CDC step so every body reaches 160 °C – the oven-extension problem that a low-bake chemistry removes. BMW notes paint shops normally need gas to reach up to 180 °C, which is why oven temperature is the first energy lever.

title: Oven-exhaust heat exchangers warm pretreatment and e-coat tanks, retiring gas boilers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 54 kWh of gas per body (60% of tank heating) is replaced by recovered exhaust heat, avoiding gas cost and EU ETS carbon cost; only loop pump electricity is added. Baseline: pretreatment degrease, rinse and zirconium stages (≈50-60 °C) and the e-coat tank heat exchanger are heated by a gas boiler, ≈90 kWh per body at 50,000 bodies a year, while the e-coat and sealer-oven exhaust leaves the thermal oxidiser at ≈150-200 °C to atmosphere. Proposal: install exhaust-to-water heat exchangers (stainless finned tube, condensing on the last stage) after the regenerative thermal oxidiser, feeding a 90/60 °C hot-water loop with a 60 m³ buffer tank that carries weekend and start-up heat; the gas boiler is kept only as back-up. Recovery target 60% of tank heating. Why it works: tank heating needs low-grade heat that the plant already rejects; a buffer tank decouples oven running hours from tank start-up. Benchmark: BMW Plant Debrecen, which builds the iX3 Neue Klasse, runs its paint shop on electricity only with an energy-recovery system and a 1,800 m³ / 130 MWh thermal store – proof that paint-shop heat can be recovered and stored at plant scale.

title: Paint-shop robots apply four die-cut patch sizes to 70 holes, retiring rubber plugs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Seven minutes of manual plugging labour per body becomes robot work, patch material is cheaper than moulded plugs, water-leak rework from mis-seated plugs drops, and 25 plug part numbers collapse to four reels. Baseline: about 70 process holes per body (e-coat drain, locator and sealer-access holes in floor, wheelhouses and closures) are closed by hand after e-coat with ≈25 different rubber and PE plugs (average €0.07 each, ≈6 s each), so ≈7 min of awkward labour, 25 part numbers and occasional water-leak repairs from mis-seated plugs. Proposal: hole diameters are rationalised into four classes (≤12, 20, 30, 45 mm) and a pair of robots after the sealer line applies die-cut butyl-backed PET or aluminium-foil patches from four reel feeders, pressed with a roller and checked by camera. Plugs remain only where a hole must be re-opened in service. Why it works: patches cost less than moulded plugs, need no orientation and are applied in under 2 s each by robot; four reels replace 25 bins. Benchmark: in the Audi Q6 e-tron paint shop, robots apply adhesive pads to seal about 70 holes per body, a task previously done manually.

title: Buy laser-blanked aluminium closure blanks instead of seven blanking dies
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Seven blanking dies and their maintenance are never bought; blank nesting and shape tuning recover about 2% of closure aluminium; the service-centre fee is higher than in-house mechanical blanking. Baseline: the closure outer and inner blanks (front/rear door outers and inners, bonnet outer and inner, tailgate outer) are cut on in-house blanking dies – seven shaped blanking dies at ≈€0.3M each – at 50,000 sets a year, so each die runs only a few shifts a month and blank shapes are frozen once the die is cut. Proposal: buy the 6016-T4 and 5182-O blanks laser-cut from coil at a service centre (coil-fed laser blanking line, 3-head, ≈60 m/min on 1 mm aluminium), delivered in racks. Blank shapes can be re-nested at any time: nest optimisation and blank-shape tuning after tryout gain about 2% of aluminium. Why it works: at 50,000 vehicles a year the die investment per part is large and its utilisation tiny; laser blanking has no tool cost and lets the blank be trimmed closer to the draw requirement. Benchmark: Audi cuts the hot-formed Q6 e-tron parts with precision lasers instead of trim dies in its Münchsmünster press shop, and that machinery switches between EV and ICE parts – laser cutting replacing dedicated cutting tools.

title: Hot-melt dry-lube aluminium coil deletes blank washing and press-line oiling
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The blank washer, re-oiler and draw-oil spraying stop for closures; galling-related die polishing and dirt/pick-up rework halve; pretreatment degreasing load falls. The dry-lube coil carries a small price premium. Baseline: closure aluminium (6016-T4, 5182-O) arrives with oil-based prelube; the press line adds draw oil at critical panels and runs a blank washer and re-oiler, and the adhesive and pretreatment processes must tolerate variable oil levels (1.5-3 g/m²). Galling pick-up on deep-draw door inners triggers die polishing every few shifts. Proposal: specify coil pre-coated at the rolling mill with a hot-melt dry lubricant (≈1 g/m², solid below 40 °C) compatible with crash-toughened epoxy bonding and zirconium pretreatment; delete the blank washer, re-oiler and draw-oil spraying for closures. Why it works: a dry film gives a steady, higher-lubricity friction coefficient (≈0.08 vs 0.12-0.15) with no drip, so galling and oil-variation adhesive faults fall, and degreasing load in pretreatment falls. Benchmark: the aluminium Range Rover body line at Solihull is glued, bonded and riveted with very little welding – an adhesive-led body where clean, consistent surface condition is critical.

title: Die-cart quick die change lets one servo tandem line press every closure panel
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Changeover press hours fall, the rack fleet for closure skins halves, handling damage on stored aluminium skins drops by about half, and inventory carrying cost shrinks with one-day batches. Baseline: the ≈18 closure panel die sets are split between two press lines with ≈25 min die changes, so each panel runs in 4-5 day batches, the rack fleet for aluminium skins is sized for a week of stock, and handling damage on class-A skins in storage is the main press-shop scrap cause. Proposal: retrofit the servo tandem line with automatic die change – die carts on rails, quick-clamping bolsters, automatic tooling-crossbar change – targeting ≤6 min changes, and run all closure dies on that line in one-day batches; the second line is freed for other parts. Why it works: shorter changes make small batches cheap, so skin inventory, racks and handling damage shrink in proportion to batch size. title: Closure lines rebuilt from carry-over robots and hemming cells, not new equipment
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Refurbishing about 40 outgoing robots at ≈€25k each instead of buying new at ≈€90k avoids ≈€2.6M of capex, about €7.4 per vehicle over 350,000 vehicles; refurbishment brings somewhat higher maintenance and older-controller energy use. Baseline: the programme plan buys ≈40 new robots, roller-hemming heads and fixtures for the door, bonnet and tailgate lines (≈€90k per robot installed), while the outgoing model's closure lines are scrapped at end of production. Proposal: refurbish and re-deploy the outgoing robots (same payload class, 165-210 kg), re-use roller-hemming heads and adhesive dispense units, and buy only new end-effectors, product-specific anvils and fixtures; controllers are upgraded where safety software requires. Simulation confirms reach and cycle before build. Why it works: closure lines are mostly generic robots plus product-specific fixtures; only the fixtures are model-specific. Benchmark: Audi reused more than 600 machines such as robots from earlier models in the body shop that builds the Q6 e-tron PPE bodies.

title: Zinc-alloy soft dies press low-volume long-wheelbase rear-door panels
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About €2.3M of hard tooling for the long-wheelbase rear doors is replaced by soft draw dies and laser trimming; the extra laser-trim cycle and some hand finishing are paid per part, and one die refurbishment is budgeted. Baseline: the long-wheelbase body (≈15% of the 50,000 mix, ≈7,500 a year) has its own rear doors, and the plan gives its four rear-door panels (LH/RH outer and inner) full hard tooling – GGG70L cast dies with tool-steel inserts, 4 operations each, ≈€3.2M – for ≈52,500 hits per die over life. Proposal: draw the LWB rear-door panels on zinc-alloy (ZA, Kirksite-type) cast draw dies with hardened steel inserts at the draw radii, and replace trim and pierce dies with 5-axis laser trimming; flanging stays on one shared hard flange die. One zinc-die refurbishment at mid-life is planned. Why it works: the hit count is within soft-tool life for aluminium skins when radii are inserted, and laser trimming removes the most expensive die stages. Benchmark: the Range Rover L460 is offered in standard and long wheelbase on the MLA-Flex architecture at Solihull, so a long-wheelbase door set is a low-volume derivative tooled alongside the main body.

title: Power-door drive doubles as door check, deleting mechanical checks on equipped doors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four mechanical door checks and their fitting are deleted on every power-door vehicle; the drive brake is upgraded to hold the door at any angle. Fleet saving scales with the 40% option take rate. Baseline: on the power-door option (≈40% take rate), each door has a spindle or rotary drive with its own holding brake and still carries a mechanical door check (zinc-cast body, steel arm, ≈€6.5 each) fitted for manual mode and as a back-up. Proposal: the power-door drive is specified with a spring-applied, electrically released brake (≥60 Nm at the hinge axis) and position sensing; detents and holding are provided by the drive in software (any angle, plus a slope-aware hold), and the mechanical check is deleted on equipped doors. A friction element in the drive gives a passive hold at zero power. Over-opening stop moves to the hinge. Why it works: the drive already resists door motion; specifying its brake for hold duty removes a duplicate component. Benchmark: Cadillac Escalade IQ power side doors open and close by touchpad and can be set to open slightly, midway or fully – drive-controlled positions – and the Range Rover L460 introduced powered doors that close at a button press.

title: MHEV active-bonnet hinge: shear-pin single pivot replaces resettable four-bar linkage
description: [MHEV] A nine-part resettable four-bar hinge pair becomes a three-part shear-pin hinge pair on MHEV bodies; after a deployment the hinge is replaced rather than reset, so reset parts and their assembly go. Baseline: the MHEV bonnet (3.0 L I6 under it, ≈45 mm head-impact clearance) uses a resettable four-bar active hinge pair: forged and stamped links, a spring-latched release lever and a reset mechanism so the bonnet can be lowered and driven after a pyrotechnic lift (≈€19 per hinge). Proposal: a single-pivot stamped hinge (S420MC 4 mm leaves) whose rear pivot is held by a calibrated shear pin; on deployment the pyrotechnic lifter shears the pin and the hinge rear rises ≈90 mm about a second pivot; after deployment the hinge is replaced (a service part) rather than reset. Why it works: deployment is rare and repaired at a body shop anyway; a shear-pin hinge has three parts against about nine, and the two-position geometry is set by the leaves. Benchmark: general practice for single-use active hinges. The Lucid Gravity's bonnet hinges are designed to hold the bonnet near 90° for frunk access – evidence that hinge kinematics are tuned to the vehicle's use rather than taken as standard.

title: Cast AlSi10MnMg mirror-sail node joins front-door frame and inner, deleting three brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three stamped corner brackets, half the corner rivets and the mirror-mount fixture adjustment are replaced by one small casting with net-shape mirror bosses, and the mirror mount is located by casting datums. Baseline: at the front corner of each front door the extruded 6063 window frame meets the 5182 door inner through three stamped parts – a frame-end bracket, a mirror-mount reinforcement and a belt-end cap (≈€4.5 together) – joined by ≈12 SPR plus adhesive, and mirror-mount position is set by a fixture with frequent adjustment. Proposal: one vacuum HPDC node in AlSi10MnMg (≈0.45 kg, 2.5-3 mm walls) with a socket that receives the frame extrusion (bonded and riveted), cast mirror-mount bosses with cored holes and a flange to the inner and belt; ≈6 SPR plus adhesive. Why it works: the corner is where three load paths meet in a small volume; a casting puts them in one part with net-shape mirror bosses, so three dies, six rivets and a fixture adjustment go. Benchmark: Rivian says large HPDC castings on the R2 cut part complexity and eliminated thousands of welds and fasteners; here the same logic is used on a small door node.

title: Laser-welded aluminium tailored-blank bonnet inner deletes hinge and latch reinforcements
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three reinforcement pressings, their three dies and 24 rivets with adhesive are replaced by two laser-welded seams in the blank; the thinner field gives back mass. The tailor-welded blank costs more than a plain blank. Baseline: the bonnet inner is 6016-T4 1.0 mm with three bolt-on reinforcements – two hinge reinforcements (5182-O 1.5 mm) and a latch reinforcement (5182-O 2.0 mm) – each with its own die, joined by 24 SPR plus adhesive. Proposal: a tailor-welded aluminium blank – 0.9 mm 6016-T4 field laser-welded (fibre-laser butt weld with AlMg5 filler wire to avoid hot cracking on the 6016 side) to 1.8 mm 5182 strips at the hinge and latch zones – formed in one inner die. Why it works: the reinforcement zones get their thickness inside the blank, so three parts, three dies and 24 joints disappear; the thinner field (0.9 mm) is acceptable because the bonnet field is driven by pedestrian head impact (softer is better) and torsion carried by the inner ribs. Benchmark: the Solihull aluminium Range Rover body is glued, bonded and riveted with very little welding; here a weld moves into the blank stage so the riveting of reinforcements is removed.

title: 800V BEV frunk depth meets head impact passively, deleting active-bonnet pyro lifters
description: [800V BEV] On BEV bodies two pyrotechnic lifters, two contact sensors, their harness branch and the more expensive active hinge are deleted; the frunk tub rim is made crushable. The MHEV keeps the active system, so the saving is per BEV and halved across the fleet. Baseline: the shared bonnet uses two pyrotechnic hinge lifters, two bumper-beam pedestrian-contact sensors and a resettable active hinge on both powertrains, because on the MHEV the 3.0 L I6 cam cover sits ≈45 mm below the bonnet inner – too little crush space for passive head impact. On the BEV the volume under the bonnet is a PP frunk tub and the nearest hard points (damper tops, cowl, front EDU) are ≥95 mm below the inner. Proposal: BEV bodies drop the active system – no lifters, sensors, harness branch or active hinge – and use the standard fixed-pivot hinge; the frunk tub rim is designed to crush (PP-T20 ribs, ≤3 kN collapse) and the inner rib pattern is tuned for the larger stroke. MHEV keeps the active bonnet. Why it works: head-impact HIC depends on available stroke; with ≥95 mm under most of the grid the passive bonnet meets the HIC 1000 target without lifting. Benchmark: Lucid Gravity has an 8.1 cu ft frunk under its bonnet with hinges that hold the bonnet near 90° – deep, hardware-free volume under the bonnet of the kind that gives passive crush stroke.

title: Hem-flange adhesive formulated as hem seal deletes post-e-coat closure hem sealer bead
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The post-e-coat PVC hem bead, its robot application and vision check and most manual touch-up are deleted; hem adhesive volume rises about 15% to form the sealing fillet. Baseline: door, bonnet and tailgate hems are bonded with a hem epoxy in the body shop, then after e-coat a PVC hem-seal bead (≈9 m per vehicle) is robot-applied along the hem edge and visually checked, with manual touch-up at corners, to keep water and filiform corrosion out of the hem. Proposal: a crash-toughened hem epoxy dosed as a two-bead profile – a structural bead inside the hem and an outer bead positioned so roller hemming squeezes a continuous fillet to the hem edge – pre-gelled by induction at the hemming cell so it survives e-coat wash; the e-coat then covers the cured fillet. The post-e-coat hem sealer is deleted except at two tailgate corners where water stands. Why it works: the fillet closes the hem gap the PVC bead used to close, and it is placed before e-coat so it is coated over rather than painted onto. Benchmark: the Solihull aluminium Range Rover body is glued, bonded and riveted – adhesive already carries joint and sealing duty in an aluminium body.

title: Robot-dispensed expanding acoustic foam replaces 14 moulded cavity baffles
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fourteen moulded baffles and their hand fitting are replaced by about 45 g of dispensed expanding foam per cavity from one robot program, cutting part numbers and clip holes. Baseline: 22 heat-expandable EVA baffles on PA66 carriers (average ≈€1.1 each) are clipped by hand into body cavities before framing (≈15 s each) to block airborne noise paths; each is a separate part number. Proposal: in the 14 cavities that are open to robot access before closing (front-door hinge-face cavity, wheelhouse-to-quarter cavities, tailgate D-ring side cavities, bonnet-side apron cavities) a robot dispenses a pumpable 1K heat-expanding acoustic foam (300-600% expansion, ≈45 g per cavity) on the inner flange; the foam rises in the e-coat oven to block the section. The 8 cavities without access keep moulded baffles. Why it works: a dispensed bead costs a third of a moulded baffle with carrier, needs no clip hole and no hand fitting, and one material and one program replace 14 part numbers. Benchmark: Audi automated the sealing of about 70 holes per Q6 e-tron body with robots applying adhesive pads, a task previously manual – the same shift of body sealing and damping tasks from hand to robot.

title: Door-inner window-opening offal blanked into door brackets instead of scrapped
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 1.3 kg of bought bracket coil per vehicle is replaced by window offal that would have been sold back as scrap, so the gap between coil price and scrap credit is recovered; offal capture and the extra small die add a little cost. Baseline: each aluminium door inner (6016-T4 / 5182-O, 1.0-1.2 mm) is drawn from a full blank and its window opening (≈0.6 m² per door) is trimmed out as scrap, returned at the scrap credit (≈€1.9/kg against ≈€4.6/kg bought), while about 0.9 kg of 1.0-1.2 mm aluminium brackets (speaker, regulator, harness, latch-cable and trim-clip brackets) are pressed from separately bought coil. Proposal: the trim die cuts the window-opening offal as a clean flat sheet onto a chute; a small progressive die blanks and forms the door brackets from it. Gauge and alloy match the inner (brackets re-specified to 1.0/1.2 mm where they were 1.5 mm, with a flange or rib to recover stiffness). Why it works: the window offal is flat, undeformed sheet in the right alloy; it is worth 2.4 times more as parts than as scrap. Benchmark: Volvo states that 25% of the aluminium in the EX90 is recycled – here the circular step goes one stage earlier by not making the scrap at all.

title: Thin-wall vacuum HPDC tailgate inner replaces nine-piece stamped and riveted inner
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Nine stamping dies, about 110 self-piercing rivets and the reinforcement joining operation are replaced by one casting; the casting costs more as a piece than the stampings it replaces. Baseline: the aluminium tailgate inner is a 6016 1.2 mm pressing plus eight reinforcements (two hinge, latch, two strut/spindle mounts, wiper, spoiler and lamp brackets) joined by ≈110 SPR and adhesive, with nine dies and a joining fixture. Proposal: one vacuum high-pressure die-cast inner in a non-heat-treated, high-ductility AlSi9MnMoZr alloy (≥10% elongation as-cast), 2.0-2.5 mm nominal wall with 3.5-4 mm local bosses at hinge, latch and spindle mounts, cast on a 2,500-3,500 t cell; the 6016 outer is bonded and hemmed over a cast 1.8 mm flange. Why it works: the reinforcements become local wall thickness and bosses in one casting; at 50,000 a year one casting die (≈€0.7M) replaces nine stamping dies and the 110-joint operation. Benchmark: Rivian says large high-pressure die castings on the R2 cut part complexity and eliminated thousands of welds and fasteners.

title: E-coat flow simulation resizes tailgate drain and vent holes, deleting cavity wax
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 0.35 kg of cavity wax, its injection labour and drip clean-up are deleted from every tailgate; a few extra drain and vent holes, two of which need patches, are added. Baseline: the tailgate has steel reinforcements and steel spindle and hinge brackets inside closed cavities; because e-coat film build in the lower cavity corners is uncertain, ≈0.35 kg of cavity wax is lance-injected after paint (≈1.2 min with drip clean-up). Proposal: run e-coat flow and throw simulation (deposition and air-pocket/drain modelling) on the tailgate cavity set, resize and add drain and vent holes (typically +4 holes, 12-20 mm), and move two baffles so liquid drains and air vents in every dip orientation; verify film build ≥12 µm in all cavity points on cut-up bodies; cavity wax is deleted. Why it works: wax only compensates for low e-coat film in trapped zones; when the geometry lets e-coat reach and drain everywhere, the protection is in the coating. Benchmark: Audi modified the cathodic dip coating process for the Q6 e-tron bodies – evidence that e-coat process and geometry are being re-engineered for new body content.

title: Robot-dispensed anti-flutter bead on bonnet inner replaces hand-laid foam pads
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Six die-cut pads and their hand placement are replaced by about 60 g of dispensed expanding rubber from the hem-cell robot, and read-through rework from misplaced pads falls. Baseline: six die-cut PU foam / butyl mastic pads (≈€0.35 each) are hand-placed between the bonnet inner ribs and the 6016 outer before marriage (≈12 s each) to stop the outer fluttering at speed and to add local dent support; misplaced pads cause read-through and rework. Proposal: a 1K heat-expanding rubber anti-flutter material (≈150% expansion, low modulus) is dispensed by the existing hem-cell adhesive robot as six short beads (≈60 g total) on the inner rib crowns just before marriage; it expands in the e-coat oven to contact the outer without read-through. Why it works: a dispensed bead is a fraction of the cost of die-cut pads, has exact placement, and uses equipment already in the cell. Benchmark: the Solihull aluminium Range Rover body is glued, bonded and riveted – adhesive dispensing is already the core joining process, so anti-flutter can be dispensed too.

title: Mechanical clinching replaces self-piercing rivets on non-structural door-inner brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 96 rivets per vehicle and their feed systems are replaced by about 110 consumable-free clinches; punch and die wear is the only running cost. The rivet stock and feeder spares for these stations go too. Baseline: each aluminium door inner carries ≈24 SPR (5 mm, ≈€0.035 rivet plus ≈€0.02 die wear and feed) fixing non-structural brackets – speaker ring, harness clips, regulator and trim-clip plates – ≈96 rivets per vehicle. Proposal: round-point mechanical clinching (die-side round button, 8 mm, no consumable) for these aluminium-to-aluminium bracket joints, with joint count raised ≈15% (to ≈110) because a clinch carries ≈60-70% of an SPR's static shear. Structural joints (hinge, latch, beam) stay SPR. Why it works: these brackets carry tens of newtons, not crash load; a clinch needs only a punch and die, no rivet feed, and runs on the same C-frame robot tools. Benchmark: the Solihull aluminium Range Rover body is glued, bonded and riveted, with riveting as the main mechanical joining method – the rivet cost that clinching removes where loads are small.

title: Robot-sprayed polyurea wheel-arch guard replaces PVC plus bolt-on stone guards off-road
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] On off-road-pack bodies the bolt-on stone guards and their fitting are deleted and PVC in the arch zones is replaced by sprayed polyurea, which costs more per vehicle than the PVC; the fleet saving scales with the 35% take rate. Baseline: on the off-road pack (≈35% take) the wheel arches and arch-adjacent underbody get PVC underbody coat (≈1.2 kg) and then bolt-on PP/TPO stone-guard plates (≈€18 per vehicle plus ≈4 min fitting) to survive gravel blasting and repeated wading; guards trap mud and need their own fixings and clip holes. Proposal: on off-road bodies a robot sprays 0.8 mm aromatic polyurea (≈1.1 g/cm³, elongation >300%) over ≈2 m² of arch and arch-adjacent underbody in the paint-shop underbody booth, replacing the PVC in those zones and deleting the bolt-on guards. Standard bodies keep PVC. Why it works: polyurea has far higher abrasion and impact resistance than PVC, so one sprayed layer does the job of coat plus plate, with no trapped mud and no fixings. Benchmark: the Defender 110 is rated for 900 mm wading, with Wade Sensing in the door mirrors – the duty (wading, mud, gravel) that this coating is specified for.

title: Cut-to-length drawn-profile door hinges replace forged-and-machined hinge halves
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Forging, flash trimming and knuckle machining are replaced by cutting and piercing drawn profile, saving about €2.6 per hinge over eight hinges; tighter bush tolerances add a little cost per hinge. Baseline: eight side-door hinges, each two forged C45 halves machined at the knuckles and bolt faces (≈€9.5 per hinge), sized for ≈38 kg dressed doors, powered doors and power-drive reaction loads. Proposal: hinge halves cut from cold-drawn steel profile (S355J2 or 34MnB5 quenched and tempered at the knuckle where needed), pierced and chamfered in one progressive die, with hardened pin and PA46 bushes; profiles carry the knuckle shape along their length so no machining is needed. Why it works: the drawn profile already has the hinge cross-section, so forging, flash trimming and machining are replaced by cutting and piercing; the profile's cold-worked grain gives high strength in the load direction. Benchmark: the Range Rover L460 introduced powered doors – heavy, driven doors whose hinges must carry drive reaction loads as well as sag, the load case these hinges are sized to.

title: Glass-bead-filled bondline isolates steel reinforcements in aluminium closures, deleting isolation tape
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 16 isolation tape patches and their hand application are deleted; a bead-filled adhesive carries a small premium and the camera check already in the cell verifies bead coverage. Baseline: where steel reinforcements (hinge plates, latch plates, check brackets, spindle mounts – ≈16 patches per vehicle) sit on aluminium closure inners, an isolating PET tape patch (≈€0.25) is hand-applied before the adhesive and SPR, to stop galvanic contact; taping takes ≈8 s per patch and taped flanges show adhesive-adhesion issues. Proposal: delete the tape and use a crash-toughened epoxy carrying 0.25-0.3 mm glass beads (≈2 wt%) so the bondline can never close to metal contact; steel parts are pre-coated (zinc-flake or e-coat) and SPRs are coated (ZnNi + sealing top-coat) so the only metal path is through the rivet coating. Why it works: the beads set a minimum gap that acts as electrical and moisture isolation, and the continuous bondline seals the flange better than a tape edge. Benchmark: reported for the Range Rover L460 (80% aluminium / 20% steel) that steel-to-aluminium bonding is camera-monitored so the metals do not touch – isolation in bonded mixed joints is the requirement.

title: 800V BEV deletes underbody PVC over the battery footprint, keeping seam sealing only
description: [800V BEV] About 2.8 litres of PVC per BEV body over the battery footprint are no longer sprayed and robot time falls; a seam-only bead program is added. The saving applies to BEV bodies and is halved across the fleet. Baseline: both powertrains get the same PVC underbody programme – ≈0.8 mm PVC plastisol sprayed over the whole floor, including the ≈3.5 m² that on the BEV sits above the battery pack, whose aluminium tray and shield cover the floor from stones and spray. Proposal: on BEV bodies the robots skip area spraying over the pack footprint and run a seam-only program (≈1.5 mm bead along the floor seams); outside the footprint (arches, front and rear floors) the full PVC stays. Why it works: underbody PVC protects against stone chipping and spray; over the pack footprint the floor faces only the pack lid in a closed space, so e-coat plus seam sealing gives the corrosion protection. Benchmark: Audi modified the cathodic dip coating process and automated hole sealing for the Q6 e-tron electric bodies – paint-shop programmes being re-engineered for what an EV floor actually needs.

title: Split tailgate: power drive on upper leaf only, gas-balanced lower leaf
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The lower-leaf power drive, its ECU channel, cinch and anti-pinch sensing are deleted on split-tailgate vehicles and replaced by torsion-spring hinges with dampers. Baseline: the split-tailgate variant (≈60% of the mix) was planned with powered upper and lower leaves – a second spindle pair or rotary drive for the lower leaf, its ECU channel, latch cinch and anti-pinch – to allow a "lower only" opening mode. Proposal: power the upper leaf only; the lower leaf (≈9 kg, 6016 aluminium) is balanced by two torsion springs in its hinges so it is near-weightless to lower and lift, with damped rotary hinges for a soft fall and two cable stays rated for two seated adults. The upper leaf's cinch latch keeps the closing experience. Why it works: the lower leaf is light and opened at waist height by a person already standing at it, so power adds little function for a lot of cost; spring balance plus damping gives a luxury feel. Benchmark: the Range Rover L460 keeps its signature split tailgate with a powered gesture tailgate and an optional Tailgate Event Suite seating area; a Land Rover patent describes a power split tailgate with both leaves driven.

title: Frunk tub perimeter lip seals the bonnet, deleting body-mounted bonnet seals
description: [800V BEV] Three body-mounted bonnet seals, two drain tubes and their fitting are deleted on BEV bodies; the frunk tub tool becomes a 2K tool with a TPE lip. The saving is per BEV and halved across the fleet. Baseline: on the BEV the bonnet closes over a PP frunk tub but still uses the MHEV sealing set – a body-mounted EPDM rear (cowl) bonnet seal (≈€3.2), two side seals on the fender rails (≈€2.1 each) and two frunk drain tubes (≈€0.7 each) – plus the tub with its own gasket. Proposal: the frunk tub is moulded as a 2K part (PP-T20 tub with a co-moulded TPE lip around its rim) whose lip seals directly against the bonnet inner, so water running through the bonnet gap is caught outside the lip and drains through moulded gutters in the tub rim; the body-mounted bonnet seals and drain tubes are deleted on BEV. Why it works: on the BEV the tub rim already sits just under the bonnet inner; one co-moulded lip does the job of three seals and the gutters replace tubes. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity has a power frunk of 8.1 cu ft under its bonnet – a frunk-led front end where the tub rim is the natural sealing plane.

title: One-sided high-speed tack setting replaces flow-drill screws in closure hinge sections
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 48 flow-drill screws per vehicle become cheaper tacks set in a quarter of the time, cutting consumable cost and robot cycle time in the closure hinge zones. Baseline: about 48 flow-drill screws (M5, ≈€0.12 each, ≈2.5 s cycle with high axial force) join steel hinge and spindle reinforcements to aluminium closed sections in the tailgate hinge area and the bonnet hinge and latch zones, where only one side is accessible. Proposal: high-speed tack (nail) setting – a hardened, coated steel tack driven at ≈30 m/s through the aluminium into the steel without pre-hole or rotation, in combination with the structural adhesive already in the flange; ≈0.6 s per joint and ≈€0.06 per tack. Why it works: like FDS it is one-sided and needs no pre-hole, but it needs no spindle rotation or thread-forming, so cycle time and consumable cost fall; with adhesive carrying shear, the tack mainly fixes the joint and resists peel. Benchmark: the Solihull aluminium Range Rover body is glued, bonded and riveted – mechanical fastening plus adhesive is the joining logic this change keeps, with a cheaper one-sided element.

title: One door check rated for 35% side slopes deletes the off-road heavy-duty variant
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A second door-check family with its cast tools, part numbers and variant fitting is removed; standard vehicles get a slightly stronger check that costs a little more than the old standard one. Baseline: two door-check families – a standard zinc-cast check (≈38 Nm detent holding at the hinge axis) and a heavy-duty off-road check with a stiffer spring pack and third detent (≈60 Nm, ≈€9.0 vs €6.0) on the off-road pack (≈35% take), so a parked door can be held open on a steep side slope. Each family has front and rear, LH and RH parts, cast tools and a fitting variant. Proposal: one check per door position sized for the off-road case – roller-and-ramp mechanism with a PA66-GF30 housing, ZnAl4Cu1 arm overmould and a tuned spring pack giving at least the ≈60 Nm of today's heavy-duty check (piece price to be re-confirmed) with a smoother effort curve (≤70 N at the handle) – fitted on all vehicles; detent count 3. Why it works: the cost step between the two springs is small, while a second family doubles tools, part numbers and line-side variants; the higher hold also helps doors without power assist. Benchmark: the Defender 110 is rated for 900 mm wading and is used where doors are opened on cambered, steep ground – the off-road use case that sets the door-hold requirement.

title: Single power-tailgate spindle with opposite gas strut replaces twin spindle drives
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One of the two spindle drives and one controller motor channel are deleted; a gas strut and a stronger single spindle take their place. Harness and connector content for the second motor also go. Baseline: the powered tailgate (standard fit) uses two electric spindle drives (≈€42 each) with a twin-motor controller channel, for a ≈24 kg aluminium tailgate. Proposal: one higher-force spindle drive (≈€48, 1,000 N stall) on the left and a matched gas strut (≈€9) on the right; the tailgate torsional stiffness (≥0.6 kNm/deg between hinges and latch) keeps the twist from the one-sided drive below 1.5 mm at the latch, and the controller drops one motor channel. Why it works: on a stiff tailgate the strut balances most of the weight and the spindle only adds the difference and controls speed, so the second motor duplicates function. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ offers an AutoSense hands-free power liftgate and the Range Rover L460 a powered gesture tailgate – powered tailgates are standard luxury content whose drive cost is worth engineering down.

title: Epoxy structural foam insert replaces door hinge-face steel reinforcement plate
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each door's full steel hinge-face plate and its rivets and isolation are replaced by a foam insert and two small nut-plates, saving cost and about 0.4 kg per door. Baseline: each front door has a CR340LA 2.5 mm hinge-face reinforcement (≈0.9 kg, ≈€3.4 with its isolation and 10 SPR) inside the aluminium door inner to carry hinge bolt loads and door sag; rear doors use a 2.0 mm version. Proposal: an epoxy-based heat-expanding structural foam on a PA66-GF carrier (≈0.35 kg, expanding ≈80% in the e-coat oven to fill the hinge-face box section) plus two small 3 mm steel nut-plates (≈0.15 kg) only at the bolt points; the foam stiffens the box against local crush and sag, and the nut-plates carry thread loads. Why it works: the steel plate is sized for stiffness of a thin aluminium box, which the foam provides more cheaply by stabilising the walls; bolt loads need only local steel. Benchmark: Kia uses hot-stamped parts in the EV9 safety cage, and a LeanDesign teardown notes the EV9 door minimises part complexity – reinforcement content in doors is a recognised cost lever.

title: Door belt reinforcement and waist-seal carrier merged into one 6063 extrusion
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The stamped belt reinforcement and the waist seal's steel carrier are replaced by one stretch-bent extrusion with a seal groove; the seal becomes a carrier-less TPV profile that is easier to recycle. Baseline: each door has a stamped CR420LA 1.2 mm belt reinforcement (≈€2.6) riveted to the inner, and an outer waist seal whose extrusion carries a steel carrier strip (≈€1.8 of the seal cost) to clip onto the door outer flange. Proposal: one 6063-T6 extrusion (≈1.6 mm walls, closed box with an open C-groove) that acts as the belt reinforcement and receives a carrier-less TPV waist seal pushed into its groove; the extrusion is stretch-bent to the belt line, pierced and riveted with the same four SPR. Why it works: the extrusion's closed section gives the belt bending stiffness that the stamping provided, and its groove replaces the seal's metal carrier, so two parts become one and the seal becomes a simpler profile. Benchmark: Lucid Gravity uses frameless doors with flush side glass, where the belt line carries glass sealing and stiffness duty on its own – the belt structure as a multi-function part.

title: Double-attached LH/RH rear-door inner die halves strokes and die sets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two rear-door inner die lines become one double-attached set, about €1.0M less tooling, and the press runs one stroke set for both hands, halving press time and die maintenance for these panels. Baseline: LH and RH rear-door inners (5182-O 1.2 mm, ≈1,050 × 900 mm) each have their own 4-operation die line (draw, trim/pierce, flange, restrike/pierce), ≈€1.6M per hand, run as two separate batches. Proposal: a double-attached die set that draws LH and RH inners together from one blank pair side by side (4.5 m bolster tandem line), trims and separates them in operation 2 and finishes both in operations 3-4 – one die set of four operations at ≈€2.2M, one stroke set per vehicle instead of two. Why it works: mirrored panels of this size fit side by side on a large bolster; die cost scales with die count and complexity, not panel count, and press time halves. Benchmark: a LeanDesign teardown of the Kia EV9 notes that the Ioniq 5 stamped door beam costs more to make because of its tooling, while the EV9 approach minimises part complexity – door tooling cost is a recognised lever.

title: Single AlSi10MnMg casting replaces seven-piece steel spare-wheel carrier weldment
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Seven pressings, their welding and the zinc-flake coat are replaced by one casting with one powder coat, about 2.4 kg lighter, which also eases tailgate drive and hinge loads. Baseline: the tailgate spare-wheel carrier for the off-road pack (full-size 20-inch spare, ≈32 kg) is a seven-piece MIG-welded S355MC weldment (two arms, hub plate, three gussets, camera bracket) with zinc-flake plus powder coat, ≈5.8 kg, ≈€46. Proposal: one vacuum HPDC carrier in AlSi10MnMg, T6-free (as-cast, F temper with Sr modification) at ≈3.4 kg with ribbed arms, a cast hub with five M14 inserts, cast camera and number-plate lamp bosses; powder-coated. Why it works: the carrier is a stiffness-and-fatigue part; ribbed casting puts material where bending stress is, and seven parts with welds and coating steps become one casting with one coat. Mass saved on the tailgate also reduces the power-drive and hinge load. Benchmark: the Defender carries an externally mounted full-size spare on its side-opening tailgate, the use case this carrier serves.

title: Fixed snap-in bonnet over-slam buffers replace screw-adjustable bump stops
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four threaded adjustable stops and about two minutes of adjustment labour per bonnet are replaced by push-in buffers picked in one of three height classes from the fitting data. Baseline: four screw-adjustable rubber bump stops (EPDM head on a threaded stem, ≈€0.55 each) support the bonnet at its front corners and sides; each is set at the final line to tune bonnet flush (≈0.5 min per stop) and re-set during audit. Proposal: once the closure-fitting cell sets bonnet height to the body (measured best-fit), the stops become fixed-height push-in TPE buffers (≈€0.18 each) in three height classes (±0.5 mm steps) chosen automatically from the fit data at the hanging cell. Why it works: adjustable stops exist to absorb build variation; when the bonnet is fitted by measurement, the residual variation is within the three classes, so threads and adjustment labour can go. Benchmark: Lucid Gravity bonnet hinges hold the large frunk lid near 90°, a big unsupported panel whose rest points must be right first time – the case for fixed, measured rest points.

title: Spindle-motor current anti-pinch replaces capacitive pinch strips on power tailgate
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two capacitive pinch strips, their connectors and harness branch and their fitting are deleted; the closure controller gets a refined pinch algorithm. The trim panel loses its strip channel. Baseline: the power tailgate uses capacitive pinch-strip sensors along both D-pillar edges (≈€6 each with connector) bonded to the tailgate side trim, plus their harness branch (≈€2), in addition to the drive's own current monitoring. Proposal: anti-pinch by the drive alone – Hall-sensor position and motor-current ripple analysis in the closure controller with a 200 Hz update, detecting a force rise of ≥40 N above the learned curve and reversing within 50 ms; the capacitive strips and their harness are deleted. Why it works: tailgate edges close slowly (≤150 mm/s near closure) so the drive sensing reacts before force exceeds the limit; strips duplicate a function the drive already provides. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ has an AutoSense hands-free power liftgate and the Range Rover L460 a powered gesture tailgate – powered tailgates whose pinch protection cost is under engineering scrutiny.

title: Self-lubricating PA46 hinge bushes replace brass bushes and line-side greasing
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Brass bushes become cheaper filled PA46 bushes with built-in washers, and greasing of 12 hinges at the line is deleted along with grease clean-up and squeak warranty. Baseline: the eight door hinges, two bonnet hinges and two tailgate hinges use sintered-brass bushes on hardened pins (≈€0.45 per bush, 2 per hinge) and are greased at the line after paint (≈10 s per hinge, grease overspray onto paint occasionally needs clean-up); squeak complaints come from grease loss. Proposal: injection-moulded PA46 bushes with PTFE and aramid fill (≈€0.18 each), flanged to also act as axial washers, on a zinc-flake coated pin; no line-side greasing. Why it works: filled PA46 runs dry with a low, stable friction coefficient (≈0.15) at hinge speeds and loads, keeps working at e-coat-free temperatures, and does not need lubrication over life; the flange deletes a separate washer. Benchmark: the Range Rover L460 introduced powered doors – driven doors whose hinge friction must stay constant for the drive's force control, which a dry bush gives more reliably than grease.

title: Zinc-flake hinge bolts with captive PA66 washers delete sealant dabs on aluminium closures
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three items per joint (bolt, loose washer, sealant dab) become one pre-assembled coated bolt, deleting sealant, washer handling and about three minutes of labour per vehicle. Baseline: the 32 hinge bolts that fix steel hinges to aluminium doors, bonnet and tailgate are ZnNi-plated M8 10.9 bolts (≈€0.28), with a separate PA isolation washer (≈€0.06) and a manually applied sealant dab under the head (≈€0.08 and ≈6 s) to stop galvanic attack and water entry into the aluminium. Proposal: zinc-flake coated bolts (zinc-aluminium flake base plus sealing top coat with integrated lubricant, ≥720 h neutral salt spray, aluminium-compatible) with a captive PA66 washer pre-assembled at the fastener supplier (≈€0.26 together); the sealant dab is deleted. Why it works: the flake coat has low galvanic potential difference to aluminium, the captive washer guarantees isolation and a seal under the head, and the line handles one part instead of three. Benchmark: the Range Rover L460 is a mixed aluminium-steel body where steel-to-aluminium contact is reportedly controlled during bonding – galvanic isolation is a design rule in such bodies.

title: In-die self-clinching nuts replace post-press blind rivet nuts in aluminium door inners
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 56 blind rivet nuts and their separate setting operation are replaced by cheaper self-clinching nuts installed by the press stroke in the last die operation. Baseline: each aluminium door inner receives ≈14 blind rivet nuts (M6/M8 for module carrier, speaker, handle and harness fixings), set after pressing by a robot or hand tool (≈€0.18 each plus ≈5 s), ≈56 per vehicle. Proposal: self-clinching nuts for aluminium (hardened steel, zinc-flake coated, knurled shank, rated for 1.0-1.5 mm 5182/6016) fed and pressed in by nut-installation heads in the last operation of the door-inner die line (8 dies across the four inners), ≈€0.11 each, no separate operation. Why it works: the press stroke already exists; installing nuts in the die removes a handling step and the rivet nut's blind-setting mechanism, and clinched nuts can meet the torque-out requirement in 1.2-1.5 mm aluminium (M8 in 1.0 mm sheet must be checked, as push-out and torque-out are lower than a flanged rivet nut). Benchmark: Rivian says R2's large castings eliminated thousands of welds and fasteners – fastener count and fastening operations are a direct cost line.

ideaData.title: In-die self-clinching nuts replace post-press blind rivet nuts in aluminium door inners
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: each aluminium door inner receives ≈14 blind rivet nuts (M6/M8 for module carrier, speaker, handle and harness fixings), set after pressing by a robot or hand tool (≈€0.18 each plus ≈5 s), ≈56 per vehicle. Proposal: self-clinching nuts for aluminium (hardened steel, zinc-flake coated, knurled shank, rated for 1.0-1.5 mm 5182/6016) fed and pressed in by nut-installation heads in the last operation of the door-inner die line (8 dies across the four inners), ≈€0.11 each, no separate operation. Why it works: the press stroke already exists; installing nuts in the die removes a handling step and the rivet nut's blind-setting mechanism, and clinched nuts can meet the torque-out requirement in 1.2-1.5 mm aluminium (M8 in 1.0 mm sheet must be checked, as push-out and torque-out are lower than a flanged rivet nut). Benchmark: Rivian says R2's large castings eliminated thousands of welds and fasteners – fastener count and fastening operations are a direct cost line.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: About 56 blind rivet nuts and their separate setting operation are replaced by cheaper self-clinching nuts installed by the press stroke in the last die operation.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Nut feeders and installation heads in eight last-operation dies; nut presence sensed in-die. Rivet-nut stations removed from the door sub-assembly line. Two robot cells are freed.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Nut holes pierced in the previous operation with ±0.05 mm tolerance; flat land ≥12 mm; nuts on the hidden side. Thread sizes standardised to M6 and M8. Nut type is common across the four inners.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium – press-shop change planned at die build
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: 56 nuts × (€0.18 − €0.11) = €3.9; setting labour/robot time 56 × 5 s × €0.0125/s = €3.5; less in-die head maintenance and nut-presence sensing €0.4. Net ≈ €7.0 (range €6-€8). Net €6-€8 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €300K-€400K per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: Push-out and torque-out of clinched nuts in 5182/6016 (spec ≥ 1.2× rivet nut values), galvanic corrosion at the nut (VDA 233-102), e-coat over threads (masking caps or post-paint thread check). Door module and handle fixings carry UN R11 / FMVSS 206 latch-related loads – verified by pull tests.

title: Bonnet outer down-gauged to 0.9 mm high-bake-response 6016 with anti-flutter support
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 10% less aluminium in the bonnet outer blank at a small grade premium, with slightly closer anti-flutter support; finished-part mass falls about 0.5 kg (0.7 kg of blank) on a high, forward panel. Baseline: the bonnet outer is 6016-T4 1.0 mm (≈1.75 m² finished, ≈7.0 kg blank at ≈€4.6/kg), sized for dent resistance after paint bake (≈190-200 MPa yield). Proposal: 0.9 mm of a high-bake-response 6016 variant (pre-aged T4P temper giving ≥230 MPa yield after a 20 min 170 °C bake versus ≈190-200 MPa for standard 6016) so static and dynamic dent resistance at the dent-critical points is maintained; anti-flutter support spacing on the inner reduced from ≈350 mm to ≈280 mm where the free span grows. Why it works: dent resistance scales roughly with yield strength × thickness², so +15-20% yield recovers most of the 19% loss from 1.0 to 0.9 mm, and closer support handles the rest at mid-panel. Benchmark: Volvo states 25% of the aluminium in the EX90 is recycled – grade and gauge choice in aluminium closures is a live cost and sustainability lever; the high-bake-response grade also tolerates higher recycled content.

title: Closure reinforcements ganged into progressive dies instead of individual transfer die sets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Twenty transfer die sets become seven ganged progressive dies, about €0.7M less tooling, and press cost per part falls with higher stroke rates and several parts per stroke. Baseline: about 20 small steel and aluminium closure reinforcements and brackets (hinge plates, latch plates, check and spindle brackets, ≤300 × 200 mm) are planned on a transfer press with one 3-4 station die set each (≈€80k per set, ≈€1.6M), each running in short batches at ≈18 strokes/min. Proposal: group the parts by material and gauge into seven progressive dies that make 2-4 parts per stroke (left/right pairs and same-gauge families), run on a 400-630 t progressive press at ≈35-45 strokes/min; ≈€130k per die, ≈€0.91M. Why it works: small parts of the same material and gauge share a strip; one die making several parts per stroke cuts tooling and press time, and progressive dies need no transfer fingers. Benchmark: the press shop supplying the Audi Q6 e-tron makes up to 20,000 parts a day on machinery that switches between EV and ICE parts – flexible, high-output small-part pressing.

title: Double-pull bonnet latch with integral safety position deletes separate safety-catch hook
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate safety-catch hook, its reinforcement and fitting are deleted in exchange for a slightly dearer latch with a built-in second position. One reinforcement die is also retired. Baseline: the bonnet has a primary latch on the front-end carrier plus a separate spring safety-catch hook riveted to the bonnet inner with its own reinforcement (≈€2.4 hook, ≈€0.8 reinforcement, ≈0.6 min fitting); the user releases the primary from the cabin and lifts the hook by hand at the front. Proposal: a double-pull latch with an integral safety position – the first cabin pull releases to the safety position, the second pull (within 5 s) releases fully – so the separate hook and its reinforcement are deleted; the latch body costs ≈€1.2 more. Why it works: FMVSS 113 requires a second latch position, not a separate hook; integrating it into the latch keeps the function and deletes a part, a reinforcement and a fitting operation. Benchmark: the BMW iX bonnet is released by two cables pulled in sequence – a sequential release in place of a hand-operated front catch.

title: Bonnet outer die line cut from five to four operations with cam piercing
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One of five bonnet-outer dies (≈€0.45M) and its maintenance are removed, and the line runs four strokes per panel instead of five; the remaining dies get more cams. Baseline: the bonnet outer die line has five operations – draw, trim, trim/pierce, flange, restrike/pierce – because washer-jet, emblem and hinge-area holes sit on surfaces that face different directions after flanging. Proposal: four operations – draw; trim with cam trim at the front edge; flange; restrike with aerial-cam piercing of the late holes – by moving the second trim into op 2 cams and the remaining pierce into op 4 aerial cams. Why it works: the fifth die exists only for hole and trim directions that cams can reach; one less die cuts tooling, die maintenance and one stroke of the tandem line. Benchmark: the LeanDesign teardown of the Kia EV9 points to tooling cost as a reason for door-beam design choices and to an EV9 door that minimises part complexity – tooling content driven down at design.

title: Tailgate latch reinforcement and wiper-motor bracket merged into one 6082 extrusion slice
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three stamped parts, three dies and six of fourteen rivets are replaced by one machined extrusion slice from a low-cost extrusion die. Joining time and part handling also fall. Baseline: the tailgate lower centre carries a 5182-O 2.0 mm latch reinforcement (≈€2.2, own die), a separate stamped wiper-motor bracket (≈€1.4, own die) and a number-plate lamp bracket (≈€0.6), joined by 14 SPR and adhesive. Proposal: one slice cut from a multi-hollow 6082-T6 extrusion (≈60 mm wide), CNC-machined with latch bolt holes and wiper-motor bosses, carrying all three functions and joined by 8 SPR plus adhesive; extrusion die ≈€15k replaces three stamping dies. Why it works: the three parts sit within 120 mm of each other and all need stiffness normal to the tailgate; a closed-section slice provides that and the bosses with one part. Benchmark: Rivian says the R2 removed about 65 body parts and about 1,500 joints – part and joint counts treated as design targets.

title: Bonded flush-handle housing stiffens door outer, deleting handle reinforcement
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four stamped handle reinforcements, their dies and fitting are deleted; the handle housings gain a bonding flange and a structural PU bead. The reinforcement die is not built. Baseline: each door outer has a stamped 5182-O 1.5 mm handle reinforcement (≈€2.1) bonded behind the handle opening to stop the 6016 outer from deflecting under handle pull (≈900 N abuse) and to stiffen the cut-out, and the flush-handle housing (PA6-GF30 / zinc) bolts separately to the inner. Proposal: the housing gets a flanged frame bonded to the back of the outer with a 2K structural PU (≈2 mm bondline), and its bolts to the inner stay; the bonded housing frame stiffens the cut-out and carries pull loads into the inner, so the separate reinforcement is deleted. Why it works: the housing already spans the cut-out; bonding it to the outer makes it act as the reinforcement. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity uses pop-out door handles – flush handles whose housings sit right behind the outer panel cut-out.

costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Four reinforcements 4 × €2.1 = €8.4; reinforcement fitting 4 × 0.5 min × €0.75 = €1.5; reinforcement die €0.12M ÷ 350,000 = €0.34; less bonding flange and 2K PU 4 × €0.35 = €1.4 and bonding fixture time plus read-through rework allowance €1.5. title: In-die hot trimming and piercing of press-hardened parts replaces 3D laser-trim cells

ideaData.title: In-die hot trimming and piercing of press-hardened parts replaces 3D laser-trim cells
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the safety cage carries 22 press-hardened parts (22MnB5 + AS150, 1.2-2.0 mm, ~48 kg per body: B-pillar and A-pillar/roof-rail reinforcements, sill reinforcements, tunnel, seat cross-members, door beams, bumper beams, rear-rail inners). Each leaves the 1,200 t hot press as martensite (Rm ≈1,500 MPa) and is trimmed and pierced in 5-axis fibre-laser cells at 45-90 s per part: 4-5 cells for 1.1M parts/yr, ≈€1.10-€1.30 per part with cell depreciation, energy, assist gas, nozzles and racking. Proposal: on the 12-14 parts whose trim and hole tolerances are ±0.5 mm or wider (seat cross-members, tunnel, sill reinforcements, door and bumper beams, roof bows, rear-rail inners), cut the outline and the Ø≥8 mm holes at the end of the forming stroke while the trim band is still at 550-650 °C, using 1.2367 hot-work shear inserts with AlCrN PVD and a local die-contact gap so the band is the last zone to quench. Parts needing ±0.2 mm (door-seal flanges on A/B-pillars, hinge pillar) stay on laser: two cells instead of five. Why it works (check): at 600 °C 22MnB5 flows at ~200-250 MPa, so trim force ≈ 3.0 m perimeter × 1.6 mm × τ 200 MPa ≈ 0.96 MN (≈98 t), well inside a 1,200 t press; cold shearing martensite needs τ ≈1,100 MPa (≈5.3 MN) and leaves edge micro-cracks prone to hydrogen-delayed fracture, which is why laser is the default. Thermal shrink of 1.4×10⁻⁵/K × 580 K ≈ 0.8% (12 mm on a 1.5 m part) is built into the trim-line CAD from thermal FE; capability is ±0.4-0.5 mm. Grade, gauge and geometry are unchanged, so crush force and E·t³ stiffness are untouched; the softer (bainitic) trim band is ≤3 mm wide and lies in flanges. Benchmark: Volvo says its SPA safety cage (XC90) is over 40% hot-formed steel; laser trimming is the industry default for such parts, and in-die hot trimming at 500-600 °C is described in the patent literature.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Moves 12-14 of the 22 press-hardened cage parts from post-quench 3D laser trimming to shear trimming and piercing inside the hot-forming die while the trim line is still soft, retiring three of five laser cells and the press-to-laser racking; the tight-tolerance parts stay on laser.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Hot-stamping dies gain shear-steel inserts and local cooling-gap control; the hot-press cycle grows by ~0.5 s (≈4%). Laser cells fall from five to two, freeing ~400 m² and removing press-to-laser racking. Insert regrind every ~60-80k strokes is added to die maintenance.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Trim lines placed in flat flange zones with ≥5 mm to any radius; holes ≥8 mm and ≥2t from edges so hot piercing does not tear; framing datum holes stay laser-cut on the two retained cells so RPS accuracy is unchanged; trim CAD carries the per-part thermal-shrink offset.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium – a process change across most of the hot-stamped cage with no change to grade, gauge or geometry
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Low: 12 parts × €1.10 laser cost = €13.2 + press-to-laser handling €0.9 − shear-insert maintenance 12 × €0.25 = €3.0 − hot-press cycle penalty 12 × €0.15 = €1.8 − extra scrap/rework €0.6 = €8.7 ≈ €9. High: 14 × €1.30 = €18.2 + handling €1.2 − €3.5 − €2.1 − €0.5 = €13.3 ≈ €13. Shear-insert tooling (€1.2M) sits in investment, not in the per-vehicle figure. Applies to every body (100%), both powertrains. €9-€13 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €0.45M-€0.65M per year.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks (seat cross-members, tunnel and roof bows are also claimed by ieb-f802db9d45ba, which takes them off the hot-stamp line, so the savings are not additive): dimensional drift with die temperature, edge quality, and a soft trim band reaching a load-bearing section. Validate with HV10 hardness traverses across the band, hole-expansion and VDA 238-100 bend tests, delayed-fracture tests on cut edges, CMM capability Cpk ≥1.33 on three lots, and subsystem crash for UN R94/R95/R135, FMVSS 214/216, Euro NCAP 2026 and IIHS small overlap. Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: The stated hot-trim capability of ±0.4-0.5 mm is applied to parts with a ±0.5 mm tolerance. That gives Cpk ≈1.0 at best, below the Cpk ≥1.33 the idea itself sets for validation. Either the in-die route is limited to parts at ±0.7 mm or wider, which probably cuts the 12-14 part count and the saving, or the capability claim must be shown.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Volvo XC90 (2025, SPA) — Steel-intensive safety cage with over 40% hot-formed steel in the structure, against 7% in the first XC90. How this differs: Volvo discloses how much of the cage is hot-formed; we change how those parts are trimmed, moving the tolerance-tolerant majority from laser cells into the hot-forming die.

title: Roll-formed CR1700M multi-cell sill beam replaces 6082-T6 pack-protection extrusion at equal mass
description: [800V BEV] Swaps the most expensive extrusion in the 800V BEV body for a roll-formed martensitic steel beam of the same mass that exceeds its plastic bending capacity, and joins it by resistance spot welds instead of flow-drill screws and isolating adhesive. Baseline (800V BEV only, 40% of volume): each steel sill carries a 1,900 mm 6082-T6 four-cell extrusion (≈140 × 80 mm, 3.0 mm walls, ≈2,300 mm², 11.8 kg) that takes the pole load (UN R135 / FMVSS 214, 32 km/h at 75°) before it reaches the pack; it is cut, end-machined and fixed with flow-drill screws and isolating adhesive (≈€72 per side). Proposal: a 2D roll-formed, inline laser-welded three-cell profile in CR1700M martensitic steel (Docol 1700M), 1.4 mm, ≈60 mm deep (load direction) × 100 mm tall with two internal webs, ≈790 mm² so mass stays 11.8 kg per side, spot-welded to the sill inner before the outer closes. Why it works (check): pole intrusion is set by the plastic bending moment. Al: 260 MPa × Zp ≈ 57,600 mm³ ≈ 15 kNm; steel: ≈1,350 MPa × Zp ≈ 13,400 mm³ ≈ 18 kNm, so ~20% more at equal mass in a section 20 mm shallower, which adds crush stroke before the pack. The trap is local buckling: σcr = 3.6E(t/b)² must reach yield, so cells are held to 33 mm (b/t ≈ 24, σcr ≈ 1,300 MPa); a single 100 mm 1.4 mm box would buckle at ≈150 MPa. Stiffness is not equal: insert EI drops from ≈139 to ≈74 kN·m², but the steel sill shells (≈1,365 kN·m²) dominate, so sill bending stiffness falls ~4% and body torsion <1%. Martensite has ~5% elongation, so bend radii are ≥3t and the laser seam sits on the neutral axis. Benchmark: Kia

Why it works (check): pole intrusion is set by the plastic bending moment. Al: 260 MPa × Zp ≈ 57,600 mm³ ≈ 15 kNm; steel: ≈1,350 MPa × Zp ≈ 13,400 mm³ ≈ 18 kNm, so ~20% more at equal mass in a section 20 mm shallower, which adds crush stroke before the pack. ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Swaps the most expensive extrusion in the 800V BEV body for a roll-formed martensitic steel beam of the same mass that exceeds its plastic bending capacity, and joins it by resistance spot welds instead of flow-drill screws and isolating adhesive.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Beam made on a 2D roll-forming line with inline laser seam welding and flying cut-off (≈20 m/min; one shift covers 40,000 beams/yr); the body shop welds it to the sill inner in the existing sill sub-assembly cell before the outer closes; the flow-drill-screw robots for the sill insert are retired.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Constant section allows cut-to-length for both wheelbases; drain holes punched inline for e-coat throw and cavity wax; ≥25 mm spot pitch on the flanges; no galvanic isolation needed against steel sill shells; same sill-inner datums as the aluminium insert.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium-High – large per-BEV material saving at unchanged mass
costSavingPotential.percentage: 50-60% of BEV sill pack-protection insert cost
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per side: aluminium insert €64-€70 plus FDS and adhesive joining €6 deleted; steel beam €27-€30, spot welds €0.8, cavity wax and drain plugs €2.5-€3.0, framing sequence change €0.75 added. Low = (64+6) − (30+0.8+3.0+0.75) = €35.5 per side; high = (70+6) − (27+0.8+2.5+0.75) = €45.0 per side; × 2 sides = €70-€90 per BEV, taken as €70-€85 to cover HAZ and corrosion margin. BEV share 40% → €28-€34 per vehicle (fleet average) × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €1.4M-€1.7M per year.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: martensite fracturing rather than folding at the pole, laser-seam HAZ softening, and delayed fracture of uncoated martensite after e-coat. Validate with 3-point-bend coupons against 6082, UN R135 and FMVSS 214 pole, UN R95, IIHS side 2.0, Euro NCAP 2026 far-side, post-crash electrical safety to the UN R95 / UN R135 annexes and FMVSS 305 (no electrolyte leak, isolation kept) with REESS mechanical integrity to UN R100, and a body torsion test for the −4% sill EI. Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: Equal plastic moment is not equal pole energy absorption. With ≈5% elongation, CR1700M may hinge and crack rather than absorb energy over the stroke before the pack keep-out, so the energy at the keep-out stroke is the right metric. This overlaps library ideas bat8-6705b2448759 and psuv107 (martensitic or CP inserts in the sill), so savings must not be added together.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Kia EV9 (2024) — Extruded aluminium pack housing through-bolted directly into the unibody, with structural crush zones at the pack leading edge. How this differs: Kia relies on aluminium extrusions around the pack; we keep the side-impact energy in the body sill but make the beam a roll-formed martensitic steel profile of equal mass.

ideaData.title: Aluminium body-side outer split at the D-pillar into aperture and rear-quarter pressings
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: each body-side outer is one 6016-T4 pressing (1.0 mm), A-pillar to tail lamp, drawn from a ≈4.30 × 1.75 m blank (7.5 m², 20.3 kg) to a ≈8.6 kg part, about 42% utilisation, because the deep rear-quarter features (wheel-arch flare and tail-lamp pocket, ~140 mm draw) set the binder and addendum for the whole panel; five operations on the largest tandem line, ≈€9M for the LH/RH die set. Proposal: split at the D-pillar into an aperture outer (A/B/C pillars, roof rail, sill; ≈3.25 × 1.45 m blank, 12.7 kg) and a rear-quarter outer (≈1.30 × 1.15 m blank, 4.0 kg): 16.7 kg per side (−3.6 kg, ~51% utilisation). The 1.1 m lap runs under the D-pillar glass finisher and behind the tail lamp and is closed with structural adhesive, self-piercing rivets at 40 mm pitch (~28 per side) and seam sealer, the joint family the aluminium body already uses. Why it works (check): sheet €4.3/kg less €2.1/kg segregated 6xxx scrap credit = €2.2/kg × 3.6 kg × 2 = €15.8 per vehicle before joint costs. Gauge is unchanged, so dent and oil-canning resistance (∝ E·t³ and panel span) are unchanged, and the quarter becomes a shorter, stiffer panel with a flanged return at the joint. The seam lies 60-70 mm inside the finisher edge, and tail-lamp gap/flush is set by the quarter alone. The outer skin carries little of the body torsion (the inner structure does), and the lap is bonded, so torsional stiffness changes by <1%. Benchmark: Range Rover's Solihull aluminium bodies are glued, bonded and riveted with very little welding; this idea uses that same joint to buy back sheet utilisation. All bodies, both powertrains.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Two smaller pressings nest far better on the coil than one A-pillar-to-tail-lamp body side, cutting aluminium blank mass by ~3.6 kg per side; the joint uses the body shop's existing adhesive-plus-rivet process and sits under the D-pillar finisher, never on a Class-A line.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Aperture outer and quarter each need four operations and fit a mid-size tandem line instead of the largest press; one bonded-and-riveted joining station built from carry-over robots is added to the body-side sub-assembly; the quarter becomes a separately replaceable repair part.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Lap flange 18 mm with three locating pins; joint placed under the existing D-pillar finisher and tail lamp; the quarter carries the tail-lamp datums so lamp gap and flush are controlled by one part; rivets set from the hidden side; same 6016 coil for both parts.

title: Camera road-preview software retires the premium damper variant on upper trims
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Upper trims stop buying the premium two-solenoid damper. The comfort gain that justified it now comes from the base one-solenoid damper, switched soft 100-300 ms before each bump that the ADAS camera and map data detect ahead. Baseline: base trims fit a CDC damper with one proportional solenoid (0.3-1.6 A). The two upper trims fit a premium version with separate rebound and compression solenoids, costing €30-€40 more per corner, to meet impact-harshness targets on broken tarmac and speed humps. Proposal: run road preview on the existing front ADAS camera (8 MP monocular) fused with navigation map data. The chassis domain estimates a height profile 5-15 m ahead and sequences each corner's one solenoid: soft just before the wheel meets the event, then firm in rebound to control the aftershock. Upper trims then use the base damper with their own calibration only. Why it works: the premium hardware's advantage is mainly that it can be soft on impact and firm afterwards at the same time. When the impact time is known in advance, one solenoid can be switched through both states in sequence, because valve response (about 10-15 ms) is far shorter than the preview time at speeds up to 120 km/h. Benchmark: Genesis added Preview ECS to the GV80 as software on its existing suspension hardware, using a monocular camera plus navigation data. Applies identically to the MHEV and the 800V BEV.

title: 800V BEV roll actuators fed straight from the HV bus, deleting 48 V DC/DC
description: [800V BEV] On the BEV the 48 V sub-net exists only for the two electromechanical roll actuators; feeding the actuators directly from the 800 V bus deletes the DC/DC converter, the buffer and the 48 V harness, at the price of HV-rated motor inverter stages. Baseline: the shared platform uses 48 V electromechanical roll actuators (brushless motor, three-stage planetary, ~1,400 Nm class) front and rear. MHEV takes 48 V from its belt starter-generator net; the 800V BEV carries a dedicated 3.5 kW 800→48 V DC/DC, a 48 V supercapacitor buffer for 200 ms torque peaks and a separate 48 V harness only for these loads. Proposal: a BEV variant of the actuator power stage using 1,200 V SiC half-bridges (or 1,200 V IGBT on a small module) and a re-wound motor (higher back-EMF constant) supplied from the HV junction box through a 10 A HV fuse, orange HV cable and HVIL loop; the MHEV keeps the 48 V stage, so gearbox, housing, bar halves and software stay common. Why it works: the HV battery is a far stiffer source than a 48 V supercap for 2-3 kW peaks, and peak current at 800 V is only ~4 A. Benchmark: Porsche Active Ride on the Cayenne Electric draws power directly from the high-voltage battery without a voltage converter. If other 48 V loads exist on the BEV, only the buffer and harness lines remain valid.
