title: Passive diagonal-interlinked dampers replace electromechanical roll actuators on performance trim
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Roll stiffness on the performance trim comes from hydraulics instead of motors: diagonally cross-connected damper chambers resist roll while leaving warp (articulation) and bounce nearly free, with no motors, power electronics or 48 V energy draw. Baseline: the performance trim carries front and rear 48 V electromechanical roll actuators with split bars, plus a roll ECU. Proposal: delete both bars and actuators; give each CDC damper an extra annular port and connect the four compression/rebound chambers in two diagonal circuits (circuit A: FL compression, FR rebound, RL compression, RR rebound; circuit B the mirror set; a literal diagonal joining FL and RR compression would stiffen warp, not roll), each with a 0.4 L nitrogen accumulator pre-charged to 20 bar and a small pressure-maintenance valve; a bridge valve lets the software soften the circuits in off-road mode. Roll stiffness comes from fluid displaced between circuits, warp is free because it moves fluid within a circuit. Why it works: passive interlinked systems deliver very high roll stiffness with low warp stiffness; the cost is a lines-and-accumulator kit, not two 1.4 kNm servo drives. Honest trade-off: no active roll levelling into a corner (body still leans ~1°); keep the CDC valves for damping. Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport SV's 6D Dynamics uses hydraulically interlinked dampers with about 25 m of lines and removes conventional anti-roll bars and Dynamic Response Pro.

title: Multi-spindle subframe marriage with joint-signature records ends click-wrench re-checks
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each safety-critical chassis bolt proves itself through its recorded rotation-and-gradient signature, stored against the VIN. The 100% click-wrench re-check after decking and most of the repair loop disappear. Baseline: front and rear subframes, strut tops and arm-to-body bolts are run down at the decking station by single nutrunners with torque-only control. Because these are category A joints under VDI/VDE 2862, two operators per shift re-check every bolt with click wrenches and paint-mark it, and about 0.6% of cars need a repair loop. Proposal: a 12-spindle servo head on the decking AGV records each bolt's full signature (torque, rotation angle, yield gradient), for example M14×1.5 10.9 subframe bolts at a snug torque of about 80-100 Nm + 90° ±10°, and writes it to the car's MES record. A bolt outside its window sends the car to an automatic repair loop at the next station. Both powertrains share the subframe pick-up positions, so one spindle layout serves the MHEV and the 800V BEV, with the programme selected by VIN. Why it works: a rotation-and-gradient signature reveals cross-threads, missing washers, soft joints and stripped threads that a torque-only reading misses, which is exactly what the click-wrench re-check is meant to catch. Benchmark: chassis built at high volume across trims, such as the Li Auto L9 at 200,000 deliveries, depend on one standard decking process. This idea makes that process self-verifying.

title: Stereo wheel-arch scanning teaches air-suspension height sensors during wheel alignment
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The air-suspension height sensors are taught automatically while the car is already in the alignment rig, so the separate height-gauging station and its operator time disappear. Baseline: after the air springs are filled, the car moves to a level platform where an operator measures the four wheel-arch-to-hub-centre heights with a mechanical gauge, then teaches the four ride-height sensor offsets through a diagnostic tester – about 3.5 min per car with occasional transcription errors. Proposal: two stereo laser-line scanner pairs added to the existing four-post alignment rig measure arch-lip and wheel-centre positions (±0.5 mm) while toe and camber are being set; the rig controller writes the four offsets to the chassis controller over DoIP and confirms by commanding a 20 mm lift-and-return and re-measuring. Why it works: the alignment rig already holds the car level on floating plates at trim load, which is the reference condition for height teach; the extra measurement adds no cycle time. Benchmark: multi-level air-suspension SUVs such as the Volvo EX90 rely on accurately taught sensors for speed-dependent ride height (210 mm road to 250 mm off-road); one shared calibration step serves MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One welded front subframe shell with bolt-in engine or EDU crossmember
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Both powertrains share one welded subframe shell and one weld line; the powertrain-specific content (engine-mount pedestals for the I6 or EDU cradle bosses for the BEV) lives in a small bolt-in crossmember, so the second set of weld fixtures, gauges and e-coat jigs is never bought. Baseline: two different welded steel front subframes – the MHEV one with engine-mount pedestals, oil-sump clearance pocket and steering-rack bosses; the 800V BEV one with front-EDU cradle bosses and a different rear crossmember – each needing its own robotic weld cell fixtures, check gauges and coating jigs (~€5M per variant) at only 30,000/20,000 per year. Proposal: one shell (side members in hydroformed S420MC tube, front and middle crossmembers stamped CR780T/420Y-DP EN 10338, all arm and rack pick-ups common) plus a bolt-in rear crossmember: vacuum-HPDC AlSi10MnMg T7 for MHEV (engine-mount towers integral) or BEV (three EDU mount bosses), each fixed by 4 × M12 10.9 bolts into weld nuts with two Ø12 h7 dowels for position. Why it works: suspension hard-points and crash load paths are identical for both powertrains; only the drive-unit interface differs, and that interface is local. Benchmark: the Audi Q6 e-tron's PPE is shared with the Porsche Macan Electric and carries an asynchronous front motor; here we share one subframe across combustion MHEV and BEV.

title: Levelling-only single-chamber air springs on base trims delete reservoir and lift hardware
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Base trims keep the air ride and automatic load levelling that customers feel, but lose the multi-height functions they rarely use, so the reservoir, the fast-lift compressor rating, one height sensor and two valves are removed. Baseline: every trim carries the full system – dual-height-mode air springs, a 6 L reservoir at 16 bar, a compressor rated to lift the car 50 mm in under 30 s, four rotary height sensors and a five-valve block (four corners plus reservoir). Proposal: on base trims (60%) fit single-chamber air springs at one road height with automatic load levelling only (±10 mm around trim, e.g. for 7 seats or a 750 kg trailer nose load), a compressor sized for levelling flow (−35% displacement), no reservoir, a three-valve block (front pair on one fill valve with each spring isolated by a check valve or a ≤0.5 mm orifice cross-port, so roll stiffness is kept, plus two rear corners) and three sensors (one front axle-average, two rear). Upper trims keep the full multi-level system from the same air-spring top caps and piston family. Why it works: levelling needs small air mass flows over minutes; the reservoir and fast compressor exist for quick lift/lower, which base-trim buyers seldom use. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity base trim uses single-chamber air springs at a fixed 178 mm clearance, with the three-chamber 5.0-9.0 in system as an option.

title: Front-axle-only active roll actuator on mid trim with stiffened passive rear bar
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] On the mid trim only the front bar is actively twisted; the rear gets a stiffer hollow passive bar. One of the two most expensive chassis actuators is deleted, while the front actuator still delivers most of the anti-roll moment and the comfort decoupling on single-wheel bumps. Baseline: active-roll vehicles carry two 48 V electromechanical actuators – front (~1,400 Nm class) and rear (~900 Nm class) – each splitting its bar, together holding body roll near 0.5°/g. Proposal: on a mid trim (25% of mix, positioned between passive bars and full active roll), keep the front actuator and fit a hollow 34MnB5 passive rear bar (Ø26×4.5 mm) about 20% stiffer than the passive-trim rear bar. The front actuator supplies the anti-roll moment the passive rear bar cannot, giving a roll gradient around 1.2-1.5°/g, against 2.5-3°/g on passive trims. The shift in lateral load transfer towards the front, which adds understeer, is compensated by the rear passive bar rate and by the CDC rebound balance; on the dual-motor 800V BEV, rear torque bias helps. Why it works: in a luxury SUV the front bar carries most of the roll moment, and most of the single-wheel comfort benefit of a decoupled bar comes from the front axle, where impacts arrive first. Benchmark: the BMW X7's Executive Drive Pro splits both bars with central electric swivel motors; we keep that hardware on top trims and offer a front-only version to cut cost.

title: Rear air spring moved to spring link lets coil and air trims share dampers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moving the rear air spring off the damper and onto the spring link, where the coil spring sits on coil trims, frees the rear damper from air-tight sealing and a special top cap, so one rear CDC damper serves coil and air trims. Baseline: rear air trims use an air strut – the bellows wrapped around the damper, with a sealed outer tube, rod pass-through seal and special top cap – while coil trims use a plain damper and a coil on the spring link: two rear damper families. Proposal: put the rear air spring (cross-ply bellows, single chamber or dual-chamber on top trims) on the same lower spring-link seat as the coil spring, with an air-spring top cap bolted to the body's spring seat, and fit the identical CDC damper on both trims. The spring link gets a larger, flatter seat pressing (CR780T/420Y-DP) and a lower piston boss. Why it works: on multi-link rears the spring-link position has a motion ratio (~0.6) that suits air-spring volume and keeps the bellows out of bending; the damper then stays a standard twin-tube part. Benchmark: Li Auto's L9 combines dual-chamber air springs and CDC on a five-link rear; our split layout is general practice on several European five-link rears and lets coil and air trims share dampers.

Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: Two points. (1) The baseline has coil trims with a 70% air share, but idea ieb-1791d9504c4b says every trim carries the full air system; the register needs one baseline. (2) dfmDfa makes the larger spring link common to all trims, yet the bridge charges it on air trims only (€3.5 × 2 × 0.7). On 100% of cars the cost is €7.0, not €4.9.

title: One long-stroke dual-chamber air corner gives access, road and 75 mm off-road heights
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Every car gets the same slightly longer air spring and damper, so the separate off-road corner set (four extra part numbers with their tooling and sequencing) disappears; the +75 mm off-road level is enabled in software on the off-road pack and capped at +40 mm on road cars. Baseline: road cars use dual-chamber air springs and CDC dampers giving −40 mm access, road, and +40 mm raised heights; the off-road pack (25% take) swaps in a longer-lobe bellows, a long-stroke damper with extended rebound and a different jounce bumper to reach +75 mm off-road height with full droop articulation. Proposal: one corner for all – rolling lobe +30 mm, damper stroke +30 mm (same bore, longer tube and rod), jounce and rebound stops positioned for the full 115 mm height range (−40 mm access to +75 mm off-road) – and software that unlocks the +75 mm level (and a hold at +55 mm up to 40 km/h) only with the off-road feature code. Why it works: the incremental material for 30 mm more stroke is small compared with a whole parallel corner family at only 25% volume. Benchmark: the Xiaomi YU7's closed dual-chamber springs offer a 75 mm five-level range from one corner design, and the Volvo EX90 raises from 210 mm to 250 mm in off-road mode. Off-road benefit: more droop travel improves articulation and approach/departure angles on every car that is later enabled.

title: Corner bushes torqued at trim height on axle sub-line, deleting under-car pit station
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Rubber-bushed pivots must be tightened with the arms at design ride height; doing this on the axle sub-line in a fixture that holds each corner at trim position removes the under-car pit station on the main line. Baseline: the link and wishbone bushes are only hand-started on the axle modules; after marriage and air-spring fill the car sits at trim height and two operators per shift in a pit tighten 16 bush joints (M12-M14, 90-180 Nm) – necessary because tightening at full droop would preload each bush by 10-15° of torsion and cut its life. Proposal: on the axle sub-line, a fixture with four servo-hydraulic positioners lifts each knuckle to its CAD trim position (±1 mm, read from the knuckle's datum holes), then a multi-spindle head torques all bush joints with torque-angle control; the module arrives at marriage already neutral. Why it works: the bush's neutral angle depends only on the geometry of the module, which the fixture reproduces exactly; it is independent of the body. Benchmark: air-suspension SUVs with wide height ranges, such as the Cadillac Escalade IQ (−2 in/+1 in), make neutral-bush torque important; this applies to MHEV and 800V BEV modules alike.

title: MHEV 48 V energy arbitration shares BSG and roll-actuator peaks, avoiding battery upsizing
description: [MHEV] During the short roll-actuator peaks (<1 s) the energy manager briefly trims belt starter-generator boost, so the 48 V battery never has to deliver both peaks at once and the upsized battery variant on active-roll MHEVs is no longer needed. Baseline: on MHEVs with front and rear 48 V roll actuators, the 48 V Li-ion battery is upsized from 0.9 kWh to 1.25 kWh (higher-power cells) so it can supply simultaneous BSG boost (up to 15 kW for 2-3 s), the roll actuators (2 × 1.5 kW peaks) and the electric air compressor/heater loads without voltage dipping below 36 V. Proposal: a 48 V power arbiter in the powertrain/chassis domain gives the roll actuators priority for up to 1 s when their predicted demand exceeds a threshold, reducing BSG boost by up to 3 kW in those moments (the I6 can make up the torque only where it has reserve at part load; at full load the 3 kW of boost is simply lost for up to 1 s), and pre-charges the battery SOC window when map data predict a twisty road. Why it works: true coincidence of full boost and full roll correction is rare and short; arbitrating it costs about 1-2% of boost energy, invisible to the driver. Benchmark: Range Rover's Dynamic Response Pro is a 48 V system that replaced hydraulics on an MHEV-equipped flagship, and BMW's 2023 X7 runs 48 V mild hybrid on all combustion engines – both show the shared 48 V net this idea manages.

title: Air springs delivered with residual pre-charge and topped up by the car's compressor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The supplier ships each air spring holding about 3 bar behind its residual-pressure valve, and the vehicle's own compressor finishes the fill during the drive to end of line, so the plant's external fill rig and its operator time are removed. Baseline: air springs arrive at atmospheric pressure held in shape by a transport clamp; after installation an operator connects an external fill rig to the valve-block service port and fills the four springs to 8-10 bar and the reservoir to 16 bar (≈2 min). Proposal: the spring supplier fills each spring to ~3 bar through the residual-pressure retention valve already in the spring cap (it normally keeps ≥2 bar to stop the bellows folding), and fits a sealing cap on the port; in the plant the line is pushed on (the push-in fitting opens the valve), and after first ignition an EOL software mode runs the vehicle compressor with cool-down pauses while the car travels the 6-8 min to the alignment rig. Why it works: from a 3 bar pre-charge the compressor only adds ~6 bar per spring, within its duty cycle when paced by the EOL mode. Benchmark: closed dual-chamber systems such as the Xiaomi YU7's recirculate air within the vehicle, showing the on-board compressor and storage can manage the air mass; this applies to MHEV and 800V BEV identically.

title: Splined press-fit joins roll-actuator bar halves, deleting forged flanges and bolts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each bar half is joined to the actuator output by a rolled involute spline pressed into the actuator's internally splined hub instead of a welded forged flange with six bolts, removing four forgings, 24 bolts and four machined faces per car. Baseline: on the split roll-control bars each bar half (hollow 34MnB5 tube, quenched and tempered) has a forged 42CrMo4 flange friction-welded to its end, faced and drilled, and is bolted with six M10 10.9 bolts to the actuator's output flange or housing flange. Proposal: cold-roll an involute spline (module 1.0-1.25, 34-38 teeth, DIN 5480 profile) directly on an upset bar-end, induction-harden it to 50-54 HRC, and servo-press it into an internally broached hub on the actuator output and housing end with 0.02-0.04 mm interference; axial retention by a cross pin plus a roll-formed or crimped collar (no weld on the quenched-and-tempered boron-steel bar, whose heat-affected zone would sit at the spline root). Why it works: roll-control torque (≤1,400 Nm) is well within a 38 mm spline's capacity with a safety factor above 2; press-fit splines remove backlash, which matters for roll feel. Benchmark: BMW's X7 Executive Drive Pro splits each bar and joins the halves through a central electric swivel motor – the joint this idea simplifies.

title: High-angle upper ball joint shared by road and off-road front arms
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One front upper ball joint with a ±32° swing angle is used on every car, so the off-road pack no longer needs its own upper arm and knuckle variant to reach full droop at the off-road height. Baseline: road cars use a ±22° upper ball joint; at the off-road height (+75 mm) and full droop the joint would bind, so the off-road pack has a different forged 6082-T6 upper arm with a high-angle joint and a knuckle with a lowered upper boss. Proposal: a high-angle ball joint on all cars – 22 mm stud with a reduced-neck design, PA66/POM bearing shell, larger housing of 38MnVS6 – fitted to one arm forging and one knuckle; software height limits keep road cars at +40 mm. Why it works: the joint's angular capacity is set by stud neck and housing opening, not by the arm; the incremental cost of a high-angle joint is a few euros, whereas a separate arm and knuckle family at 25% volume carries tooling, PPAP and sequencing costs. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S reaches 14.9 in (380 mm) maximum clearance on its air suspension, showing the travel a luxury off-roader's joints must accommodate. Off-road benefit: full droop articulation available at the off-road height on every enabled car.

title: Subframe bushes with bonded rebound flanges delete loose snubbing washers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each subframe bush is moulded with a steel rebound flange bonded to its rubber, so the large loose washer that limits axial (rebound) travel is no longer a separate part. At marriage the operator handles one part per joint instead of two. Baseline: the eight subframe-to-body joints (four front, four rear) each use a voided rubber bush pressed into the subframe plus a separate stamped steel rebound washer (Ø70 mm, 4 mm, zinc-flake coated), held under the bolt head. The washer's rubber-faced lip limits subframe drop in rebound and crash and is placed by hand at marriage; washers are sometimes missing or upside-down. Proposal: mould a Ø68 mm S355 flange, welded or crimped to the bush's inner sleeve, into the bush's lower face, with a 6 mm moulded rubber snubbing pad that gives the same progressive axial stop (gap 3 mm, then about 4 kN/mm). The bolt clamps the flanged inner sleeve metal-to-metal, as it clamped the washer, so subframe retention in a crash stays mechanical; the rubber bond carries only the snubbing pad. Why it works: the washer has no function the bush moulding cannot carry, and bonding fixes its orientation and position. Benchmark: luxury SUVs with wide air-suspension ranges, such as the Escalade IQ (lowers 2 in, lifts 1 in), put large rebound and jounce excursions through their subframe mounts, which these stops must control. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One hub-bearing unit size for all four corners on both powertrains
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The heaviest-duty corner (BEV front, highest axle load) sets one Gen 3 hub-bearing unit that is used at all four corners and on both powertrains, doubling volume per part number and deleting three part numbers with their tooling and validation. Baseline: four Gen 3 driven hub-bearing units – MHEV front, MHEV rear, BEV front, BEV rear – differing in pitch diameter (Ø 88-94 mm), ball size, spline and flange, each with its own forging dies, grinding set-ups, PPAP and validation; the 800V BEV, ~300 kg heavier, needs the larger units. Proposal: one unit (pitch Ø 94 mm, 100Cr6 balls and inner rings, C56E2 induction-hardened flange, 5 × M14 PCD 112) with a common CV spline agreed with the driveline supplier and one knuckle bore across all corners. Why it works: bearing life at the lighter MHEV corners simply rises (L10 margin +40%), and the knuckle interface is common anyway on shared hard-points; the volume of a single part number lowers forging, heat-treat and grinding cost. Benchmark: the Audi Q6 e-tron's PPE is shared with the Porsche Macan Electric, a deliberate cross-model commonisation of chassis hardware; here we commonise across corners and powertrains.

title: Conical rubber front-subframe mounts on BEV, hydromounts kept only for the I6 MHEV
description: [800V BEV] The hydraulic front-subframe mounts exist to damp the I6 engine's shake around 10-14 Hz; the BEV has no such excitation, so it gets simpler voided rubber mounts tuned for road impact and EDU frequencies. Baseline: the front subframe's two rear mounts are hydraulically damped (glycol-filled inertia-track mounts) on both powertrains to suppress engine shake of the 3.0 L I6 at idle and on rough roads and the coupled shake of the front axle, at €26-€32 each. Proposal: on the 800V BEV, a conical voided natural-rubber mount (NR/BR blend, 55 Shore A, progressive stop) of the same outer geometry and bolt pattern, with radial-to-axial stiffness tuned for impact harshness and a voided axis softened for longitudinal compliance; damping comes from the CDC dampers and rubber hysteresis. Why it works: hydromount damping peaks over a narrow frequency band, chosen for engine shake; front EDU orders are above 200 Hz, where hydromounts give no benefit and can even stiffen dynamically. Benchmark: premium BEVs such as the Porsche Cayenne Electric achieve comfort through active chassis control rather than engine-shake hardware; our change is general BEV practice that must be proven in our own NVH tests.

title: Polyamide-bodied front air-strut top module replaces five-piece isolator stack
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One moulded polyamide module per side carries the vulcanised rubber isolator, the stop face and the end-stop snap. The steel can, its retaining ring, the stop cup and the clip are deleted, so the strut top is fitted as a single part. Baseline: the top of the front air strut is a stack of five pieces on the rod nut: the air-spring cap, a rubber isolator pressed into a steel can and held by a retaining ring, a stamped steel stop cup, and a clip that holds the end-stop. Proposal: one module in which the natural-rubber isolator (60 Shore A) is vulcanised with a one-coat adhesive onto a PA66-GF35 body. The body has a moulded stop face carrying a 2 mm steel wear washer and a snap groove for the end-stop, and it seals to the air-spring cap with an O-ring. Why it works: on a double-wishbone front the air strut does not turn with the steering, so no top bearing is needed. The stack only isolates vibration and carries end-stop loads up to 25 kN, which PA66-GF35 can take with the steel washer at the contact face. Benchmark: the Xiaomi YU7's closed dual-chamber air springs show how much function is now packaged at the strut top; this idea consolidates the parts around it. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Extended front subframe side members take small-overlap loads without bolt-on outriggers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The subframe's own side members are extended forward with crush-initiation beads and a welded end plate so that they engage the barrier in a small-overlap crash, replacing the bolt-on outrigger brackets and their bolts. Baseline: the welded steel front subframe carries two bolt-on outriggers (stamped CR780T/420Y-DP EN 10338, 2.0 mm, four M12 bolts each) that extend the lower load path outboard to engage the barrier in the IIHS small-overlap and Euro NCAP 2026 frontal tests. Proposal: hydroform the side members (S420MC tube) 120 mm longer with a swept-outboard tip, two crush-initiation beads and a 3 mm welded end plate; the tip lies in the same position as the outrigger face, so the load path into the wheel and sill is unchanged. Why it works: the outriggers are load-path extensions, not energy absorbers; making them part of the tube removes the joint, the bolts and the bracket flanges. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90's air suspension and off-road raise (210 → 250 mm) show why the lower load path must work at several ride heights; extending the subframe tube keeps it in place at each height. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV front subframes alike.

title: Four-bore co-extruded air-line ribbon replaces six separate suspension air lines
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The four corner air lines run together in one co-extruded PA12 ribbon with four bores from the valve block to front and rear split blocks, so the plant routes and clips one profile instead of six separate tubes. Baseline: six individual PA12 Ø6×1 mm air lines (four corners, reservoir, supply) are routed separately along the underbody, held by about 60 single clips with 12 push-in connectors. Proposal: a co-extruded PA12 (PA12-PHL, DIN 73378) four-bore ribbon, each bore Ø4 mm ID, joined by a 1.5 mm web, routed as one profile from the valve block to a moulded front and a rear split block (PA66-GF30 with brass inserts) where it branches into short single lines to each air spring; clips are wide double-hook clips every 400 mm. Why it works: the lines already follow the same path for most of their length; one profile halves clip count and connector count while keeping each corner's line independent (no cross-flow). Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport SV's 6D system uses about 25 m of hydraulic lines – routing length is a real cost in chassis systems with corner-to-corner connections, which this idea attacks for air. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV underbodies.

title: Sealed rear-subframe crossmember tube doubles as the air-suspension reservoir
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear subframe's closed extruded crossmember is sealed with welded end caps and a port boss to store the system air, so the separate reservoir, its brackets, isolators and one installation step disappear. Baseline: a 6 L aluminium reservoir at 16-20 bar sits under the rear floor on two brackets with rubber isolators, connected by a line to the valve block. Proposal: the rear subframe's rear crossmember (6082-T6 extrusion, Ø90 mm, wall 4.0 → 4.5 mm) is closed by two friction-stir-welded 6082 end caps and carries an M12×1.5 port boss, providing ~4.5 L at 20 bar; burst ≥ 80 bar (4× working), leak-tested with helium. Lift-speed loss from the smaller volume is offset by the higher 20 bar storage pressure (same stored air mass ≈ 6 L × 16 bar). Why it works: the crossmember is already a closed, thick-walled tube; hoop stress at 20 bar is pr/t ≈ 2 MPa × 45/4.5 ≈ 20 MPa, modest against 6082-T6 strength but additive to structural stress at the FSW end-cap seams. Benchmark: closed air systems like the Xiaomi YU7's dual-chamber design depend on onboard storage; integrating that storage in structure is our step. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV rear subframes alike.

title: Single 46 mm working-bore family for front and rear CDC dampers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Front and rear CDC dampers use the same 46 mm working bore, piston, rod guide, seals and tube stock, differing only in lengths, valving and attachments, so the damper line runs one component family at doubled volume. Baseline: front air struts use a 46 mm working-bore twin-tube CDC damper and the rear separate dampers a 36 mm bore, each with its own piston (sintered Fe with PTFE band), rod guide, seals, inner and outer tube stock, valving tools and EOL test fixtures. Proposal: one 46 mm bore for all four dampers, with the rear damper's piston valving retuned for the larger area (lower pressures for the same force, which also improves CDC valve resolution and reduces cavitation), same 22 mm rod, rod guide and seal pack; length and lower eye differ. Why it works: piston, guide and seals are the precision parts that drive damper cost; length variants are cheap. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 fits four-corner adaptive dampers on its air-sprung trims, making the damper set a high-value, four-off part; we standardise the bore across the four. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Face-spline hub-to-driveshaft joint replaces involute spline and collared axle nut
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Torque passes from the outer CV joint to the hub through a radial face spline clamped by one central bolt, so the long splined stub shaft through the bearing, its machining, the large collared nut and the anti-click spline adhesive are deleted. Baseline: each driven corner (all four on the AWD MHEV and dual-motor 800V BEV) uses a CV outer joint with an integral stub shaft carrying an involute spline through the Gen 3 hub-bearing inner bore, clamped by a collared M24-M27 nut torqued to 300-450 Nm and staked; spline backlash can 'click' under regen torque reversals, so a micro-encapsulated adhesive is applied. Proposal: a radial face spline (Hirth-type, ~40 teeth) cold-formed on the hub's orbitally formed inner-ring face and on the CV bell face, clamped by a single M16×1.5 10.9 bolt through the hub with ~120 kN preload. Why it works: a preloaded face spline carries torque without backlash and centres the joint; deleting the stub shaft shortens the CV bell and removes ~0.4 kg per corner. General practice: face-spline wheel-bearing joints are in production at several European OEMs. Benchmark: the Audi Q6 e-tron drives both axles (140 kW front ASM, 280 kW rear PSM), so every corner carries drive and regen torque reversals – the clicking case this joint removes.

title: Welded steel lower clevis on front damper replaces forged aluminium clamp fork
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The front damper's lower attachment to the wishbone becomes a stamped steel clevis welded to the damper outer tube at the damper supplier, deleting the separate forged aluminium fork, its machining and the pinch bolt that clamps it to the tube. Baseline: on the double-wishbone front, the air-strut damper's lower end is clamped into a forged 6082-T6 fork (machined bore, slot and pinch bolt) that straddles the drive shaft and bolts to the lower wishbone through a rubber bush. Proposal: a two-piece stamped S500MC (EN 10149-2) 4 mm clevis, laser-welded to the E355 damper outer tube with a pressed-in bush sleeve, giving the same straddle geometry; the damper is delivered with clevis attached, so the plant just bolts it to the wishbone. Why it works: the fork's function is a load path and drive-shaft clearance, not adjustability; a welded steel clevis carries the 25 kN jounce and 8 kN lateral loads with less machining, at the cost of ~0.35 kg more unsprung mass per side. Benchmark: double-wishbone fronts remain standard on luxury SUVs including the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology, so the damper fork is a common, high-volume part. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Rod-top CDC connector at the strut tower removes damper flying leads and clips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] With the CDC valve inside the piston, the valve wires already exit through the hollow rod; terminating them in a connector at the rod top lets the body harness plug in at the strut tower, deleting the flying lead, its clips and grommet. Baseline: each CDC damper has a 350 mm flying lead from the valve to an inline connector on the body, with three clips and a grommet through the wheel-house; leads are exposed to stones and need routing care during strut installation. Proposal: where the platform uses a piston-integrated CDC valve (wiring through a hollow 22 mm rod), terminate the two conductors in a sealed 2-pin connector (IP6K9K) moulded on the rod-top nut, inside the top mount; the body harness connector clips onto it from the engine-bay/strut-tower side after strut installation. Why it works: the rod top moves only a few millimetres relative to the body through the top-mount isolator, so a short strain-relieved lead sees far less motion than one on the damper tube and stays protected, and the harness branch shortens by ~300 mm. Benchmark: CDC continuous damping is fitted to every Li Auto L9 with its dual-chamber air springs, typical of the high CDC penetration in luxury SUVs that multiplies this four-corner saving. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Air-supply unit hung on rear subframe isolators, deleting body bracket and second mount stage
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The compressor, dryer and valve block unit is mounted on the rear subframe through one set of isolators, using the subframe's own body mounts as the second isolation stage, so the body bracket and its second isolator set are removed and rear air lines shorten. Baseline: the air-supply unit (12 V dry-running compressor, regenerative dryer, five-valve block) is fixed by three rubber isolators to a stamped steel bracket that is itself isolated from the floor by three further grommets – double isolation to keep compressor noise below 35 dB(A) in the cabin. Proposal: hang the unit on three conical isolators from two bosses on the rear subframe (welded or cast), between the rear crossmember and the spring links; the subframe bushes give the second stage, and the unit is pre-assembled to the subframe before marriage, shortening rear lines by ~1.6 m. Why it works: compressor excitation (≈20-40 Hz fundamental, harmonics to 500 Hz) is well isolated by two rubber stages in series regardless of whether the middle mass is a bracket or a subframe – and the subframe is a much larger intermediate mass, improving isolation. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity's three-chamber air suspension illustrates how much air-supply hardware a luxury SUV carries under the floor; we simplify its mounting. Not compatible with a rigidly bolted BEV rear subframe – see that alternative.

title: One dual-chamber air spring for both axles, tuned by axle-specific rolling pistons
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Front and rear use the same bellows, top cap with auxiliary chamber, and switching valve; the different spring rates and load capacities are obtained by axle-specific rolling-piston contours that set the effective area and its progression. Baseline: front air struts and rear air springs have different bellows (diameter, length), different top caps with different auxiliary-chamber volumes and different chamber switching valves – four families once powertrain-specific rates are counted. Proposal: one bellows (cross-ply, 2-ply, polyamide cord, NR/CR compound), one cap with 0.9 L auxiliary chamber and one solenoid switching valve; axle- and powertrain-specific rates come from PA66-GF50 rolling pistons with different diameters and contour (effective area 85-105 cm², progressive flare), and from the software pressure level. Why it works: for an air spring, rate is set by effective area, volume and pressure; the piston controls the first, the common chamber the second, software the third – the bellows only needs to cover the stroke and burst requirement. Benchmark: Li Auto's L9 uses dual-chamber air springs on both axles (with CDC); our idea commonises the bellows and valve hardware across axles. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Hook-in polyamide anti-roll-bar bush shells delete steel clamp brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each bar bush is moulded into a glass-filled polyamide shell that hooks into a slot in the subframe and is held by one bolt, replacing a stamped steel clamp bracket and halving the bolts per bush. Baseline: on trims with passive anti-roll bars (no active roll), front and rear bars are held by four rubber bushes, each in a stamped steel clamp bracket (S355MC 3 mm, e-coated) with two M10 bolts into weld nuts on the subframe. Proposal: bush rubber (NR, bonded to the bar or slip type) moulded into a PA66-GF50 half-shell with a hook tongue that engages a punched slot in the subframe and a single M10 bolt on the opposite side; metal compression limiter in the bolt hole. Why it works: bar bush loads are modest (≤ 6 kN radial), within polyamide shell capability with a hook taking the main reaction; the hook gives a defined position and one-hand assembly. Benchmark: the Toyota Land Cruiser 250's front stabiliser with disconnection mechanism shows how central anti-roll-bar mounting is to off-road and on-road tuning; our change is to how the bar is clamped. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV passive-bar trims.

title: Forged sacrificial skid rib on rear spring link replaces bolt-on off-road arm guard
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear spring link forging gets a 4 mm sacrificial skid rib and a shroud boss around the height-sensor link pick-up on its underside, so the off-road pack no longer needs a bolt-on aluminium guard and a separate sensor shield on each link. Baseline: the rear lower spring links (forged 6082-T6) are the lowest suspension parts behind the rear wheels; the off-road pack bolts a 3 mm 6082 guard plate (four M8 bolts) under each link and a stamped steel shield around the height-sensor link to survive rock and log strikes. Proposal: modify the forging die to add a longitudinal 4 mm-deep, 25 mm-wide sacrificial rib along the link's underside (on the lower face, which is the link's highest-stress fibre in bending, so the rib is treated as non-structural, given a generous root radius and excluded from the strength section) and a forged-in boss shrouding the sensor ball-stud; standard on all links (+0.15 kg). Why it works: a guard plate's value is a sliding surface and an abrasion allowance; both can be forged into the part at low cost, deleting fasteners that loosen off-road. Benchmark: the Toyota Land Cruiser 250's front stabiliser disconnection gives more articulation, which puts the lowest suspension links in contact with terrain more often – the case this rib protects. Off-road benefit: smoother sliding over rocks and no snag points.

title: Triple-lip wading cassette seal on every hub bearing deletes knuckle slinger and variant
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Every hub bearing gets the cassette seal previously reserved for off-road builds – three radial/axial lips with an integrated encoder – so the separate knuckle-side slinger and the off-road bearing variant disappear. Baseline: road builds use a double-lip inboard cassette seal plus a stamped steel slinger pressed on the knuckle to deflect water; off-road builds (rated for 900 mm wading) use a different bearing part number with a triple-lip seal. Proposal: one inboard cassette seal on every bearing: two radial HNBR lips plus an axial lip against a stainless flinger, with the magnetic wheel-speed encoder (NdFeB-filled elastomer) bonded to the flinger; outboard seal unchanged. The knuckle slinger is deleted because the axial lip and labyrinth replace its function. Why it works: seal drag rises by only ~0.05-0.1 Nm per corner with low-friction lip geometry, while ingress protection improves for every customer (car washes, flooded roads). Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 110 is specified to 900 mm wading on air suspension (850 mm on coil) – the immersion case the seal must survive; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Solid-solution ferritic GJS-500-14 rear knuckles replace pearlitic GJS-600-3 castings
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Solid-solution-strengthened ferritic ductile iron has a uniform hardness and higher elongation than pearlitic grades, so the rear knuckle machines faster with longer tool life and its walls can be thinned at the same strength. Baseline: rear knuckles (heavy SUV, both powertrains) are sand-cast EN-GJS-600-3 (pearlitic-ferritic) – hardness spread 190-270 HB across sections, so machining parameters are set for the hardest zones and walls are sized for its low 3% elongation in misuse loads. Proposal: EN-GJS-500-14 per EN 1563 (silicon ~3.8%, fully ferritic, Rp0.2 ≥ 400 MPa, A ≥ 14%), with hardness 170-200 HB uniform; walls thinned 0.5-1 mm in low-stress zones (mass −0.5 kg per knuckle) because higher ductility raises misuse margin. Why it works: GJS-500-14 offers yield close to GJS-600-3 with far better elongation and uniform machinability – documented by foundries as up to 30% higher tool life. Benchmark: heavy electric SUVs like the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology keep robust, iron-and-steel-intensive axles for rugged use; we pick a better iron rather than a costlier aluminium knuckle. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Form-tapped wheel-bolt threads in hub flanges replace cut taps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Wheel-bolt threads in the hub flange are cold-formed instead of cut, so taps last about three times longer, no chips are produced near the bearing, and the work-hardened thread flanks are stronger. Baseline: the C56E2 hub flange's five M14×1.5 wheel-bolt holes are drilled and cut-tapped; chips must be washed out to protect the bearing seals, taps break occasionally, and thread tearing causes rejects. Proposal: drill to the form-tap pre-hole (Ø13.4 mm, H8), then form-tap with a TiCN-coated roll tap and emulsion; thread flanks are cold-worked (+10-20% strip strength), and no chips are generated. Why it works: C56E2 in the normalised flange zone (≈200-230 HB, elongation >14%) is formable enough for roll tapping; form taps run at higher speed with longer life. Benchmark: heavy three-row 800V BEV SUVs like the Kia EV9 carry high wheel loads (it adds self-levelling rear dampers for load), the case where wheel-bolt thread strength matters; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Single-stroke segmented swaging of air-spring clamp rings with force-path monitoring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The aluminium rings that clamp the bellows to piston and cap are swaged in one stroke by a 12-segment tool with force-path monitoring, replacing a two-stage crimp and catching under-clamped rings in-process instead of at leak test. Baseline: each bellows end is clamped by a 6060-T66 aluminium ring crimped in two stages on an 8-jaw radial press (pre-crimp, final crimp), followed by leak test at 1.5× working pressure; under-crimps appear only at leak test (≈0.8% rework). Proposal: a 12-segment swaging head closes the ring in one stroke to a monitored diameter; the force-displacement curve is checked against an envelope for every ring; rings get a fine inner knurl (0.3 mm) to increase rubber grip. Why it works: more segments give more uniform radial compression in one stroke; monitoring verifies the clamp directly. Benchmark: closed dual-chamber air springs such as the Xiaomi YU7's hold air across two chambers and five height levels, making clamp integrity central to the system; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV springs.

title: Fixed-length rear toe link on a post-machined subframe pick-up deletes eccentric cam bolts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear toe link's inboard bore position on the subframe is machined after welding in the subframe datum fixture, so rear toe lands inside tolerance without adjustment and the eccentric cam bolts and their adjustment time are deleted. Baseline: the five-link rear's toe link mounts to the subframe through an eccentric cam bolt with cam washers; at the alignment rig the operator sets rear toe by rotating the cams (≈2 min), and service retains the adjustment. Proposal: weld the subframe's toe-link bracket with a 1.5 mm undersize hole, then in the existing post-weld datum machining fixture (used for arm bores) bore it to final size (±0.15 mm relative to subframe datums) so that toe is within ±5' with stack-up of knuckle and link tolerances; fit a plain M12 10.9 bolt. Alignment rig only verifies; out-of-tolerance cars (target <1%) are corrected with an offset-bush service part, since a plain round bore cannot take a cam bolt. Why it works: most toe scatter comes from weld distortion of the bracket, which post-machining removes. Benchmark: Li Auto's L9 uses a five-link rear, like ours, where the toe link is the adjustment point; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

ideaData.title: Fixed-length rear toe link on a post-machined subframe pick-up deletes eccentric cam bolts
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the five-link rear's toe link mounts to the subframe through an eccentric cam bolt with cam washers; at the alignment rig the operator sets rear toe by rotating the cams (≈2 min), and service retains the adjustment. Proposal: weld the subframe's toe-link bracket with a 1.5 mm undersize hole, then in the existing post-weld datum machining fixture (used for arm bores) bore it to final size (±0.15 mm relative to subframe datums) so that toe is within ±5' with stack-up of knuckle and link tolerances; fit a plain M12 10.9 bolt. Alignment rig only verifies; out-of-tolerance cars (target <1%) are corrected with an offset-bush service part, since a plain round bore cannot take a cam bolt. Why it works: most toe scatter comes from weld distortion of the bracket, which post-machining removes. Benchmark: Li Auto's L9 uses a five-link rear, like ours, where the toe link is the adjustment point; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: The rear toe link's inboard bore position on the subframe is machined after welding in the subframe datum fixture, so rear toe lands inside tolerance without adjustment and the eccentric cam bolts and their adjustment time are deleted.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One additional boring spindle in the subframe machining fixture; plant alignment cycle shortens for rear toe. Service kit kept for repairs. Alignment rig cycle drops by about 1.5 min.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Requires a capable knuckle-to-link tolerance chain (±0.1 mm toe-link length, knuckle bore ±0.1 mm); document the stack in a 3D tolerance analysis. Plain bolts use the same M12 grade and torque as the other link joints.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low-medium – adjusting hardware and alignment time removed
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Eccentric cam bolts with washers €3.5 × 2 = €7.0 → plain bolts €1.8 (€5.2); rear toe adjust at alignment 2 min × €0.95 = €1.9 → €0.3 verify (€1.6); minus subframe pick-up post-machining €2.8 (low) / €1.2 (high, shared with existing machining op). Low = 5.2+1.6-2.8 = €4.0; high = 5.2+1.6-1.2 = €5.6 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €200K-€280K per year.

ideaData.riskNotes: Toe outside tolerance on some cars (tyre wear, pull) – validate stack-up statistically on 500 cars, Cpk ≥1.33 for rear toe. Steering/handling homologation UN R79 not affected (rear toe), but stability under UN R13-H ESC tests must be confirmed with the tolerance band.

How this differs: Li Auto's five-link rear is the layout reference; machining the pick-up to delete toe adjustment is our process change.

title: Edge-protecting thicker e-coat lets steel subframes drop cavity wax and stone-chip PVC
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] An edge-protecting cathodic e-coat at 30 µm, combined with drain and vent holes designed for full cavity throw, protects tube interiors and edges well enough that the subframe cavity wax and PVC stone-chip spray are no longer needed. Baseline: welded steel front and rear subframes (S420MC, CR780T/420Y-DP) are zinc-phosphated and e-coated to 25 µm, then the rear subframe tubes are cavity-waxed and the front subframe's lower edges sprayed with PVC stone-chip protection. Proposal: an edge-protection cathodic e-coat (high-build, edge coverage ≥ 12 µm on sheared edges) at 30 µm average, with drain/vent holes repositioned (CAE e-coat simulation) so interior surfaces get ≥ 15 µm; delete cavity wax and PVC. Why it works: wax and PVC compensate for poor interior throw and thin edge coverage; edge-protecting formulations and hole design address both causes. Benchmark: off-road-capable SUVs face water and salt exposure – the Land Rover Defender 110 is specified to 900 mm wading on air suspension – so the subframe protection must meet that duty; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Injection-moulded TPC-ET jounce bumpers replace cast microcellular polyurethane
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Bellows-shaped copolyester (TPC-ET) jounce bumpers are blow-moulded in seconds instead of cast and cured over minutes like microcellular polyurethane, and their convoluted shape gives the progressive stop in a shorter length. Baseline: each corner uses a cast microcellular polyurethane (MCU, ~500 kg/m³) jounce bumper, moulded in heated tools with a cure time of several minutes, then demoulded and post-cured. Proposal: an injection-blow-moulded thermoplastic copolyester elastomer (TPC-ET, e.g. 47-55 Shore D grade) convoluted bellows, wall 1.8-2.5 mm, giving a progressive force curve to 25 kN with 15-20% shorter block length than MCU; recyclable thermoplastic. Why it works: TPC bumpers are in production on several platforms; cycle time and material use are lower than MCU, and the shorter solid height returns usable travel. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ's Low Ride Mode drives with the suspension fully lowered, which shows how much jounce travel matters on air-sprung luxury SUVs; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One-coat rubber-to-metal bonding agent for all chassis bushes deletes primer step
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Bush inner and outer metals are coated with a single-coat bonding agent instead of a primer plus a topcoat, removing one spray, one flash-off and one handling step for every rubber-to-metal bush on the chassis. Baseline: all bonded chassis bushes (control arms, links, subframe, damper eyes, anti-roll bar; ≈24 per vehicle) use a two-coat bonding system – a phenolic primer then a polymer topcoat adhesive – each sprayed and dried before rubber injection/transfer moulding. Proposal: switch to a qualified one-coat bonding agent for natural rubber on zinc-phosphated or grit-blasted steel and aluminium inserts, applied by spray-dip in one step; adjust mould temperature profile (150-165 °C) to keep bond strength (rubber-tear failure mode, R ≥ 95%). Why it works: one-coat systems are well established for NR compounds and remove handling and drying capacity. Benchmark: the BMW X7's split active anti-roll bars still rely on conventional rubber bushes at the bar and link mounts, typical of the two dozen bonded bushes in a luxury SUV chassis this process change touches; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Glass-filled PA66 outer sleeves replace plated steel sleeves on rear subframe bushes
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear subframe bushes' outer sleeves are injection-moulded in glass-filled polyamide with an axial collar and anti-rotation ribs, replacing pressed steel sleeves that need zinc-nickel plating against corrosion. Baseline: four rear subframe bushes with natural-rubber bodies bonded between a steel inner tube and a pressed S235 steel outer sleeve, zinc-nickel plated (8 µm) to prevent red rust in the subframe eye. Proposal: PA66-GF35 (heat-stabilised, hydrolysis-resistant) outer sleeve, 4 mm wall, bonded to the rubber, with a moulded collar for axial location, three anti-rotation ribs and a press-in retention bead; a clip on the collar side secures against push-out. Why it works: the outer sleeve transfers bush loads into the subframe eye (≤15 kN radial in service but several times that in misuse and rear impact, so press-fit retention after polymer creep governs), a compressive load polyamide handles well; corrosion protection becomes unnecessary. Benchmark: premium BEVs like the Porsche Cayenne Electric put more of their comfort into the chassis, raising the number and quality of isolation elements – the bushes this lowers in cost. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Orbitally rolled housing lip closes ball joints, deleting cover plates and circlips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The ball-joint housing is closed by orbitally rolling its own lip over the bearing shell instead of fitting a cover plate held by a circlip, deleting two parts and a machined groove on each of the eight joints per car. Baseline: the car's eight ball joints (front lower and upper wishbones, rear links and toe links where ball-jointed) are closed by a stamped steel cover plate retained by a circlip in a machined groove, over the POM bearing shell and preload spring. Proposal: extend the 38MnVS6 (or C45) housing by 2.5 mm and orbitally form the lip over a chamfered bearing shell, setting the joint's breakaway torque during forming (closed-loop on forming force); grease volume unchanged. Why it works: rolled closures are a proven high-volume method; they remove the circlip's stack tolerance, giving tighter friction-torque scatter (±15% → ±10%). Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 with EQ Technology keeps a double-wishbone front – four of the eight ball joints in a layout like ours sit in its wishbones; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Cast-to-size sensor bore and clip lugs remove six drilling ops on rear knuckles
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear knuckle casting carries the wheel-speed sensor bore cast close to size and cast-in lugs and T-slots for harness clips and the dust shield, so six drilling/tapping operations and five screws are deleted. Baseline: low-pressure cast AlSi7Mg0.3-T6 rear knuckles are machined for the bearing bore and arm interfaces, plus six secondary features: a drilled and reamed Ø18 wheel-speed sensor bore with an M6 retaining hole, two M6 harness-clip holes and three M6 dust-shield holes, each needing a screw. Proposal: cast the sensor bore with a core pin to Ø17.6 (ream only), add cast-in T-slots for push-in fir-tree harness clips and three cast lugs onto which the dust shield clips; sensor retained by a push-in clip on a machined ledge that sets the air gap. Why it works: low-pressure casting holds ±0.3 mm on cored features, sufficient for clips; only the sensor air-gap face needs a light ream. Benchmark: the Kia EV9's self-levelling rear axle shows how much is packaged on a heavy BEV SUV's rear corner; our change trims the knuckle's secondary machining. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Scalloped near-net forged hub flanges cut turned stock and unsprung mass
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The hub flange is forged with five scallops between the wheel-bolt bosses instead of as a full round disc, removing 0.35 kg of steel per hub that was previously turned away or carried as unsprung mass. Baseline: the Gen 3 hub's C56E2 flange is forged as a Ø150 mm round disc and turned on both faces and the periphery, leaving a full disc between the five wheel-bolt bosses. Proposal: forge the flange near-net with five scallops (web thickness 8 mm, bosses unchanged) so only the wheel-mounting face and pilot are machined; induction-hardened raceway zone unaffected. Mass −0.35 kg per hub (−1.4 kg unsprung per car). Why it works: the material between bolt bosses carries little load in wheel bending; FEA confirms flange stiffness change <5%, keeping brake-disc runout within limits. Benchmark: high-performance BEV SUVs like the Porsche Cayenne Electric pursue low unsprung mass for ride on active suspension; scalloped flanges are general practice; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: PA66-GF50 contoured rolling pistons replace anodised aluminium pistons on rear air springs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear air springs' rolling pistons are injection-moulded in 50% glass-filled polyamide, deleting aluminium forming, turning and anodising, and the moulded contour can shape the effective-area curve for a progressive spring rate at no extra cost. Baseline: the rear air springs' rolling pistons are deep-drawn and turned 6060 aluminium, hard-anodised against abrasion of the rolling lobe, with a machined seal groove and a bolted lower mount. Proposal: a PA66-GF50 (hydrolysis-stabilised) injection-moulded piston with ribbed interior, a free-form outer contour (flare from Ø88 to Ø102 mm over the stroke) giving progressive effective area, a moulded seal groove and an over-moulded steel insert for the lower mounting bolt. Why it works: rear pistons on separate springs carry only axial compressive loads (≤ 15 kN at 12 bar) and lobe friction, well within PA66-GF50 capability; free-form contours are expensive to turn in aluminium but free in moulding. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity offers single-chamber and three-chamber air springs across trims, showing how spring-rate shaping is used to differentiate trims – the contour does part of that work here; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Press-quenched 6008-T6 extrusions replace 6082-T6 in aluminium rear subframe rails
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] EN AW-6008 extrudes faster and can be press-quenched with air or mist, so the subframe rails cost less to convert and distort less than water-quenched 6082, at the price of a slightly thicker wall for equal strength. Baseline: the rear subframe (aluminium version used on both powertrains) has two side rails of EN AW-6082-T6 extrusion (6.5 kg total) – high strength but slow to extrude, needing water quench and post-quench straightening. Proposal: EN AW-6008-T6 (Mn/V microalloyed, Rp0.2 ≈ 250-270 MPa vs 6082's ≈ 280-310 MPa) extruded ~30% faster, press-quenched by mist, aged in a shorter T6 cycle, with wall +0.2 mm in high-stress zones, which gives parity only where the rails are governed by welded-joint/HAZ fatigue; where parent-metal yield governs, the ~10-15% lower Rp0.2 needs ~10-15% more section and would consume most of the saving. Why it works: 6008 was developed for crash-relevant automotive extrusions with good extrudability and quench insensitivity; conversion cost scales with press speed and quench severity. Benchmark: the Audi Q6 e-tron's PPE carries a 280 kW rear motor, typical of the rear-axle loads such subframe rails must take in premium BEVs; applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Hot-flattened and pierced ends replace forged welded eyes on hollow anti-roll bars
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The ends of the hollow passive anti-roll bars are induction-heated, flattened and pierced in one press stroke to form the link eye, replacing separately forged eyes welded onto the tube. Baseline: passive front and rear anti-roll bars on non-active-roll trims are hollow 34MnB5 tubes (Ø28×5 / Ø24×4.5 mm), quenched and tempered, with forged 38MnVS6 end eyes friction-welded to each end, then machined and inspected. Proposal: induction-heat each tube end to 950-1,000 °C, flatten to a 12 mm paddle and pierce Ø12.2 mm in a single press stroke, before the bar's quench-and-temper cycle so the end gets the same hardness; drop-link ball studs bolt through the paddle. Why it works: flattened-end hollow bars are in wide production; paddle stiffness is adequate for link loads (≤ 8 kN) and the forging plus weld (a fatigue-critical joint) disappears. Benchmark: the Toyota Land Cruiser 250's front stabiliser with disconnect shows anti-roll bars remain central even on modern off-roaders; our change lowers the bar's cost on passive-bar trims of MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Vacuum-HPDC AlSi10MnMg engine-mount arms replace forged 6082 arms on the I6 MHEV
description: [MHEV] The two arms that carry the 3.0 L I6 engine mounts to the front subframe are cast near-net in vacuum high-pressure die-cast AlSi10MnMg with cast-in bolt holes and faces, replacing forged 6082 arms that need full machining. Baseline: the MHEV's two engine-support arms, bolted between the hydraulic engine mounts and the front subframe, are forged 6082-T6 (≈1.2 kg each) with all bolt holes and mount faces machined. Proposal: vacuum HPDC AlSi10MnMg (T7 or T5 heat treatment, Rp0.2 ≥ 150 MPa, A ≥ 7%) arms with ribbed I-sections, cast-in cored bolt holes, and only the two mount faces and one locating bore machined; mass +0.15 kg each. Why it works: engine-mount arm loads (3 g vertical, 1.5 g longitudinal) include high-cycle engine-shake loading, and vacuum-HPDC AlSi10MnMg has roughly half the yield and fatigue strength of forged 6082-T6, so the ribbed section must be sized by FEA (the +0.15 kg per arm is a first estimate that may grow), and HPDC removes the forging's machining. Benchmark: the BMW X7 (2023) runs 48 V mild hybrid on all combustion engines, typical of the longitudinal I6 MHEV layouts where the engine is carried on arms like these; the 800V BEV does not use them.

title: Vacuum-fill with one-box valve-cycling purge deletes the second brake bleed station
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The manual bleed operation and its operators at the second station disappear, because the one-box ECU itself opens every isolation, inlet and outlet valve while the fill rig evacuates and pressure-fills; long-pedal rework falls and purge-fluid waste is cut. Baseline: the line vacuum-fills DOT 4 LV (ISO 4925 class 6) brake fluid to <1 mbar and pressure-fills at 3-5 bar, but the integrated one-box unit (motor-piston pressure supply, pedal simulator, ABS/ESC valves) holds trapped volumes behind normally-closed solenoid valves. A second end-of-line station therefore connects a diagnostic tester, cycles the valves and has two operators open each caliper bleed screw in turn (four corners, 5.5-6.5 min), and ~3% of vehicles still return for long-pedal or simulator-air rework. Proposal: the fill head talks UDS to the brake ECU over the OBD/CAN link during filling; a supplier-released purge routine energises every valve group in sequence (5 Hz pulsing) during two evacuation holds at 0.5 mbar, strokes the pressure-supply piston to sweep its chamber, then the one-box runs a closed-valve leak and pedal-travel versus pressure check with its own redundant pressure sensors. Why it works: residual air sits in valve galleries that only connect to the fill path when energised; opening them while the system is under vacuum removes the air before fluid arrives, so nothing is left for a manual bleed to chase. title: Electric parking brake drivers moved into the one-box ECU, standalone EPB module deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate EPB ECU, its die-cast housing, bracket, fuse and long 4 mm² feed lines are deleted; the one-box already owns wheel speeds, pedal state and a power stage, so adding two H-bridges to its board is far cheaper than a second box. Proposal: specify the one-box variant with integrated EPB drivers – two independent H-bridges on the existing power board, a separate supply pin and separate ground for the parking-brake path – and wire the two EPB motors directly through the rear corner harness. title: Single EOL roller rig checks service brake, ABS, parking brake and rear-steer

Baseline: three end-of-line stations – a brake roller dyno for axle brake force (UN R13-H conformity of production), a diagnostic bay where ABS/ESC valves are pulsed with the wheels lifted, and a separate low-speed roller for EPB clamp checks – plus a rear-steer actuator sweep on the alignment stand; about 4.5 min aggregate and three operators. title: Steering column lock deleted; anti-theft met by authenticated park-lock immobilisation

title: Fail-operational dual-wound steering fitted only to hands-free trims, not the whole fleet
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Base and mid trims get a single-channel EPS (3-phase motor, one inverter, one feed) on the same rack, housing and belt drive; only the hands-free trim carries the dual-wound, dual-ECU, dual-feed fail-operational version. Baseline: the platform specifies one fully redundant electric power steering for every car – a dual-wound 6-phase motor, two inverters and microcontrollers, two torque-sensor dies and two independent power feeds – so that hands-free (SAE L2+/L3) driving can be sold on any vehicle. Three quarters of buyers never order it but carry ~€55 of redundancy. Proposal: two EPS variants sharing the rack, ball-screw, belt drive, housing, motor flange and connector body; the base variant uses a 3-phase single-wound stator and one inverter board and is fail-safe (degrades to reduced assist with warning) rather than fail-operational, while the hands-free variant keeps the full dual channel. Stator lamination stack, housing and end-of-line test are common; only winding, PCB population and one connector cavity set change. Why it works: fail-operational steering is needed only when the system, not the driver, is the steering fallback; for a driver-supervised car a fail-safe design meeting the failed-assistance effort limits is the industry norm. Benchmark: BMW runs steering sub-functions in its central Heart of Joy controller on the new iX3; we keep a central software stack but split the hardware redundancy by trim. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: EPS torque-based hands-on detection on base trims deletes the capacitive rim sensor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The capacitive hands-on-detection mat under the rim leather, its sensing electronics in the hub and two clock-spring circuits are removed from base and mid trims; driver hands are detected from the EPS torque sensor and motor current, as on earlier lane-keeping systems. Baseline: every steering wheel carries a capacitive hands-on-detection (HOD) layer – a conductive textile or printed-foil electrode under the leather, a sensing ECU in the hub, and extra clock-spring circuits – so lane-centring can verify the driver is holding the wheel. Proposal: on trims without the hands-free option, detect hands from the EPS: the torque sensor sees the small corrective torques a holding driver applies (0.1-0.3 Nm band-passed 0.5-5 Hz), and an observer on motor current and column inertia distinguishes a held from a free rim even on straight roads; a short haptic micro-pulse can be used to probe when signals are ambiguous. Capacitive HOD is kept only on the hands-free trim, where the driver-monitoring camera and UN R171 logic need it. The heated rim element is retained on all trims. Why it works: torque-based HOD was the standard method for driver engagement before capacitive mats; lane-centring on a driver-supervised car needs an engagement cue, not a contact map. Benchmark: Toyota says the Land Cruiser 250 EPS enables Lane Tracing Assist; the EPS signal itself carries the steering-hold information. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Base trims fit a forged rigid tie-bar on the rear-steer mounts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Instead of fitting the rear-steer actuator to every car and unlocking it in software, cars sold without rear-wheel steering get a forged rigid tie-bar with the same ball joints and mounting points, so the €200 actuator is bought only when it is sold. Baseline: the platform plan copies the "hardware on every car, unlock in software" model – every vehicle leaves the plant with the central rear-steer actuator (BLDC motor, ball-screw, ECU, position sensors) and rear-steer angle is enabled by trim or subscription. Proposal: two rear-axle builds on identical mounts: (1) actuator for cars ordered with rear-wheel steering, (2) a rigid tie-bar (42CrMo4 QT forged, Ø25 mm tube section, same outer ball joints and length at mid-stroke) bolted to the same subframe bosses for base cars. Toe is set by the same threaded outer joints. Rear-axle kinematics, bushings and alignment targets stay identical, so handling tuning only changes for the steer function itself. Retrofit by dealers remains possible because mounts, harness connector position and software exist. Why it works: the actuator is the expensive item; mounts and joints are cheap, so sharing them while varying the actuator gives most of the commonality benefit at a fraction of the cost. Benchmark: Mercedes fits the EQS SUV with 4.5° rear-axle steering as standard and offers up to 10° via over-the-air activation – i.e. the hardware is built into every car. We take the opposite, cost-led route for base trims of a 50,000/yr platform. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Wheel range cut from four diameters and eleven designs to three and seven
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four wheel designs and one rim diameter (21 inch) are never tooled or homologated; OE tyre development, wheel validation and inventory are spread over fewer variants, and the remaining designs gain volume leverage. Baseline: the plan offers 20, 21, 22 and 23-inch wheels in eleven designs and finishes across MHEV and 800V BEV, each needing a low-pressure-casting die set (A356.2-T6), finishing fixtures, wheel fatigue and impact tests, brake and suspension clearance checks, TPMS and handling tuning, plus OE tyre development per size with two tyre makers. Proposal: three diameters – 20-inch (all-terrain, winter and efficiency fitment), 22-inch and 23-inch – and seven designs; 21-inch is removed because it sits between the efficiency and the style choices without owning either. Brake packages must be confirmed to clear 20-inch; the 400 mm BEV and sport-pack front discs cited elsewhere in this register may limit 20-inch to the base brake. Why it works: each additional diameter multiplies tyre development, homologation and calibration work far more than it multiplies sales; buyers of large luxury SUVs cluster at the efficiency end and the style end. Benchmark: BMW lists the new iX3 with a 20-inch standard fitment and 21 and 22-inch options, and a public highway test showed a 20-inch low-rolling-resistance set adding about 25 km of range over a 21-inch set – evidence that the smallest wheel is the efficiency anchor. We use it to prune the middle of the ladder for MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Regen-aware disc-cleaning stops let BEV use uncoated grey-iron friction bands
description: [800V BEV] Ferritic nitrocarburising of all four BEV disc friction bands is removed; the brake ECU instead schedules short friction-only decelerations that wipe corrosion off the bands, so plain grey-iron friction faces stay clean despite regenerative braking doing almost all the work. Baseline: because regeneration carries almost all everyday braking on the BEV, friction bands sit unused for weeks, rust, then cause noise, judder and inspection failures; the plan therefore specifies ferritic nitrocarburising (FNC) of all four BEV discs plus zinc-flake hats. Proposal: keep the zinc-flake coating on the hats (visible corrosion) but leave the friction bands as plain GJL-250 high-carbon grey iron (EN 1561), and add a disc-conditioning function to the one-box: a model integrates km since the last friction event, ambient humidity, rain-sensor and wiper activity and road-salt season; when a threshold is passed, the next moderate stop (0.15-0.25 g from above 40 km/h) is carried by friction on the affected axle for 1-2 s while motor torque is reduced so the driver feels identical deceleration. Energy cost is ~10-15 Wh per event, about two events a week, below 0.1% range. Why it works: light rust is removed in a few pad contacts; regular contact prevents it growing into pitting. Benchmark: Audi describes the Q6 e-tron sequence as rear-axle regen first, then front regen, then front friction, with the rear friction brakes joining only towards ABS intervention – exactly the duty pattern that leaves bands unused. 800V BEV only; MHEV discs keep their specification.

ideaData.title: Regen-aware disc-cleaning stops let BEV use uncoated grey-iron friction bands
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: because regeneration carries almost all everyday braking on the BEV, friction bands sit unused for weeks, rust, then cause noise, judder and inspection failures; the plan therefore specifies ferritic nitrocarburising (FNC) of all four BEV discs plus zinc-flake hats. Proposal: keep the zinc-flake coating on the hats (visible corrosion) but leave the friction bands as plain GJL-250 high-carbon grey iron (EN 1561), and add a disc-conditioning function to the one-box: a model integrates km since the last friction event, ambient humidity, rain-sensor and wiper activity and road-salt season; when a threshold is passed, the next moderate stop (0.15-0.25 g from above 40 km/h) is carried by friction on the affected axle for 1-2 s while motor torque is reduced so the driver feels identical deceleration. Energy cost is ~10-15 Wh per event, about two events a week, below 0.1% range. Why it works: light rust is removed in a few pad contacts; regular contact prevents it growing into pitting. Benchmark: Audi describes the Q6 e-tron sequence as rear-axle regen first, then front regen, then front friction, with the rear friction brakes joining only towards ABS intervention – exactly the duty pattern that leaves bands unused. 800V BEV only; MHEV discs keep their specification.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Same disc casting and machining for MHEV and BEV friction bands; only the surface treatment routing differs, identified by laser part marking. Fewer surface-treatment part numbers in service.

title: Uniformity match-mounting at the tyre-wheel assembler halves balance weight and shimmy claims
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Tyre and wheel are rotated relative to each other so the tyre's radial-force high point meets the wheel's run-out low point; the residual imbalance and road-force variation fall, so less balance weight is applied and fewer cars come back with steering shimmy. Baseline: tyre-wheel assemblies for the 22-23-inch fitments are mounted without regard to tyre or wheel uniformity, then balanced; they average 85-110 g of adhesive weight per wheel, ~6% need a second balance pass, and first-harmonic radial-force variation drives a steering-shimmy warranty rate near 0.4%. Proposal: the tyre maker marks the first-harmonic radial-force high point (measured on its uniformity machine), the wheel maker laser-marks or encodes in the DMC the first-harmonic radial run-out low point measured at final machining; the assembler's vision system reads both and rotates the tyre on the bead seat before inflation (vectoring for best combined result), then measures road-force and balances. Typical industry results are 30-50% lower first-harmonic force and roughly half the balance weight. Why it works: most residual imbalance and force variation come from the superposition of two independent eccentricities; aligning them to cancel is cheaper than adding weights. Benchmark: tyre choice is a measurable lever on BMW's new iX3, where a low-rolling-resistance 20-inch set added about 25 km range; uniformity is the refinement counterpart. We apply match-mounting to every MHEV and 800V BEV wheel.

title: BLE tyre sensors read by the digital-key anchors delete TPMS receiver and initiators
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 433 MHz TPMS receiver, the four wheel-arch LF initiator antennas and their harness are removed; Bluetooth Low Energy tyre sensors are received by the six-to-eight BLE/UWB digital-key anchors the car already carries for phone-as-key. Baseline (to be confirmed: most current 433 MHz systems already auto-locate by ABS phase correlation without initiators, which would leave only the receiver saving): direct TPMS with 433 MHz sensors, a dedicated RF receiver, and four 125 kHz low-frequency initiators in the wheel arches that trigger each sensor in turn so the system knows which wheel is where (auto-location). Proposal: BLE 5 tyre sensors (same valve-mounted package) transmit to the existing BLE/UWB anchors used for phone-as-key; auto-location combines received-signal-strength patterns across the anchors with rotation-phase correlation – each sensor's accelerometer phase is matched to the ABS wheel-speed tone-ring phase of each corner over a few hundred metres – so no initiator is needed. The body controller hosts the TPMS function. Why it works: phone-key anchors are already distributed around the cabin and sills and listen continuously; the tyre sensors are just more BLE nodes, and wheel-phase correlation is a proven localisation method. Benchmark: Tesla moved the Model Y to Bluetooth Low Energy TPMS sensors that the car recognises and syncs to automatically after driving; we combine that sensor type with the digital-key anchor network on MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: BEV carries a compressor-sealant mobility kit instead of a temporary wheel and jack
description: [800V BEV] The BEV no longer carries a space-saver tyre on a steel rim, scissor jack, brace and holder; a 12 V compressor with integrated sealant bottle clips into a side pocket and the former underfloor tub becomes sellable storage for charging cables. Baseline: the BEV inherits the MHEV puncture strategy – a 19-inch space-saver tyre on a steel rim, scissor jack, brace and moulded holder in an underfloor tub above the rear drive unit, about 20 kg in all. Proposal: on the 800V BEV fit a mobility kit (12 V compressor with integrated 450 ml latex sealant cartridge) in the boot side pocket and turn the tub into an 80-90 l covered storage well. Buyers who want a temporary wheel can order a dealer kit; markets that expect one can be configured with it. Why it works: most punctures are tread punctures that sealant closes; for an electric luxury SUV, 20 kg less mass and a usable storage well are worth more than a speed-limited temporary wheel. Benchmark: Rivian ships the R1S without a spare tyre and stores its tyre sealant kit in the rear cargo compartment, limited to tread holes up to 6 mm. We adopt that for the BEV only; the MHEV keeps its spare wheel (full-size on off-road MHEVs).
