title: Inductive PCB sensor reads steering twist and absolute angle, deleting the column angle sensor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The gear-driven angle sensor in the column, its clip, connector and harness are deleted; one magnet-free inductive PCB at the pinion reads both torsion-bar twist and absolute steering-wheel position for every function that needs it. Baseline: the rack EPS measures driver input with a magnetic twist sensor (multipole NdFeB ring on the input shaft, soft-iron flux concentrators, two Hall ICs), while a separate gear-driven angle unit in the column (two vernier gears, AMR die, own CAN node) supplies absolute wheel position to stability control, lane keeping and rear steer. Proposal: an inductive position sensor – excitation and receive coils printed on a 4-layer PCB around the pinion, with stamped rotor targets on both ends of the torsion bar. The phase difference between the two targets gives twist (driver effort); two further tracks with 37 and 38 periods form a vernier that gives absolute angle within one pinion revolution; the turn count over ±3 turns comes from a keep-alive EPS rotor-turn counter (or a geared target), re-referenced after battery disconnect; a dual-channel ASIC reports effort to ASIL D and position to ASIL C. Why it works: inductive sensing needs no magnet, is immune to the DC fields of nearby 48 V and HV cables, and one coil set can read several targets, so the column unit becomes redundant. Benchmark: general steering-supplier practice; Toyota introduced EPS on the Land Cruiser 250 to cut off-road kickback and enable Lane Tracing Assist, both of which depend on clean effort and position signals. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One motor with a selector clutch drives both column reach and rake
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The second adjustment motor, its worm gear, Hall sensor and wiring are removed; a single motor drives either the reach or the rake spindle through a small bistable dog clutch, and memory positions are reached sequentially. Baseline: the electrically adjustable steering column has two 12 V brushed DC motors with worm reductions – one driving the telescopic (reach) spindle, one the tilt (rake) spindle – each with a Hall pulse sensor, controlled from the memory-seat module for easy-entry and driver profiles. Proposal: one motor drives a short output shaft carrying a bistable solenoid-operated dog clutch that engages either the reach or the rake spindle; the unused spindle is held by its self-locking trapezoidal thread. Position is counted by one Hall sensor plus learnt end-stops; easy-entry and memory moves are made sequentially, adding ~1.2 s to a full move that already takes 4-6 s. Crash energy-absorption straps, column lock-out under load and spindle self-locking are unchanged. Why it works: the two axes are rarely moved together and both use self-locking spindles, so a shared motor loses almost nothing functionally; the same principle was used for decades in single-motor mirror and seat adjusters. Benchmark: general practice; Range Rover sets a manoeuvrability benchmark with four-wheel steering and an under-11 m kerb-to-kerb circle – a reminder that luxury steering value sits in the axle, not in adjustment motors. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Spring-loaded wedge rack yoke self-adjusts, deleting the screwed adjuster and lock nut
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The threaded adjusting plug, lock nut and the end-of-line adjust-and-stake operation are removed; a spring-loaded one-way wedge behind the yoke keeps a small fixed clearance for life, cutting rack-rattle warranty. Baseline: the rack yoke (thrust piece) presses the rack against the pinion through a POM-faced yoke, a coil spring and a threaded adjusting plug; at the EPS supplier the plug is torqued, backed off a set angle to give 0.02-0.08 mm clearance, locked by a nut and staked. Clearance grows with wear, giving the "clunk" over rough roads and off-road kickback that drives warranty adjustments. Proposal: a self-adjusting yoke – a sintered Fe-Cu-C wedge (PTFE-coated) between the yoke and a pressed-and-caulked plug, pushed by a small spring so it moves only in the take-up direction; the main spring sets 300-450 N preload. No adjustment, lock nut or staking. Why it works: the one-way wedge converts any clearance growth into wedge travel, so clearance is held at a small set gap (0.02-0.05 mm, fixed by the wedge's stop geometry) within which the preload spring lets the rack ride over pinion runout. Benchmark: Toyota reports that the Land Cruiser 250's EPS reduces off-road kickback; low rack-yoke clearance is part of that refinement. We make it maintenance-free for MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Membrane vent on the steering rack deletes the wading snorkel breather line
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 1.8 m breather tube that routes the rack bellows to a high point above the wading line is removed, together with its clips, elbow and routing operation; a membrane vent on the rack housing breathes air but holds back water. Baseline: the left and right rack bellows breathe through the rack, and on a 900 mm wading platform the breather is extended by a 1.8 m PA12 tube routed up the bulkhead to a high point with a cap, like an axle breather, so muddy water is not sucked into the bellows when a hot rack is submerged. Proposal: an ePTFE membrane vent (0.2 µm pore, IP69K, water-entry pressure >0.6 bar) pressed into a cast boss on the rack housing above the belt-drive cover, plus the internal bellows-to-bellows transfer path. Physics check: a rack at 60°C plunged into 15°C water cools its air volume, creating at most 1 bar × 45/333 ≈ 0.14 bar under-pressure; adding 900 mm of water head (0.09 bar) gives ~0.23 bar, well below the membrane's water-entry pressure, so water does not pass while air equalises within minutes. Why it works: the snorkel solves a pressure problem the membrane solves locally. Benchmark: Land Rover lists wading depths of 850 mm (coil) and 900 mm (air suspension) for the Defender, the target class for this platform. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Dual-die motor-angle sensor gives rear-steer rod position, deleting the linear stroke sensor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate absolute linear stroke sensor on the rear-steer push rod is removed; rod position is computed from a dual-die motor-angle sensor plus a low-power multi-turn counter and referenced against the ball-screw lead. Baseline: the central rear-steer actuator (BLDC motor, ball-screw, push rods) uses two independent position paths for ASIL D: a motor rotor-angle sensor for commutation and an absolute linear stroke sensor (inductive PLCD) on the push rod. Proposal: one motor-angle sensor package with two independent tunnel-magnetoresistive (TMR) dies on separate supplies, each feeding a multi-turn counter kept alive at ≤20 µA from the permanent supply, so the counter tracks motor turns even when the vehicle sleeps (the ball-screw is back-drivable). Rod position = turns × lead; two independent dies give the diverse channels, and plausibility is checked against the vehicle's rear-wheel-angle estimate from yaw rate and wheel speeds. After a battery disconnect, the actuator re-references to its mechanical centre detent at standstill before enabling rear steer. Why it works: with a rigid ball-screw, motor angle already defines rod position; the linear sensor only adds a second measurement that two independent dies can provide. Benchmark: Porsche offers rear-axle steering of up to five degrees on the Cayenne Electric; such actuators are an ASIL-heavy, cost-sensitive subsystem. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV cars with rear-wheel steering.

title: Polyamide-coated involute spline replaces the ball-spline telescopic intermediate shaft
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two-row ball-spline with cages in the telescopic intermediate shaft is replaced by an involute spline whose male half is coated with polyamide 11 and formed with a slight elliptical preload, removing balls, cages and precision grinding. Baseline: the intermediate shaft between column and EPS pinion has a ball-spline telescopic section (two rows of balls in cages between ground grooves) to give low sliding force (<30 N) for crash collapse and for body-to-subframe relative motion on the 2.7 t SUV. Proposal: a cold-formed involute spline (C45E male, 20MnCr5 case-hardened female tube), the male spline fluidised-bed coated with PA11 (Rilsan type, 0.3 mm) and calibrated by broaching to an elliptical form that preloads the joint to below 0.05° backlash, with 20-80 N sliding force – adequate for subframe compliance and well inside the crash-collapse requirement. Why it works: coated splines are the industry standard for intermediate shafts; the ball-spline is only justified where very low sliding force is needed, which elastic subframe mounts on this platform do not demand. Benchmark: Toyota highlights the Land Cruiser 250 EPS for crisper steering feel; the coated, preloaded spline keeps that feel without the cost of a ball-spline. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Stop lamps driven from the one-box pedal-travel sensor; brake-light switch deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The pedal-box brake-light switch, its bracket, harness branch and the set-and-check adjustment are removed; the one-box's redundant pedal-travel sensor, which already senses every brake application, commands the stop lamps over the chassis network. Baseline: with a one-box brake system the pedal travel is measured by a dual-channel sensor in the unit, yet the car keeps a separate dual-contact brake-light switch on the pedal box, adjusted on the line, wired to the body controller for stop lamps and as a plausibility signal. Proposal: delete the switch. The one-box broadcasts a brake-apply flag derived from both pedal-travel channels (and hydraulic pressure where available) on the chassis CAN; the body controller drives the stop lamps; a dedicated wake line from the one-box keeps the function alive when the vehicle is asleep and the pedal is pressed. Fault handling: on loss of the message the body controller defaults to lamps on with brake-pressure plausibility. Regen deceleration above the R13-H threshold already lights stop lamps through the same path. ideaData.title: Stop lamps driven from the one-box pedal-travel sensor; brake-light switch deleted

Fault handling: on loss of the message the body controller defaults to lamps on with brake-pressure plausibility. Regen deceleration above the R13-H threshold already lights stop lamps through the same path. Why it works: the brake pedal state is already measured to ASIL standards; a second, simpler measurement only adds cost and an adjustment that can be set wrong. Benchmark: Audi's Q6 e-tron combines brake boosting and ABS/ESC in one electronic brake control unit, making the unit the natural source of brake-state signals. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Reservoir mounted directly on the brake one-box replaces the remote reservoir and hoses
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The bulkhead-mounted remote brake-fluid reservoir with its bracket, two feed hoses and clips is replaced by a reservoir clipped directly on the one-box, reached through a short filler neck; leak paths and fitting time fall. Baseline: because the one-box sits low in the engine bay or front compartment, its fluid reservoir is mounted remotely on the bulkhead for filling access, with a steel/plastic bracket, two EPDM feed hoses with spring clips and a separate level sensor. Proposal: a PP-T20 reservoir mounted directly on the one-box ports with push-in grommets (as on most integrated units), integrated reed-type level sensor, and a 120-180 mm blow-moulded PA6 filler neck to the service position; the BEV front compartment and MHEV bay both reach it. Hose leak paths fall from four connections to zero. Why it works: the remote position solved a filling-access problem that a filler neck solves for a fraction of the cost; integrated reservoirs are the default of one-box suppliers. Benchmark: BMW's new iX3 consolidates braking with other vehicle-dynamics functions under the Heart of Joy controller; the matching hardware step is a compact, self-contained brake unit. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Laser-welded, membrane-vented parking-brake motor unit deletes the wading breather hose
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The breather hose and splash cap that keep wading water out of the rear parking-brake motor-gear units are removed; the gearbox cover is laser-welded and breathes through an integrated membrane vent instead of an O-ring and hose. Baseline: each rear caliper's electric parking-brake motor-gear unit (motor, two-stage planetary/belt reduction, spindle drive) has a clipped PBT cover with an O-ring and breathes through a 0.6 m hose routed up into the wheel arch, plus a splash cap over the connector, because at 900 mm wading the unit (~250 mm above ground) is fully submerged and a hot unit sucks in water as it cools. Proposal: the PBT-GF30 cover is laser transmission-welded to the housing (no O-ring), an ePTFE membrane vent (water-entry pressure >0.6 bar) is moulded into the cover, and the connector is upgraded to an IPX7/IP6K9K sealed design. A submerged 70°C unit cooling to 15°C sees ≤0.17 bar under-pressure plus 0.07 bar head, inside the vent rating. Why it works: welded covers remove the O-ring leak path, and the vent handles thermal pumping locally, so the hose and cap become redundant. Benchmark: Land Rover quotes 900 mm wading for the air-suspended Defender and a Wade programme that raises the vehicle; our parking-brake hardware is sealed for that depth on MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One sealed corner connector joins wheel-speed, parking-brake and pad-wear circuits
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Ten separate two-way connections at the four wheel corners (speed sensors, parking-brake motors, pad-wear sensors) become four sealed multi-way corner connectors on short pigtails, removing harness branches, grommets, clips and assembly operations, and halving the number of ingress points below the wading line. Baseline: each rear corner has three separate sealed 2-way connectors – wheel-speed sensor, EPB motor, pad-wear sensor – and each front corner two, every one with its own harness branch, grommet, clip and routing to the body, and all of them submerged at 900 mm wading. Proposal: one 6-way (rear) or 4-way (front) mat-sealed corner connector (IP6K9K, IPX7) on a bracket at the wheel-arch body flange; components arrive with short pre-terminated pigtails that are clipped to the brake hose or knuckle as today. The body harness has one branch per corner. Connections at the line fall from 10 to 4. Why it works: fewer, better-sealed interfaces reduce both cost and water-ingress failure modes; mat seals tolerate thermal pumping better than many small single-wire seals. Benchmark: Mercedes quotes an 850 mm fording depth for the G 580; all corner electrics in that class sit well below the water line, which is the design case here. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Front skid plate wings shield rack and tie-rods, deleting two steel guards
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two separate pressed-steel tie-rod and rack guards on the off-road pack are removed; the aluminium front skid plate gets formed side wings that cover the rack and inner tie-rods, sharing its fixings. Baseline: the off-road pack fits a front aluminium skid plate under the front subframe plus two separate 3 mm S355MC pressed guards (1.6 kg each, e-coated, three bolts each) protecting the steering rack bellows and inner tie-rods from rock strikes. Proposal: the 4 mm 6082-T6 front skid plate is blanked wider and formed with two 25° up-turned wings that sit 25 mm below the rack bellows and tie-rods, with drain slots; the wings are fixed by the skid's rear mounts and two additional captive nuts on the subframe. Total aluminium added ≈1.4 kg against 3.2 kg steel removed. Why it works: a single formed plate with continuous load path is stiffer than three separate plates and its fixings already exist; wing geometry deflects rather than stops the rock. Benchmark: Lexus fits a large aluminium skid plate as standard on the GX 550 Overtrail; we extend that kind of plate to cover the steering. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV off-road packs.

title: Tyre pressure sensor with captive clamp-in valve replaces screwed two-part assembly
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate clamp-in valve stem, sensor fixing screw and washer of each tyre-pressure sensor are replaced by a sensor body with a captive metal valve, so the tyre fitter fits one part with one nut. Baseline: each direct TPMS sensor is a PBT-GF30 housing screwed (Torx, 1.2 Nm) to a separate anodised aluminium clamp-in valve stem with grommet, washer and nut; the tyre-wheel assembler assembles the sensor to the valve, then fits and torques the valve nut (4 Nm), then audits. Proposal: the valve stem is pressed into the sensor housing at the sensor supplier with a captive swivel joint (to accommodate rim angle), so the assembler inserts one part and torques one nut; the metal clamp-in valve is retained because the car exceeds the speed rating of snap-in rubber valves. Why it works: the screw joint only exists to allow one sensor to fit several valve angles, which a captive swivel provides. Benchmark: Tesla's BLE TPMS sensors are recognised automatically by the car after installation, simplifying service; our captive design simplifies the mechanical side in the same spirit. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: EPS power stage cooled through the motor end-shield, separate heatsink casting deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The EPS electronics' separate die-cast aluminium heatsink and its machining are removed; the power-stage substrate is clamped to the motor's existing end-shield, which is machined flat and becomes the heat sink. Baseline: the rack EPS power-pack ECU, mounted axially on the motor, carries its own ADC12 die-cast heatsink (≈380 g) with a machined face; MOSFETs on an insulated metal substrate (IMS) are pressed against it through a thermal pad, and the heatsink is screwed to the motor flange. Proposal: the IMS is clamped directly against the motor's A380 die-cast end-shield, whose face is machined flat to Ra 1.6 / 0.05 mm, using a dispensed gap filler (3 W/m·K); the end-shield's mass and its contact with the rack housing spread the heat. The electronics cover becomes a PBT-GF30 moulding. Thermal model: MOSFET losses peak ~60 W for a few seconds at parking; the end-shield plus rack housing provides more thermal capacity than the old heatsink. Why it works: the end-shield is already a large, conductive casting a few millimetres away; adding a second casting only adds an interface. Benchmark: Toyota's first-ever Land Cruiser EPS (250 Series) shows EPS reaching heavy off-road SUVs, where thermal duty is highest; integration lets us meet that duty with fewer parts. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Tube rack friction-welded to a forged tooth section replaces gun-drilled solid bar
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 820 mm deep gun-drilled bore in a solid bar is replaced by a seamless tube friction-welded to a short forged tooth section; the drilling operation and 1.0-1.3 kg of drilled-out steel per rack are no longer paid for. Baseline: the EPS rack is machined from solid C45E bar (Ø28 mm) and gun-drilled with a Ø15 mm, 820 mm-deep bore to save mass, then the teeth are broached or warm-forged, the ball-screw thread rolled and both induction hardened. Gun-drilling is slow (3+ min) and turns ~1.2 kg of bought steel into chips. Proposal: a two-piece rack – a seamless C45E tube Ø28 × 5.5 mm for the ball-screw and tie-rod sections, rotary friction-welded to a solid warm-forged C45E tooth section (variable-ratio teeth net-forged), flash removed in-line, weld 100% ultrasonically inspected, then induction hardening and thread rolling as today. Mass equals the gun-drilled rack. Why it works: the bore only exists for mass; starting from a tube puts the material only where it is needed, and friction welding of medium-carbon steels is a mature, fully monitorable process. Benchmark: general steering-supplier practice; Toyota's first EPS on the Land Cruiser 250 shows EPS racks reaching heavy off-road SUVs, where rack strength and mass matter most. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Blow-moulded copolyester steering rack bellows replace compression-moulded chloroprene
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two chloroprene rack bellows made by compression moulding are replaced by thinner blow-moulded thermoplastic copolyester bellows, which cost less, cycle faster and resist splitting from cold, ozone and stone damage. Baseline: the steering rack bellows are compression-moulded chloroprene rubber (CR), 2.0 mm wall, vulcanised in multi-cavity tools with deflashing, held by ear clamps. Proposal: extrusion blow-moulded thermoplastic copolyester (TPC-ET, ISO 18064, Shore 40D class), 1.2 mm wall, with convolution geometry optimised for the ±80 mm rack stroke and ±25° tie-rod angle; same clamps and clamping grooves; TPC is recyclable and needs no vulcanisation or deflashing. Cold flexibility to -40°C and resistance to ozone, grease and stone chipping are better than CR, which matters for off-road and salt-belt use. Why it works: TPC bellows are the standard for drive-shaft CV boots exposed to much higher speeds and angles; the rack boot is a less demanding duty. Benchmark: Land Rover lists 900 mm wading for the air-suspended Defender; boots that do not split are the first line of defence keeping water and grit out of the rack in that use case. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Glass-filled polyamide ball-nut belt pulley replaces machined aluminium in the EPS drive
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The large driven pulley on the EPS ball-nut, today turned and hobbed from 6082-T6 aluminium, is injection-moulded in glass-filled polyamide over a steel hub ring, removing bar stock, machining of the HTD tooth profile and balancing. Baseline: the rack-parallel EPS uses a toothed belt (HTD-type) from the motor pinion pulley to a Ø105-115 mm driven pulley clamped on the ball-nut; the driven pulley is turned from 6082-T6 bar, the tooth profile hobbed, then anodised and balanced. Proposal: PA66-GF30 (or PA46-GF30 where the thermal model shows >120°C) injection-moulded with the tooth profile in the tool, overmoulded onto a knurled 16MnCr5 steel ring that is pressed onto the ball-nut as today. Belt tension (≈0.8-1.2 kN) and tooth shear stresses are within polyamide capability with a 2.0 safety factor at 120°C; moulded teeth also run quieter against the belt. Why it works: plastic gears and pulleys are standard in column EPS worm wheels, which carry higher tooth stress than a belt pulley. Benchmark: Toyota's Land Cruiser 250 EPS is said to reduce kickback – the shock loads that the belt drive must transmit; the moulded pulley is sized for those transient loads. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Single-coat high-temperature powder finish on calipers replaces two-coat liquid paint
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Visible brake calipers get one coat of high-temperature polyester powder instead of a 2K liquid base plus clear, and the logo is laser-marked instead of pad-printed, removing a paint pass, solvent handling and most rework. Baseline: all four calipers (aluminium fixed fronts, iron or aluminium floating rears) are finished in a coloured 2K liquid basecoat plus clear, with pad-printed logos, each coat flashed and oven-cured; masking of bores, threads and abutments is manual, and paint runs are a common rework. Proposal: pre-treat (zirconium conversion for aluminium, zinc phosphate for iron), then a single high-temperature super-durable polyester powder coat (rated 200°C continuous, 250°C peak) applied electrostatically and cured once; colour and gloss match the brand palette; the logo is laser-marked through a contrasting layer or in a dedicated logo powder spot. Silicone masking plugs are reusable. Why it works: one powder coat delivers 60-80 µm with near-100% transfer efficiency and no solvent; regen-dominated braking on the BEV and moderate duty on the MHEV keep caliper temperatures inside the powder rating. Benchmark: Porsche offers ceramic composite brakes as an option on the Cayenne Turbo Electric, signalling that visible caliper finish is a luxury cue; we deliver it at lower cost. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Handed-neutral front caliper body with twin bleed bosses serves both sides
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Left and right front fixed calipers become one part: the body is made symmetrical with a bleed boss at each upper corner and a central inlet, so one casting die, one machining programme and one part number serve both sides; the unused bleed port is closed with a plug. Baseline: the 4-piston aluminium fixed front calipers are handed – left and right bodies differ because the bleed nipple must sit at the top and the inlet is offset – so there are two die sets, two machining programmes, two part numbers per colour and handed inventory. Proposal: a mirror-symmetric monobloc body (A356-T6 gravity cast) with two bleed bosses, one at each upper corner, a centrally placed inlet port and a symmetric internal gallery; on each side the lower bleed port is fitted with a sealed screw plug and the upper one with the bleed nipple. Pad abutments and mounting bolt pattern are symmetric already; the piston layout becomes symmetric only once the staggered 38/42 mm bores are replaced by equal bores (the equal-bore caliper idea), so this idea depends on that one. Why it works: the only real asymmetry is fluid routing, which a second boss and plug remove for under €1; everything else is shared, doubling volume per part number. Benchmark: Audi fits four-piston fixed front calipers on the Q6 e-tron; that caliper architecture is inherently symmetric except for its ports. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Plain friction faces replace cross-drilled discs on the sport brake package
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 72-hole cross-drilling, chamfering and magnetic-particle crack inspection of the sport-pack discs are removed; plain friction faces cost less, crack less under thermal cycling and keep pad wear even. Baseline: the sport brake package (400 mm front, 380 mm rear vented grey-iron discs) is cross-drilled with 72 holes per disc, each chamfered, followed by magnetic-particle inspection for drilling-initiated cracks; the holes are largely visual. Proposal: plain friction faces with the same vane design, the visual differentiation moved to the hat (laser-etched logo and contrasting zinc-flake colour). Drilled holes reduce thermal mass and are crack initiators under repeated hard braking, and on BEVs with regen-dominated use their claimed wet-weather and degassing benefits are irrelevant with modern pads. Why it works: friction-face drilling is a styling feature with a cost and durability penalty; a plain face has more thermal capacity per kilogram. Benchmark: Porsche states ~97% of everyday braking on the Cayenne Electric is done electrically – the friction face is used rarely and briefly, so cosmetic drilling buys nothing. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV sport packs.

title: Mechanically keyed pad backplates replace shot-blast and adhesive friction bonding
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Pad backing plates get a field of raised, undercut hooks formed into their face that lock the friction material mechanically, so shot-blasting and the phenolic adhesive layer are removed and corrosion can no longer lift the lining off the plate. Baseline: brake pad backing plates (fine-blanked S355MC, 5-6 mm) are shot-blasted, coated with a phenolic adhesive, then the friction mix and underlayer are hot-pressed on. On low-use BEV pads in salt-belt markets, corrosion creeping under the bond ("rust jacking") can delaminate linings and causes noise and warranty. Proposal: a mechanical retention plate – hundreds of small raised, hooked barbs raised from the plate surface by a toothed tool after fine-blanking (the NRS-type process used widely in aftermarket and some OE pads) – hot-pressed with the same friction mix and a thinner underlayer; no shot-blasting or adhesive. Shear strength ≥ adhesive-bonded values (≥4 MPa at 300°C). Why it works: mechanical interlock does not depend on surface chemistry, so corrosion cannot undermine it, and two process steps leave the line. Benchmark: Audi says about 95% of everyday braking on the Q6 e-tron is regenerative – the low-use, corrosion-dominated duty where mechanical retention pays off. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Swaged tube-nut hose ends replace caliper banjo bolts and copper washers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] At each caliper the banjo bolt and its two copper sealing washers are replaced by a swaged hose end with a captive tube nut and inverted flare seat screwed directly into the caliper; three parts and two leak paths per corner disappear. Baseline: each flexible brake hose connects to its caliper through a banjo fitting – hollow bolt, banjo eye, two copper sealing washers, 30-35 Nm – chosen historically to allow hose orientation at assembly. Proposal: the hose end is swaged with a captive M10×1 tube nut and an inverted 90° double-flare seat (SAE J533 / ISO 4038 type) that screws straight into a matching caliper port; orientation is fixed by a small anti-rotation clip on the caliper and a flat on the hose end, so the hose cannot be twisted when the nut is torqued. Why it works: the same inverted-flare seat already seals the rigid brake pipes at 250+ bar; extending it to the hose end removes the parts that exist only for orientation. Benchmark: BMW says about 98% of braking on the new iX3 is done by recuperation; with friction-brake duty this low, simplifying corner hydraulics is pure cost. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Equal-bore pistons in the front fixed caliper replace staggered two-size bores
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The front fixed caliper's leading and trailing piston pairs, today of two different diameters to control tapered pad wear, become one diameter; piston, seal, dust boot and bore-tool variants halve. Baseline: the 4-piston front fixed caliper uses staggered bores (e.g. 38 mm leading, 42 mm trailing) to counter the pad's tendency to wear tapered under the self-servo effect, requiring two piston, square-seal and dust-boot sizes and two bore-finishing tools. Proposal: four equal 40 mm bores (same total piston area), with taper control moved to the pad: a 0.3 mm leading-edge taper and chamfer, and a slightly offset abutment that shifts the centre of pressure trailing. With friction braking reduced by regeneration (BEV) and blended BSG recuperation (MHEV), taper wear over a pad life is smaller than in the era when staggered bores were introduced. Why it works: taper wear is a pressure-distribution problem that pad geometry and abutment position can also solve; piston variety only adds cost. Benchmark: Audi's Q6 e-tron runs four-piston fixed front calipers with friction brakes engaged late in the blend, a duty with little taper-wear pressure. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Rear brake dust shields deleted on BEV, with automatic post-wade brake drying
description: [800V BEV] The pressed-steel dust shields behind the BEV rear discs and their bolts are removed; with almost no rear friction duty there is little heat to shield, and the one-box's automatic brake-drying routine clears water and grit after wading or rain. Baseline: all four corners carry 0.7 mm zinc-coated pressed dust shields (DX54+Z) with three bolts each, protecting knuckle bushings and wheel-speed sensor leads from radiant heat and the disc inboard face from spray. Proposal: delete the rear shields on the 800V BEV, whose rear friction brakes see very low duty because regeneration covers almost all everyday braking; the MHEV keeps them. The one-box runs a brake-drying routine – light pad contact pulses of ~0.5 bar for a few seconds – triggered by wipers on, wade-mode exit or ambient/rain-sensor logic, so pads and discs stay dry and clean. The rear-steer actuator and sensor leads are checked for radiant temperature at the worst-case repeated-stop test. Why it works: the shield's functions are heat and spray management; regen removes the heat, software handles the spray. Benchmark: Porsche says the vast majority of braking manoeuvres on the Macan in everyday driving are performed by the electric motors without activating the friction brakes. 800V BEV only.

title: Parking brake applied from the park button and auto-logic; console switch deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The illuminated, dual-contact parking-brake switch in the centre console and its harness are removed; the parking brake applies automatically on park selection, door opening or seatbelt release, and manually by the existing park button, which is upgraded to dual contacts. Baseline: a dedicated EPB pull/push switch in the console (two redundant contact sets, illumination, harness to the brake ECU), duplicating functions already provided by shift-by-wire park selection, auto-hold and auto-apply logic. Proposal: delete the switch. Apply: automatically when P is selected, the driver door opens with the seatbelt unbuckled, or the vehicle is switched off; manually by pressing the shift-by-wire P button (made dual-contact, ASIL B) – it applies the EPB statically at standstill and, if pressed and held while moving, requests an emergency deceleration through the one-box hydraulics, falling back to EPB dynamic application. Release: automatic drive-away logic or brake pedal + selector. Why it works: every function of the switch already has an input in the car; the switch is legacy HMI. Benchmark: Tesla's Model Y has no gear stalk and handles drive selection through other controls – general practice in shift-by-wire BEVs is to merge park and parking-brake control. We apply it to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Zinc-flake-coated steel balance weights replace zinc adhesive weights
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Adhesive wheel balance weights change from zinc to low-carbon steel with a zinc-flake and paint finish, which costs roughly half as much per kilogram and is fully recyclable with the wheel. Baseline: tyre-wheel assemblies are balanced with adhesive zinc segment weights (5 g segments on strips), chosen after the EU end-of-life vehicle directive banned lead; zinc is expensive and its price volatile. Proposal: low-carbon steel segment weights (DC01) with zinc-flake (ISO 10683) base and colour-matched topcoat, on the same acrylic foam tape and in the same dispenser magazines; steel is denser than zinc (7.85 vs 7.1 g/cm³), so strips are slightly shorter and fit better on the narrow inner barrels of 22-23-inch wheels. Galvanic contact with the aluminium wheel is prevented by the coating and the tape. Why it works: the weight only needs mass, adhesion and corrosion resistance; coated steel provides all three for less. Benchmark: BMW's iX3 shows how tyre and wheel choices affect efficiency and cost at the vehicle level; balance weights are a small but universal line item that all wheel sizes share. Not additive with the match-mounting idea, which reduces the total weight applied. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Laser-ablated two-tone wheel face replaces diamond-turning and second clear coat
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Bicolour wheels no longer go back on a lathe to have their face diamond-cut through the paint and then re-clear-coated; a laser removes a tinted clear layer from the spoke faces over a bright silver base, giving the two-tone look without bare machined aluminium. Baseline: bicolour wheels are powder primed, painted dark, cured, then diamond-turned on a CNC lathe to expose bright aluminium on the spoke faces (≈2.5 min per wheel), then clear-coated again; the bare cut aluminium is the starting point of filiform corrosion, a well-known warranty item on machined-face wheels. Proposal: primer, bright silver metallic base and a tinted dark clear over the whole wheel; a 2D-scanned pulsed fibre laser then ablates the tinted clear from the spoke faces (≈1 min), exposing the bright base, followed by one clear coat. The aluminium is never exposed, so filiform risk largely disappears. Why it works: the bright look comes from the metallic base, not from bare metal, and removing a few tens of microns of clear by laser is faster and gentler than turning through paint. Benchmark: BMW offers the iX3 with 20, 21 and 22-inch wheels – the large luxury wheels where bicolour finishes and their corrosion issues are concentrated. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Full-size steel reserve wheel replaces the matching flow-formed alloy on off-road MHEV
description: [MHEV] The off-road MHEV's fifth wheel becomes a painted 20 × 8.5J steel rim with the same offset, bolt circle and load rating instead of a matching flow-formed alloy, and carries no pressure sensor; it wears the same all-terrain tyre. Baseline: on the off-road MHEV the fifth wheel is a full-size match for the four on the car – a 20-inch flow-formed A356.2-T6 alloy rim with all-terrain tyre and a pressure sensor – so the trip can continue after a sidewall cut far from help. Proposal: a 20 × 8.5J steel rim (S420MC disc, rim roll-formed and flash-butt welded, e-coat plus powder topcoat) with identical offset, centre bore, bolt seats and ≥1,000 kg load rating, mounted with the same all-terrain tyre; no pressure sensor, so after fitting it the monitoring system reports a missing sensor until the repaired wheel goes back on, which UN R141 permits. The steel rim is ~4 kg heavier, so its carrier is checked and locally reinforced. Why it works: the fifth wheel is used rarely; full-size capability, not appearance, is what matters on a trail, and steel can be hammered straight. Benchmark: Land Rover specifies an 18-inch steel wheel in lieu of the 19-inch on Defender Hard Top versions and carries a full-size reserve on the side-hinged tailgate. MHEV with off-road pack only.

title: Front recovery hooks rated as transport lashing points, separate tie-down brackets deleted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two front transport tie-down brackets bolted under the front rails are removed on off-road cars; the forged front recovery hooks, already designed for higher loads, are proof-tested and documented as the lashing points for ship, rail and truck transport. Baseline: off-road-pack vehicles carry two forged front recovery hooks bolted through the bumper beam into the rail ends, plus – on every vehicle – two pressed steel transport tie-down brackets under the front rails used once, for outbound logistics lashing. Proposal: on off-road cars the recovery hooks (forged 38MnVS6, rated for 1.5× vehicle mass in recovery) are specified, proof-tested and drawn as transport lashing points; the logistic lashing instruction references them, and the tie-down brackets are deleted on that variant. Road cars keep the brackets. Why it works: recovery loads (≈4.3 t) far exceed lashing loads (≈1.5-2 t per point under maritime acceleration factors), and both act through the same rail ends; one rated interface serves both. Benchmark: Rivian's R1 tow-operator guide has dedicated sections on recovery connections and tow-eye use, documenting the vehicle's rated pull points for third parties – the same documentation approach we use for transport lashing. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV off-road packs.

title: In-mould-decorated wheel centre caps replace caps with bonded metal badges
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The four wheel centre caps lose their separately stamped and bonded aluminium badges; the logo, colour and metallic effect are applied by an in-mould-decorated film during moulding of the PC/ABS cap, removing a part and a bonding step per cap. Baseline: each wheel centre cap is a PC/ABS moulding with a stamped, anodised and printed aluminium badge bonded on with double-sided acrylic tape or adhesive, placed by hand or a pick-and-place unit, then inspected for alignment. Proposal: in-mould decoration (IMD) – a formed, printed polycarbonate film with logo, colour field and metallic-effect ink is placed in the tool and back-moulded with PC/ABS in one shot; a hard-coat on the film gives car-wash and stone resistance. Optional: a vacuum-metallised logo ink for a premium bright look without chrome plating. Why it works: the badge is decorative; IMD delivers the decoration in the moulding cycle, and the part becomes a single material family that is easier to recycle. Benchmark: BMW offers the new iX3 with 20-inch to 22-inch wheels; every option carries centre caps, so a single cap process change applies across the full wheel range. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One Euro 7 brake-emission test family covers MHEV and BEV corner hardware
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] MHEV and BEV share one front and one rear brake corner specification and one pad formulation per axle, so brake-dyno particle-emission testing runs on two families instead of four; the BEV result uses the same hardware data with its own regenerative friction-share factor. Baseline: Euro 7 adds brake particle (PM10) limits – 7 mg/km for the MHEV and 3 mg/km for the pure-electric vehicle – measured on a brake dynamometer to the UN GTR 24 WLTP-brake cycle per brake family. The plan has four families (MHEV front and rear, BEV front and rear) with different pad formulations, each needing a test campaign (bedding, repeat runs, both axles, worst-case inertia) of €0.25-€0.35M, plus separate friction-material development. Proposal: harmonise the corner hardware and use one low-emission, low-steel pad formulation per axle for both powertrains, test the worst-case inertia once per axle, and assess the BEV against its 3 mg/km limit using the regulation's friction-share approach for vehicles that brake regeneratively. Why it works: particle emission is driven by pad, disc and braking energy; with identical hardware the dyno result is shared and only the friction share differs. Benchmark: Audi reports that ~95% of everyday braking in the Q6 e-tron is regenerative, with rear friction brakes joining only near ABS – exactly the low friction share that lets one hardware set meet the stricter BEV limit. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Steering rack arrives with tie-rods laser-preset to nominal length, cutting toe adjustment
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The EPS supplier sets both outer tie-rods to nominal length with the rack on its electrical centre and pre-torques the jam nuts; with machined subframe datums most vehicles need no front toe correction, so alignment time and one alignment pit are saved. Baseline: the steering rack arrives with tie-rods screwed to an arbitrary length (±3 mm), so at the alignment stand every car needs both tie-rods turned to set toe and centre the steering wheel – 2.3 min average, 8% needing a second pass – and the alignment area is the chassis takt bottleneck with three pits. Proposal: at the supplier's end-of-line, the rack is driven to its electrical centre (EPS rotor position stored), each tie-rod is set by laser gauge to nominal ball-centre length ±0.3 mm and the jam nuts are pre-torqued; the subframe is located on machined datums, so total toe lands within ±0.1° on ~60% of vehicles without adjustment. Operators only fine-trim the rest, and the steering-angle zero is written electronically. Why it works: most front toe variation comes from the arbitrary tie-rod length, not from body or subframe tolerance; removing it at source turns adjustment into an exception. Benchmark: Range Rover combines front steering with rear-wheel steering that turns in phase above 50 km/h; such systems need precise front toe and centre so the rear axle can be calibrated against them. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One parking-brake motor-gear unit serves MHEV and BEV with software clamp-force targets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Instead of two electric parking-brake motor-gear units (a higher-ratio one for the heavier BEV), one unit sized for the BEV serves both powertrains; the brake ECU sets the clamp-force target per vehicle mass by motor current, so the second gear set, its tooling and its part numbers disappear. Baseline: the rear calipers of both powertrains share a body, but the parking-brake motor-gear unit comes in two variants – the BEV, ~250 kg heavier, uses a higher reduction ratio to reach the clamp force for holding on a 30% gradient at gross mass, the MHEV a lower ratio for faster apply. Proposal: one motor-gear unit with the BEV reduction ratio on both powertrains; the brake ECU applies a clamp-force target scaled to the coded vehicle mass and gradient (current-based end-of-apply detection), and drive-away release time is kept within target by starting release on brake-pedal lift. Apply time on the MHEV rises by ~0.15 s, unnoticeable in normal use. Why it works: clamp force is controlled by motor current, so the only physical difference between variants was the gear ratio; using the stronger one everywhere costs almost nothing per unit while halving variety. Benchmark: Audi fits single-piston floating rear calipers with an electromechanical parking brake on the Q6 e-tron, the same actuator architecture used here. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: Stator busbar ring plugs straight into the EPS control board, deleting phase leads
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The EPS motor's flexible phase leads, crimps, terminal screws and sealing grommet are replaced by a moulded busbar ring welded to the winding ends, whose press-fit pins enter the control board when the electronics are joined to the motor. Baseline: the axially mounted EPS power pack connects to the motor through three phase leads (six on dual-wound variants): flexible copper cables welded to the winding terminations, crimped to ring terminals and screwed to the power board, passing through a sealing grommet in the end-shield. Proposal: the winding ends are TIG- or resistance-welded to a PA66-GF overmoulded copper busbar ring on the stator; its pins (several press-fit, tin-plated CuSn pins per phase, sized for the ~100-150 A peak phase current) project through the end-shield and enter plated holes in the power board as the electronics are pressed on, in the same stroke as the motor-position sensor alignment. Sealing moves to the end-shield-to-housing O-ring that exists anyway. Why it works: the leads only bridge a few millimetres between stator and board; press-fit is a proven high-current interconnect (used in inverter power modules) and removes screwed joints that can loosen. Benchmark: Toyota's first-ever Land Cruiser EPS (250 Series) shows EPS reaching heavy off-road SUVs, where vibration makes screwed electrical joints a reliability item; press-fit removes them. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One stainless spring stamping per pad end replaces abutment liners and cross spring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] At each end of each front pad, the stainless abutment liner, the anti-rattle cross spring and one of the two retaining pins are replaced by a single formed stainless spring that is both sliding liner and radial-tangential preload spring. Baseline: each 4-piston front fixed caliper carries four stainless abutment liners (one per pad end), a stamped anti-rattle cross spring, and two pad retaining pins with a spring clip; each is a separate part fitted by hand at the caliper supplier. Proposal: one 1.4310 (301) stainless spring stamping per pad end that clips into the caliper abutment, provides the low-friction sliding surface for the pad ear and, through two formed spring fingers, preloads the pad radially and tangentially against rattle; pads are retained by a single centre pin. Spring rates are chosen so residual pad drag stays below about 0.5 N·m per corner (2 N·m would cost ~150 W per corner at 100 km/h), which matters for BEV range. Why it works: liners and springs act on the same pad ears; one formed part can do both, and stainless spring steel already serves as the liner material. Benchmark: Audi uses four-piston fixed front calipers on the Q6 e-tron, the caliper type whose multiple pad hardware parts this consolidates. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

title: One-piece TPU end-stop rings replace bonded rubber-steel rack travel dampers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rack's two travel end-stop dampers – rubber vulcanised to steel washers, held by circlips in machined grooves – become one-piece thermoplastic polyurethane rings that snap onto the inner tie-rod joint housings. Baseline: at each end of the rack, a bonded NBR-to-DC04 steel washer cushions the inner tie-rod joint against the rack housing at full lock, retained by a circlip in a groove machined on the joint housing; the dampers limit end-stop impact noise and peak loads when the driver or a kerb drives the steering to lock. Proposal: an injection-moulded TPU ring (Shore 95A, polyether type for hydrolysis resistance) with an internal snap lip that engages a shoulder formed on the forged joint housing, and a profiled face giving a progressive force-travel curve over 3 mm. No vulcanising, no circlip, no groove. Why it works: TPU has higher energy absorption per volume and better fatigue life than NBR at end-stop strain levels, and snap retention needs no separate fastener. Benchmark: Porsche quotes an 11.1 m turning circle for the electric Macan with rear steer – manoeuvring at full lock is where rack end-stops work hardest. Applies to MHEV and 800V BEV.

Proposal: one cartridge per axle (tube, rod, piston valve, base valve, CDC proportional valve, fail-safe orifice), with mass-class and trim differences set only in the CDC current maps; top mounts, spring seats and air-strut interfaces stay variant-specific. Why it works (check): damping ratio ζ = c/(2√(k·m)). Front sprung corner mass spans ~560 kg (MHEV coil) to ~690 kg (BEV air); wheel rates are tuned to hold ride frequency, so k ∝ m and the required c ∝ m, a 1.23:1 spread. A CDC valve spans about 4-5:1 between soft and firm at 0.5 m/s, so the spread uses ~15% of its authority. The passive fail-safe (de-energised) characteristic is set for the heaviest car at ζ ≈ 0.30; on the lightest car the same valve gives ζ ≈ 0.37, firmer but stable, and reached only after a fault. The fail-safe needs no software because a passive valve sets it, and no brake, steering or restraint function depends on the maps. Low-speed bleed is the compromise: the map cannot change the bleed, so one cartridge bleed is set at the geometric mean of the light- and heavy-car needs: slightly soft on the heaviest car and slightly firm on the lightest below 0.05 m/s. Benchmark: Xiaomi YU7 fits CDC dampers across its range while adding dual-chamber air springs only on Pro/Max trims, so one damping technology spans coil and air variants.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: The supplier assembles two cartridge types; the EOL bench runs two hydraulic recipes plus a CDC current sweep instead of sixteen; variant top mounts are fitted at the module stage. The vehicle plant writes the CDC map by VIN at EOL, as it already does for chassis calibration.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Cartridge interfaces (rod thread, tube OD, valve connector) frozen across variants; mass-class map chosen by build code, not hardware, so a wrong-damper fit cannot happen; air-strut and coil-over modules keep their poka-yoke top-mount geometry.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Medium – complexity and development saving on every damper
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle (4 dampers): variant shim kits and tune parts €1.0-€1.4 × 4 = €4.0-€5.6; EOL bench recipe changeovers €0.30-€0.45 × 4 = €1.2-€1.8; physical tuning loops 14 × €60k = €0.84M replaced by map calibration €0.30M → €0.54M ÷ 350,000 = €1.5; minus map data management €0.3 (low) / €0.2 (high). Low = 4.0 + 1.2 + 1.5 − 0.3 = €6.4 ≈ €6; high = 5.6 + 1.8 + 1.5 − 0.2 = €8.7 ≈ €9. Every vehicle. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €0.3M-€0.45M per year.

ideaData.riskNotes: Risks: comfort compromise at the light end and harshness in fail-safe mode. Validate ride and handling sign-off for each mass class, ISO 3888-2 lane change and ISO 7401 step steer in fail-safe mode on the heaviest and lightest variants, 1.5M-cycle damper durability, and UN R79 handling behaviour unchanged; no regulated fail-safe function depends on the calibration. Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: Two cartridges still need piston and base-valve shim stacks. Commonising removes shim variety, not shims, yet the bridge takes €6.0 of 'variant shim kits and tune parts' down to €1.6 (−73%) at €1.0-€1.4 per damper. Shim stacks cost cents per damper, so the real gain is supplier complexity and set-up. That gain is plausibly well under €1 per damper and probably halves the saving. Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: This overlaps library idea psuv019 (one CDC valve across damper sizes, differences set by discs and software maps) and is adjacent to ieb-628d6811edeb (one 46 mm bore family). The savings are not additive.
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Xiaomi YU7 (2025) — CDC continuous damping control dampers across the range, with closed dual-chamber air springs added only on Pro and Max trims. How this differs: Xiaomi shares the damping technology across trims; we also share the damper hydraulic hardware across mass classes and powertrains and move the differences into current maps.

title: Chassis bolt catalogue cut from 46 to 18 part numbers, one coating and drive
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Fewer, higher-volume fastener part numbers buy a lower piece price and remove line-side bins, nutrunner sockets and per-variant friction and corrosion approvals; one coating and one friction window also make torque-angle tightening more repeatable. Baseline: about 130 chassis bolts and nuts per vehicle (subframes, arms, knuckles, dampers, calipers, steering gear, stabilisers) across 46 part numbers: M8-M16, lengths in 5 mm steps, hex-flange and hexalobular heads, zinc-nickel with sealer and zinc-flake finishes, two friction windows and several torque-to-yield variants. Proposal: 18 part numbers – M8/M10/M12/M14/M16 class 10.9 (ISO 898-1) plus three nut types, one zinc-flake system (ISO 10683, μtot 0.09-0.14), one external hexalobular drive per size, lengths in 10 mm steps, torque-angle tightening throughout. Sizes are not reduced. Why it works (check): an M14 10.9 bolt tightened by torque-angle to ~90% of proof gives Fv ≈ 85-95 kN; one friction window cuts preload scatter from about ±20% to ±12%, so no joint needs a larger size and none loses clamp. ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: brake judder comes from disc thickness variation that builds when lateral runout (LRO) lets the pad touch the disc off-brake. The platform holds assembled LRO ≤40 µm at the friction ring with tight parts: Gen3 hub flange face finish-turned after bearing assembly to ≤15 µm at Ø150 mm, and discs double-finished to ≤25 µm. Proposal: at the corner sub-line a laser probe measures the spinning hub's flange runout vector (amplitude and phase); each disc carries its own runout vector from the supplier's EOL gauge in a data-matrix code; the station picks the one of five bolt positions that minimises the vector sum, and a 100% re-measure confirms ≤40 µm. Hub spec opens to 25 µm (post-assembly face turning deleted) and disc to 35 µm (one finishing pass). Why it works (check): hub tilt scales with radius, so 25 µm at Ø150 becomes ≈60 µm at the Ø360 mm ring. With five positions the residual phase error is at most ±36°, so worst-case assembled LRO = √(60² + 35² − 2·60·35·cos 36°) ≈ 38 µm, inside the 40 µm target even with both parts at their upper limits; typical values are about half. Braking torque, disc mass and thermal capacity are unchanged, and the friction brake works exactly as before with no software in its path; only geometric error is managed. Service discs keep the tight 25 µm spec, but because the relaxed hub alone can contribute ≈60 µm at the ring, a dealer replacement must be indexed to the minimum-runout bolt position with a dial gauge (added to the service procedure and validated). Benchmark: Audi says about 95% of everyday Q6 e-tron braking is regenerative; such BEV discs are seldom cleaned by hard stops, so runout-driven thickness variation and corrosion judder matter more, which raises the value of controlling LRO at assembly (Audi does not disclose doing so).
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Instead of buying runout out of each part with extra finishing passes, the corner sub-line cancels hub and disc runout against each other by choosing the bolt position, so the hub's post-assembly face turning and the disc's second finishing pass can be deleted.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: One measuring station on the corner sub-line (laser probe, hub spinner, code reader, ~12 s, within takt); the disc supplier publishes per-part runout data; the hub supplier drops its post-assembly hard-turning cell; judder warranty claims are tracked by VIN against matching data.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Disc hat with five equally spaced holes and a marked index; the chosen position is written to the corner build record; a wrong-position fit is caught by the 100% assembled-LRO re-measure before the corner leaves the cell.

Low = 5.6 + 2.0 + 0.6 − 0.6 − 0.4 = €7.2 ≈ €7; high = 6.4 + 2.4 + 0.7 − 0.5 − 0.4 = €8.6 ≈ €9. Every vehicle. × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €0.35M-€0.45M per year.

title: Long-wheelbase chassis signed off by rig replay of scaled road loads, not prototypes
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three of the four long-wheelbase chassis durability prototypes and their proving-ground running are replaced by one road-load mule and rig replay of the standard car's drive files scaled to long-wheelbase loads; one confirmation car remains for system effects. Baseline: the platform builds standard and long-wheelbase (LWB, ~25% of volume) bodies, and the LWB gets its own chassis durability fleet of four proving-ground (PG) prototypes (≈€0.7M each to build, ≈€0.35M each to run) even though axles, subframes, arms, knuckles, brakes and steering are shared with the standard car. Proposal: instrument one early LWB mule with wheel-force transducers for road-load data (~6 weeks of PG), compare pseudo-damage per channel with the standard car, replay the standard car's drive files scaled to the LWB loads on the existing spindle-coupled axle rigs, and keep one LWB PG confirmation car for system effects (squeaks, harness chafe, body interfaces). Why it works (check): LWB adds ~3-6% rear axle load and changes pitch inertia. Fatigue damage scales with load^k (Basquin k ≈ 5 for forged and cast chassis parts, 3-4 for welds), so 6% more load gives 1.06⁵ ≈ 1.34× damage; replaying the drive files at a 1.07 load factor covers it without new parts. Any channel above 1.10× standard-car pseudo-damage (likely the rear spring link and subframe rear mounts) gets its own component rig test. Brake (UN R13-H) and steering (UN R79) hardware keep their full physical tests, and nothing safety-related is signed off by simulation alone. The figure is a programme saving: €2.15M net spread

title: One pad-wear sensor per axle instead of one per corner on fixed calipers
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Halves the number of pad-wear sensors and harness legs on cars without the off-road pack, relying on the left/right wear symmetry of an axle (to be confirmed in the validation fleet); both pads on an axle are always replaced together, so one sensor per axle still triggers the service. Baseline: the platform's fixed four- and six-piston calipers carry a wear sensor in every corner: four sensors with harness legs, clips and connectors. Proposal: one sensor per axle (front-left and rear-right inboard pads), while the off-road pack (~15% of vehicles, with frequent single-side brake-based traction control) keeps four. Calipers and pads keep both sensor pockets so all variants share them. Why it works (check): pads are 11 mm new and the sensor trips at 3 mm, so 8 mm of wear is monitored. Normal left/right asymmetry is ≤15% (caliper drag, camber, road crown), so when the monitored pad trips the other side still has ≥ 11 − 8 × 1.15 = 1.8 mm of friction material ahead of the backing plate. On the off-road pack, brake-based traction control can push asymmetry to 25-30% (11 − 8 × 1.3 = 0.6 mm), which is why it keeps four sensors. The driver warning and the easy visual wear check that UN R13-H requires are kept. The friction brake itself is unchanged and depends on no sensor or software; only the service reminder is affected. 800V BEV pads wear more slowly because of regeneration, but the asymmetry argument is the same on both powertrains. Benchmark: BMW X5 (G05) uses one pad-wear sensor per axle, on the front-left position at the front.

title: Sequenced front-end module: fascia, grille, shutters, lamps and radar fitted as one lift
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Moves about 8 minutes of nose fitting from the OEM trim line to a cheaper supplier module line, sets gap and flush once in a fixture rather than on every body, and cuts line-side part numbers and their logistics. Baseline: the front fascia, upper and lower grille, active grille shutter (AGS), two headlamps, front radar bracket, six ultrasonic sensors and the bumper harness branch are delivered as separate parts and fitted at four trim-line stations (≈12.5 min of direct labour per vehicle), with gap and flush to bonnet and wings set by hand on the line. Proposal: the exterior supplier builds the complete nose as a just-in-sequence module on a PP-LGF30 front-end carrier (fascia PP/EPDM-T20, AGS in PP-T20, lamps clipped to carrier datums), tests lamp, sensor and shutter function at end of line, and ships it in build sequence; the plant lifts it with a manipulator onto four M10 body bolts and two harness connectors (≈4.5 min). Gap and flush are set once in the supplier fixture against a body-representative datum gauge. Why it works: the nose is the most crowded trim-line zone and its tolerances stack across five suppliers; one module turns five stacks into one and moves labour to a supplier rate about 35% below the OEM line rate. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse integrates its headlamps into the illuminated grille as one front graphic, which only works if lamps and grille are aligned to each other rather than individually to the body.

title: Headlamp aim station deleted: lamps located on carrier datums, supplier-aimed, software-trimmed
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes 100% end-of-line aiming labour and most of the aim-station capex, deletes the horizontal adjuster on each lamp, and replaces it with one supplier calibration and a 5% plant audit. Baseline: at end of line every vehicle passes a headlamp aim station (screen or camera aimer) where an operator turns the vertical and horizontal adjuster screws on each lamp, ≈1.6 min per vehicle; each lamp carries two adjusters because the chain body → bracket → lamp holds only about ±0.4° of beam aim. Proposal: lamps sit on three moulded datums on the front-end carrier that is itself located on body datums (±0.15° measured chain); the lamp supplier aims the cut-off to the lamp datums at its end-of-line photogoniometer and writes a residual offset to the lamp memory; the pixel or matrix light source then applies any horizontal correction in software, so the horizontal adjuster is deleted and only the vertical (service and levelling) adjuster stays. The plant runs a 5% camera audit instead of 100% aiming. Why it works: with a matrix or DMD source the horizontal beam position is a software value (this holds only where every trim has a matrix or DMD headlamp; trims with a conventional LED projector keep the horizontal adjuster), and with datum mounting the vertical scatter fits within the R48 initial-aim band. Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport digital LED headlamps use 1.3 million micro-mirrors to shape the beam in software.

title: Low-bake 90 °C clearcoat lets fascias be painted on the body line
timeToImplement: 30-36 months (paint shop change at a model launch)
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the supplier paint process and its margin for fascias and mirror caps, removes colour-harmonisation rejects and painted-part logistics, and lowers the body oven temperature from about 140 °C to 90 °C. Baseline: front and rear fascias, mirror caps and spoiler are painted at a supplier plastics paint line (flame, adhesion promoter, waterborne base, 2K clear, 80 °C bake) while the steel/aluminium body is painted at about 140 °C at the OEM. The two shops must be colour-harmonised for every shade (luxury palette of 16 colours), 2-3% of fascias are rejected for colour mismatch, and painted fascias travel in protective racks. Proposal: after e-coat and its 180 °C bake, fascias are fitted to the body on a removable paint jig and the body and plastics go through primer-less base and clear together with a low-temperature system curing at about 90 °C (body e-coat stays separate). Fascias, made from PP/EPDM-T20 with heat deflection above 100 °C, need plasma activation plus a conductive surface (a conductive adhesion promoter or a conductive compound, see ieb-dc614acc8cef), so the electrostatic bells lay down the same film build and flake orientation as on the steel body; that step is not yet priced. Why it works: if the parts are painted together in one pass they match by construction, the supplier paint line and its margin disappear, and the plant oven runs cooler. Benchmark: PPG showed at SURCAR Asia 2026 a three-layer automotive system designed to cure together at 90 °C, aimed at painting bodies and bumpers in one process.

title: Deflectometry defect map plus four-robot cell replaces manual paint spot repair
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces about 4 of 5.4 minutes of manual sanding and polishing per vehicle with a robot cell, cuts abrasive use and re-inspection, and lowers repaint loops through defect data fed back to the booths. Baseline: after clearcoat, inspectors mark dirt inclusions, craters and runs by eye under a light tunnel and finishers sand and polish them by hand. At luxury quality about 45% of bodies need spot repair at an average of 12 min each (≈5.4 min per vehicle), plus re-inspection, and defect data are not fed back to the booths. Proposal: a deflectometry tunnel projects stripe patterns and maps every defect in 3D (position, size, type); a four-robot cell with automatic abrasive and pad change sands and polishes only the mapped spots; finishers handle only edges, door joints and the filler flap; the defect map is fed back to booth air and applicator settings each shift. Why it works: the robot follows a defect-specific path with controlled force, so it removes less clearcoat and causes fewer re-repairs, and the data loop lowers the defect rate at its source. Benchmark: BMW Regensburg (BMW X1/X2) uses deflectometry cameras to map defects in 3D and a four-robot booth that sands and polishes each body only where needed, for up to 1,000 bodies a day.

title: Low-loss colour change at the applicator for a 16-colour, two-tone palette
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts purge losses of basecoat and solvent at every colour change by about 75-80%, reduces VOC abatement and paint-sludge disposal, and lets a wide luxury palette run at small batch sizes without a cost penalty. Baseline (applies only where the basecoat booths still have wall-mounted colour valves; most current shops already use on-arm changers): a luxury SUV offers 16 body colours plus contrast roofs and lower bodies, so at 50,000/yr the basecoat booths change colour at about 0.35 changes per body. Each change on eight bell robots purges about 0.18 l of basecoat and 0.5 l of solvent per robot from the colour valve to the bell, all of which goes to waste and VOC abatement. Proposal: move the colour changer onto the robot arm right behind the applicator with short dosing lines (pig-type or dosing-pump changers, general industry practice), cutting the purged volume to about 0.04 l of paint and 0.15 l of solvent per robot; group two-tone bodies so the second colour is applied by nozzle-plate applicators that change colour in a closed-loop cleaner. Why it works: purge loss scales with the line volume between colour valve and atomiser, and on-arm changers cut that volume by about 80%. Benchmark: BMW Plant Dingolfing applies two-tone designs without masking using the Dürr EcoPaintJet, whose Pro version is designed for fast colour change with minimal losses and a closed-loop cleaner.

title: One mirror base and door harness accept either a glass head or camera head
description: [800V BEV] Avoids a second mirror base tool and its validation, a second door-sail patch and a harness variant; the CMS option becomes a head swap, so its take rate can follow demand without new tooling. Baseline: offering a camera-mirror system (CMS) as an option on the 800V BEV, where its drag saving is worth range, usually means a second mirror base casting, a second door-sail patch in the door outer, a separate harness variant through the door and different inner door trim, because the camera arm and the glass mirror head share nothing. Proposal: one die-cast mirror base (AlSi9Cu3, HPDC) and one three-bolt door-sail interface for both heads; a common 12-way sealed connector in the base carries glass actuator, fold, heater and indicator lines on glass versions and LVDS/GMSL camera, heater and indicator on CMS versions; the head (glass or camera arm) bolts to the base with one M8 and a locating spline. Why it works: the base and door interface are the costly tooling and validation items; the head is where variants belong. Benchmark: the Audi Q8 e-tron offers virtual exterior mirrors, a camera in a flat support with 7-inch OLED displays, which cut drag from Cd 0.28 to 0.27, worth about 35 km of range.

title: Single satin PVD brightwork finish across trims; trim lines differ by lighting
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Reduces brightwork from 33 to 14 part numbers and from three finish processes to one PVD finish plus one MIC black moulding, removing masking and paint of the black pack and the gloss-matching loops between finishes. Baseline: eleven exterior brightwork parts (grille surround, side-window finishers, side vents, lower fascia blades, tailgate finisher, mirror lower bar) are offered in three finishes – bright electroplated Cr(III) on ABS, satin anodised aluminium and painted gloss black – across trim lines, giving 33 part numbers, three finish processes and three colour/gloss matching loops. Proposal: one satin PVD finish (CrN over a base coat on PC/ABS, or on stainless strip for the window finishers) for every brightwork part, with the black pack done in mould-in-colour high-gloss ASA instead of painting; trim lines differ by lit signature (illuminated grille contour, welcome animation) and badges instead of by metal finish; any lighting content added for that purpose is not in this bridge and must be netted off (window finishers overlap ieb-1e28c164901d, black grille overlaps ieb-32e3ff020741). Why it works: three finish processes with matched gloss cost more than the parts; one finish and one black MIC moulding halve part numbers and remove masking. Benchmark: BMW says with the iX3 Neue Klasse that exterior lighting is the new chrome – its headlights carry no chrome and the illuminated grille provides the highlight instead.

title: Inline terahertz film-build control trims clearcoat and basecoat overspec
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts average clearcoat by 7 µm and basecoat by 2 µm without moving the minimum, by narrowing film-build variation with 100% inline measurement and zone-level feedback to the applicators. Baseline: film build is checked by magnetic/eddy-current gauges on a few panels per shift and by destructive cross-sections, so booths aim high to keep the thinnest spot above the minimum: clearcoat targets 50 µm (minimum 40 µm) and basecoat 2-3 µm above hiding need. On about 14 m² of painted surface per body that margin is all paint. Proposal: two robot-mounted terahertz sensors measure wet base and clear thickness layer by layer at 40 points on every body after the clear booth; the data adjust bell flow, shaping air and robot paths per zone each shift, so the process runs at clearcoat 43 µm target with the same minimum and basecoat 2 µm lower. Why it works: the margin is set by variation, not by the minimum; closed-loop measurement narrows the variation and lets the mean come down safely. Benchmark: the Dürr EcoPaintJet Pro used by BMW camera-measures each body and adapts the paint programme to tenths of a millimetre – the same principle of body-specific programmes we apply to film build.

Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: A 43 µm clearcoat target with a 40 µm minimum met on 99.9% of points needs a film-build standard deviation of about 1 µm. title: Pressure-decay leak test with vent plug replaces helium testing of lamps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes helium consumption on every lamp, shortens the leak-test cycle from 45 s to about 12 s, and cuts test-chamber maintenance, while keeping a leak limit tied to the wading requirement. Baseline: the six exterior lamps (two headlamps, two body rear lamps, two tailgate lamps) are leak tested at the lamp suppliers by helium sniffing or chamber tests (≈€0.35 of helium per lamp, 45 s cycle) because the lamp vents make a simple pressure test read the vent, not the seal. Proposal: a test head that closes the ePTFE vent with a soft plug, then a temperature-compensated differential pressure-decay test at +30 mbar against a reference volume (8-12 s) with a reject limit equal to the helium-equivalent leak that admits water at 900 mm wading; helium is kept only for an audit sample and for root-cause work. Why it works: lamp seal leaks that matter (laser- or hot-plate weld voids, adhesive gaps) are in the 10⁻² mbar·l/s range that pressure decay resolves once the vent is plugged; helium resolution is far beyond the need. Benchmark: Land Rover rates the Defender for 900 mm wading on air suspension, which sets the leak class that exterior lamps must hold if this SUV carries a comparable wading rating.

title: Wading-rated lamp breathers: high-hydrostatic ePTFE vents replace snorkel tubes
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four snorkel tubes, their clips and routing labour, replacing them with higher-grade membrane vents that work submerged; the lamp keeps its wading rating with fewer parts. Baseline: to keep the headlamps and lower front lamps breathing during 850-900 mm wading – where the bow wave covers the lamp rear – each lamp vent is routed through a rubber snorkel tube clipped up into the upper engine bay or front-end carrier (two tubes per headlamp pair plus one per rear lower lamp), with clips, routing labour and a risk of kinks. Proposal: replace snorkel tubes with high-hydrostatic ePTFE membrane vents (water entry pressure ≥ 150 mbar, i.e. above 1.5 m water column, oleophobic treated) welded directly on the lamp housing, plus a shield rib that keeps the bow-wave jet off the vent face; the front-end architecture is set so lamps sit above the static wade line with the vent on the highest point of the housing. Why it works: a membrane with a water entry pressure well above the wade head stays dry when submerged; it cannot breathe while covered, so a hot lamp cooled by the water builds an under-pressure (≈200 mbar for 80 → 5 °C) that exceeds 150 mbar unless the vent stays above the wade line or a higher-WEP membrane is used; the cold-shock wade test decides whether the snorkel can go. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 EQ is rated for 850 mm wading, 150 mm deeper than the combustion G-Class, so its front-end hardware is submerged deeper than in any combustion off-roader.

title: Lit grille contour driven from spare headlamp channels, deleting the grille ECU
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the separate grille LED ECU, its connector and most of its harness branch; the headlamp driver gains four channels at a fraction of an ECU cost. Grille lighting software moves into the headlamp driver as one more channel set. Baseline: an illuminated grille contour and light-guide plate carry its own LED driver ECU with a LIN or CAN node, buck-boost converter, diagnostics and connector, plus its own harness branch, alongside the two headlamp ECUs that already contain multichannel LED drivers. Proposal: the left headlamp driver is specified with four spare constant-current channels (a multichannel automotive linear LED driver IC; the TPS9261x parts are single-channel), and the grille becomes a passive LED board fed through a 6-way connector from the headlamp; welcome and signature animations run in the headlamp driver, commanded by the body domain controller over the existing bus; on the MHEV the lamps keep the 12 V rail, on the 800V BEV the same. Why it works: the grille LEDs draw under 6 W and switch in step with the DRL, so a separate ECU duplicates power conversion, microcontroller and diagnostics. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ lights its Black Crystal grille and vertical edge DRLs as one choreographed animation, which shows grille and headlamp lighting already act as one function.

title: Outside door handle fitted from the exterior as a pre-tested cartridge
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts handle fitting from about 1.6 to 0.6 min per door, deletes four access-hole covers and their sealing, and lowers flush rework because the cartridge seats on the skin pocket it sits in. Baseline: flush outside handles are fitted from inside the door through access holes in the door inner before the trim goes on: the operator feeds the module in, holds it against the skin, torques two nuts blind and plugs the latch and lamp connectors, then gap and flush are checked against the skin (≈1.6 min per door), with access-hole covers sealed afterwards. Proposal: the handle becomes a sealed cartridge (housing, lever, microswitch, approach lamp, e-latch connector and mechanical Bowden pull) tested at the supplier, slid into a reinforced pocket in the door skin from outside and fixed by two Torx screws hidden behind the lever; a blind-mate connector on the pocket floor carries power and signals; the access holes and covers are deleted. Why it works: fitting from outside lets the cartridge set its own flush against the skin it sits in, and the door-inner work disappears. Benchmark: the 2022 Range Rover uses flush door handles; owner reports note how sensitive flush handles are to operation and feel, which a supplier-tested cartridge controls better.
