title: Cross-car light strip mounted on the front-end carrier, not bonnet and lamps
description: [800V BEV] Replaces three housings and two driver boards with one lamp and one driver, deletes the bonnet-crossing harness, grommet and flexible guard, and removes gap tuning between three lamp pieces. Baseline: a closed-face 800V BEV front with a continuous light strip usually builds it from three lamps – a centre bar mounted on the bonnet leading edge and two end sections inside the headlamps – with three housings, lenses and seals, two driver boards, a harness that crosses the bonnet hinge with a flexible guard and grommet, and hand gap/flush tuning so the three pieces read as one line. Proposal: one 1.9 m strip lamp (PMMA lens, PC-HT housing, volume-diffusing light guide fed from both ends) fixed to the front-end carrier just below the bonnet shut line, with one driver board, one connector and no harness on the bonnet; the bonnet closes over its upper edge with a 4 mm gap. Why it works: the strip stays still when the bonnet opens, so there is no moving harness, and one housing removes two lens-to-lens joints that are the hardest gaps on the face. Benchmark: the Li Auto L9 runs a continuous front light strip across the face, without a grille interrupting it.

title: Split headlamp: common hidden main-beam module behind powertrain-specific DRL lamps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One main-beam module tooled and validated once at double volume replaces two integrated headlamps; only a low-cost DRL/indicator lamp varies by powertrain, and the facelift can carry the main module over. Baseline: the MHEV (open cooling face) and 800V BEV (closed face) are styled differently, so each gets its own integrated headlamp – matrix low/high beam, DRL, indicator in one housing – which doubles the lamp tooling, photometric validation and part numbers and halves the volume of each lamp (25,000/yr each). Proposal: split the function: a slim upper lamp (DRL, position, indicator) carries the styling and is unique per powertrain, while the main low/high-beam matrix module sits lower behind a tinted, common PC panel and is identical for both powertrains and for the mid-life facelift. Why it works: the expensive optics and electronics live in the main module, which now runs at 50,000/yr with one validation; the styling lamp is a simple light-guide lamp that is cheap to tool twice. Benchmark: the 2023 BMW X7 facelift was the first BMW with split headlights – slim upper LED DRL housings with the main beams hidden behind tinted glass lower down – which BMW said gave more freedom to restyle the front.

title: One global semi-flush door handle built to the China 2027 mechanical-release rule
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four deploy actuators and four ice-break heaters, and avoids a separate China handle variant, replacing them with one fixed semi-flush handle and Bowden release that meets the 2027 rule worldwide. Baseline: power-deploying flush outside handles on four doors, each with a DC motor and gearbox, position sensor and ice-break heater, and from 2027 a separate China variant to meet the new MIIT rule that every door must have a mechanical release and that pop-out electric handles are banned – two handle families, two validations. Proposal: one global semi-flush fixed handle: a body-colour pocket with a finger recess of at least 25 × 60 mm, a fixed grip bar in PA6-GF30 with PVD trim, a microswitch that triggers the e-latch for normal opening, and a mechanical Bowden pull to the latch that opens the door when the grip is pulled through its full travel; no deploy motor, no gearbox, no heater. Why it works: the motor and heater exist only to make the handle disappear; a semi-flush pocket keeps most of the aero and look while meeting the China rule everywhere. Benchmark: China's MIIT rule, effective 1 January 2027, requires a mechanical release on every door and bans pop-out electric handles; Tesla Model Y, BMW iX3 and many Chinese models with retractable handles are affected.

title: One actuator drives upper and lower grille shutter banks through a cross-link
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the second shutter actuator, its bracket and harness branch, replacing them with a bellcrank and cross-link rod that reproduce the sequenced opening the calibration already uses. Baseline: the front end has two active grille shutter (AGS) banks – an upper bank behind the grille (6 blades) and a lower bank in the bumper intake (8 blades) – each with its own LIN smart actuator (brushed DC motor, gear train, Hall position sensing, ≈€12), bracket and harness branch, so that the calibration can open them independently. Proposal: one actuator on the lower bank drives the upper bank through a PA66-GF30 bellcrank and a 6 mm steel cross-link rod with a lost-motion slot: the first 40% of actuator travel opens the lower bank only (cooling for the MHEV intercooler loop or 800V BEV chiller at moderate load), the remaining travel opens the upper bank too (towing, DC fast charging, high ambient). Why it works: in practice the calibration almost always opens lower first and upper second, so a mechanical sequence reproduces nearly every state used; the second actuator buys only rarely used combinations. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric uses fully variable cooling flaps that close on the road for Cd 0.25 and reopen when temperature sensors call for cooling of battery, motors, cabin and brakes.

Why it works: in practice the calibration almost always opens lower first and upper second, so a mechanical sequence reproduces nearly every state used; the second actuator buys only rarely used combinations. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric uses fully variable cooling flaps that close on the road for Cd 0.25 and reopen when temperature sensors call for cooling of battery, motors, cabin and brakes.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: Deletes the second shutter actuator, its bracket and harness branch, replacing them with a bellcrank and cross-link rod that reproduce the sequenced opening the calibration already uses.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: AGS supplier fits the cross-link at sub-assembly; one fewer LIN node to flash and test at end of line; harness loses one branch. The AGS sub-assembly test rig checks the lost-motion sequence (lower bank first, then upper) on every unit.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Cross-link rod snaps into ball sockets on both banks, one orientation only; lost-motion slot is moulded into the bellcrank, no adjustment needed. Both banks keep their own return springs, so a broken link leaves the upper bank in the failsafe-open position.

Net €11.9; low €9.0 if a stronger single actuator is needed (+€2.9), high €12.0. Net €9-€12 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €450K-€600K per year (estimate; amortisation over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: Loss of independent control and a single-point failure for both banks. Validate failsafe-open by spring on actuator loss, thermal performance in towing at 40 °C and 350 kW DC charging, ice-breaking torque at -20 °C, UN R127 / GTR 9 pedestrian lower-leg loads through the AGS zone, and fuel/energy consumption on WLTP.

title: Shutter frame with 2K TPE lips and integral side ducts seals MHEV radiator
description: [MHEV] Deletes four foam seals and two side air guides with their fitting labour by moulding a TPE lip and the ducts onto the shutter frame, and recovers cooling airflow lost to bypass. Baseline: on the MHEV (3.0 L I6 with low-temperature intercooler and condenser stack), the AGS frame sits ahead of the cooling pack with four die-cut EPDM foam seals and two separate PP side air guides that close the gaps between frame, radiator and headlamps so that air does not bypass the cores; the seals are hand-applied and often misplaced, and bypass leakage costs core performance. Proposal: the AGS frame is moulded in PP-T20 with a 2K TPE-V lip seal (Shore 60A) around its rear face and with the two side ducts moulded on as wings, sealing directly to the radiator side tanks and headlamp backs. Why it works: a moulded lip has a defined interference (3 mm) and cannot be misplaced, and integral ducts remove two parts and their joints; closing the bypass recovers 3-5% of core airflow, which keeps the existing cooling pack size. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric relies on sealed variable cooling flaps that close fully on the road and open on demand – sealing at the shutter is what makes that work.

title: Moulded parking-knock crush ribs on the rear fascia replace the EPP absorber
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the rear EPP absorber, its clips and fitting labour; crush ribs moulded into the fascia take over parking-knock protection at a small fascia mass increase. Baseline: behind the painted rear fascia sits a full-width EPP 45 g/l absorber (≈1.1 kg) in front of the aluminium reinforcement; the EPP is there for 4 km/h contact and to keep the fascia from denting in parking knocks. Proposal: delete the EPP and mould a field of 2.2 mm vertical crush ribs (30 mm deep, 25 mm pitch) on the fascia inner face over the beam, tuned to buckle at about 8 kN; a flat closing plate on the reinforcement gives the ribs an even reaction face. The rear has no pedestrian leg requirement, so the energy target is set by ECE R42 and the RCAR 10 km/h test, where the metal structure does the work. Why it works: in a 4 km/h knock the energy (≈1.5 kJ for a 2.6 t SUV share) is absorbed by fascia rib buckling and tyre/suspension compliance; EPP adds little once ribs are present. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail uses multi-piece bumper construction, treating the bumper as layers that each do one job – here the fascia takes over the absorber's job.

title: High-gloss mould-in-colour ASA grille frame and mesh replace piano-black paint
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the paint process on the grille (flame, base, clear, handling) and most paint rejects, replacing it with a mould-in-colour 2K PMMA/ASA part at a small resin and energy premium. Baseline: the grille surround and mesh are moulded in PC/ABS and painted piano black (flame treatment, black base, 2K clear) at a supplier paint line, ≈€9.8 of paint cost per grille plus about 6% paint rejects for dust and runs in the deep mesh. Proposal: mould the frame and mesh in high-gloss black ASA with a PMMA cap layer (2K, PMMA 0.6 mm Class-A skin over ASA core) on a variotherm (rapid heat-cycle) tool that heats the cavity to 120 °C at injection and cools to 60 °C, giving a 90+ GU gloss without paint; the PMMA skin carries scratch and UV resistance. Why it works: the grille is black anyway, so paint only adds gloss and depth; variotherm moulding reproduces the gloss of the tool surface and removes weld-line visibility. Benchmark: BMW states with the iX3 Neue Klasse that exterior lighting is the new chrome, with no chrome on the headlights – the front face is built from lit and black surfaces, not bright paint and plating.

title: Illuminated and unlit grilles share one lattice tool; unlit gets opaque film
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Avoids the second lattice tool and most of the second frame tool and validation by making lit and unlit grilles the same moulding with different in-mould films and inserts. Baseline: an illuminated grille (clear PC lattice with backlit dots and a light-guide plate) and the unlit base grille (silver or dark-chrome slats) are different mouldings with different frames, so the range carries two lattice tools, two frame tools and two validations for one aperture. Proposal: one PC lattice tool for both; on the unlit variant the same lattice is moulded with an in-mould decorated opaque film (dark-chrome or satin silver print) and no LED board, while the illuminated variant uses a smoked IMD film with dot windows and the LED board; frames differ only by two tool inserts (connector boss, LED-board clips). Why it works: the lattice geometry, fixings, radar window and pedestrian behaviour are identical, so only the decoration and the electronics vary; one validation covers both. Benchmark: the Mercedes GLC with EQ Technology offers an illuminated grille with 942 backlit dots in a chrome frame, and plain silver or dark-chrome grilles for buyers who do not want the lighting.

title: Headlamp washers deleted by holding low-beam flux below the 2,000 lm threshold
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the headlamp cleaning system (two telescopic nozzles, pump, hoses, extra washer volume and painted covers) by designing the low beam to stay under the flux threshold that triggers it. Baseline: a high-output LED low beam of about 2,400 objective lumens per lamp brings in the UN R48 requirement for a headlamp cleaning system: two telescopic pop-up nozzles in the fascia, a dedicated pump with check valve, hoses, about 1.5 l of extra washer capacity and two painted nozzle covers. Proposal: design the low-beam optics for high utilisation – chip-scale LEDs with efficacy above 200 lm/W and a free-form reflector or projector optic with ≥ 45% optical efficiency (micro-lens-array optics are compact but usually less efficient, so they are not the route to this target) – so the beam meets UN R149 and IIHS targets at 1,900 objective lumens, and delete the cleaning system (the matrix high beam is not counted in the threshold). Why it works: road illuminance depends on how much of the flux reaches the useful pattern, not on raw source flux; better utilisation buys back the lumens. Benchmark: the 2024 Genesis GV80 uses Micro Lens Array headlamps with chip-scale WICOP LEDs for all front functions, an example of chip-scale LEDs in a slim lamp; the MLA optic itself is not a high-efficiency design, so the anchor supports the LED choice rather than the efficiency target.

title: Headlamp inner bezels moulded in black low-fog PC instead of vacuum-metallised
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes base coat, vacuum metallising and protective topcoat on the inner bezels, and the yield losses and fogging that come with them, at a small premium for low-fog black PC and tool texture. Baseline: each headlamp has inner bezels and reflector masks in PC-HT that are base-coated, vacuum-metallised with aluminium and top-coated with a protective siloxane layer (≈€6.2 per lamp), a process that also causes fogging and outgassing problems and 5-8% yield losses on large bezels. Proposal: mould the bezels in black low-fog PC-HT (glass transition ≥ 180 °C, low-volatile grade) with a laser-etched micro-texture in the tool for a deep satin look, and let the lit signature – not metallised surfaces – carry the design; only the functional reflector surfaces stay metallised. Why it works: on a dark-face design the metallised bezel is barely visible by day and becomes a glare source at night; a textured black bezel looks more technical and removes a coating process. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse headlights carry no chrome, and BMW states that exterior lighting has replaced chrome as the styling highlight.

title: One headlamp housing carries two styling variants via swappable inner module carrier
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Avoids a second housing and lens tool set and most of its validation for an edition lamp graphic; only the inner carrier, light guides and bezel are variant. Photometry validation remains per graphic. Baseline: a luxury SUV range that offers a heritage-style or off-road edition with a distinct lamp graphic normally tools a second headlamp: housing, outer lens, mounting and full photometric and environmental validation, because the graphic is fixed by the lens and housing shape. Proposal: one PC-HT housing and one PC outer lens for all versions; the graphic is set by an inner module carrier (PC-HT, with the DRL light guides and bezel) that clips into the same housing datums, and the low/high-beam modules are common. The edition lamp differs only in the inner carrier, light guides and bezel. Why it works: housing and lens are the costly tools and the long validation items (sealing, condensation, stone-chip, vibration); the inner carrier is small and validates mainly for photometry. Benchmark: the Toyota Land Cruiser 250 offers round and rectangular headlights that fit the same housing, giving two very different looks.

title: Through-tinted rear lamp outer lens deletes separate smoked inner screens
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four smoked inner screens and their clips and fitting, moving the tint into the outer lens; LED power rises slightly to keep intensities, which partly offsets the saving. Baseline: dark "blacked-out until lit" rear lamps use a clear PMMA outer lens with a separate tinted inner screen (2 mm smoked PMMA, ≈€3.8 per lamp) clipped in front of the light guides, across four rear lamps (two body-side, two tailgate). Proposal: mould the outer lens in through-tinted neutral-grey PMMA (≈40% transmission, red areas in tinted red PMMA, 2K), and check each function against UN R148 minimum intensities; at equal tint the two surfaces removed gain about 8%, so LED drive or count rises only if the outer lens is made darker than today's screen; delete the inner screens. Why it works: the inner screen only reduces transmission; doing it in the outer lens removes a part, two surfaces (≈8% reflection loss) and the clips. Benchmark: the 2022 Range Rover has rear lamps that are blacked out until they light up.

title: Frameless outside mirror: ground-edge glass deletes the bezel ring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes two bezel rings and their paint, adding only edge grinding and a slightly larger glass, and gives more mirror area for the same head size. Same actuator is used. Baseline: each outside mirror glass sits in a PP carrier plate inside a separate bezel ring (PC/ABS, painted gloss black, ≈€4.8 with paint), which frames the glass and provides the rounded edge that UN R46 requires; the bezel adds a gap, a paint process and a part number per side. Proposal: a frameless mirror – the glass is enlarged to the full head outline, its edge is C-ground and polished to a radius ≥ 2.5 mm, and it is bonded to the actuator carrier with a PU foam tape; the housing cap closes to the glass edge with a 1 mm shadow gap. Why it works: the bezel exists only to finish the edge; a ground glass edge meets the edge-radius requirement directly and gives a larger mirror area within the same head. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 uses frameless door mirrors, in high-gloss black on some trims.

title: UWB approach detection replaces capacitive sensor electrodes in four door handles
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four capacitive electrode PCBs and four LF antennas from the handles and simplifies handle connectors; two added UWB anchors and two microswitches partly offset the saving. Baseline: each of four outside handles carries a capacitive unlock/lock electrode PCB and a 125 kHz LF antenna for passive entry (≈€8 per handle with connector pins), even on vehicles that already have ultra-wideband (UWB) anchors for a smartphone digital key. Proposal: use the UWB anchors (one added in each B-pillar trim, giving six) to locate the key or phone to within ±10 cm and unlock the approached door on approach; locking is by walk-away or by a single microswitch on each front handle; the LF antennas in the handles are deleted, with one LF antenna kept in the cabin for key-in-car detection. Why it works: UWB time-of-flight localisation is more precise than LF field strength and resists relay attacks, so handle-mounted sensing is no longer needed for approach unlock. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse uses flush door handles; the Car Connectivity Consortium Digital Key 3.0 standard (general practice) uses UWB for secure passive entry.

title: One handle module per side serves both front and rear doors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts handle modules from four to two part numbers, avoids two tools and validations, and doubles the volume per part, with a small cable adapter as the only variant. Baseline: front and rear outside handle modules differ in length, lever arc and pocket depth because the front and rear door skins have different curvature at the handle line, giving four handle part numbers (LH/RH front, LH/RH rear), two tools per side and four validations. Proposal: set the handle line so front and rear skins have the same local curvature (±0.5 mm over the 180 mm pocket) at the handle position – a styling constraint agreed early – and use one module per side for both doors; only the Bowden or e-latch lead length differs, handled by a clip-on cable adapter. Why it works: the handle is a precision mechanism that is expensive to tool and validate; the skins can carry the geometry change, which costs nothing on the press tool. Benchmark: the 2022 Range Rover uses flush handles on all doors as part of its flush-surface exterior, where identical handles front and rear read as one design line.

title: Tailgate wordmark moulded as one tied script instead of seven loose letters
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces seven letters and seven tapes with one tied script and one tape, cutting application time and spacing defects and lowering finish cost per vehicle. Audit time also falls. Baseline: the model name on the tailgate is applied as seven separate electroplated ABS letters, each with die-cut acrylic foam tape, positioned by an operator with a template (≈1.4 min), plus a separate powertrain badge; misaligned letters are a common audit defect. Proposal: mould the script as one part in PC/ABS with 1.2 mm tie bars hidden in the letter baseline shadow, finish it with satin PVD, and apply it with a single die-cut foam tape from a one-hit applicator that locates on two tailgate pierce holes or on the lamp edge. Why it works: one part and one tape remove six placements and the spacing error between letters; tie bars sit below the letters where the shadow hides them. Benchmark: BMW cites refined badging on the iX3 Neue Klasse, which uses fewer, cleaner exterior badges.

title: Lit front badge becomes a decor insert lit by the grille light-guide
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the stand-alone lit-badge module (board, housing, potting, connector and harness branch), replacing it with a decor insert lit by four extra LEDs on the grille board. Baseline: an illuminated front badge is a sealed module of its own: PMMA badge with printed decor, LED board, reflector, potting, housing, connector and harness branch (≈€38), mounted in the middle of an illuminated grille that already has a light-guide plate and LEDs behind it. Proposal: the badge becomes a thin decor insert (PMMA with IMD print and a metallised outline, ≈€9) clipped into the grille lattice in front of the existing light-guide plate; four extra LEDs on the grille LED board light it through a local extraction pattern; one seal and one harness branch disappear. Why it works: the badge and the grille are lit by the same physics and the same driver; the badge module duplicates sealing, board, connector and harness for a few LEDs. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ has a backlit Cadillac badge in its illuminated grille, lit together with the grille in one animation.

title: Shutter frame lower rail doubles as the pedestrian lower-leg stiffener
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes the separate lower-leg stiffener and its clips by giving the shutter frame lower rail the stiffener function, at a small material upgrade from PP-T20 to PP-LGF30. Baseline: below the lower grille a separate lower-leg stiffener (PP-GF30 blade, ≈0.9 kg) is clipped to the bumper beam brackets to support the pedestrian's lower leg and reduce knee bending in the UN R127 / GTR 9 flex-PLI test, and immediately behind it the AGS frame has its own lower rail. Proposal: mould the AGS frame in PP-LGF30 and extend its lower rail forward by 45 mm with a 3 mm ribbed C-section to act as the lower-leg stiffener, fixed to the crash-box brackets at both ends with two M6 screws; delete the separate stiffener. Why it works: the stiffener only needs to stand at the right height and stiffness (≈60-80 N/mm); a long-glass PP rail, already present and spanning the same width, can provide it with small extra mass. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric integrates fully variable cooling flaps into its front intake as part of an aero-led front end – the shutter frame is already a full-width structural part of the nose.

title: One rotation-symmetric tail/stop light engine used in all four rear lamps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Consolidates four rear LED board designs and collimator tools into one rotation-symmetric engine at four times the volume, with one binning and one end-of-line test. Baseline: the four rear lamps (LH/RH body-side, LH/RH tailgate) each have their own tail/stop LED board and collimator design, giving four PCB part numbers (≈€9 each), four collimator tools and four sets of LED binning and end-of-line tests. Proposal: one tail/stop light engine – a 6-LED board with an integrated PMMA TIR collimator, 180° rotation-symmetric so it fits LH and RH – used in all four lamps; the lamp housings, light guides and outer lenses keep the styling. A 4-way connector jumper adapts the harness side. Why it works: the tail/stop function needs the same intensity class in every lamp, so one engine at 200,000 pieces a year replaces four at 50,000, with one binning recipe and one test. Benchmark: the Audi Q6 e-tron builds its rear lights from six OLED panels with 360 segments controlled by software, a modular light source repeated across the lamps.

Proposal: one tail/stop light engine – a 6-LED board with an integrated PMMA TIR collimator, 180° rotation-symmetric so it fits LH and RH – used in all four lamps; the lamp housings, light guides and outer lenses keep the styling. A 4-way connector jumper adapts the harness side. Why it works: the tail/stop function needs the same intensity class in every lamp, so one engine at 200,000 pieces a year replaces four at 50,000, with one binning recipe and one test. title: One wide CMS sensor per side also supplies the 360° door view
description: [800V BEV] Deletes the two downward door imagers and their links on CMS vehicles; a higher-resolution sensor and dual-output serialiser per side offset part of the saving. Baseline: on 800V BEV vehicles with the camera-mirror system (CMS), each side carries a rear-facing camera-mirror sensor in the arm and a separate downward fish-eye unit under the mirror base for the 360° parking view, each with its own coax/GMSL link (≈€22 per camera plus €4 of harness). Proposal: one 5 MP camera per side with a 190° lens in the CMS arm, angled 20° down; the ISP crops a high-resolution rear field for the CMS door display and dewarps a second, downward field for the 360° parking view; a dual-output serialiser feeds both domains, with the CMS path given priority and its own latency budget. Why it works: the two imagers look at overlapping fields from almost the same point on the door; one higher-resolution sensor covers both with margin. Benchmark: the Audi Q8 e-tron virtual exterior mirrors place a camera at the end of a flat support and show highway, turning and parking views on 7-inch OLED displays, and cut drag from Cd 0.28 to 0.27.

ideaData.dfmDfa: One camera per side with a single sealed connector in the arm; no separate camera boss under the base. The arm has one camera window with a hydrophobic coating and heater, which keeps both views clear in rain and frost.

Net €32.0; low €26 if a separate ISP is needed, high €34. Net €26-€34 per CMS vehicle; the annual value below assumes all 50,000 vehicles carry CMS, so scale it by BEV mix × CMS take rate (≤ 40% gives ≤ €10-€13.5 fleet average). Net €26-€34 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €1.3M-€1.7M per year (estimate; amortisation over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: UN R46 CMS requirements on availability, latency and image quality must hold while the same camera also serves surround view. Validate UN R46 / ISO 16505 class II/III fields and latency (≤ 200 ms), functional independence of the CMS path (ISO 26262), 360° view stitching quality at the doors, Euro NCAP 2026 assistance features using side views, and lens contamination in rain. title: Puddle-lamp logo projector: one moulded micro-lens array replaces glass gobo optics
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the glass gobo, condenser, two-element lens and focus barrel of each logo puddle lamp with one moulded micro-lens-array stack, cutting part cost and deleting the focus adjustment step. Baseline: the logo-projecting puddle lamps in both outside mirrors (and often in the front doors) use a single-channel projector: LED, condenser lens, a printed or chrome-etched glass gobo slide carrying the logo and a two-element glass or PMMA projection lens in a die-cast or PBT barrel with focus adjustment, ≈€6.5 per lamp. Proposal: a micro-lens-array (MLA) projector – two moulded PC or PMMA plates with several hundred lenslets each, the logo printed as a chrome mask between them – placed directly over the LED; the array images the logo without a focus barrel and with a depth of focus that tolerates the 0.9-1.1 m projection height of an air-suspension SUV. Why it works: each lenslet projects the same small image and the images overlap on the ground, so the projector needs only 6-8 mm of build depth, no focusing and no glass. Benchmark: the 2024 Genesis GV80 uses Micro Lens Array technology in its Two-Line headlamps, showing MLA optics are now produced in volume for exterior lighting.

title: Screen-printed self-regulating PTC heater on mirror glass replaces foil heater pad
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the foil heater pad and its temperature limiter with a printed self-regulating PTC layer on the glass, cutting part cost and removing the adhesive bonding step. Baseline: each outside mirror glass has an etched aluminium or copper foil heater on a PET carrier, bonded to the glass back with a pressure-sensitive adhesive, with a bimetal or NTC temperature limiter to avoid overheating (≈€3.4 per glass plus the limiter). Proposal: screen-print a carbon-polymer PTC ink (self-regulating, resistance rising sharply above ≈60 °C) with silver busbars directly on the glass back, then laminate the anti-splinter film over it; on the MHEV and 800V BEV it stays on the 12 V net (≈12-15 W per glass). The PTC characteristic removes the separate temperature limiter. Why it works: the PTC ink limits its own power as it warms, so it de-ices quickly from cold and cannot overheat; printing on the glass removes the PET carrier and its adhesive, and improves heat transfer. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 uses frameless door mirrors, where the glass is the visible surface and must stay clear without a frame to hide a heater pad edge.

title: Mirror base cover with 2K TPE seal lip replaces separate foam gasket
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes two die-cut foam gaskets and their placement by moulding the seal onto the base cover, cutting part count and wind-noise and water-leak rework. Seal set also improves. Baseline: the mirror base seals to the door sail through a die-cut EPDM foam gasket (≈€1.6 per side) placed by hand before the base cover is clipped on; misplaced gaskets cause wind noise and water entry into the door, and the foam takes a compression set over time. Proposal: the PP-T20 base cover is moulded with a 2K TPE-V lip (Shore 55A, 1.2 mm lip, 2.5 mm interference) around its door-side face, so the seal comes with the cover and cannot be misplaced. Why it works: a moulded lip has repeatable interference and recovers better than foam, and it removes a hand operation that is a known source of wind-noise complaints. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 uses frameless door mirrors and flush door details, where mirror-to-door joints must stay tight and quiet.

title: Headlamp aim adjusters in PA66-GF30 and POM replace zinc housings and aluminium gears
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces zinc die-cast housings and aluminium gears with moulded PA66-GF30 and POM parts and deletes screw fixings with a snap-in lock, cutting adjuster cost by about 45%. Baseline: each headlamp has two aim adjusters (vertical and horizontal) with a zinc die-cast housing, a steel ball stud, an aluminium bevel gear pair and screw fixing to the lamp housing (≈€2.2 each, four per vehicle). Proposal: snap-in adjusters with a PA66-GF30 housing, POM bevel gears and the steel ball stud retained, clipped into the housing boss with a quarter-turn lock; the adjuster thread is a moulded PA66 lead screw with a self-locking flank angle. Why it works: aim adjusters carry only the lamp optic module load (≈30 N) and move a few times in life; glass-filled PA66 with a POM gear pair holds the aim position under vibration if creep is controlled by a short load path. Benchmark: the Range Rover uses ZKW LED modules with 1.2 million pixels steered by electronically controlled mirrors, so beam shape is electronic and the mechanical adjusters only need to hold the base aim.

title: Rear lamp outer lens thinned from 3.0 to 2.4 mm with high-flow PMMA
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts PMMA mass by about 20% and lens moulding cycle time by about 30% through a thinner nominal wall and a high-flow grade, with stiffening ribs to keep weld stiffness. Baseline: the four rear lamp outer lenses are moulded in standard-flow PMMA at 3.0 mm nominal wall, a thickness inherited from older lamps; cooling time, which scales with the square of wall thickness, sets most of the 70-80 s cycle. Proposal: 2.4 mm nominal wall in a high-flow PMMA grade (MVR ≈ 8 cm³/10 min) with local 3.0 mm only at the weld flange and mounting bosses, and two hidden stiffening ribs along the long edge to keep stiffness for hot-plate or laser welding. Why it works: cooling time falls to about (2.4/3.0)² ≈ 64% of today's, i.e. by about 36%, so the cycle shortens by roughly 30%, and material falls by about 20%; impact resistance for gravel and car-wash loads is still met at 2.4 mm. Benchmark: the 2025 Tesla Model Y uses a single cross-car rear lamp that Tesla calls the first indirect reflective body-panel taillight – a large lamp where lens mass and cycle time are significant cost drivers.

title: Rear crash boxes as cut 6063-T6 extrusions bolted to the aluminium beam
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces two welded and e-coated steel crash boxes with cut-to-length aluminium extrusions, deleting welding, e-coat and galvanic isolation and saving about 0.8 kg. Baseline: the rear bumper system uses a 6082-T6 extruded beam on two stamped and MIG-welded steel crash boxes (two half-shells in DC04/HX340LAD, ≈1.0 kg each, e-coated), joined to the aluminium beam through isolating washers and a coating to prevent galvanic corrosion. Proposal: crash boxes cut from a 6063-T6 octagonal multi-cell extrusion (2.0 mm wall, ≈0.6 kg each) with two machined crush initiators, bolted to the beam with the same M10 pattern and to the rear rails with a cast end plate; no welding, no e-coat, no galvanic isolation. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail uses a multi-piece bumper construction built for repair and accessory fitment, the same modular logic we apply to the rear crash-box joint.

title: Side-window bright finishers roll-formed in 1.4509 stainless instead of anodised aluminium
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces anodised aluminium with mill-finished bright stainless, cutting strip and finishing cost and most of the colour-matching rejects. Car-wash durability also improves. Baseline: the bright side-window (daylight opening) finishers on four doors and two quarters are roll-formed from bright-rolled 5xxx aluminium strip, then chemically brightened and anodised; colour and gloss matching between batches and parts gives 10-15% rejects and the anodised layer is attacked by alkaline car-wash chemicals. Proposal: roll-form and stretch-bend the finishers from 0.5 mm EN 1.4509 (441) ferritic stainless strip in bright-annealed (2R) finish, clipped to the same PP carriers; the stainless finish is uniform from coil and needs no anodising. Why it works: bright-annealed ferritic stainless gives a consistent bright finish from the mill, resists alkaline washes and road salt, and costs less than anodised aluminium once rejects are counted, at a small mass penalty (≈+0.25 kg). Benchmark: the Mercedes-Benz GLC with EQ Technology frames its grille with a wide chrome frame and offers dark-chrome alternatives, showing bright metal remains a core luxury cue.

title: Latch inertia lock replaces zinc counterweights in four outside handles
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four zinc counterweights and their fixing from the handles by blocking inertial opening at the latch, cutting part cost and about 0.3 kg. The handle also gets lighter. Baseline: each outside handle with a mechanical release carries a zinc die-cast counterweight (60-90 g) on its lever so that side-impact acceleration does not swing the handle and open the latch, as UN R11 and FMVSS 206 require. The counterweight must balance lever, grip and cable so the net inertial moment about the handle pivot stays below the release threshold at 30 g. Proposal: delete the counterweights and put an inertia lock in each latch – a small pendulum or mass-blocker that locks the release lever above about 20 g lateral acceleration and resets itself – so that the mechanical path cannot open the door during a crash. Why it works: one inertia blocker in the latch protects the whole release chain (handle, Bowden, lever) instead of balancing the handle; the latch already has the space and the lever. Benchmark: the Tesla Model Y uses retractable handles that are among the designs affected by new rules demanding a mechanical release path; any such path must be protected against inertial opening, which is cheapest at the latch.

title: Fascias at 2.5 mm wall in high-stiffness PP/EPDM-T15 instead of 3.0 mm
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts fascia compound by about 1 kg per vehicle and moulding cycle by about 15%, with a small grade premium; flange ribs restore stiffness where fixing and sensor loads need it. Baseline: front and rear fascias are moulded at 3.0 mm in a standard PP/EPDM-T20 (flexural modulus ≈1,900 MPa, MFR ≈20), total ≈6.4 kg; the wall was set to control waviness and sink on large Class-A surfaces. Proposal: 2.5 mm nominal wall in a high-crystallinity, high-flow PP/EPDM-T15 (flexural modulus ≈2,200 MPa, MFR ≈35, low CLTE) with sequential valve gating and ribbed fixing flanges, giving ≈5.4 kg; local 3.0 mm at fixing bosses and sensor brackets. Why it works: bending stiffness scales with modulus × t³, so 2,200 × 2.5³ ≈ 67% of 1,900 × 3.0³, which is recovered in the zones that need it by flange ribs; most of the fascia surface carries no structural load, and the cycle shortens because cooling time scales with t². Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail front fascia is designed to raise the approach angle to 26° and to accept aftermarket bumpers – fascias are styling skins over separate structure.

title: Front lower-leg absorber in EPP 45 g/l with deeper section instead of 60 g/l
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Cuts EPP bead mass by about 15% and shortens the steam-chest cycle by moving to 45 g/l with a deeper, ribbed section that keeps the energy absorbed. Absorber mass falls by about 0.18 kg. Baseline: the front bumper energy absorber ahead of the beam is moulded in EPP 60 g/l (≈1.3 kg), sized for the pedestrian lower-leg test and low-speed impact; its depth is limited to 70 mm by the fascia position. Proposal: EPP 45 g/l with the section deepened to 85 mm where the fascia allows (centre zone) and a ribbed back face that keeps the crush stiffness in the corners; mass ≈1.12 kg. Plateau stress of EPP falls roughly with density (≈0.45 vs 0.60 MPa), so the deeper section restores the energy (stress × crush distance) while lowering the force peak that drives tibia acceleration. Why it works: lower density gives a softer, longer crush that suits the flex-PLI test, and a lower bead mass and shorter steam cycle cut cost. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail redesigns its front fascia for a 26° approach angle, which leaves the absorber depth as the main variable behind the fascia.

title: Fascia guide and slide-lock brackets in PP-T20 instead of PA6-GF30
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Switches eight fascia brackets from PA6-GF30 to PP-T20, cutting resin cost and removing moisture conditioning, with a little extra section to keep retention. Squeak risk also falls. Baseline: the eight guide brackets that hold the fascias to the wings, headlamps and rear quarters (slide-lock rails and snap pockets) are moulded in PA6-GF30 (≈0.09 kg each), which needs moisture conditioning to avoid brittle snaps and costs about €3.9/kg. Proposal: mould them in PP-T20 (≈€2.1/kg) with sections and snap geometry re-sized to keep retention force (PP-T20 has about a third of the modulus of conditioned PA6-GF30, so a 10% thickening alone recovers only about 1.3× of the 3× stiffness gap; it has much higher strain at break), no conditioning. Why it works: the brackets carry only fascia mass and thermal movement; PP-T20 matches the fascia material, so thermal expansion is the same and squeak and rattle are lower. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 Overtrail uses a multi-piece bumper, where many small brackets and joints carry the pieces – the cost of those small parts adds up.

title: Sealed LED headlamp housing deletes rear access caps and their O-rings
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four access caps, four O-rings and the bayonet seal features in the housing tool, removing four leak paths; a warranty provision for module service is charged against the saving. Baseline: although the headlamps are all-LED, each housing still carries two rear access caps (PP with EPDM O-ring, bayonet) inherited from bulb lamps, used only to reach module screws in service; the cap seals are also a leak and condensation path. Proposal: close the housing back with moulded walls; LED modules are serviced by removing the lamp (four bolts from the front-end carrier) or by replacing the lamp (a laser- or hot-plate-welded lens cannot be opened at a repairer); delete the caps, O-rings and bayonet seal lands. Why it works: LED modules last the vehicle life in most cases, so access caps are rarely used, while every cap is a sealing interface in production. Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport headlamps use digital LED units with 1.3 million micro-mirrors – sealed electronic modules with no bulb to change.

title: Rear lamps fixed by one nut and two self-retaining darts instead of three nuts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Removes two nuts and studs per lamp, most of the blind torquing time and part of the trim access flaps, replacing them with two self-retaining darts. Rattles fall as well. Baseline: each of the four rear lamps is held by three M6 studs with flange nuts, torqued from inside through trim access flaps; the operator works blind and the flaps add parts and rattles. Proposal: one M6 stud and nut at the lamp's datum point carries the clamp load, and two moulded darts with a spring-steel retaining clip snap into body holes, biased so they pull the lamp onto its seal; the lamp seats with a push and one nut is torqued. Access flaps shrink to one small opening per lamp. Why it works: the lamp needs location and seal compression, not three bolted joints; darts provide location and retention, and one bolt sets the clamp and the electrical ground path if needed. Benchmark: the 2025 Tesla Model Y uses a single cross-car rear lamp, showing how much rear-lamp fixing and fitting can be simplified on a modern design.

title: Ripple counting replaces potentiometers in memory mirror glass actuators
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Deletes four position potentiometers and their harness wires and pins, using motor current ripple counting in the door controller instead, at a small software and calibration cost. Baseline: memory-function outside mirrors use a two-motor glass actuator with two potentiometers per side to read glass position for driver memory and reverse-dip, each needing a reference and wiper wire through the door harness (≈€1.1 per sensor plus connector pins). Proposal: delete the potentiometers and count commutation ripples in the motor current in the door zone controller, which already drives the motors; the position is re-zeroed against the mechanical end stops at a slow speed once a month or after battery disconnection, and stored in non-volatile memory. Why it works: brushed DC motors produce current ripples per commutation, which the controller can count reliably at a resolution well below 0.1° of glass angle; end-stop recalibration removes drift. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 uses frameless door mirrors, a design where the actuator and its sensors sit directly behind a large visible glass.

title: Conductive PP fascia compound removes conductive adhesion promoter before electrostatic paint
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Replaces the conductive adhesion promoter with a thin standard promoter and raises electrostatic transfer efficiency on fascias by making the compound itself conductive, at a compound premium. Baseline: PP/EPDM-T20 fascias are flame treated and then sprayed with a conductive adhesion promoter (chlorinated polyolefin with carbon black, 5-8 µm) so the waterborne basecoat and 2K clear can be applied by electrostatic bells; without conductivity, transfer efficiency drops to that of air spray. Proposal: compound the fascia with about 0.8-1.5% multi-wall carbon nanotubes (conductive carbon black would need several times more and costs impact strength) to reach a surface resistivity below 10⁶ Ω/sq, so the part itself is grounded through its jig; after plasma activation a thin non-conductive promoter (2-3 µm) is enough, or none on some grades. Why it works: electrostatic painting needs a grounded surface, not a conductive coating; a conductive substrate gives an even field at edges and recesses, raising transfer efficiency. Benchmark: PPG showed at SURCAR Asia 2026 a low-temperature system intended to paint metal bodies and plastic bumpers in one process – which only works if the plastic parts accept electrostatic application like the body.

title: Hidden J-hook crossbar anchors make rail-free tops the base specification
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Raised roof rails, their feet, seals and fasteners are deleted from the 55% of the mix that never carries a roof load; every body instead gets eight low-cost anchors under the roof-ditch seal, so roof-load capability is sold as a dealer crossbar kit rather than built into every car. Baseline: the platform fits raised 6063-T6 anodised longitudinal bars (≈€88 a pair with four feet, gaskets and eight M8 fasteners) to all but the entry trim, although customer clinics on luxury SUVs typically show only a minority ever carry cargo up there; the bars also add ≈0.004-0.006 Cd and wind noise at 130 km/h. Proposal: the body-side gutter flange receives eight clinched M8 J-hook anchor blocks (zinc-flake coated S355MC, 22 g each) at fixed crossbar stations, hidden under the gutter seal and marked by moulded arrows. Raised bars stay as an option for the off-road and tow trims; all other cars leave the line with a clean top, and an accessory crossbar pair (6082-T6 aero profile, clamp feet with stainless studs) clips in through a seal flap with only a trim key. Why it works: crossbar loads (75-100 kg dynamic) go straight into the side-frame ring through the anchor rather than through a decorative extrusion, so the load path is shorter and the anchor costs a fraction of the bar it replaces; the clean top also helps BEV range. Benchmark: Tesla Model Y racks clip under the glass-top seal and anchor to J-hooks beneath the glass, so nothing is visible on cars that never carry a rack. General practice for load carriers is ISO 11154 City-crash and dynamic testing.

title: Tilt-only front glass panel replaces tilt-and-slide panoramic roof mechanism
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The long slide guide rails, the full-stroke cable drive, the wind deflector and most of the water-management channel are deleted; the front panel only tilts, so the cassette needs short tilt levers and a smaller motor while keeping ventilation and the full-length glass view. Baseline: the optional opening panoramic roof is a spoiler-type tilt-and-slide module: the front glass (≈0.55 m²) rises, then slides 420 mm rearward over the fixed rear panel on two 1.1 m 6063 guide rails driven by a 12 V motor and twin helical cables, with a pop-up wind deflector and a four-corner drain channel; module ≈€620 and 17 kg. Proposal: keep the same two-panel glass layout and frame footprint, but the front panel only tilts its rear edge up 45 mm (venting mode) on two short 6063-T6 lever sets with a single-stage cable stroke of 60 mm. Guide rails shrink to 280 mm, the wind deflector is deleted because a tilted panel does not create the buffeting of an open aperture, and the drain channel only needs to handle seal seepage. Why it works: usage logging on fleet vehicles generally shows tilt is the mode most used; full slide-open is rare at motorway speed in a luxury SUV because of noise. Mass falls ≈4.5 kg high in the body, helping both the MHEV (CO2) and the 800V BEV (range). Benchmark: Range Rover Sport makes a fixed panoramic roof standard and sells the sliding roof and powered blind as options, showing that luxury buyers accept non-sliding glass; our proposal sits between fixed and sliding.

title: Air-suspension reservoir pulses clean rear and side cameras without washer fluid
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two fluid solenoid valves, ≈7 m of washer line to the tailgate and wings and three fluid nozzles are deleted; the already-fitted air-suspension compressor and reservoir supply dry air pulses through one small valve and PA12 line, so camera cleaning reuses hardware the car already carries. Baseline: the rear camera and the two front-wing surround cameras each have a fluid nozzle fed from the front reservoir through two 12 V solenoid valves and ≈7 m of 4 mm line, routed through the tailgate hinge grommet; every clean uses 15-20 ml of fluid. Proposal: tap the dry side of the air-suspension circuit (dryer outlet, 16-18 bar reservoir) with one normally-closed 2/2 solenoid valve (≈0.5 W hold) feeding a 4×1 mm PA12 line to three laval-profile air-knife nozzles moulded in PA66-GF30. Each 150 ms pulse uses ≈0.2 NL of air, so ten pulses drop reservoir pressure by well under 0.5 bar and the compressor tops up in seconds; ride-height levelling always has priority in the air-suspension controller. A single fluid shot for dried mud remains available at the rear camera by re-aiming the existing rear-screen washer jet. Why it works: air pulses shed water droplets, spray and light snow, which cause most camera-occlusion events; air from the dryer is dry so the line cannot freeze. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 gives almost every exterior camera its own fluid sprayer, which shows the content a fluid-only approach carries.

title: Sequenced cowl module drops wiper drive, scuttle and washer plumbing in one install
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two trim-line stations and the bonnet washer jets with their hinge-crossing hose are deleted; the supplier pre-assembles wiper linkage, motor, scuttle panels, arm-mounted washer nozzles and plumbing into one sequenced module that is fixed with three bolts and one connector. Baseline: the wiper linkage and motor are bolted into the plenum at one station, washer hoses are routed and clipped at another, the bonnet carries two heated washer jets fed by a hose that crosses the hinge through a grommet, and the upper and lower scuttle panels (PP-T20) are clipped on after glazing — ≈7.6 min of labour across two stations. Proposal: the lower scuttle panel becomes a PP-GF30 carrier onto which the supplier mounts the wiper frame, motor, washer manifold and hoses; the washer nozzles move onto the wiper arms (fluid travels through the arm), so there is no hose to the bonnet at all. The module arrives sequenced, is lowered in after windscreen bonding, located on two pins, fixed by three M8 bolts and one connector: ≈2.6 min. Why it works: plumbing that never leaves the cowl does not need to cross a moving panel, and pre-assembly moves fiddly hose clipping to a bench where it is cheaper and leak-tested before shipping. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 carries its washer nozzles on the wiper arms, so the arms also spray the roof lidar. Mercedes MAGIC VISION CONTROL showed blade-edge delivery is reported to use up to 50% less fluid.

title: Off-road pack swaps aero panels for aluminium skids on one common fixing grid
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Off-road cars no longer carry an aero panel beneath or around their skid plates, and the separate skid bracket set and the weld nuts unused on road cars are deleted; one 14-point rivet-nut grid serves both the road aero panels and the off-road aluminium skids. Baseline: road cars carry PP-T20 and PET-fleece aero panels; the off-road pack adds 3 mm steel skid plates on their own welded brackets and captive nuts, with the aero panels cut around or left beneath them, so off-road cars carry two layers in the front and centre zones and every body carries 12 weld nuts used only by the off-road pack. Proposal: define one fixing grid of 14 M8 rivet-nuts on the subframes and rails. Road cars use PP-T20 aero panels with moulded-in steel compression limiters; off-road cars use 4 mm 5083-H111 aluminium skids pressed to the same aero shape (swaged ribs, NACA-style relief for the EDU/engine air) that take the aero panel's place one for one. Why it works: a skid that is also shaped to the aero surface needs no panel under it; one grid means one body variant and one set of jacking/recovery clearances. Benchmark: the Lexus GX 550 dealer-fit middle skid plate uses the vehicle's existing attachment mounts, so it installs with no drilling; we extend that principle to the whole underbody and to factory fit.

title: Regen-dominant braking lets 800V BEV close its front brake-cooling ducts
description: [800V BEV] On the 800V BEV, the two brake-cooling ducts, their brackets and their fitting labour are deleted, and the underbody panel is moulded closed, because regenerative braking does most of the stopping; the MHEV keeps the ducts. Friction-only fade performance is still proven before deletion. Baseline: the shared platform carries MHEV-sized front brake cooling on both powertrains: a scoop in the front underbody panel and a PP-T20 duct per side feeding air to the caliper, plus clips and brackets (≈€19 per car with labour). Proposal: on the 800V BEV the underbody panel is moulded closed by a tool insert, and ducts and brackets are deleted. Regen of up to ≈0.3 g covers the large majority of decelerations, so mean disc temperatures in customer use are far lower than on the MHEV. A brake-temperature estimator in the brake controller is calibrated to warn and derate if regen is unavailable (full battery, cold pack) during long descents. Why it works: duct cooling is sized for repeated friction stops; on a BEV the friction brake mostly sees low-energy events, while the closed panel removes a drag source next to the wheel. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric runs a flat, closed floor with flexible underbody covers and closes its active cooling flaps to reach Cd 0.25 in Eco; we apply the same closed-floor logic to the brake-cooling ducts.

title: Glass supplier pre-applies latent-cure PUR bead, deleting the in-plant glazing cell
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The plant no longer buys, purges and maintains a robot urethane dispensing cell for windscreen, backlite, roof and quarter glass; the bead arrives already applied to the glass, and the plant only activates it with a short IR or induction pulse before setting, removing purge waste and most cell upkeep. Baseline: five bonded glazing parts are primed, then a robot applies a 1K moisture-cure or 2K PUR bead (≈380 g per car) at a dedicated cell with heated pumps and drums. Purge, start-up and skin-over waste runs at 6-8%, and the cell needs two operators per shift and planned maintenance. Proposal: the glass supplier, which already runs encapsulation and primer lines, applies a latent-cure PUR bead profile (triangular 8×10 mm) in a controlled environment and protects it with a release liner. At the vehicle plant a robot removes the liner, an IR/induction station activates the bead for 20-30 s, and the existing glass-setting robot places the glass. Why it works: bead geometry is more consistent at the supplier (fixed glass on a fixture, no body tolerance), purge waste disappears, and the activation station is much cheaper than a dispensing cell. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ fits a large fixed panoramic glass roof as standard, showing the growth of large bonded glazing on luxury SUVs that makes bead cost and quality matter more.

title: Robot roll-in of door-aperture weatherstrips with vision-checked joint position
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Hand roll-in of four door-aperture seals and the tailgate seal is replaced by two robots with roller heads, which removes most of the labour, the 40 mm overlap allowance per seal and much of the water-leak rework caused by uneven seating and misplaced joints. Baseline: operators push and roll five aperture weatherstrips (EPDM sponge bulb on steel carrier, ≈20 m in total) onto the flanges, ≈1.6 min each; joint position varies ±60 mm, and partial seating causes water-test failures on ≈1.5% of cars, each needing about €45 of rework. Proposal: two six-axis robots with compliant roller heads follow the flange using the body's RPS and a 2D vision check; the operator only loads the seal start at a marked index. Seating force is controlled at 60-90 N/mm, the joint is placed in a defined low-exposure zone (lower rear corner), and seating depth is checked by a laser line before the car leaves the station. Why it works: uniform seating gives uniform compression load deflection, which governs water tightness, wind noise and door closing effort; the robot removes the overlap allowance used to cover hand variation. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 110 is rated to wade 900 mm, which sets a body-sealing quality bar that robot seating helps hold in volume.

title: Nose-weight estimated from air-suspension height sensors deletes tow-ball load cell
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The strain-gauge load pin in the towbar neck mount, its harness branch and its module input are deleted; nose weight is calculated from the rear ride-height sensors and air-spring pressures the car already has, giving the trailer-loading readout through software. Baseline: the tow-pack specification includes a strain-gauge load pin in the towbar neck mount (≈€38), a 1.2 m harness branch and a module input, so the driver sees nose weight while loading a trailer. Proposal: the air-suspension controller already reads rear corner height (±0.5 mm) and air-spring pressure. With levelling paused for the loading phase, the change in rear spring pressure × effective piston area gives the vertical load added at the rear axle; the controller subtracts cargo load using the front/rear pitch change and resolves the tow-ball load through the known axle-to-ball lever arm. Accuracy target ±10 kg across 0-195 kg after an EOL zero, displayed with a tolerance band. Why it works: the air spring is itself a load cell; only the geometry and a calibration are new. Benchmark: Land Rover's electrically deployable Defender tow bar, rated 3,500 kg and 195 kg nose load, is offered only on air-suspension vehicles, which means the air-suspension sensors are always present on the towing car.

title: Behind-windscreen lidar in the wiped zone deletes roof pod, heater and nozzle
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The painted roof-header lidar pod, its hard-coated window, PTC heater, dedicated washer nozzle and line, and the roof reinforcement and seal are deleted; a thin in-cabin lidar looks through an IR-optimised zone of the windscreen that the wipers already keep clean. Baseline: cars with the laser-scanner option (assume 40% take on the Pilot pack) carry a header-mounted housing: painted PC/ASA shell, PC hard-coated optical window, 25 W PTC heater, dedicated washer nozzle and line, and a local reinforcement with its own seal (≈€65 of content around the sensor). Proposal: package a thin solid-state scanner (≈25 mm tall) behind the windscreen, above the camera cluster, inside the wiped area. The windscreen gets a local IR window: low-iron outer ply, no IR-absorbing interlayer and no frit in that zone, giving high transmission at 905 nm. The existing camera heater and wipers clean the field. Why it works: the windscreen is already a cleaned, heated, impact-tested optical surface; the main added cost is a more complex glass (≈€22) and a bracket. Detection range drops with glass in the path, which current sensors are specified to tolerate. Benchmark: Volvo EX90 puts its lidar on the roof header and cleans it with the wiper-arm nozzles; Hesai's ET25 in-cabin lidar is quoted at 250 m without and 225 m with a windscreen, with FAW Hongqi as first customer.

title: Air-suspension low aero height replaces active front underbody flap actuators
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The active front underbody flap, its actuator, linkage, harness and diagnostic output are deleted; the air suspension, which already lowers the body at motorway speed, gives most of the same drag reduction, and a fixed flexible TPO lip recovers the rest. Baseline: an active front underbody flap deploys 50-60 mm at >90 km/h to cut underfloor flow, using a 12 V actuator, steel linkage, PP-GF30 flap and position sensor (≈€42 with harness), and it retracts for off-road approach angle. Proposal: the air suspension already drops 15-25 mm in its aero mode above 105 km/h; that lowering reduces underfloor mass flow and frontal area beneath the bumper in the same way. A fixed 25 mm-deep lip in flexible TPO (Shore D 40) is added at the bumper-to-undertray joint; it bends back on contact, so approach angle in off-road height is unchanged. Why it works: both measures reduce the gap that feeds the underfloor; wind-tunnel experience on air-sprung SUVs is that lowering gives the larger share of the gain. Residual Cd penalty versus flap plus lowering is expected at ≈0.002-0.003 and must be confirmed. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric reaches Cd 0.25 in Eco by closing its flaps and lowering the chassis together, which shows how much of the gain comes from ride height.

title: Zonal controllers drive sensor-cleaning valves, deleting the dedicated cleaning ECU
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The standalone sensor-cleaning control unit, its bracket and much of its harness branch are deleted; spare high-side outputs in the front and rear zonal controllers switch the cleaning valves, and the cleaning logic runs as software next to the ADAS availability manager. Baseline: a dedicated sensor-cleaning ECU (≈€32) with six valve drivers, its own CAN node and bracket, sits behind the front bumper and drives camera, lidar and radar-cover cleaning valves through a dedicated harness branch (≈€9). Proposal: the front and rear zonal controllers, which already sit near the valves, get two populated smart high-side drivers each (≈€1.25 per channel); the cleaning strategy (spray timing, fluid budget, freeze lockout, priority per sensor) moves into the zonal software and is triggered by the perception stack's occlusion flags. Harness shrinks to short local runs. Why it works: valve drive is simple PWM/on-off switching at <2 A, which zonal controllers are designed for; the separate ECU mainly added housing, connector and CAN overhead. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 fits a washer sprayer to almost every exterior camera, which is the kind of valve count that makes a central cleaning ECU tempting; we absorb it into the zonal architecture instead.

title: Weld-in towbar nuts on every rear rail delete the tow-body variant and dealer drilling
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate tow-prepared body variant, its framing fixture and logistics, the reinforcement plates in the retrofit kit and most retrofit corrosion claims are removed; every body carries six projection-welded M12 nuts and a small doubler, so a factory or dealer towbar simply bolts on. Baseline: line-fit towbar cars (≈35%) use a tow-prepared rear-rail variant with welded nuts and doublers, built on its own framing fixture program; dealer retrofits (≈15% of cars over life) drill the rails, add reinforcement plates and re-wax the cavities, which leads to cavity-corrosion claims on ≈3% of retrofits. Proposal: all bodies get six M12 projection-welded nuts (property class 10) and two 2 mm HC420LA doublers in the rear rails, e-coated with the body. Plug-caps keep the threads clean until a towbar is fitted. Why it works: the doublers cost ≈€3.2 per body and remove an entire body variant, while the retrofit kit loses its plates, drilling template and wax kit. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender offers an electrically deployable tow bar approved for 3,500 kg and 195 kg nose load as a genuine accessory, which shows the size of the after-sales towbar business our body prep supports.

title: Fixed aero step moulded into sill cover replaces power-deployable running boards
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two motors, linkages, control module and most harness of the power running boards are deleted; a slim fixed step is integrated in a structural sill cover, so the option becomes a moulded part with an extruded tread instead of a mechatronic system. Baseline: the optional power-deployable running boards (≈25% take) use two 12 V motors with worm gears, four-bar linkages per side, extruded aluminium boards and a control module with door-ajar inputs (≈€420 per car). Proposal: a structural sill cover moulded in PP-LGF30 with an integrated 90 mm-deep fixed step, a 6063-T6 extruded tread insert with TPE grip strips, and three steel brackets per side picking up the sill jacking points. The step sits inside the body's plan view and above the sill bottom line, so ground clearance and breakover angle are unchanged. Cost ≈€160 per car. Why it works: a fixed, well-faired step costs a fraction of a deploying one and carries no motors, sensors or anti-trap logic; in aero terms a faired fixed step can be tuned as a side skirt. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ uses fixed running boards instead of power-deployable boards, citing aerodynamics and foot room.

title: Common BIW aperture ring takes an SMC solid top, fixed glass or opening glass
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two roof-skin die sets and a framing variant are never bought; every body is framed with one large roof aperture ring, and the roof closure is a bonded module chosen at trim: fixed glass, opening glass, or a painted SMC solid panel for the minority who want a solid roof. Baseline: three top variants need three BIW solutions: a welded steel skin with bows, a fixed-glass panel on a large aperture flange, and an opening aperture with a cassette ring. That means two extra skin die sets (≈€2.2M) and a framing variant (≈€0.8M). Proposal: the BIW always carries the large aperture ring (side rails, front header, rear header and one bow, all common), and the closure is chosen at trim: fixed glass and opening glass as today, and for the ≈15% who choose a solid top a class-A SMC panel (UP-GF, ≈2.5 mm) painted in body or contrast colour, attached with the same urethane bead path. Why it works: on luxury SUVs the glazed top is the majority choice, so the solid top becomes the low-volume closure, and a low-volume SMC compression tool (≈€0.35M) is far cheaper than steel skin dies; the framing line builds one body. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 fits a fixed, non-opening panoramic glass top with an optional sun shade, showing that a glazed top as the default is accepted in this class.

title: Rear wiper pivots from the roof spoiler, so the backlite needs no drilled hole
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The hole drilled and edge-finished in the tempered backlite, the scrap it causes in tempering, and the grommet, seal nut and cap are deleted; the rear wiper motor moves into the roof-spoiler cavity and the arm sweeps down from the top edge of the glass. Baseline: the rear wiper motor is bolted to the tailgate inner panel and its spindle passes through a 22 mm hole drilled in the 3.85 mm tempered backlite before toughening. The hole needs drilling, edge grinding and stress-relief positioning, causes extra tempering breakage, and needs a grommet, seal nut and cosmetic cap. Proposal: the motor (same 12 V unit) mounts in a PP-GF30 boss in the roof-spoiler cavity under the spoiler's upper skin, and the arm pivots from the spoiler underside, parking hidden under the spoiler lip. The backlite becomes an undrilled tempered panel with heater grid and antenna only. Why it works: spoiler cavities on SUVs are already large, dry and close to the screen top edge; holes in tempered glass are a known cost and breakage driver, so the glass gets cheaper and more robust. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse packages its antenna hardware in the leading edge of the roofline instead of a shark fin, the same idea of hiding function hardware inside roof-edge mouldings; spoiler-mounted rear wipers are general practice in published patents.

title: Dual-bulb body-side aperture seal deletes the tailgate-mounted secondary seal
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 4.8 m tailgate-mounted secondary seal, its adhesive tape and the hand application are deleted; the body-side aperture seal is co-extruded with two sponge bulbs, so one part gives the primary water barrier and the secondary acoustic line. Baseline: the tailgate opening uses a body-side EPDM sponge-bulb weatherstrip on a steel-carrier U-section (5.2 m) and a tailgate-mounted secondary EPDM sponge seal (4.8 m) taped to the tailgate inner, mainly for acoustics and dust. Proposal: one co-extrusion with dense EPDM U-section, a 0.65 g/cm³ outer sponge bulb and a 0.5 g/cm³ inner sponge bulb 12 mm inboard, with moulded corners. Compression load deflection is tuned so that the power-tailgate cinch force and closing effort stay within target. Why it works: both seal lines contact the same tailgate flange; putting them on one carrier removes the second part, its tape and the tolerance stack between tailgate and body. The tailgate inner flange needs only a simplified hem sealer. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S is quoted with a wading depth over three feet, showing the sealing robustness luxury EV SUVs now claim; we keep sealing performance while removing a part.

title: One full-length sunblind spans both panoramic glass panels, deleting a motor
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The second blind motor, the second roller tube and fabric, and the guide-rail joints between the front and rear blind sections are deleted; one 1.75 m blind runs the full length of both glass panels from a single roller at the rear header. Baseline: the two-panel panoramic roof uses separate front and rear roller blinds, each with its own 12 V motor (≈€38), roller, fabric and guide rail section, so occupants can shade each row independently. Proposal: one warp-knit PET blind with a reflective back coating runs the full 1.75 m length from a 34 mm roller behind the rear header, pulled forward by a single up-rated motor (≈€44) via twin cables in continuous rails. Intermediate stops let the blind shade the rear row only (it deploys from the rear header); front-row-only shading, the usual glare request, would need the roller at the front header. A stronger spring and edge-tension beads keep the fabric flat over the length. Why it works: a full-length blind needs one drive, one roller and one set of end stops; partial-row shading is still possible by position. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 fits a fixed panoramic glass roof with the sun shade sold as an option, showing that the shade is a content line worth simplifying.

title: Opening-roof cassette ring moulded in PP-LGF40 replaces the steel weldment
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Six steel stampings, their spot welding, e-coat and the bonded water channel are replaced by one injection-compression moulded long-glass PP ring with the water channel and mechanism bosses moulded in, saving parts, coating and ≈2.6 kg. Baseline: the opening-roof cassette ring is welded from six 0.8 mm DX54D+Z stampings, e-coated, with a bonded PU water channel and clinch nuts for the mechanism rails (≈€58, 6.8 kg). Proposal: one injection-compression moulded PP-LGF40 ring (12 mm fibre pellets) with 2.8 mm walls, a ribbed box section along the sides, moulded water channel and drain spigots, and moulded-in brass M6 inserts for the 6063-T6 guide rails, ≈€41 and 4.2 kg. The ring is bonded to the roof aperture as today. Why it works: the ring carries mechanism and sealing loads, not body loads; LGF-PP keeps its stiffness at the 85-90 °C a dark roof reaches, and moulding removes the weld-coat-seal chain. Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport sells a sliding panoramic roof as an option, the module this frame belongs to; LGF-PP roof frames are general supplier practice.

title: Wheel-arch cladding carries the liner outer flange, deleting foam strips and screws
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Liner rim material, four screws per arch and the foam strip that seals the cladding-to-liner gap are deleted; the cladding is moulded with a return flange that forms the visible arch lip, and the shortened liner snaps into it. Baseline: each arch has a PP-EPDM-T15 cladding (2.8 mm, 9 clips) and a separately screwed wheel-arch liner (PP-T20 front, needle-punched PET rear) whose outer rim is trapped behind the cladding, with a foam strip to close the gap; four screws per arch fix the rim. Proposal: the cladding gets a 60 mm moulded return flange that forms the full arch lip; the liner is trimmed 40 mm shorter and engages the cladding return with four dart clips and a tongue-in-groove. Foam strips and rim screws are deleted. Why it works: two parts that overlap and need sealing become one edge with a positive engagement; the visible arch edge is now one moulded surface with better gap and flush. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 reaches Cd 0.28 with air curtains and a sculpted underbody cover, showing how much attention the wheel-arch flow region gets; a closed, single-edge arch lip helps that region too.

title: Sill cover TPV lip closes the door-bottom gap, deleting four clip-on lower seals
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four clip-on door lower seals and their fitting labour are deleted; a 2K TPV lip co-moulded on each sill cover seals against the door bottom skin, keeping mud and water out of the sill rabbet during wading and muddy use. Baseline: each side door carries a clip-on EPDM sponge lower seal along its bottom edge (≈€6 each) that closes against the sill, plus the sill cover below. Off-road use packs mud into the gap between door skin and sill, and in deep fords the sill rabbet floods. Proposal: each PP-EPDM-T15 sill cover is two-shot moulded with a 64 Shore A TPV lip (12 mm high, 1.6 mm root) that contacts the lower skin of both doors with 2-4 mm interference. The lip sheds spray outward and wipes mud as the door shuts. Why it works: the sill cover is already one continuous part beneath both doors, so a single lip on it replaces two separate seals per side and gives an unbroken line. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 110 is rated to ford 900 mm, which puts the lower door edges below the surface; a continuous lip is a robust way to keep that zone clean.

title: Front tyre spats moulded into the wheel-arch liner, deleting separate deflectors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two separate TPO tyre deflectors, their six push-pins and fitting labour are deleted; the deflector shape is moulded into the front wheel-arch liner with a flexible hinge zone so it still bends back on kerb contact. Baseline: ahead of each front tyre a separate TPO tyre spat (≈€3.5) is fixed with three push-pins to the underbody panel and liner, to cut tyre-wake drag. Proposal: the PP-T20 front liner is extended downward with a spat lobe joined by a co-injected TPE (or unfilled PP copolymer) hinge strip that lets it fold back 60° on contact and spring back (a thinned hinge in talc-filled PP-T20 would crack after few cold folds); a TPE-coinjected tip is used where approach-angle strikes are expected. Shape is tuned in CFD to the same position as today's spat. Why it works: the liner is already located precisely at that spot, so the spat inherits its position; one tool replaces two. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse reaches Cd 0.24 with aero wheels and an air curtain in the front bumper leading edge, showing how much attention the front-wheel flow gets; integrating the spat keeps that flow control at lower part count.

title: Front camera, washer jet and lens heater delivered as one sealed sensor pod
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate washer-jet bracket, jet, its fixings and aiming step and the camera heater lead are deleted; the camera supplier delivers a pod whose housing carries the fluid channel, a fan jet at the lens edge and the heater pins in the camera connector, fixed by one bracket. Baseline: the forward surround-view camera is clipped into its own PP bracket, a washer jet sits on a second bracket aimed at the lens and is adjusted at end of line, and the lens-cover heater has its own two-pin lead; three suppliers, four fixings and an aiming step meet at one small sensor. Proposal: one sealed pod in PA66-GF30: the camera module, a moulded internal fluid channel ending in a flat fan jet 6 mm from the lens edge (spray angle set by the tool, so no aiming), a printed heater on the lens cover and heater pins added to the camera's existing connector. The pod clips to a single bracket with two snap features and one screw, and its hose port is a push-fit. Why it works: lens-to-jet geometry is fixed in one moulding instead of a tolerance chain across two brackets and the fascia, so spray coverage is repeatable and no adjustment is needed. Benchmark: the 2025 Tesla Model Y added a front bumper camera fitted with its own washer sprayer, carried over from the Cybertruck, showing that forward cameras now need cleaning hardware.

title: Towbar receiver doubles as a rated rear recovery point on tow-pack cars
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] On tow-pack cars the separate forged rear recovery eye, its rail bracket and fitting are deleted; the towbar receiver is sized and certified as the rear recovery point, with a recovery pin in the tool kit, so one strong node does both jobs. Baseline: every car has a forged 42CrMo4 rear recovery eye (≈€26) bolted through its own bracket to the rear rail, and tow-pack cars also carry the towbar receiver bolted to the towbar beam. Proposal: on tow-pack cars (≈35%) the receiver casting or forging (38MnVS6 microalloyed forging) is sized for a recovery load of 1.5 × GVW at ±30° horizontal and 15° vertical, with a 19 mm cross-pin hole for a soft shackle or recovery pin supplied in the tool kit. Non-tow cars keep the eye. Why it works: the towbar load path (receiver → beam → rail nuts) is already designed for 3,500 kg dynamic tow loads; recovery loads (1.5 × GVW ≈ 45-50 kN) are about three times the towbar D-value (≈17 kN at 3,500 kg), so the receiver, beam, beam-to-rail bolts and rail nuts must all be rated for them, not only the receiver. Benchmark: Land Rover approves its electrically deployable Defender tow bar for 3,500 kg and 195 kg nose load; we extend that rated node to recovery duty.
