title: BEV washer reservoir blow-moulded as the frunk tub side wall
description: [800V BEV] On the 800V BEV, the reservoir's three brackets, one section of the frunk tub wall and most of the filler neck are deleted; the reservoir is blow-moulded with a class-B flat face that forms the frunk side wall and fills at the frunk lip. Baseline: the BEV front compartment holds an injection-moulded PP-T20 frunk tub, and the 4.5-6 L HDPE washer reservoir sits beside it on three brackets with a 600 mm filler neck to a filler under the bonnet. Proposal: an extrusion blow-moulded HDPE reservoir (with a textured, flat face toward the frunk) forms the frunk side wall; the tub is shortened and seals to the reservoir face with a TPE lip. The filler moves to the frunk opening lip, so the neck is 150 mm. Why it works: the reservoir is a large hollow part anyway; making one face of it the frunk wall replaces a section of tub and its brackets. More camera washers on luxury EVs push reservoir size up, so a wall-integrated reservoir finds volume without extra packaging space. Benchmark: the 2025 Tesla Model Y added a front bumper camera with its own washer sprayer, one example of rising washer demand per car.

title: Hydrophobic sensor window sprayed by wiper-arm jets deletes its dedicated washer
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The lidar's own solenoid valve, high-pressure nozzle and the 4 m line routed up the A-pillar are deleted; a fluorinated hydrophobic hard coat on the lidar window sheds water, and an extra orifice in the wiper-arm jet reaches the window for dirt. Baseline: cars with the header-mounted laser scanner (assume 40% take) carry a dedicated 2.5 bar nozzle aimed at its window, a solenoid valve and ≈4 m of hose routed up the A-pillar and across the header (≈€13.6 with labour). Proposal: the polycarbonate scanner window gets a fluorinated silane topcoat over its abrasion hard coat (water contact angle >105°), so rain beads and blows off at speed; for dirt, the wiper-arm jet gains a third, upward-aimed orifice that reaches the window at the top of the stroke. A fine-wire heater outside the optical aperture keeps ice off. Why it works: at road speed most soiling of that window is water film, which a hydrophobic surface clears; the arm jet already sweeps an arc that can reach the header. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 sprays its header-mounted lidar with the nozzles carried on the windscreen wiper arms, so it needs no separate washer for that sensor.

title: Single-piece flexible TPE wind deflector replaces mesh pop-up deflector
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The mesh fabric, its plastic frame, two spring-steel bows and two pivot arms of the pop-up wind deflector are replaced by one injection-moulded TPE profile whose shape springs up when the glass slides back and lies flat under the glass edge when it closes. Baseline: the opening roof's wind deflector is a mesh fabric stretched on a PA6 frame, raised by two spring-steel bows on pivot arms when the front glass opens (≈€19 with assembly). Proposal: one 1.0 m TPE (SEBS-based TPS, 70 Shore A) moulding with a perforated or slotted upper lip and a living-spring S-section; when the glass moves rearward the section unloads and rises 35 mm, and the closing glass edge presses it flat into the frame gutter. Ends clip into the frame. Why it works: the deflector only needs to trip the boundary layer at the aperture leading edge; a tuned elastomer lip does that without a mechanism, and it cannot jam or rattle. For roofs that only tilt, the deflector can be deleted altogether (see the tilt-only idea; the two are alternatives). Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport sells the sliding panoramic roof as an option, the module this deflector serves.

title: PA6-GF50 wiper linkage frame replaces welded steel tube frame
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The steel tube, stamped pivot housings, welding, zinc plating and pivot machining of the wiper frame are replaced by one glass-filled polyamide moulding with over-moulded steel inserts at the motor mount, saving ≈1 kg and several process steps. Baseline: the wiper linkage frame is a 25×1.5 mm E235 steel tube with two stamped pivot housings and a motor plate MIG-welded on, zinc-plated, with machined pivot bores (≈€16.5, 2.1 kg). Proposal: one PA6-GF50 injection moulding with box-rib section, moulded pivot housings carrying sintered bronze bushes, and an over-moulded DC04 steel plate at the motor mount to take motor reaction torque and three M6 inserts for body fixing (≈€11.2 incl. inserts, 1.1 kg). Why it works: frame loads are moderate (blade stall torque on snow, ≈30 N·m at the motor); PA6-GF50 has adequate stiffness and fatigue strength at plenum temperatures, and the moulding replaces weld-plate-machine steps. A plastic frame also deforms more benignly in pedestrian head impact over the cowl. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 carries washer nozzles on its wiper arms, showing that wiper hardware is being given extra functions; a moulded frame can host the washer manifold clips too.

title: BEV rear underbody panel in GMT doubles as the rear EDU stone guard
description: [800V BEV] The separate aluminium stone-guard plate under the rear EDU and its brackets are deleted; the rear underbody aero panel is moulded in GMT with local thickening under the EDU, so one part provides both the closed floor and the stone protection. Baseline: the 800V BEV rear underbody has a PP-T20 aero panel (≈€11) cut around a separate 2 mm 5754-H22 aluminium stone guard under the rear EDU (≈€19) on three brackets. Proposal: one compression-moulded GMT panel (PP-GF40, 3.5 mm general, 6 mm under the EDU sump and inverter) spanning the rear subframe, with NACA-type relief for EDU oil-cooler airflow if needed. Why it works: stone impacts under a road car are low-energy (gravel at speed), which 6 mm GMT absorbs; the closed panel also improves underfloor flow. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric uses a flat floor closed even in the rear-axle area with flexible underbody covers; we give that closed panel the protection role too.

title: Sloped press-hardened glancer at the pack front edge lets BEV pack shield downgauge
description: [800V BEV] The pack bottom shield can drop from 3.0 to 2.0 mm aluminium over most of its area because the most severe strikes, at the pack's leading edge, are deflected by a sloped press-hardened steel glancer, so less aluminium is bought while protection where it matters improves. Baseline: the 800V BEV pack has a 3.0 mm 6061-T6 aluminium bottom shield over ≈1.9 m², sized for the worst case of a bollard, kerb or rock hitting the pack front edge and sliding under. Proposal: a 15° sloped glancer in 1.5 mm 22MnB5 Al-Si press-hardened steel (≈1,500 MPa) ahead of the pack front edge, bolted to the front subframe and pack front flange, lifts the car over obstacles and spreads the load; behind it the shield drops to 2.0 mm 6061-T6 with pressed swage ribs. Why it works: the leading edge is where an obstacle first meets the pack, so a glancer there deflects the most concentrated hits; behind it the 2.0 mm shield must still pass the bottom-impact tests on its own, because GB 38031-2025 and OEM drop tests strike any point on the pack bottom. Spending steel at the edge and saving aluminium over the area is cheaper and better targeted. Benchmark: the Mercedes G 580 protects its battery with 26 mm-thick underbody protection in a material mix that includes carbon, about 58 kg, which shows how much the off-road BEV case can cost when one material does everything.

title: Longitudinal bar extrusion carries a TPE gutter lip, deleting the finisher strip
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] On cars fitted with raised rails, the separate roof-ditch finisher strips and their installation are deleted; the rail base extrusion carries a TPE lip insert that closes the roof ditch along its length, so the rail and the finisher become one subassembly. Baseline: every car has a co-extruded TPV/PVC finisher strip (≈€7 per side) pushed into the gutter between top panel and body side, and cars with raised bars then fit the bars over it, so most of the strip is hidden. Proposal: the 6063-T6 bar base extrusion gets a T-slot holding a TPE (SEBS, 75 Shore A) lip strip fitted by the supplier; the lip closes the gutter between the feet, and short moulded end caps finish the gutter beyond the bar. Cars without bars keep the strip. Why it works: on those cars the strip's job is mostly done by the bar already; a lip on the bar closes the remaining gap with less material and no separate fitting. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 110 rates 300 kg static and 168 kg dynamic loading with its Expedition rack, showing that bars on a luxury off-roader are load hardware first; here the bar also does the trim job.

title: Two-shot PA6-GF50 roof-rail foot replaces zinc die-cast foot and snap cover
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four zinc die-cast rail feet, their PC/ABS snap covers and separate gaskets become four two-shot PA6-GF50 feet with a moulded-in stainless insert and an integral TPE gasket, cutting material and the cover-fitting step. Baseline: each raised roof rail has two ZAMAK 5 (EN 12844 ZP0410) die-cast feet (≈€3.8 each) with a separate PC/ABS cosmetic cover (€0.9), a foam/EPDM gasket (€0.4) and two M8 screws into the roof nuts. Proposal: a two-shot injection moulding: PA6-GF50 black mould-in-colour body with a moulded-in A2-70 stainless M8 threaded insert, and a TPE (SEBS 60 Shore A) gasket shot onto the base (≈€2.4 per foot). The cosmetic surface is grained or high-gloss from the tool, so no cover. Why it works: the foot carries roof-load crossbar forces as compression and bending into the insert; PA6-GF50 at 50% glass gives the stiffness and creep resistance needed at roof temperatures, and the stainless insert carries the thread. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 110 rates its roof at 300 kg static and 168 kg dynamic with its Expedition Roof Rack, the level of roof loading a rail foot design must be validated against.

title: Panoramic roof glass laminate thinned to 2.6/0.76/1.6 mm heat-strengthened plies
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Less float glass is bought and bent per roof, and the roof sheds ≈5 kg at the highest point of the car, by moving from 3.15/2.1 mm plies to a heat-strengthened 2.6 mm outer and 1.6 mm inner ply with the same PVB. Baseline: the large fixed panoramic roof (≈1.8 m², fitted to ≈85% of cars) is laminated 3.15 mm outer + 0.76 mm PVB + 2.1 mm inner soda-lime, annealed and gravity-bent, ≈24 kg. Proposal: 2.6 mm heat-strengthened outer ply (surface compression 30-50 MPa, EN 1863) + 0.76 mm PVB + 1.6 mm inner ply, the outer ply bent and heat-strengthened singly on a press-bend and quench line and the inner ply matched to it (a heat-strengthened ply cannot be pair-bent). Glass mass falls ≈4.7 kg (1.05 mm × 2.5 kg/m²/mm × 1.8 m²). Two extra bonded PU support pads at mid-span on the cross bows keep deflection under wind and snow load inside today's limit. Why it works: heat-strengthening raises the outer ply's resistance to hail and stone impacts, while thinner glass is cheaper per square metre and lighter to bend and ship. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 uses a fixed, non-opening panoramic glass roof; thinner roof laminates are general glazing-supplier practice, with thin plies already used in windscreens.

title: Bonnet-to-scuttle seal co-moulded on the scuttle panel as a 2K TPV lip
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The push-on EPDM sponge seal between bonnet and scuttle and its hand fitting are deleted; a TPV lip is two-shot moulded onto the PP-T20 upper scuttle panel, so the seal comes with the panel. Baseline: a 1.4 m EPDM sponge-bulb seal on a U-clip is pushed by hand onto the scuttle flange to seal the bonnet rear edge against water and air recirculation into the HVAC intake (≈€4.8 + 0.6 min). Proposal: the PP-T20 upper scuttle panel is moulded on a rotary 2K tool with a 70 Shore A TPV (PP/EPDM) hollow-lip profile bonded along its front edge; the TPV bonds to PP chemically, so no adhesive. Why it works: the scuttle panel already runs the full width under the bonnet edge; making the seal part of it removes a part and gives a consistent seal line set by the tool. Keeping water out of the plenum also protects the HVAC intake during deep-water driving. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 110 is rated to wade 900 mm, which makes cowl and plenum water management a real design load for luxury off-roaders.

title: Tongue-and-slot underbody panel edges cut fasteners from 46 to 24
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Twenty-two plastic nuts and quarter-turn fasteners and their overhead fitting time are deleted because adjacent underbody panels interlock at their joints, one panel's tongue sliding under the next panel's lip and held by snap hooks. Baseline: five underbody aero panels are held by 46 fasteners (plastic speed nuts, quarter-turns and screws, ≈€0.18 each), with joints overlapping flat and each panel fixed independently around its perimeter, needing ≈6 s per overhead fastener. Proposal: joints between neighbouring panels become a 20 mm tongue-and-slot with two snap hooks per joint, panels are fitted in a fixed sequence (front to rear), and only the outer perimeter and service openings keep fasteners: 24 in total. Why it works: shared joints only need to resist flutter and peel, which the tongue and hooks carry; the outer edge carries the panel weight and air loads. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 reaches Cd 0.28 with a 3D-sculpted underbody cover, which shows that fully covered underbodies are standard on luxury EVs and fastener count is a significant cost of them.

title: UHMW-PE glide runners on a 4 mm aluminium skid replace a 6 mm plate
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A third of the aluminium in the front skid plate is removed because two riveted UHMW-PE runners take the sliding and abrasion along the strike lines, and pressed swage ribs restore the bending stiffness that the thicker plate gave. Baseline: the off-road pack front skid is a 6 mm 5083-H111 plate (≈0.9 m², 14.4 kg, ≈€94 material). Proposal: a 4 mm 5083-H111 plate (9.6 kg) press-formed with three longitudinal swage ribs, plus two 8 mm PE-UHMW (ISO 11542, molecular weight >5×10⁶ g/mol) glide runners riveted with countersunk stainless rivets along the lines where rocks contact the plate. The runners present a low-friction (μ ≈0.15-0.2 on rock) sacrificial surface so the car slides off obstacles rather than gouging and hanging up; worn runners are replaceable. Why it works: thickness in a skid plate mostly buys dent resistance and abrasion life; ribs restore stiffness and the runners give abrasion life at a fraction of the aluminium cost. Benchmark: the Toyota Land Cruiser 250 ships a plastic factory front skid which aftermarket suppliers replace with 3/16 in (4.8 mm) aluminium, showing that 4-5 mm aluminium is the accepted off-road gauge.

title: Breakaway fir-tree fixings on the cladding lower edge survive off-road strikes
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Twelve screws with U-nuts and four internal anti-tear brackets on the cladding lower edge are deleted; defined-pull-out fir-tree clips in replaceable PA6 carriers let the cladding pop off on a rock or rut strike and be pushed back on, so neither the cladding nor the body flange is damaged. Baseline: the lower edges of the wheel-arch claddings and sill-adjacent cladding are fixed with 12 screws and spring U-nuts, backed by four stamped steel anti-tear brackets inside the cladding; an off-road strike tears clip towers or cracks the cladding, and it must be replaced. Proposal: lower-edge fixings become PA66 fir-tree clips with a designed pull-out force of 160-200 N into replaceable PA6 clip carriers on the body flange; upper edges keep their fixed hooks so the cladding hinges down rather than detaching. The anti-tear brackets are no longer needed. Why it works: the load that damages cladding in off-road use is a short, high-displacement event; a part that releases and re-seats survives it, while aero loads at 250 km/h stay well below the pull-out force. Benchmark: the Toyota Land Cruiser 250 has a 32° approach and 22° departure angle, typical of the class, which still puts the lower cladding edges in reach of ruts and rocks.

title: 48 V supply for the MHEV heated windscreen cuts cable, relay and busbar copper
description: [MHEV] On the MHEV, the 50 A 12 V heated-windscreen feed is replaced by a 12.5 A 48 V feed, so the 6 mm² cable becomes 1.5 mm², the relay and fuse become a zonal 48 V switch, and the glass busbars and connectors carry a quarter of the current. Baseline: the wire-heated windscreen (fine tungsten wires, ≈600 W) runs at 12 V, drawing ≈50 A through ≈3 m of 6 mm² cable each way, a 60 A relay and fuse, and wide silver/copper busbars with heavy-duty tabs. Proposal: on the MHEV, feed the screen from the 48 V board net through a smart high-side switch in the front zonal controller. Power stays at 600 W, so current is 12.5 A: 1.5 mm² cable, smaller tabs and narrower busbars. The wire pattern is re-designed for 16× resistance (finer, longer wires in series-parallel groups), which the glass supplier sets in the same wire-laying process. 48 V stays below the 60 V DC protective-measure threshold, so no HV touch protection is needed. Why it works: resistive heating does not care about voltage, but cable and switch cost scale with current. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender is sold with 48 V D MHEV powertrains, the kind of luxury off-roader whose 48 V net makes this possible.

title: One-piece PA6-GF50 wiper arm with in-arm washer channel replaces zinc head and steel rail
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The zinc die-cast arm head, the stamped steel rail and their powder coating are replaced by one glass-filled polyamide moulding per arm that also contains the washer fluid channel, so the arm costs less and carries the washer function itself. Baseline: each front wiper arm is a ZAMAK die-cast head riveted to a stamped steel rail with a tension spring, powder coated black (≈€9.5 per arm with spring), with washer jets separately on the bonnet. Proposal: a one-piece PA6-GF50 arm (head and rail) with a moulded internal 2.5 mm fluid channel ending in two fluidic jets at the blade adaptor; the steel spring and a steel insert at the spline remain. The arm is mould-in-colour black with a textured finish. Why it works: arms are stiffness-led; PA6-GF50 with a U-section of increased depth matches the steel rail's bending stiffness, and the moulded channel removes external hoses on the arm. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 places washer nozzles on its wiper arms, which also spray the roof lidar; Mercedes MAGIC VISION CONTROL delivers fluid through the arms and blade and is reported to use up to 50% less fluid.

title: Sill cover lower lip replaces separate underbody side strakes
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two separate PP side-strake panels, their clips and fitting are deleted; the sill cover is moulded with a 30 mm inboard lower lip that controls the floor-edge airflow the strakes used to manage. Baseline: two PP-T20 side strakes (≈€4.5 each, six clips) run along the underbody edge inboard of the sill to stop side flow entering under the floor. Proposal: the PP-EPDM-T15 sill cover gets a 30 mm horizontal lip along its lower edge, turning inboard under the sill flange, with the same edge height as today's strake. The lip is flexible enough to yield on contact. Ramp breakover and ground clearance stay the same because the lip sits within the sill's existing lowest line. Why it works: the strake and the sill cover sit within 40 mm of each other; extending the sill cover reaches the same edge and removes a joint that leaked air anyway. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 attributes its Cd 0.28 partly to a 3D-sculpted underbody cover, showing the value of controlling floor-edge flow on a large SUV.

title: Printed silver camera-window heater on the windscreen replaces bracket PTC heater
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The PTC heater element clipped into the ADAS camera bracket and most of its separate harness lead are deleted; a silver heater track printed on the inner ply around the camera window, fed through the windscreen's existing connector, keeps the camera field clear. Baseline: the forward ADAS camera bracket holds a PTC heater pad (≈€4.2) pressed against the glass behind the camera field of view, with its own lead and connector to the harness. Proposal: the glass supplier prints a silver-paste heater track (≈8 W, 12 V) on the inner surface of the inner ply around the camera aperture, in the black frit zone, fired during bending, with a soldered tab next to the rain-sensor connector; the camera bracket loses its heater pocket. Why it works: printed heater grids are routine on backlites and in wiper park zones; heating the glass directly is more efficient than conducting heat through a pad. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 relies on its windscreen and wipers to keep its forward sensors usable, with the wiper-arm nozzles also spraying the roof lidar; keeping the camera window clear is the same requirement.

title: Aluminised-fleece underbody panel takes over most of the MHEV exhaust heat shield
description: [MHEV] The separate centre underbody aero panel is deleted and the embossed aluminium exhaust heat shield shrinks to the hot zone only; a compression-moulded PET/glass fleece panel with an aluminium foil face does both jobs elsewhere. Baseline: on the MHEV, an embossed 0.5 mm aluminium heat shield (≈€14) runs along the exhaust tunnel under the floor, and a separate PP aero panel (≈€7) is cut around it. Proposal: one compression-moulded PET/glass fleece panel (1,600 g/m²) with a 50 μm embossed aluminium foil face covering the tunnel and floor beyond 150 mm from the pipe surface; the metal shield is kept only over the catalyst and the hottest 600 mm of pipe (≈€6). Fixings fall from 12 to 4. Why it works: beyond about 150 mm from the pipe, radiant and convective heat flux are low enough for foil-faced fleece, which is already used for underfloor acoustic shields; it is also aerodynamically smooth. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric runs a flat, fully closed floor with flexible underbody covers; our MHEV gets the same closed floor while keeping heat protection.

title: Washer reservoir downsized from 6 to 4 litres with wiper-arm jets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A smaller blow-moulded reservoir, a smaller bracket and less factory-fill fluid are bought, because spraying from the wiper arm right in front of the blade wastes much less fluid than bonnet jets do, so the same refill interval needs less volume. Baseline: the platform reservoir is a 6 L HDPE blow moulding sized for bonnet jets plus camera cleaning, filled with ≈3 L at EOL. Proposal: with washer jets on the wiper arms (as in the cowl-module and arm ideas), fluid is placed in front of the blade instead of over-spraying the glass and the roof, so windscreen fluid use per wash falls. The reservoir drops to 4 L, the bracket shrinks and EOL fill drops to ≈2 L; camera cleaning volumes are budgeted separately. Why it works: refill interval is set by fluid per wash × washes; cutting the first term keeps the interval with less volume. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 places its washer nozzles on its wiper arms; Mercedes MAGIC VISION CONTROL feeds fluid through the arms to the blade edge and is reported to cut fluid use by up to 50%.

ideaData.title: Washer reservoir downsized from 6 to 4 litres with wiper-arm jets
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: the platform reservoir is a 6 L HDPE blow moulding sized for bonnet jets plus camera cleaning, filled with ≈3 L at EOL. Proposal: with washer jets on the wiper arms (as in the cowl-module and arm ideas), fluid is placed in front of the blade instead of over-spraying the glass and the roof, so windscreen fluid use per wash falls. The reservoir drops to 4 L, the bracket shrinks and EOL fill drops to ≈2 L; camera cleaning volumes are budgeted separately. Why it works: refill interval is set by fluid per wash × washes; cutting the first term keeps the interval with less volume. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 places its washer nozzles on its wiper arms; Mercedes MAGIC VISION CONTROL feeds fluid through the arms to the blade edge and is reported to cut fluid use by up to 50%.
ideaData.costReductionMechanism: A smaller blow-moulded reservoir, a smaller bracket and less factory-fill fluid are bought, because spraying from the wiper arm right in front of the blade wastes much less fluid than bonnet jets do, so the same refill interval needs less volume.
ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Smaller blow-moulding parison and tool insert; EOL fill program changed. Reservoir supplier changes the parison programme and EOL fill volume and a tool insert, so the main mould is reused and changeover costs stay low.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Same filler neck, pump and level-sensor positions, so the BEV and MHEV packaging is unchanged; 2 kg less fluid mass at the front. Filler, pump, level sensor and bracket interfaces stay in the same positions as on the 6 L part.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: Low – small saving that follows from arm-mounted jets
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Reservoir €8.5 → €6.6 (−€1.9), EOL fill €1.5 → €1.0 (−€0.5), bracket €0.6 → €0.4 (−€0.2), minus spray-pattern recalibration €0.1. Net €2.5. Low €1.8 if camera volume needs 4.5 L; high €2.6 central case. Net €1.8-€2.6 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €90K-€130K per year (engineering estimate; tooling amortised over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: Refill interval perceived as shorter in winter with camera cleaning. Validate with a fluid-consumption duty cycle (winter salt road, camera cleaning included), customer clinic of refill interval, freeze tests, and UN R94 / R137 frontal crash (smaller part only helps). Engineering review (8 Oct 2026) — open point: The idea only works if ieb-50e5f438ef6e or ieb-a7ed45da866e (arm jets) is adopted, and 'up to 50%' fluid saving is a best case. It also runs against rising camera-cleaning demand (ieb-84a95d31456f).
ideaData.benchmarkReference: Inspired by / benchmarked against: Volvo EX90 (2024-2025) — Roof-header lidar above the windscreen whose protective screen is sprayed by the washer nozzles carried on the windscreen wiper arms. How this differs: Volvo uses arm nozzles for coverage; we take the fluid saving that arm delivery brings and shrink the reservoir.

title: PA6-GF30 towbar socket bracket with moulded cable clip replaces stamped steel bracket
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The stamped, e-coated steel bracket for the 13-pin trailer socket, its separate cable clip and cover are replaced by one PA6-GF30 moulding with the socket mount, cable clip and drip edge built in. Baseline: the 13-pin socket (ISO 11446) sits on a 2 mm stamped S235 bracket (≈€4.5) bolted to the towbar beam, e-coated, with a separate cable P-clip and a plastic cover (≈€1.2). Proposal: one PA6-GF30 injection moulding (≈€2.0) with a three-screw socket face, a moulded cable clip and a drip edge, held by one M8 bolt and an anti-rotation tab on the beam. Why it works: the socket bracket carries only plug insertion and cable loads (a few hundred newtons); glass-filled PA handles that with no corrosion protection needed. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender's electrically deployable tow bar, approved for 3,500 kg and 195 kg nose load, is offered as a genuine accessory, which is the towbar family this bracket serves.

title: Silicone duckbill check valves insert-moulded into each cleaning nozzle body
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Eight inline check valves and sixteen extra hose connections are deleted; a liquid-silicone duckbill is insert-moulded into each nozzle body, so every nozzle holds its own column of fluid and fires immediately. Baseline: each camera, lidar and screen nozzle (assume eight on a well-equipped car) has an inline check valve (≈€0.55) spliced into its feed hose with two barbed connectors (≈€0.2), to stop the line draining back and delaying the spray. Proposal: each PA66-GF30 nozzle body is moulded around an LSR duckbill (Shore A 50, opening pressure 0.2-0.3 bar) seated at its inlet, so the nozzle and valve are one part (≈€0.32 added per nozzle). Why it works: the check valve only needs to sit somewhere between pump and outlet; putting it at the outlet holds the whole line full and removes two joints per nozzle, which are also leak points. Benchmark: the Volvo EX90 gives almost every exterior camera its own small washer sprayer, which multiplies the number of nozzles and check valves on the car.

title: Low-profile 22 mm roof-rail section replaces 45 mm raised rail extrusion
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A smaller aluminium extrusion section with less anodised area is bought for rail-equipped cars, and the lower rail reduces frontal area and wind noise; crossbar clamp feet are redesigned to grip the lower section. Baseline: rail-equipped cars (≈45%) use a 45 mm-high hollow 6063-T6 rail extrusion, bright anodised, about 2.4 kg per pair of aluminium. Proposal: a 22 mm-high, 38 mm-wide 6063-T6 section with an internal web and a T-groove on the inboard face for crossbar clamps; aluminium ≈1.7 kg per pair and anodised area ≈20% lower. Rail feet (2K PA, see the foot idea) keep their spacing. Why it works: rail section height is mostly styling; the crossbar clamp only needs a grip face and a groove, which a lower section provides, and roof loads pass through the feet. Benchmark: on the Kia EV9, the GT-Line's larger roof rails raise overall height from 1,755 mm to 1,780 mm, showing that rail size is a styling variable with a visible packaging and frontal-area cost.

title: Extruded-on-glass TPE seal on the sliding panel replaces push-on frame seal
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 3.6 m push-on EPDM perimeter seal of the opening front glass panel and its hand fitting are deleted; a TPE profile is extruded by robot directly onto the panel edge at the glass supplier, so the seal arrives on the glass at its final position. Baseline: the sliding front panel of the optional opening panoramic top seals against a push-on EPDM sponge-bulb profile on a steel-carrier U-clip, fitted by hand around the cassette opening (3.6 m, ≈€7.9, ≈0.8 min) with a moulded corner joint. Proposal: a 65 Shore A TPE (SEBS-based) hollow-bulb profile is extruded directly onto the primed glass edge by a robot-guided nozzle die (extruded-on-glass, EOG), with the start-stop joint closed by a short in-situ moulded patch. The profile bonds to the glass primer, needs no carrier, and its position relative to the glass edge is set by the robot path rather than by hand. Why it works: the panel moves, so a seal that travels with it sees the same compression all round; EOG removes the carrier, the corner mould and the plant fitting step, and TPE scrap is regrindable. Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport sells a sliding panoramic top as an option over the fixed one, the module whose moving-panel seal this changes; EOG profiles are established glazing-supplier practice on fixed glass.

ideaData.title: BEV charge inlet sits in the MHEV fuel-filler aperture behind one common flap module
ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: MHEV refuels through a rear-right quarter flap (PP bucket, hinge, push-push latch, locking actuator); BEV charges through a separate powered flap in the front-left wing. That means a wing variant with a pierced and flanged aperture, a quarter with or without filler hole, two flap modules, and for BEV a DC charge cable running about 2.6 m from the front wing to a high-voltage junction at the rear of the pack (rear-EDU side). Proposal: both powertrains use the rear-right quarter aperture and one flap module (hinge, powered latch, actuator, LED); only the bucket insert differs – filler-neck seat for MHEV, CCS2 inlet housing with drain spigot for BEV. Packaging check: a CCS2 inlet face is about 95 × 140 mm including latch, so the common flap opening is set at 130 × 165 mm (fuel alone needs about 110 × 140), +39% area; a pressed flange ring and the bucket rim keep the 0.8 mm quarter panel’s oil-canning margin (local E·t³ restored by the 3-sided flange). Cable check: DC run shortens from 2.6 to 1.4 m; at 2 × 70 mm² shielded 800 V cable (≈€9/m per conductor) that is 2 × 1.2 × 9 = €21.6 per BEV, and 2 × 1.2 m × 70 mm² × 8.96 g/cm³ ≈ 1.5 kg of copper. Crash: the MHEV filler already lives in this zone; DC pins are dead except when the pack charge contactors close during charging, and AC pins are isolated behind the OBC, so post-rear-impact electrical safety is held by design. Why it works: the filler and inlet are both a hole, a door and a bucket – only the bucket content is powertrain-specific. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 places its CCS inlet on the rear right, where the petrol X3 has its fuel flap.

title: Non-dimming heated convex glass on the passenger mirror; electrochromic kept on driver side
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The passenger exterior mirror changes from electrochromic to heated, blue-tinted chrome convex glass, and its EC drive wires and pins are deleted; the driver mirror and interior mirror keep electrochromic dimming, where headlamp glare actually matters. Baseline: both exterior mirrors carry electrochromic (EC) heated glass, about €21.5 each, driven from the interior mirror over two extra wires per door. Proposal: passenger side gets heated chrome convex glass with a blue anti-glare tint (≈€6.0, reflectance ≈50%, above the 40% minimum of UN R46), driver side unchanged. Glare check: a convex mirror of R = 1,400 mm (f = 0.7 m) images a headlamp 20 m behind at magnification m = f/(u + f) ≈ 0.034, so the image intensity falls by m² ≈ 0.00115 and the virtual image sits ≈0.68 m behind the glass. Illuminance at the eye E ∝ ρ·m²/(v + u′)²: passenger mirror with eye distance v ≈ 1.2 m → 0.00115/1.88² ≈ 3.3e-4; driver mirror (also convex in Europe) v ≈ 0.6 m → 0.00115/1.28² ≈ 7.0e-4, so the passenger mirror delivers ≈47% of the driver mirror’s glare illuminance. It also sits ≈45° off the line of sight against ≈30° for the driver mirror, and veiling glare falls roughly with 1/θ², giving (0.47) × (30/45)² ≈ 0.21: passenger-side disability glare is about a fifth of the driver side’s, and lower still against the flat interior mirror. Why it works: dimming is valuable where the glare is, and the passenger mirror’s geometry already suppresses most of it. It also sits ≈45° off the line of sight against ≈30° for the driver mirror, and veiling glare falls roughly with 1/θ², giving (0.47) × (30/45)² ≈ 0.21: passenger-side disability glare is about a fifth of the driver side’s, and lower still against the flat interior mirror. Why it works: dimming is valuable where the glare is, and the passenger mirror’s geometry already suppresses most of it. Benchmark: BMW deleted the automatically dimming function from the passenger exterior mirror on the X5 while keeping it on the driver’s mirror and the interior mirror; G05 X5 parts listings show EC glass on the driver side.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Passenger glass becomes a non-electrical part, removing the mis-connection mode of the EC pigtail; the door harness passenger variant loses two circuits and one connector cavity, and the glass is fully interchangeable on the same backing plate.

title: One seat domain controller per front seat absorbs memory, climate and massage ECUs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three controller housings, three MCUs and supplies and about six connectors per seat are deleted; the single domain controller costs less than the sum of the modules it replaces, and in-seat circuits and the EOL test time fall because all drivers sit on one board. Baseline: each luxury front seat carries three or four separate controllers – a memory-seat module with six to eight motor H-bridges, a seat-climate module PWM-driving two heater mats and a vent blower, a pneumatic lumbar/massage ECU built onto the pump, and discrete belt-reminder and occupancy wiring – each with its own housing, MCU, transceiver, supply filter and connector, roughly €80 of controller electronics per seat (bridge: €158 for two seats) and about 40 in-seat circuits. Proposal: one seat domain controller (SDC) under the cushion pan: a 32-bit automotive MCU, an eight-half-bridge motor pre-driver with current sensing (enabling ripple-count position), two high-side PWM heater channels, one blower PWM output and a LIN master for a valve-only pneumatic slave; one CAN-FD link to the body zone controller. The pump keeps its valves but loses its MCU board. Why it works: the separate ECUs duplicate power supply, MCU, protection, housing and connectors; one PCBA (FR4, 4-layer, PA66-GF30 housing) carries the same driver silicon with one supply and one connector, and in-seat routing shortens because drivers sit in one place. Benchmark: the Cadillac Escalade IQ Executive Second Row package combines heating, ventilation, 10-point massage, 14-way adjustment and power lumbar/bolster in a single seat

title: Contact-heating-first BEV climate mode trims HV PTC air heater from 7 to 5.5 kW
description: [800V BEV] The HV PTC heater shrinks one power step (7 → 5.5 kW) with a smaller HV fuse and lighter HV cable; the added cost is two heated armrest pads and a calibration loop, both far cheaper than the PTC power removed, and winter range improves as a side effect. Baseline: the 800V BEV pairs an R1234yf heat pump with a 7 kW HV PTC air heater sized for cold soak below −10 °C, while heated seats and wheel are treated as independent comfort options, so cabin air must reach 22 °C before occupants feel warm. Proposal: on BEV trims where heated front and second-row seats and the heated wheel are already standard (the bridge prices only the added armrest pads – if any of this content is optional today its cost must be added), add heated front armrests (≈0.45 kW combined contact heating) and calibrate a contact-first climate mode: below 0 °C the air set point runs 2-3 K lower for the first 20 minutes while contact surfaces deliver comfort, the heat pump covers more operating points and the HV PTC is resized to 5.5 kW – sized by the windscreen defrost case of EU 672/2010 at −18 °C rather than by cabin warm-up. Why it works: contact heating delivers perceived comfort at roughly a tenth of the power of air heating because heat goes straight to the occupant; once the occupant is warm, the residual PTC duty is defrost, which needs less power than full cabin warm-up. Benchmark: the BMW iX offers radiant interior surface heating with heated armrests and 3-stage steering heating as part of its climate concept.

title: Thermal-comfort layer laminated onto trim cover at the cover sewer, not the seat line
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Hand layup and spray adhesive at the seat line are removed, three part streams become one, and the consolidated thermal content is bought from one source at a better price; the added lamination step at the cover supplier costs less than the layup it replaces. Baseline: heated and ventilated seats are built up at the seat assembly line from separately sourced layers – a CuNi wire heater on non-woven, a 3D polyester spacer-fabric vent plenum, an NTC sensor and a scrim – each placed and spray-glued onto the PU foam pad by hand, about six minutes per seat, with three suppliers, three packaging streams and adhesive spray booths. Proposal: the trim-cover supplier hot-melt laminates the heater, 8 mm PET spacer and NTC onto the B-side of the cut cover panels in a flat-bed laminating press (PA/PES co-polyamide web, 130 °C, 25 s) before sewing, so each surface arrives as one thermal cover; the seat line simply dresses the cover over the pad. Supplier-integrated thermal-comfort trim covers are reported to be entering production (not verified here). Why it works: lamination flat, before sewing, is fast and repeatable; layup on a contoured foam pad is slow and variable. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S offers heated and cooled seats in its first two rows, a content level that multiplies these layup steps across four seats.

title: One second-row seat structure for both powertrains via a bolt-on anchor riser
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A second row-2 lower-structure variant – its weld fixtures, rail and leg tooling and duplicate sled validation – is never bought; the MHEV pays only for a small stamped riser and its fitting, so the net is a clear tooling and complexity saving. Baseline: at row 2 the battery-electric underbody is flat over the pack, while the combustion-hybrid underbody has a tunnel and a kick-up over the tank that puts its rear seat anchors about 45 mm higher than the front ones; programmes therefore release two second-row lower structures – different rear legs, rail inclinations and anchor brackets welded into the rails – with two weld-fixture sets and two R14/R17 sled campaigns. Proposal: design one second-row structure (rails, legs, cushion frame, foam and cover) to the flat anchor plane and give the hybrid body a bolt-on riser block – a 2.0 mm CR420LA (EN 10268) hat-section stamping with captive M10 nuts – that lifts its two low-side anchors (the front pair, if the MHEV rear anchors are the 45 mm higher ones) onto the same plane. On MHEV the H-point to heel-point height changes by up to the riser height, because the floor does not move with the seat, so re-check package, belt geometry and UN R14 anchorage zones. Why it works: the anchor-height difference is a local offset at two bolts, not a difference in seat geometry, so a 0.4 kg riser absorbs it. Benchmark: the Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV uses its bespoke EV platform to give the entire second row electric adjustment as standard (130 mm fore-aft).

title: Trim-cover-last postponement cuts front-seat sequence variants from 180 to 12
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Finished-seat inventory, obsolescence write-offs, sequence-break rework and buffer floor space all fall because the variant explosion happens in the last 25 minutes instead of at the start of the build; the cost is extra cover kitting and handling. Baseline: the JIS seat plant builds complete trimmed front seats against the OEM broadcast – about 12 colour/material combinations × 5 function levels (heat, heat-vent, massage, sport, lounge) × handedness gives 120 finished-seat part numbers (about 180 with powertrain and market sub-variants); a 4-6 hour finished-seat buffer, obsolescence when trims change and premium freight when the sequence breaks. Proposal: postpone the colour decision. Build about 10-12 functional core seats (frame, foam, thermal layer, electronics, function level × hand, plus sub-variants) in a pull loop, and fit the trim cover, headrest and side shields in a dedicated 25-minute trim cell triggered by the broadcast; covers arrive pre-kitted in sequence from the cover sewer. Why it works: colour and material drive about 90% of the variant count but only the last 20% of the build content; postponing them shrinks the buffer to core seats that never go obsolete and makes sequence breaks a cover swap rather than a seat rebuild. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse standardises leather-free Econeer recycled fabric, illustrating how far trim-variant reduction can go; we keep customer choice but move it to the end of the line.

title: Seat controller self-test replaces supplier end-of-line seat function rigs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Rig depreciation and maintenance, operator rig-loading time and the duplicate OEM functional check fall away; the only added cost is self-test software, amortised over the programme. Baseline: every power seat spends 90-120 s on a dedicated end-of-line rig at the seat supplier – motors run to end stops, heater current ramps, blower tach, pneumatic pressure decay, squib loop resistance – and the OEM repeats a 60 s functional check after installation with a hand-held diagnostic tool. Proposal: a built-in self-test routine in the seat controller (or existing seat ECUs) triggered through a pallet-mounted docking contact (12 V, GND, CAN-FD): it runs each motor over a short stroke with ripple-count verification, ramps heaters and checks current against a window, reads blower tach and valve pressure decay, and writes a VIN-traceable result record; the airbag ECU checks squib resistance at first power-up. The OEM check becomes a DTC read during the vehicle EOL. Why it works: the controller already has the drivers and current sensing the rig duplicates; testing on the conveyor pallet removes rig hardware, fixturing time and duplicate checks. Benchmark: the Li Auto L9 has electric adjustment and heating in all three rows plus ventilation and 10-point massage in two, the kind of function count that makes rig-based EOL testing expensive.

title: Seatback haptic exciters carry tactile bass and directional ADAS alerts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two redundant haptic actuator sets and their driver channels and wiring are deleted on trims that already pay for seat exciters; the alert function moves into the audio DSP at a small software and amplifier-channel cost. Baseline: the trims that offer a tactile-audio seat still carry a separate steering-wheel rim vibration motor for lane-departure haptics (≈€9), a pair of cushion vibration motors for ADAS alerts (≈€12), their ECU driver channels and wiring – three haptic systems in one cockpit. Proposal: on tactile-audio trims (≈35% take), the two moving-magnet exciters per front seatback (40 W, 20-80 Hz) carry both the low-frequency audio and a directional ADAS haptic channel (left or right exciter pulses at 40-60 Hz for lane departure, both for forward collision); the audio DSP mixes the alert with priority and mutes music in that band. The wheel motor and cushion motors are deleted on those trims. Why it works: an exciter is a far more capable actuator than an ERM motor – faster rise time and selectable frequency – so one actuator set covers all seat-borne haptics. Benchmark: the Range Rover Sport SV Body and Soul Seat uses SUBPAC transducers and membranes in the front seats alongside the 29-speaker, 1,430 W Meridian system.

title: One row-2 lower structure serves bench, captain chairs and lounge seats
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Variant rail and frame tooling and duplicate structure validation are avoided, rail volume concentrates on two part numbers for a better price, and the body shop runs one anchor pattern; the only added cost is anchor nuts fitted on bodies that do not use them all. Baseline: the second row exists as a 60/40 bench, a pair of captain's chairs and an executive lounge pair, each with its own rails, rail length, cushion-frame side members, leg brackets and floor anchor pattern – six rail part numbers, three anchor patterns in the body and three structure validation sets. Proposal: a common row-2 lower structure: one floor anchor pattern (eight nuts at fixed Y positions, fitted on every body), one roll-formed rail family in two lengths (standard and long-slide lounge), common cushion-frame side members in 22MnB5 hot-formed tube, and a common leg/riser casting; the bench, captain and lounge uppers bolt onto this lower via a four-bolt interface. Why it works: the variants differ in what the occupant sits in, not in how the seat attaches to the floor; standardising the interface lets one validated lower carry three uppers. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S (2027 six-seat) swaps the second-row bench for two heated, fold-flat captain's chairs that keep the child-seat mounting points and open a walk-through.

title: Steering wheel shipped with driver airbag fitted, clocked and tested
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One OEM line station and its labour are removed, a hazmat logistics stream and store are merged, and gap/flush rework drops; the supplier charges a smaller marriage and EOL cost. Baseline: the steering wheel and the driver airbag module come from different supply streams; the DAB travels as Class 1.4G dangerous goods (UN 0503) to a segregated store, and at the line one station fits the wheel, connects the clockspring and torques the bolt, and a second station fits the DAB, checks gap and flush and runs the squib check – about 110 s and a recurring gap/flush rework on non-round wheels where clocking tolerance shows. Proposal: the wheel supplier marries DAB and wheel in its plant, runs 100% EOL (squib resistance, horn function, gap and flush by vision, wheel clocking), and ships one wheel module as 1.4G; the OEM line fits one module with one bolt and one connector at a single station. Why it works: wheel-to-DAB fit is controlled best where both parts are made, on a fixture referenced to the armature, not on a moving vehicle; one hazmat stream replaces two. Benchmark: the BMW iX polygonal steering wheel shows how a non-round rim makes clocking and gap appearance more visible to the customer.

title: Single blind-mate seat docking connector replaces six hand-plugged under-seat plugs
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Under-seat plugging labour and missed-connection rework disappear and the long service-loop pigtails shorten; the hybrid connector costs more than the separate plugs, which limits the net saving but buys quality. Baseline: each powered chair has five to seven body-side plugs – supply, CAN/LIN, side-airbag squib, buckle pretensioner and switch, occupancy and comfort feeds – mated by an operator reaching under it after bolt-down, about 45 s each, with service-loop pigtails long enough to reach and a missed-plug rate near 300 ppm that shows up as airbag warning lamps at vehicle EOL. Proposal: one hybrid 26-way docking plug (power, signal and USCAR-compliant squib cavities with shorting clips) on a floating bracket at the rear of the rail, mating with a body-side half fixed to the floor bracket; the chair drops onto its locating pins and the plug mates under the bolt-down stroke (±2.5 mm float, CPA closed by a lever). Why it works: the chair already lands on pins to ±1 mm, so a floating half can mate blind; nobody reaches underneath and pigtails shrink to fixed lengths. Benchmark: the Tesla Model Y 2025 refresh carries ventilated front seats and heated, power-folding second-row seats, multiplying body-side connections across four powered positions.

title: Remote laser welding cell replaces MIG on front and row-2 seat frames
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] MIG consumables, straightening and spatter cleaning are removed, cycle time per frame falls by about 60%, and narrower flanges save steel; the laser cell adds energy and optics consumables, and its net capex (after avoiding MIG cell replacement) pays back within the programme. Baseline: front back and cushion frames and row-2 frames are joined by robotic GMAW (MIG) – about 45 seams and 2.2 m of weld per front seat set – in six-robot cells: wire and shielding gas, spatter cleaning, 12-15 mm flanges for torch access and heat distortion that needs a straightening press; cycle about 140 s per frame. Proposal: remote laser welding (6 kW fibre laser with scanner optic) of lap and flange joints on HC420LA (EN 10268) stampings and 22MnB5 tubes, using stitch seams placed by the scanner while the robot moves; gap held below 0.2 mm by clamping fixtures; flanges narrowed to 8 mm; one cell replaces two MIG cells at about 55 s per frame. Why it works: laser heat input is a fraction of MIG, so distortion and straightening go away; no consumable wire or gas; scanner positioning cuts non-productive robot motion. Remote laser welding of seat structures is established general practice at major seat suppliers. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 130 seats eight in a 2+3+3 layout, an example of the frame volume a three-row luxury SUV puts through its seat structure cells.

title: 48 V seat and wheel heaters on MHEV let the 48/12 V DC/DC downsize
description: [MHEV] The 48/12 V DC/DC converter drops a power step and heater feed copper and fuses shrink fourfold in current; the added cost is 48 V-rated heater mats and drivers, smaller than the converter and copper saved. Baseline: on the MHEV every seat heater, the heated steering wheel and the vent blowers run from the 12 V net; four heated seats (two zones each, 50-55 W per zone) plus the wheel load the 48/12 V DC/DC converter with up to 0.5 kW in winter, which is one reason it is specified at 3.0 kW, and each heated seat needs 2.5 mm² feeds and a 15-20 A fuse. Proposal: on MHEV, move the resistive heater loads to the 48 V rail: heater mats redesigned with 16× the element resistance (P = V²/R: four times the voltage at the same power, current falling fourfold) (finer CuNi44 wire or printed carbon) and 60 V-class insulation, 48 V high-side drivers in the seat controller, feeds downsized to 0.5 mm²; motors and blowers stay on 12 V. With 0.5 kW off the 12 V net, the DC/DC drops to 2.5 kW. Why it works: resistive heaters are voltage-agnostic loads ideally suited to 48 V (ISO 21780 range), and moving them is the cheapest way to cut 12 V peak demand. Benchmark: the Li Auto L9 has electric adjustment and heating in all three rows, showing how large the seat heating load of a three-row luxury SUV becomes.

title: Correlated virtual seat-comfort models halve physical prototype seat builds
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 120 prototype seats and their soft tooling are not built, and fewer clinics are run; the cost is simulation licences, people and correlation tests. Development time per comfort loop also shortens from weeks to days. Baseline: a luxury SUV seat programme builds about 260 prototype seats at €6-9k each for comfort clinics, H-point checks, foam-hardness loops, durability and sleds, with soft-tooled trim covers re-cut after every comfort loop. Proposal: a correlated virtual seat: FE seat models with hyperelastic foam calibrated on three physical iterations, a digital SAE J826 H-point machine, pressure-map correlation against 30 clinic subjects and human body models for posture and comfort indices; physical seats are kept for homologation sleds (UN R17, R14), durability and final clinics, cutting builds to about 140. Why it works: most comfort loops change foam hardness and contour, which the calibrated model predicts within the scatter of clinic data; physical builds are then reserved for decisions the model cannot make. Benchmark: Genesis had its Ergo Motion seats approved by Germany's AGR for posture support – evidence that comfort attributes can be specified and verified against objective criteria.

title: Pressure-only front side-impact sensing deletes B-pillar acceleration satellites
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two satellites, their harness legs, brackets and fitting are deleted; the cost is extra crash calibration and misuse testing, amortised over the programme. B-pillar trim also loses the sensor access cut-out. Baseline: front seat thorax-pelvis side airbags and curtains are triggered by a combination of front-door pressure sensors (2), B-pillar acceleration satellites (2) and C-pillar satellites (2), plus the central airbag ECU lateral channel. Proposal: on this body – sealed front-door inner cavities and a stiff BEV/MHEV rocker – trigger the front side bags from the door pressure sensors with the central ECU lateral and yaw channels as safing; delete the two B-pillar acceleration satellites; keep the C-pillar satellites for rear-row events. Pressure sensing reacts earlier for door impacts, and safing from the ECU guards against slam and misuse. Why it works: in modern bodies most front-row side impacts (MDB at the R-point, pole at the front door) load the door cavity directly; door pressure sensing with ECU safing is used on some platforms, but deleting the B-pillar satellites must be proven across the full side, pole, oblique and off-road misuse matrix; keep the satellites if any time-to-fire target is missed. Benchmark: the Volvo EX60 multi-adaptive belt selects among 11 load-limiting profiles from exterior, interior and crash sensors – the restraint fusion of existing sensors this idea relies on.

title: One brushless radial blower per seat ventilates cushion and backrest through a Y-plenum
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two of the four fans, their mounts, harness legs and driver channels are deleted; the remaining blower is brushless and pricier, and a Y-plenum with bellows is added, but the net per vehicle is clearly positive. Baseline: each ventilated front seat carries two brushed axial fans (≈€10 each) – one under the cushion, one in the backrest – each with its own mount, harness leg, connector and driver channel; four fans per vehicle. Proposal: one 12 V brushless radial blower (70 mm, 4-5 W, 150-250 Pa) under the cushion feeding a moulded EPP 45 g/l Y-plenum: one branch into the cushion spacer, the other through a TPE (TPS-SEBS, Shore 60A) bellows that crosses the recline pivot into the backrest spacer; a fixed orifice sets a 60/40 cushion/back flow split, and the blower's integrated driver takes a single PWM line. Why it works: a radial blower develops several times the static pressure of an axial fan of the same size, so it can drive the longer path through the bellows while delivering the same 8-10 m³/h per surface; one brushless motor with integrated electronics costs less than two brushed fans with separate drivers. Benchmark: the Tesla Model Y 2025 refresh added ventilated front seats, bringing seat ventilation to a high-volume price point.

title: Steering-rim heater element doubles as the capacitive hands-on-detection electrode
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A sensor mat layer, its wrapping step and a dedicated HOD controller PCB are deleted; the heater controller is upgraded to measure capacitance, which costs less than the parts removed. Baseline: the heated wheel has a resistive heater mat under the leather, and the hands-on detection required for assisted driving uses a separate capacitive sensor mat with its own shield layer and a dedicated HOD controller PCB in the hub – two conductive layers wrapped on the rim and two electronics boards. Proposal: use the heater element as the capacitive electrode. A combined heater/HOD controller interrupts the heater PWM for 2 ms measurement windows at 50 Hz and measures self-capacitance of the heater mesh against a thin metallised shield film (kept from the baseline stack) driven as an active guard; heating and sensing share one zone layout (left, right, top). Why it works: the heater mesh covers the rim grip zones just as a sensing electrode must; time multiplexing removes 10% of heater on-time (2 ms in every 20 ms), so the PWM duty is raised to keep heating power within 3% of baseline outside full-power warm-up while the guard removes the heater supply's influence on the measurement. Combined heater/HOD rims are established general practice at wheel suppliers. Benchmark: the BMW iX offers 3-stage steering heating on its polygonal wheel alongside its assisted-driving functions.

title: Second-row cushion-dive fold driven by the recline motor through a cam pushrod
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A cushion motor, its driver channel and harness leg are deleted on each power-fold section; a cam, pushrod and lost-motion link are added at a fraction of the cost. Baseline: power-folding second-row 60/40 sections use two motors each – one spindle actuator to fold the backrest and a second to flip the cushion forward into the footwell – plus two driver channels and harness legs per section. Proposal: one recline/fold spindle motor per section drives the backrest; a cam on the recliner side plate drives a steel pushrod (C45E, Ø10 mm) to a four-bar cushion-dive linkage, so the first 25° of fold travel flips the cushion forward and down before the back continues onto it; a lost-motion slot lets the backrest recline normally in seated mode without moving the cushion. Why it works: the fold sequence is fixed – cushion must clear before the back drops – so it can be encoded in a cam rather than in a second motor and software. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity second row power-folds in a two-stage motion – the cushion flips forward into the footwell and the backrest folds onto it – from buttons in the cargo area.

title: Moulded PP-LGF30 centre-20% backrest module replaces steel frame and cupholder insert
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A welded steel frame, a separate cupholder insert and most fasteners are replaced by one moulding with inserts; the moulding costs a little less than the frame and removes assembly steps. Baseline: the centre 20% section of a 40:20:40 second-row backrest – used as through-load hatch and fold-down armrest – is a MIG-welded steel tube-and-sheet frame (≈€14) carrying a separate moulded cupholder insert, a hinge bracket, a latch bracket and foam and trim, assembled with about ten fasteners. Proposal: one injection-moulded PP-LGF30 (long-glass PP, 30%) structural back with ribbed core (3.0 mm walls, 2.5 mm ribs), integral cupholder pocket, moulded hinge bosses with steel pins and a moulded-in steel latch striker plate; foam and cover as today. Why it works: the centre section carries no belt anchorage loads (the centre belt sits in the 40% section), so its load cases are luggage impact and armrest abuse, which a long-glass PP structure handles with local steel inserts at the hinge and latch. Benchmark: the Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV second row uses a 40:20:40 split backrest with an armrest and through-loading feature.

title: Electronic tilt-sensing locks seat-mounted retractors, ending off-road washboard lock-ups
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Three recline-compensated gimballed sensors are replaced by simpler solenoid pawls and short wiring legs through the existing seat harness; the electronics are already in the vehicle. Baseline: seat-mounted retractors in the reclining second-row captain chairs and third row need a vehicle-sensitive sensor that stays level as the backrest reclines and folds, so they use a gimballed, recline-compensated ball sensor (≈€7 each). On off-road tracks, washboard corrugations and steep crests make ball sensors chatter and lock the belt, pinning occupants as they lean to spot. Proposal: the vehicle-sensitive function on these three retractors becomes a solenoid locking pawl commanded by the airbag ECU from its accelerometers and vehicle tilt (from the chassis IMU), meeting UN R16 limits – locking by 27° tilt and at 0.45 g, no locking below 12° – while filtering corrugation vibration (>8 Hz) that trips a mechanical ball. The mechanical webbing-sensitive lock stays as a power-independent backup. Why it works: an electronic threshold is precise and immune to seat recline angle, so the gimballed compensation mechanism goes away, and the filter removes nuisance lock-ups. Benchmark: the Volvo EX60 belt selects among 11 load-limiting profiles from exterior, interior and crash sensors – restraint behaviour set from vehicle sensors rather than mechanics.

title: Off-road side-slope rollover algorithm uses chassis IMU, deleting airbag-ECU roll gyro
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The airbag ECU roll gyro and part of its PCB area and filtering are removed; the cost is a private CAN-FD link, E2E software and an off-road rollover calibration campaign. Baseline: the airbag ECU carries its own roll-rate gyro and low-g lateral/vertical sensors to deploy curtains and fire belt pretensioners in a rollover, while the chassis domain already has an ASIL D-capable 6-axis IMU for ESC, air suspension and terrain modes. Off-road, the roll algorithm must not fire on 40° side slopes, rock steps or articulation. Proposal: the airbag ECU receives roll rate and lateral and vertical acceleration from the chassis IMU over a private CAN-FD link with AUTOSAR E2E protection (profile 7) at 1 kHz; its own low-g lateral sensor stays as the independent plausibility channel; the roll algorithm uses terrain-mode and air-suspension height states to widen the misuse envelope off-road. The ECU roll gyro and its filtering are deleted. Why it works: the IMU already measures roll at higher quality than the ECU gyro, and knowing the terrain mode lets the algorithm separate a sustained 40° side slope from a trip-over. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 130 seats eight in three rows, so its rollover protection must cover curtains and pretensioners across all three rows.

title: Single outboard recliner and passive hinge on each second-row 40% backrest
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One recliner and the synchronising cross tube are deleted from each 40% section; a passive hinge and a frame doubler are added at less than half the cost. Fewer recliners also reduce the backrest release effort and the number of synchronisation adjustments at the seat line. Baseline: each outboard 40% section of the 40:20:40 second-row backrest uses two taumel recliners (≈€10 each), inboard and outboard, synchronised by a cross tube, even though the outer shoulder belt is pillar-mounted and the centre belt lives in the other section. If the centre-belt retractor and upper anchorage are integrated into one 40% section (as the centre-20% PP-LGF30 backrest idea assumes), that section keeps both recliners and the saving roughly halves. Proposal: keep the outboard recliner and replace the inboard one with a passive bushed hinge (PA66 bush on a 16 mm pin) while stiffening the back frame against torsion with a CR780T/420Y-DP (EN 10338) U-doubler along the inboard upright, so luggage and occupant loads still flow into the outboard recliner and the inboard hinge carries shear. Why it works: in a section that carries no belt anchorage, the governing case is UN R17 luggage retention, which loads the back in bending and torsion; a stiffened frame with one locking recliner meets it, as many single-recliner rear seats show. Benchmark: the Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV second row uses a 40:20:40 split backrest, the layout this idea targets.

title: Front-row pneumatic massage module reused unchanged in second-row executive seats
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Front module volume rises by about a third, earning a price step; the row-2 module, its tooling and validation are avoided; the only cost is reworking the row-2 foam pocket. Baseline: front seats use a 10-cell pneumatic massage/lumbar module (pump, valve block, RF-welded TPU cell mat) from supplier A, while the second-row executive seats carry a different 8-cell module from supplier B with its own pump, cell layout, software and validation, because row 2 was developed later by a different team. Proposal: carry the front module – pump, valve block, cell mat geometry and massage programmes – into the row-2 executive seats unchanged; differences in backrest height are absorbed by foam pocket position, and the seat controller sends the same LIN commands. Why it works: massage programmes are defined by cell geometry and timing, not by seat row; one module at higher volume gets a better price and avoids a second tool and validation. Benchmark: the Li Auto L9 offers 10-point massage in both first and second rows, showing the same massage content can serve both rows.

title: Front belt-height adjusters deleted by fixing the D-ring to memory-seat geometry
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two adjuster rails, their trim slots and covers and part of the fitting time are deleted; a welded boss and a belt-fit validation study are added. Trim variants for adjuster covers also disappear from the parts list. Baseline: both front B-pillars carry a five-position belt-height adjuster rail (≈€4 each) with a trim slot and cover, fitted and torqued at the trim line. Proposal: a fixed D-ring anchorage at an optimised height chosen from a 5th-female to 95th-male RAMSIS study combined with the front seats' 60 mm power height range and memory: the seat height positions each occupant's shoulder relative to the fixed D-ring, so belt fit across the population stays within the target zone (webbing on mid-clavicle). The B-pillar inner gets a welded M10 boss instead of the rail. Why it works: with power height adjustment as standard, the seat already moves the occupant's shoulder line, which is what the height adjuster did; many current vehicles use fixed D-rings for the same reason. Benchmark: the Genesis GV80 Smart Posture Assist adjusts seat and air cells to the driver's body, showing that seat-side adjustment can manage occupant geometry.

title: Grip-zone rim heater with smaller driver replaces full-circumference steering-wheel heating
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Heater mat area, wire length and laminate shrink by about a third, the driver and fuse drop one current class and winter energy draw falls; the only cost is a zoned layout and a comfort clinic to confirm perception. Baseline: the heated steering wheel wraps a CuNi wire heater mat around the full rim circumference, including the 5-to-7 o'clock section and the spoke junctions that hands rarely touch, drawing 60-70 W at 12 V with a 6 A high-side driver, a dedicated fuse and a mat of about 0.11 m². Proposal: heat only the grip zones – two arcs from 8 to 11 and 1 to 4 o'clock plus a short 12 o'clock arc for hand-over-hand steering – using a printed or wire heater laid as three zones in one laminate; unheated sections carry only the foam and leather. Heated area falls by about 35% and power to about 40 W for the same 30 °C skin-contact target in 3 minutes, allowing a 4 A driver and smaller fuse (clockspring carried over). Why it works: by general ergonomics practice drivers hold the rim at the 9-3 and 10-2 positions for most of a journey, so heating the lower rim and spoke junctions mostly warms foam that is seldom touched. Benchmark: the BMW iX offers 3-stage steering heating on its polygonal wheel, a rim shape that already separates grip zones from straight non-grip sections.

title: One rear comfort controller drives row-2 and row-3 heating, ventilation and power fold
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Four rear seat modules are replaced by one controller with more channels; housings, MCUs, connectors and part of the harness disappear and the controller costs less than the modules it replaces. Baseline: rear seats are served by a collection of small controllers: a climate ECU in each second-row outboard seat, a third-row heater module and a power-fold motor driver module for rows 2 and 3 – four modules at about €66 combined, each with housing, MCU and connector, wired separately to the rear zone. Proposal: one rear comfort controller mounted under the row-2 floor console: eight heater PWM channels, four blower outputs, six motor H-bridges with current-sense (fold and recline), LIN to the seat switches and one CAN-FD link to the rear zone controller; it sits within 1.2 m of every rear seat. Why it works: rear seats are close together and their loads are simple, so a single controller with more channels costs less than four lightly loaded modules, and wire runs are shorter. Benchmark: the Li Auto L9 has electric adjustment and heating in all three rows, with ventilation and massage in two – exactly the rear-seat load set this controller hosts.

title: Handed-symmetric captain-chair armrest fits both left and right seats
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Half of the armrest foam, frame and cover tooling is not bought, per-part volume doubles for a small price step, and handed sequencing and inventory go away; the extra boss costs a few cents. Baseline: second-row captain's chairs carry an inboard flip-up armrest that is mirrored left and right – two foam tools, two frame dies, two cover patterns and two part numbers per trim colour. Proposal: an armrest symmetric about its own mid-plane: pivot bosses on both sides of a PA6-GF30 frame (only one used per side), a symmetric friction-detent mechanism, a cover pattern with identical stitching on both faces and a symmetric foam pad. One part number per colour fits both chairs; the unused boss is hidden by a snap-in cap. Why it works: the armrest's function is symmetric; only the pivot side differs, which a duplicated boss resolves for a few grams of material. Benchmark: the Tesla Model Y L six-seat version uses second-row captain's chairs that power-fold and slide, the layout in which handed armrest pairs appear.

title: Coupled cam height-tilt link deletes the cushion-tilt motor on passenger zero-gravity seat
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] One motor, its gearbox, driver channel and harness leg are deleted on the passenger seat; a cam front link and roller are added and validated. Passenger seat mass falls by about 0.9 kg with the motor removed. Baseline: the front passenger seat with zero-gravity mode uses separate height and cushion-tilt motors (front link driven by the tilt motor) plus recline and legrest motors; zero-gravity is reached by tilting the cushion nose up 12-14° while reclining. Proposal: on the passenger seat only, drive both four-bar links from the height motor and shape the front link with a cam slot (fine-blanked S500MC) so that the last 30% of the height stroke raises the front faster, adding up to 13° of cushion tilt; normal height use runs in the first 70% where tilt stays near constant. Zero-gravity is then height-to-top plus recline plus legrest. The driver seat keeps independent tilt for driving posture. Why it works: passengers use cushion tilt mainly for the relax posture, which correlates with the top of the height range, so the two motions can be coupled without losing useful adjustment. Benchmark: the Xiaomi YU7 offers zero-gravity front seats with 123° recline, leg rests and 10-point massage.

title: One thorax-pelvis bag fits left and right seats via symmetric fold and bracket
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Per-part volume doubles for a price step, handed folding fixtures are not bought and handed inventory and sequencing disappear; the symmetric bracket uses slightly more steel. Baseline: the thorax-pelvis bags fitted in the outboard bolsters of the front and second-row seats are handed – left and right versions differ in fold direction, bracket and connector exit – giving separate part numbers per position, handed folding fixtures and handed stock. Proposal: a symmetric module: a roll-and-tuck fold that is mirror-symmetric about the module mid-plane, a centred tubular hybrid gas generator, a two-stud bracket symmetric about the same plane and a connector exit on the centreline; the same unit fits the left and right outboard positions without rotation, because a module mirror-symmetric about its deployment plane is its own mirror image (rotating it 180° about the vertical axis would point the cushion rearward). Why it works: a thorax-pelvis cushion is a flat two-panel bag close to symmetric inboard-to-outboard; handedness came from fold and bracket conventions, but fold direction sets how the bag unfolds between occupant and door, so deployment kinematics must be proven on both sides. Benchmark: the Genesis GV80 adds a centre side airbag on the console side of the driver's seat, illustrating how seat-mounted restraint variants multiply per seat.

title: Heated rear-seat mats double as capacitive occupancy sensors for belt reminders
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Five pressure mats and most of their harness are deleted; capacitive channels in the rear controller and guard layers in the heater laminate are added for less. Baseline: rows 2 and 3 carry five membrane pressure occupancy mats (≈€6.5 each) under the cushion foam so the belt reminder can show which occupied seats are unbuckled, in addition to heater mats in the same cushions. Proposal: where rear heating is already standard in every rear position (including the row-2 centre seat – otherwise add its heater mat to the bridge), the cushion heater mat becomes a capacitive occupant electrode measured by the rear comfort controller in loading mode during 2 ms heater-off windows; a thin guard layer in the heater laminate shields it from the seat frame, and a humidity-compensated threshold separates occupant from wet seat or shopping bag. Why it works: a seated adult or child changes the electrode capacitance by tens of picofarads, far above the drift from moisture with a driven guard; the heater already lies exactly where an occupancy mat would. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S heats its third row as well as the first two rows, the precondition for using heater mats as sensors in every rear seat.

title: EPP anti-submarining block replaces stamped steel ramp in front seat cushions
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Stamped ramps, their welds and part of the steel mass are removed and replaced by an EPP insert that is foamed in place; cost and about 0.4 kg per seat are saved. Baseline: each front cushion carries a stamped steel anti-submarining ramp (HC420LA, 1.5 mm) welded or bolted between the side members ahead of the pelvis, plus a front cross tube, under the PU foam; the ramp stops the pelvis sliding under the lap belt in frontal crashes. Proposal: a moulded EPP 60 g/l anti-submarining block (with a 2 mm PA6-GF30 load-spreading face) seated on the existing front cross tube, shaped to the same ramp angle and engagement height, and foamed into the PU pad as an insert; the steel ramp and its welds are deleted. Why it works: anti-submarining needs the pelvis to meet a rising, stiff surface early; dense EPP crushes at a controlled plateau stress (~0.6-0.8 MPa) and spreads the load onto the cross tube, which carries it to the side members. Foam or EPP anti-submarining features are used in some cushion designs, but replacing a steel ramp must be proven with THOR-50M. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 offers second-row relaxation seats with massage, part of a trend to reclined postures where anti-submarining design is critical.

title: Third-row head restraints tip forward by Bowden cable from the backrest release
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Two solenoids, their driver channels and wiring are deleted; a Bowden cable and latch lever per seat are added at less than half the cost. Electrical load and two connector cavities per seat also go, simplifying the third-row harness. Baseline: on seven-seat vehicles the third-row head restraints are tipped forward by electromagnetic latch actuators (≈€9 each, with driver channel and wiring) triggered from a button, so the backrest can lie flat and rear visibility improves. Proposal: a Bowden cable from the backrest release lever pulls the head-restraint latch: when the occupant or strap releases the backrest, the restraint springs forward first and the backrest then goes down; raising the backrest leaves the restraint tipped until the occupant lifts it, which is clearly noticeable as UN R17 requires for retractable head restraints. Why it works: the restraint only needs to tip when the backrest goes down, so the motion can be taken mechanically from the release, removing electronics entirely. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity third row stows manually into the floor with strap-and-handle releases, showing a mechanical third row is accepted at the top of the market.
