title: Third-row 50% seat shares back frame and recliner with second-row 40% section
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A third-row back-frame tool set is not bought, frame and recliner volumes concentrate on one part, and third-row luggage validation reuses row-2 results; the third row carries a slightly heavier frame. Baseline: the third-row 50/50 backrests use their own tube-and-panel back frame and recliner, while the second-row 40% sections have a different frame of near-identical width (≈580 vs 600 mm), so two frame tool sets and two recliner variants are released. Proposal: size the third-row back to the second-row 40% frame: common 22MnB5 hot-formed perimeter tube, common stamped HC420LA back panel with luggage-retention ribs, common recliner and headrest guides; height and contour differences sit in foam and cover. The third row inherits the row-2 strength, which it needs anyway because its back faces the luggage area. Why it works: both backs are governed by the same UN R17 luggage-retention case, so one frame that passes it serves both rows; the width difference is small enough for foam to absorb. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender 130 seats eight in a 2+3+3 layout with a sliding and folding middle row, illustrating how many back frames a three-row SUV needs.

title: Self-regulating PTC-ink seat heater deletes NTC thermistors and closed-loop control
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Eight NTCs, their wiring and pins are deleted and closed-loop channels simplify to monitored switches; the PTC film costs slightly more than wire, which leaves a modest net saving. Baseline: each heated seat zone uses a CuNi44 wire heater sewn or laminated on a PET non-woven, an NTC thermistor glued in the zone and a closed-loop PWM channel that regulates to the set temperature; four heated seats × two zones = eight elements, eight NTCs with their wiring and connector pins. Proposal: a screen-printed positive-temperature-coefficient (PTC) carbon/polymer ink heater on a 100 µm perforated PET film with silver bus bars, whose resistance rises steeply around 45 °C so the element self-limits; three comfort levels are set by open-loop duty cycle and the controller only monitors current. Why it works: a PTC heater limits its own surface temperature, so the NTC and regulation loop that protect against overheating become unnecessary; printed films also heat more evenly, with no hot spots at wire crossings. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse fits heated front seats as standard, the kind of volume at which heater element cost matters.

title: Snap-fit mould-in-colour PP-T20 steering-wheel rear cover replaces painted PC/ABS shells
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Painting, one moulding and five of six screws are removed, and felt pads become moulded bumpers; the PP part costs less than the PC/ABS painted pair. Paint emissions and paint-line capacity for this part also go. Baseline: the steering-wheel rear cover is two painted PC/ABS shells (upper and lower) screwed to the armature with six screws, with felt anti-rattle pads, about €6.5 plus 50 s of assembly. Proposal: one mould-in-colour PP-T20 (talc-filled PP, grain K29 matched to the IP) rear cover retained by four snap hooks onto the magnesium armature and one locking screw at 6 o'clock for anti-rattle, with moulded TPE bumpers in place of felt pads. Why it works: the rear cover is a non-structural, low-visibility part in the driver's lower field of view; mould-in-colour grained PP gives the same appearance as painted PC/ABS at this distance and removes paint and most screws. Benchmark: the BMW iX polygonal wheel uses gloss-black controls and a non-round rim, where rear cover fit and seams are visible to the driver.

Why it works: the rear cover is a non-structural, low-visibility part in the driver's lower field of view; mould-in-colour grained PP gives the same appearance as painted PC/ABS at this distance and removes paint and most screws. Benchmark: the BMW iX polygonal wheel uses gloss-black controls and a non-round rim, where rear cover fit and seams are visible to the driver.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Wheel supplier fits one cover with a snap-on motion and one screw (≈15 s instead of 50 s); paint line volume drops. One 2K tool (PP + TPE) replaces two single-shot tools.
ideaData.dfmDfa: Snap hooks engage cast-in armature windows with a 1.5 mm undercut; asymmetric hook spacing prevents wrong orientation. Locking screw position chosen for tool access from below, without removing the airbag.

title: ISOFIX bars welded directly to the captain-chair cushion cross-tube, deleting brackets
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The bracket carriers, bolts and part of the funnel content are deleted; bars are welded in the existing frame cell with an added weld and pull-test step. Frame mass also falls by about 0.3 kg per seat with the carrier removed. Baseline: sliding second-row captain's chairs must carry their ISOFIX anchorages on the seat; each seat uses a separate ISOFIX bracket assembly – a stamped carrier with two 6 mm bars, bolted to the cushion frame – plus guide funnels in the trim. Proposal: keep the mandated 6 mm round bars (UN R145 / ISO 13216) but resistance-weld them directly to the 22MnB5 rear cushion cross-tube through formed saddles, deleting the carrier and its bolts; guide funnels are clipped into the cover's listing seam. Why it works: the cross-tube is already the stiffest member at the right position and carries load straight into the side members and rails; the carrier was an interface part, not a structural need. Benchmark: the Rivian R1S six-seat captain's chairs keep the child-seat mounting points while folding flat, the same requirement this idea serves.

title: Fixed-hub driver airbag with membrane horn switch replaces floating horn module
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Horn springs, contacts and most dampers are deleted and gap/flush rework at the wheel plant falls; a membrane sensor and connector are added for less. Rattle complaints from floating modules are also removed at source. Baseline: the driver airbag module floats 2-3 mm on three spring-loaded horn contacts with damping elements, so pressing the pad sounds the horn; the floating gap (≈3.5 mm) around the module, its springs, contacts and dampers cost about €4 per wheel and cause rattle and gap/flush variation. Proposal: snap the DAB rigidly to the armature and sense horn presses with a thin-film force-sensing membrane (printed silver/carbon on PET) under the pad cover's horn zone, read by the wheel electronics node or as a direct switch; the pad gap shrinks to 2 mm. Why it works: a membrane switch needs only 0.3 mm of travel and can be laid under the cover skin, so the whole module no longer has to move; fixed mounting also improves DAB positioning. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse redesigned its steering wheel and hub around a new four-spoke layout, where tight pad gaps are part of the design language.

title: Camera-scanned hide nesting with automatic flaw grading lifts leather yield five points
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Hide consumption per leather seat set falls by roughly 7% for the same panels, and flaw-marking labour disappears; the scanning cutters add depreciation at the cutting supplier. Baseline: Nappa hides for seat trim are inspected by eye, flaws marked by chalk or pen and nested semi-manually on CNC knife cutters; utilisation for seat panels is typically 68-72% and flaw marking takes about two minutes per hide. Proposal: hide-scanning cutters with multi-spectral cameras and a trained classifier that grades every area of the hide into quality zones (A visible faces, B sides, C hidden) and nests each pattern piece into the zone its seat position needs, with grain-direction rules, before cutting; utilisation rises to 74-77%. Why it works: manual marking is conservative and nesting cannot use small B/C areas reliably; automated zoning lets hidden panels absorb natural marks that would otherwise be scrap. Automated hide scanning and nesting is established general practice in leather cutting. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse goes leather-free with recycled Econeer fabric; for a luxury SUV that keeps leather, cutting hide waste is the equivalent lever.

title: Ultrasonic quilting replaces sewn diamond quilting on PU-microfibre seat inserts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Quilting stitch time, thread and needles are removed on synthetic trims and PU foam laminate is replaced by cheaper heat-bondable PET wadding; sonotrode wear and tooling are added. Baseline: diamond-quilted seat inserts are sewn through the cover, a 5 mm PU foam laminate and a scrim on multi-needle quilting machines, roughly 18-25 minutes of quilting per seat set and significant thread, with frequent needle-mark rework. Proposal: on PU-microfibre and textile trims (≈40% of vehicles), form the quilting pattern by ultrasonic bonding with a rotary patterned sonotrode (20 kHz) through face material and a heat-bondable PET wadding (replacing PU foam laminate), creating the embossed diamonds in one pass; a single perimeter accent stitch keeps the hand-made look. Leather trims keep sewn quilting. Why it works: thermoplastic faces and PET wadding weld locally under ultrasonic energy, producing a durable quilt line without thread; the process is faster and has no needle holes to leak or tear. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse uses leather-free Econeer recycled seat fabric as standard, the class of synthetic trim where ultrasonic processing applies.

title: Motor-current ripple counting replaces Hall position sensors in memory-seat motors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Ten Hall sensor boards, their wires and pins are deleted; current-sense channels and end-stop re-zero software are added at a fraction of the cost. Seat harness weight also falls with 20-30 fewer circuits. Baseline: memory-seat motors (fore-aft, height, tilt, recline, plus row-2 slide and recline) each carry a Hall sensor board on the armature shaft, with two or three extra wires and connector pins per motor to report position – about ten Hall-equipped motors per vehicle. Proposal: sensorless position by commutation-ripple counting: the seat controller's H-bridge current sense samples motor current at 20-50 kHz and counts the current ripples produced by each commutator segment transition (12-segment motors give 12 ripples per revolution); software compensates for start/stop transients and re-zeroes at mechanical end stops during normal use. Accuracy of ±2 mm is enough for memory recall. Why it works: the motor already encodes its rotation in its current waveform; reading it in the driver silicon replaces a sensor, magnet ring and wires. Ripple counting is established general practice for window and seat drives. Benchmark: the Li Auto L9 provides electric adjustment in all three rows, multiplying the number of positioned seat motors.

title: Flat flexible printed seat harness replaces round-wire under-cushion loom
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Round-wire loom, tape and most clips are replaced by an FFC laminate and short round pigtails; routing time falls by about half. The flat format also frees space under the cushion for ventilation ducts. Baseline: each front power seat carries a round-wire in-seat loom of about 45 circuits (roughly 7 m of bundle length, several tens of metres of FLRY wire), taped and clipped under the cushion pan and up the backrest, ≈€31 per seat plus about two minutes of routing and clipping at the seat line. Proposal: a flat flexible cable (FFC) harness – 0.1 mm copper conductors laminated between PET films, die-cut to the cushion-pan shape – bonded to the pan with pressure-sensitive adhesive and terminated in standard FFC connectors; round-wire pigtails are kept only across moving joints (height links and recline pivot). Why it works: under the cushion the routing is fixed, so a flat laminate is cheaper per circuit, lighter, faster to fit and cannot be pinched; flexing joints keep proven round wire. Benchmark: the Tesla Model Y 2025 refresh carries ventilated front seats and heated, power-folding rear seats, the circuit density that makes in-seat harness cost significant.

title: EPP third-row cushion core with thin PU topper replaces steel pan and foam
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The steel pan and two-thirds of the PU foam are replaced by one EPP core with a wire frame; material and handling costs fall and stow effort improves. Seat mass falls by about 1.4 kg per cushion, which also lowers manual stow effort. Baseline: each third-row cushion is a 1.5 mm stamped steel pan carrying 80 mm of HR PU foam (55 kg/m³) and the trim cover, ≈€24 of structure and foam and about 3.2 kg per seat, which the occupant must lift when stowing the seat into the floor. Proposal: a bead-moulded EPP 30 g/l structural core (60 mm) with a moulded-in 5 mm steel wire frame that carries the pivot and latch attachments, topped with 25 mm of PU 50 kg/m³ comfort foam; the cover attaches to moulded EPP hook channels. Why it works: third-row cushions see low occupant mass and short trips; EPP provides structure and shape in one lightweight part, and the wire frame carries the hard points. Mass drops by about 1.4 kg per seat, easing manual stow. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity third row folds manually into the floor with strap-and-handle releases, where cushion mass sets the effort.

title: Seat outer side shield moulded with integrated switch bezel and harness clips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The painted bezel, separate clips and most screws are removed; the side shield tool becomes 2K with IMD, raising its piece price by less than the parts deleted. Baseline: each front power seat's outboard side shield is a grained PP-T20 moulding to which a separate painted PC/ABS switch bezel, four harness clips or brackets and two screws are added; the switch is screwed into the bezel – ≈€11.5 per seat and about 70 s of assembly. Proposal: a 2K side shield – PP-T20 carrier with TPE soft-touch zone – with switch-retaining snaps, moulded harness clip towers and an in-mould-decorated (IMD) satin-chrome film surround replacing the painted bezel; the switch clicks in from the back. Why it works: the bezel and clips are interface parts whose geometry can be moulded into the shield; IMD gives the bright surround without painting. Benchmark: the Genesis GV80 Ergo Motion seat carries a dense set of seat controls (posture assist, stretching), the kind of switch cluster this shield hosts.

title: EPP-core head restraints with slip-on covers replace pour-in-place PU
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] PIP foaming and its cover scrap are removed; an EPP core and thin comfort layer cost less than the PIP foam and cycle, and covers can be changed for repair. Repairable covers also cut warranty replacement cost. Baseline: front and second-row outboard head restraints are pour-in-place (PIP): the sewn cover is loaded into a heated mould with the steel armature and PU foam is poured inside it, with long cycle times, foam strike-through scrap of covers and dedicated PIP tools per trim. Proposal: an EPP 45 g/l core moulded around the armature, an 8 mm PU slab or 3D spacer comfort layer, and a sewn cover slipped on and closed by a hidden J-strip; for textile trims a knitted-to-shape cover can be used. Why it works: EPP is an excellent energy absorber for the head-restraint impact test, its moulding cycle is short, and covers no longer risk strike-through scrap because foam is not poured inside them. Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse uses recycled Econeer textile trims, which suit slip-on covers on EPP cores.

Proposal: an EPP 45 g/l core moulded around the armature, an 8 mm PU slab or 3D spacer comfort layer, and a sewn cover slipped on and closed by a hidden J-strip; for textile trims a knitted-to-shape cover can be used. Why it works: EPP is an excellent energy absorber for the head-restraint impact test, its moulding cycle is short, and covers no longer risk strike-through scrap because foam is not poured inside them. title: Wire-rope stalk buckles replace stamped strap and moulded sleeve on rear seats
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The stamped strap and most of the moulded sleeve are replaced by a cheaper swaged wire rope and extruded sleeve, and the anchor plate is shared with the front family. Baseline: non-pretensioned rear buckles (rows 2 and 3, about six per vehicle) are mounted on a stamped steel strap with a rigid moulded PP/TPE sleeve that holds the buckle upright, ≈€2.3 per buckle in stalk and sleeve. Proposal: a galvanised 7×19 steel wire-rope stalk (sized for a breaking load > 25 kN, about Ø6 mm as on front pretensioner buckles; a Ø4.5 mm 7×19 rope breaks at only ≈17-19 kN) swaged into the buckle frame and the anchor plate, covered by a thin extruded TPE sleeve that gives upright presentation; the anchor plate is common with the front buckle pretensioner family. Why it works: wire-rope stalks already carry front pretensioner buckles at higher loads; using them at the rear removes a stamping and the heavy moulded sleeve. Benchmark: the Volvo EX60 multi-adaptive belt shows restraint hardware being re-engineered around common, sensor-managed components; this idea commonises the stalk.

title: PVD-coated PC/ABS spoke inserts replace machined anodised aluminium wheel trims
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Machining, anodising and edge diamond-cutting of three aluminium parts are replaced by moulding and PVD at much lower cost; cosmetic rework also falls. Bright insert supply moves from a machining specialist to the interior moulder, simplifying the supply chain. Baseline: the steering-wheel spokes carry three machined and anodised 6061-T6 aluminium inserts (diamond-cut edges), ≈€5 each, bonded or clipped to the spoke covers. Proposal: injection-moulded PC/ABS inserts with laser-textured brushed pattern in the mould and a PVD aluminium/chromium layer under a UV-cured hard coat, satin finish to avoid glare; retained by moulded clips. Why it works: on the wheel the inserts are decorative, not structural; PVD on a textured moulding reproduces the metal look (though not the cool touch of solid aluminium) at a fraction of the machining cost and satisfies the edge radii of UN R21 by design. Benchmark: the BMW iX polygonal wheel uses gloss-black controls and decorative surfaces on its spokes, the trim content this idea addresses.

title: Long-glass PA6 paddles with PVD finish replace die-cast magnesium shift/regen paddles
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Die-casting, machining and finishing of magnesium paddles are replaced by one moulding and PVD; the switch housing integration is simplified. Paddle mass falls only modestly (PA6-LGF50 at ≈1.56 g/cm³ against magnesium at 1.8 g/cm³, offset by the thicker ribbed section). Baseline: the steering-wheel paddles – gear selection on the MHEV 8-speed, regen levels on the 800V BEV – are AZ91D magnesium die-castings, machined and painted or PVD-finished, ≈€8 per pair before the microswitch housing. Proposal: PA6-LGF50 (long-glass PA6, 50%) injection-moulded paddles with a moulded-in steel pivot pin and PVD metal finish, snapping directly into a common switch housing; stiffness comes from a ribbed I-section. Why it works: paddle loads are small (≤ 50 N finger force, 500 N abuse) and a long-glass PA6 at E ≈ 16 GPa with a ribbed section matches the perceived stiffness of the magnesium part; the metal look is kept by the PVD layer (a sub-micron coating cannot give the cool touch of solid magnesium – confirm in clinics). Benchmark: the BMW iX3 Neue Klasse four-spoke wheel, with a sports wheel in the M Sport package, shows how much wheel content carries variant-specific hardware.

title: Robotic rim-closure stitching cell replaces hand-stitched steering-wheel leather wrap
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] About 20 minutes of skilled hand stitching per wheel is replaced by robot time; robot depreciation and thread allowance are charged, and stitch rework falls. Labour content becomes less sensitive to wage inflation. Baseline: the leather rim cover is skived, glued to the foamed rim and closed by hand with a decorative cross or baseball stitch along the inner contour – 25-32 minutes per wheel at the wheel supplier, with stitch-tension variation and rework. Proposal: a robotic stitching cell: a six-axis robot rotates the wheel past a single-needle curved-needle sewing head that closes the inner seam with a programmable decorative stitch; operators only prepare and load (≈8 minutes per wheel including spoke junctions finished by hand). Why it works: the rim seam is a long, regular, repeatable path – ideal for automation – while the hard-to-reach spoke junctions remain manual; robots also give constant stitch pitch and tension. Robotic steering-wheel stitching is in production at some wheel suppliers but is not yet general practice. Benchmark: the BMW iX polygonal wheel has a non-round rim where stitch regularity along the straight sections is highly visible.

title: One-piece rail skirts replace eight clipped end caps on front seat tracks
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Eight end caps, four lateral trims and their clips are replaced by four mouldings; fitting time halves. Missing-cap warranty and rattle complaints also disappear. Baseline: each front seat track carries four rail end caps (front and rear of inner and outer rails) plus two lateral trims, with separate clips – about €4.2 per seat and 40 s of fitting – and caps that go missing and rattle. Proposal: one PP-T20 rail skirt per rail (four per vehicle) that clips along the fixed lower rail, covering front and rear ends with a moulded living-hinge flap that flexes as the upper rail travels, plus integrated harness clip points. Why it works: the lower rail is fixed to the floor, so a single fixed cover along it can replace end caps and side trims; the flap accommodates upper-rail travel. Benchmark: the Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV gives its second row 130 mm of electric fore-aft travel, the rail exposure this kind of skirt covers.

title: Two seat-motor frame sizes cover every seat function across all three rows
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Motor volume concentrates on two cores for a price step, motor validation and spare-part variants shrink, and gear-stage adaptation parts add a little cost. Dual sourcing also improves supply resilience. Baseline: the seat motors on the vehicle – fore-aft, height, tilt, recline, cushion extension, legrest, headrest, row-2 slide and fold, row-3 fold – come from six or seven motor types and three suppliers, about 16 motors worth ≈€182 per vehicle, each with its own validation and spare-part number. Proposal: standardise on two DC motor frame sizes (Ø32 mm and Ø40 mm) with common brush, commutator and magnet designs, varying only worm/spindle gear stages and output interfaces; dual-source both frames. Why it works: seat motors differ mainly in torque and speed, which the gear stage sets; a common motor core gains volume pricing, simpler validation and two-source competition. Benchmark: the Xiaomi YU7 front seats offer zero-gravity recline, leg rests and cushion extension, an example of how many motor functions a luxury seat accumulates.

title: Under-windscreen soundbar replaces door mid-range speakers, grilles and door audio wiring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Front and rear door mid-range drivers, their perforated metal grilles, brackets, gaskets and door-speaker harness branches are replaced by one IP-top soundbar enclosure with six drivers and two cowl woofers, so four door grille parts and four door audio circuits disappear and door bins grow. Baseline: premium audio places a 165 mm mid-bass plus a tweeter in each of four doors (8 drivers), each behind a perforated aluminium grille with a clip frame, an EPDM gasket and a speaker bracket, wired through the door grommet. Proposal: a full-width soundbar enclosure moulded in PP-GF20 sits in the IP topper below the windscreen, carrying four 80 mm mid-range and two 25 mm tweeters with DSP-steered imaging, plus two 130 mm cowl-side woofers in sealed 3-litre volumes at the IP ends; low bass stays with the existing tailgate subwoofer. One long fabric-covered grille replaces four door grilles. Door trims lose speaker apertures, so the bin volume grows ≈2.5 l per door. Why it works: modern DSP (delay, beam-steering) recovers a stereo image from a frontal array, and mid-bass from rigid sealed IP-end volumes beats leaky door cavities. Benchmark: the Volvo EX30 groups its speakers in a soundbar spanning the dashboard under the windscreen, which removes door speakers and frees door storage; Volvo also cites less wiring and material.

title: Centre-console window switch bank deletes four door switch packs and door circuits
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The driver four-window pack, the three passenger window switches and their door bezels are replaced by one console switch bank shared by both front occupants, with rear-door switches kept only as a child-locked option; door harnesses lose the switch circuits and door connectors shrink. Baseline: four door-mounted switch packs – a driver pack with four window switches, mirror joystick and lock (≈€22), three single window switches (≈€6 each) – each in a bezel in the door armrest, wired through the door grommet on LIN plus discrete lines. Proposal: one centre-console switch bank (four window rockers + child-lock + lock) on the console LIN bus beside the gear selector, reachable by both front occupants; mirror adjustment moves to a screen menu with the steering-wheel roller as input; rear-door switches are deleted on the standard trim and offered as a factory option with the existing door module. Armrest moulds close the switch apertures. Why it works: window use is infrequent and the console is equidistant to both front seats; the door then carries only lock/handle and ambient circuits, letting the door connector drop from 40 to 16 ways. Benchmark: the Volvo EX30 places its window switches in the centre console, grouped for both front occupants, as part of a de-contented door.

title: Trim-carrier zonal node drives all door loads over two-wire Ethernet
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Every load in the door – lock, mirror, window motor, ambient LEDs, switches, speaker – is driven locally by a zonal node mounted on the trim carrier, so the body-to-door wiring shrinks to supply, return and a two-wire 10BASE-T1S Ethernet link and long point-to-point copper runs back to body ECUs disappear. Baseline: each door has a body-control-driven architecture – a door control module plus a 35-60 circuit bundle running 2-4 m from body ECUs to individual door loads (ambient LEDs, switch packs, mirror heater and fold motor, puddle lamp, speakers), each with its own copper. Proposal: a zonal node (MCU, six half-bridges for lock, mirror and window, eight LED channels, a class-D audio channel) sits in a moulded pocket of the PP-LGF30 trim carrier, located by snap datums; the body side supplies 12 V, return and a 10BASE-T1S multidrop pair. Rear doors get a smaller satellite node. Software differentiates left and right. Why it works: door wiring cost is dominated by long single-load wires; serving loads from 0.5 m away cuts copper mass and splice count, and the trim pocket is a dry, serviceable location. Benchmark: Rivian’s Gen 2 R1S zonal architecture cut ECUs from 17 to 7 and removed about 1.6 miles of wiring and 44 lb per vehicle.

title: Roof-zone harness segment pre-clipped to the headliner and installed with it
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The roof harness becomes a separate zone segment that the headliner supplier clips into moulded clip towers on the substrate back, so the plant fits headliner and wiring in one lift and makes one A-pillar connection instead of hand-routing, taping and clipping a loose roof harness overhead. Baseline: the roof harness (overhead console, reading lamps, rear-view mirror, microphones, DMS camera feed, roof antenna pigtails, rear-seat reading lights) is a branch of the body harness; operators route it overhead on the bare roof with fir-tree clips and tape (≈4.5 min), then lift in the headliner and connect four to six local connectors through openings. Proposal: following a roof-zone split, the roof harness is a stand-alone 3.2 m segment terminating in one sealed 20-way connector at the left A-pillar. The headliner supplier presses it into 22 clip towers moulded on the PET-felt/PU substrate back and pre-connects the overhead console and lamps, then runs a continuity test. In plant the headliner goes in through the tailgate with a manipulator and a single connector is mated. Why it works: overhead work is the slowest and least ergonomic in trim; moving it to a bench at the supplier saves time and quality, and a zone split shortens the roof wiring. Benchmark: BMW Neue Klasse splits its zonal harness into four zones including a dedicated roof zone, installs the parts separately, and quotes 600 m less cable and 30% less weight.

title: Headliner 60 GHz cabin radar also runs the intrusion alarm, deleting ultrasonic sensors
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The headliner-mounted 60 GHz radar already fitted for Euro NCAP child-presence detection is given an intrusion-detection mode, so the ultrasonic intrusion transducer pair, its control electronics, grilles in the overhead console and their wiring are deleted. Baseline: the overhead console carries an ultrasonic interior-intrusion module (two 40 kHz transducers, a small control PCB, two perforated grilles and a harness branch) for the alarm, while a separate 60 GHz FMCW radar in the headliner behind the rear-view mirror area performs child-presence detection (CPD) for Euro NCAP. Proposal: the radar firmware adds a low-duty intrusion mode (micro-Doppler detection of arm or body entry, 1 Hz wake cycle, ≈15 mA average at 12 V) while the vehicle is locked, reporting to the alarm controller over CAN-FD; the ultrasonic module, grilles and harness branch are removed and the overhead console mould closes the two grille apertures. Why it works: a radar that can detect a sleeping infant’s breathing can detect a person reaching in, and it is less prone to false alarms from air movement in a sun-heated cabin. title: One ceiling flip-down rear screen replaces two seatback entertainment displays
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The optional rear-seat entertainment package drops from two seatback-mounted displays with their housings, mounts and seat harness runs to one motorised ceiling display in the headliner, sharing one video link from the head unit. Baseline: the rear-entertainment option (≈25% take rate) fits two 11.4-inch displays in housings on the front seatbacks, each with its own mounting bracket, seat-harness branch through the seat track and a video/power link. Why it works: one larger centred screen gives the same viewing angle to both outer seats and the centre seat, and removes all screen content from the seats, simplifying seat variants. title: Daisy-chained smart RGB LEDs replace per-zone LIN ambient lighting modules
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Twelve LIN ambient modules, each with its own MCU, LIN transceiver and connector, are replaced by RGB LEDs with an integrated driver and factory colour calibration chained on one serial bus per zone from four gateways, deleting modules, harness branches and end-of-line colour calibration. Baseline: ≈140 RGB LEDs in 30 ambient zones are driven by 12 LIN ambient modules (MCU, LIN transceiver, constant-current drivers, 6-pin connector, ≈€4.5 each) on four LIN branches, and every vehicle needs an end-of-line colour/brightness calibration because LED binning varies. Proposal: RGB LEDs with a built-in driver IC, temperature compensation and factory-stored colour calibration data (smart-LED class, e.g. bidirectional differential daisy-chain) are chained on a 2-wire bus; four zone gateways (IP, two doors, rear) translate from the body CAN/LIN. Light-guides and trim are unchanged. Why it works: the module content (MCU, drivers) moves into the LED package where it is cheaper at volume, the calibration is done once at LED test, and one twisted pair replaces several LIN plus current branches. Benchmark: the Mercedes-Maybach EQS SUV runs active ambient lighting with 253 individually controlled LEDs and 64 colours; the EQS sedan’s band uses about 190 real-time controlled LEDs.

title: Body-side harness trunks routed in sill trim channel, clear of footwell wading water
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The left and right body harness trunks move from the floor pan under the carpet into a moulded channel in the sill scuff trim, so floor-level inline connectors no longer sit where seepage water collects after wading; eight sealed connectors become unsealed, floor conduit and many floor clips are deleted. Baseline: the body harness trunks run along the floor pan beside the sill under the carpet and underlay, with eight inline connectors at the A- and B-pillar bases. Because a wading vehicle (900 mm) can take seepage water that pools under the carpet, these connectors are IP67 sealed and the trunks carry corrugated conduit. Proposal: the trunks rise into a C-section channel moulded in the PP-T20 sill scuff trim (≈120 mm above the floor pan, above the carpet water-retention zone), retained by integrated snap fingers; inline connectors sit in the channel at the pillar bases, unsealed (IP54 with drip loop). The sill trim gets a TPE seal lip to the carpet edge. Why it works: wading seepage collects in the lowest 30-60 mm of the footwell under the underlay; lifting the electrical trunk 120 mm takes it out of that zone and lets cheaper connectors and no conduit be used, while improving post-wade robustness. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender is rated to wade 900 mm on air suspension (850 mm coil) and fits a Wade Sensing programme as standard, so cabin-floor electrics on such vehicles must tolerate seepage.

title: One wide display housing replaces separate cluster and centre-screen housings and bezels
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate instrument cluster and centre display, each with its own housing, bezel, cover lens, bracket and video link, become one wide display module under one cover glass in one housing with one bracket and a single serialiser link. Baseline: a 12.3-inch instrument cluster under a cluster hood and a separate 14.9-inch floating centre display, each with its own die-cast rear housing, cover glass, optical bonding, bezel, IP bracket, GMSL2 video link and connector; two aiming/gap-setting operations at cockpit build. Proposal: one wide display module (≈27-inch diagonal class, two LTPS panels or one wide panel behind one 0.7 mm cold-formed cover glass), one PA6-GF30/Al rear housing, one IP bracket at three points on the cross-car beam, one serialiser link from the cockpit domain controller carrying both streams. Why it works: housing, glass, bonding and bracket cost scale with part count more than with area, and one gap/flush setting replaces two; the wide format hides the panel joint behind a black-print band. Benchmark: the 2024 Genesis GV80 combines its formerly separate digital cluster and infotainment touchscreen into a single 27-inch OLED display.

title: One 15.6-inch panel part number for centre, passenger and ceiling displays
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Panel purchasing volume is pooled by using one 15.6-inch LTPS panel and backlight design for the centre display, the optional passenger display and the optional rear ceiling display, cutting panel price, qualification and service-part costs. Baseline: the cockpit uses three different panel sizes – a 14.9-inch centre display, a 12.3-inch passenger display (≈60% take) and an 11-13-inch rear display option (≈25% take) – each with its own panel qualification, backlight, optical bonding fixture, spares and supplier minimum orders. title: Console centre-zone controller with eFuses replaces cabin fusebox, relays and console feeds
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] A centre-zone controller under the console replaces the passenger-footwell fusebox, its 35 blade fuses and 8 relays with eFuse channels, and direct-mounts the console switch packs, so the fusebox housing, relays and several console feed wires are deleted and protected wires can be downsized. Baseline: a cabin fusebox behind the passenger kick panel with ≈35 blade fuses and 8 relays feeds console loads (wireless charger, USB-C, cool box, rear climate panel, console lights, seat heaters) through individual feed wires sized for fuse blow characteristics. Proposal: a centre-zone controller in a PA66-GF30 housing under the console bridge integrates 24 smart high-side eFuse channels (programmable I²t), the console switch-pack LIN master and a CAN-FD/Ethernet link to the central computer; console switch packs plug directly onto the controller board edge. Why it works: eFuses trip faster and more precisely than blade fuses, so wire gauges can follow load current rather than fuse curves (e.g. 1.0→0.5 mm² on several runs), relays disappear because the eFuse switches, and the fusebox becomes unnecessary. Benchmark: BMW’s Neue Klasse uses eFuses that replace up to 150 conventional fuses per vehicle in a zonal harness 600 m shorter and about 30% lighter.

title: Flat exciters behind door-trim fabric replace door woofers, baskets and grilles
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each door’s cone woofer, metal grille, clip frame, bracket and gasket are replaced by two flat electrodynamic exciters bonded to the back of the fabric-covered door upper panel, which radiates as a distributed-mode panel; grilles and speaker apertures disappear from all four door trims. Baseline: each door carries a 165 mm cone mid-bass driver on a bracket with EPDM gasket behind a perforated aluminium grille and clip frame cut into the trim. Proposal: two 25 W flat exciters (voice coil on a 40 mm puck) are bonded with a structural acrylic tape to the back of a stiffened PP-LGF20 upper door panel zone (≈350×200 mm, ribbed at 2.5 mm) under acoustic knit fabric; the panel radiates 150 Hz-8 kHz as a distributed-mode loudspeaker, tweeters stay in the mirror sail, and bass below 120 Hz moves to the existing subwoofer. DSP equalisation corrects panel modes. Why it works: a stiff, light trim panel is already a radiator; exciting it deliberately removes grille, basket and cut-out, and the hidden source suits a clean luxury door. Benchmark: the BMW iX "Shy Tech" interior hides its speaker panels under the cabin surface in the door panels and headrests, behind acoustic fabric.

title: One recycled-PET knit family wraps headliner, visors and pillar trims on every trim
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The greenhouse fabrics (headliner, sun visors, A/B/C pillar wraps) collapse from eight material/colour combinations to one recycled-PET warp knit in two colours, pooling yarn and dye volume, cutting dye-lot scrap, changeovers and obsolescence; a microsuede headliner stays as a paid option. Baseline: headliner, visors and pillar trims are wrapped in four colours of polyester tricot and a microsuede on upper trims – eight combinations, each needing its own dye lot (minimum 2,500 m), laminate run and stock of wrapped parts, with ≈4% cutting and mismatch scrap. Proposal: one 100% recycled-PET (rPET) warp knit, 180 g/m², flame-retardant to FMVSS 302 without halogens, laminated to 3 mm PU or PET foam, in two colours (light/dark) used on every greenhouse part; microsuede only as an option on the headliner. Why it works: greenhouse fabric is low-visibility, high-area (≈4.2 m² per vehicle); pooling volume moves price per m², and two colours cut dye-lot and changeover losses. rPET also helps the recycled-content target. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 uses recycled-PET fabric across the headliner, sun visor, garnish and other interior parts, and 100% recycled-PET carpets.

title: Wireless charger cooled by bleed from console air duct, deleting its fan
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The 15 W wireless-charging module loses its 40 mm fan, fan driver, connector and NVH foam; a 1.5 l/s bleed from the existing rear-console air duct is ducted under the charging tray, so the phone and coil are cooled by conditioned cabin air instead. Baseline: the console wireless charger (Qi/Qi2, 15 W) uses a 40 mm 12 V axial fan drawing cabin air through a grille under the phone tray to keep the coil and phone below 40-45 °C, with a fan driver stage, two-wire connector and foam to suppress fan whine. Proposal: a short PP-T20 branch with a fixed 8 mm orifice taps the rear-console HVAC duct, which already passes under the tray, delivering ≈1.5 l/s across the coil and phone underside; a thermistor in the module derates power when the HVAC blower is off, and the phone tray gets a 0.5 mm aluminium heat-spreader plate. Why it works: in cooling mode the HVAC duct carries conditioned air at 15-25 °C, better than cabin air at 30+ °C in summer; in heating mode the same duct carries 40-60 °C air, so the branch needs a passive thermostatic shut-off (or must tap a cold-deck/bypass duct) and the charger derates in winter; a bleed of 1.5 l/s is <1% of rear-console flow and imperceptible at the outlet. Benchmark: general practice in several premium consoles; the 2025 Tesla Model Y Juniper redesign of its console and dash shows how the console area is being re-packaged around fabric, ambient light and charging pads.

title: EPP rear auxiliary HVAC case with integral insulation replaces PP-T20 shells and pads
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear auxiliary HVAC case on three-row vehicles changes from two PP-T20 injection shells plus three die-cut PU insulation pads and screws to two EPP 60 g/l moulded shells that insulate, seal the heat-exchanger cores and clip closed. Baseline: the rear auxiliary HVAC unit (three-row trims) uses two PP-T20 injection-moulded shells (≈1.4 kg), three die-cut PU foam pads for thermal/condensation insulation, foam gaskets around the evaporator and heater core, and eight screws. Proposal: two EPP 60 g/l steam-chest moulded shells (≈0.45 kg) with moulded-in core pockets that grip the evaporator and heater with 1 mm interference, moulded blend-door bearing bushes in PA6 inserts, and four snap clips plus two screws at the blower flange. EPP’s λ ≈ 0.038 W/mK removes the insulation pads and its compliance replaces core gaskets. Why it works: a rear unit has low structural load and benefits from insulation and NVH damping; EPP tooling is cheap and the part count halves. Benchmark: general practice for rear HVAC and duct housings; the Lucid Gravity shows the luxury three-row BEV format where rear climate units must stay compact and light.

title: Two-shot glovebox bin and door with moulded hinge and rotary damper
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The glovebox inner and outer door welding, separate linear damper, hinge pins and bump stops are replaced by a two-shot door with TPE bump stops and a silicone-fluid rotary damper moulded around the hinge axis, cutting four parts and one vibration-welding operation. Baseline: glovebox assembly with a PP-T20 bin, an ABS outer door skin and PP inner door vibration-welded together, steel hinge pins, a linear air/oil damper with bracket, two rubber bump stops and a latch with bowden cable. Proposal: a one-piece PP-LGF20 inner door with integrated hinge knuckles, a TPE second shot for bump stops and seal, a compact silicone-fluid rotary damper (Ø 18 mm) pressed onto the hinge axis, and the outer skin as a grained PP-T20 panel heat-staked to the inner (no welding). Why it works: rotary dampers at the pivot are smaller and cheaper than linear dampers with their brackets, and the second shot replaces separate rubber parts. Benchmark: general practice in volume interiors; the Defender L663 exposed-beam IP shows how luxury SUV storage can be re-thought around the beam rather than added parts.

title: A-pillar trim with moulded living hinge and captive tether replaces tether clips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two tether clips and separate fabric tether strap that keep the A-pillar trim from becoming a projectile during curtain-airbag deployment are replaced by a moulded TPO living-hinge zone and one dual-lock clip with captive tether, saving parts and fitting time per side. Baseline: each A-pillar upper trim (PP-T20, fabric-wrapped) is retained by two tethered fir-tree clips and an additional woven tether strap riveted to the trim, so that when the curtain airbag deploys the trim swings open but stays attached. Proposal: the trim is moulded in a TPO-T15 grade with a 0.9 mm living-hinge band along the windscreen edge that lets the rear edge rotate ≈25° under airbag load; one dual-lock clip with a captive steel tether (pre-assembled by the clip supplier) holds the lower end; the separate strap and second tethered clip are deleted. Why it works: a hinge band gives the trim a controlled opening path, so only one tether is needed to prevent detachment; TPO tolerates the high strain rate without cracking at −30 °C. Benchmark: general practice in recent pillar-trim designs; the Kia EV9 shows rPET-wrapped greenhouse trims on a luxury three-row SUV, the trim family this design applies to.

title: Rear-console face as one module: climate keys, USB-C and registers on one PCB
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The rear console end’s separate rear-climate control panel, twin USB-C module, register housing and bezel become one moulded face with a single PCB carrying keys and USB-C PD controller, cutting one PCB, two connectors and two housings. Baseline: the rear end of the centre console carries a register housing with two vents (PP), a rear climate control panel with its own PCB and LIN node, a separate USB-C PD module (two ports, own PCB and connector), a decorative bezel and three harness connectors. Proposal: one PC/ABS face moulding with register vanes and housings integrated, behind which one 4-layer PCB hosts the capacitive/mechanical climate keys, LIN node and a dual-port 45 W USB-C PD controller; one 12-way connector. Why it works: two small PCBs and their connectors, housings and assembly steps cost more than one larger PCB; the rear console face is a natural single module. Benchmark: the 2025 Tesla Model Y adds an 8-inch rear touchscreen that controls rear climate and media in the console end, consolidating rear-occupant controls in one place.

title: Moulded harness channels with snap fingers on IP substrate replace tape-on clips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Most of the 45 fir-tree and cable-tie clips that fasten the cockpit harness to the beam and IP substrate are replaced by moulded channels with flexible snap fingers, so the harness is pressed in along tape-marked locators, cutting clip cost, clipping time at the cockpit supplier and rattles. Baseline: the cockpit harness (≈9 m of branches across displays, registers, switches, airbag, HVAC actuators) is attached by ≈45 fir-tree clips and cable ties to holes in the CCB brackets and IP substrate, plus foam tape for anti-rattle; clipping takes ≈7 min per cockpit. Proposal: the PP-T20 IP substrate and two PA6-GF30 beam brackets get U-channels (12-25 mm) with flexible snap fingers every 120 mm; the harness carries coloured tape-marks at matching positions; 12 clips remain at heavy or 3D branch points. Why it works: moulded features cost almost nothing at 50,000/yr once in the tool, pressing a harness into a channel is faster than fitting clips, and channels damp rattles. Benchmark: general practice; BMW’s Neue Klasse zonal harness, split into separately installable parts and 30% lighter, shows how lighter harness segments suit moulded routing.

title: Capacitive sensing film behind overhead console decor replaces seven of eight mechanical switches
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The overhead console’s eight mechanical switches, chrome caps, switch frames and the separate lamp lenses are replaced by one printed capacitive sensing film laminated behind the decor face with backlit icons, sharing the lamp PCB, so switch parts and assembly operations disappear. Baseline: overhead console with eight mechanical switches (two reading lamps, interior lamp, roof/shade, SOS, garage, two spare), each with a chrome-plated cap, switch frame and plunger to a PCB, plus separate lamp lenses. Proposal: the console face (PC with IMD decor or thin wood veneer laminated to PC) carries a printed silver/PEDOT capacitive sensing film with eight pads and laser-etched backlit icons; a single PCB hosts the touch controller, LEDs for icons and reading lamps and a 30 ms haptic pulse via a small LRA; SOS keeps a recessed mechanical key with guard to meet eCall rules. Why it works: touch pads cost a fraction of mechanical switches and caps, and one laminate replaces many parts; icons only show when lit, giving a clean luxury look. Benchmark: the BMW iX "Shy Tech" interior conceals haptic controls behind open-pore wood trim.

title: Air-purification ioniser emitter moulded into the HVAC blower scroll
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The stand-alone ioniser module with its own housing, bracket, duct section and harness branch is replaced by an emitter PCB that snaps into a pocket moulded in the blower scroll outlet and shares the blower connector, deleting a housing, bracket, duct joint and connector. Baseline: the cabin air-purification option places an ioniser/hydroxyl-radical generator module in a separate housing spliced into the front HVAC duct behind the IP, with its own bracket, two duct seals and a harness branch from the body controller. Proposal: the emitter board (high-voltage generator, needle electrode, ozone-limited output) is potted into a PBT-GF30 carrier that snaps into a pocket moulded in the blower scroll outlet, where flow velocity is highest – but in a blow-through module this is upstream of the evaporator and heater core, whose wet fins capture much of the ion/radical output, so cabin delivery must be measured against the duct-mounted baseline (fallback: an outlet-plenum pocket downstream of the heater core); power and enable come through two extra pins in the blower motor connector, with control via the existing HVAC LIN. Why it works: the blower outlet sees all cabin airflow at the highest velocity, so the emitter is as effective there; the duct splice, housing and bracket are pure packaging cost. Benchmark: the Range Rover integrates Panasonic nanoe X ionisation into its HVAC together with CO2 management and PM2.5 cabin air filtration.

title: D-pillar upper and cargo-side upper trims merged into one moulding per side
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each side’s D-pillar upper trim and cargo-side upper trim become one injection moulding with the shared joint line removed, cutting one tool pair, three clips, a screw and one fitting operation per side, and eliminating a visible gap that needs gap-and-flush control. Baseline: in the cargo area each side has three trims – D-pillar upper (wrapped in headliner fabric), cargo-side upper (grained PP-T20 with tie-down and lamp apertures) and cargo-side lower – joined by visible split lines, eight clips and two screws per side. Proposal: the D-pillar upper and cargo-side upper are moulded as one PP-T20 part (≈1.3 m tall) with a grain change at a styled character line instead of a split, the fabric zone replaced by a flocked-in-mould or knit-laminated insert only where visible from the second row; the lower stays separate for load-floor tolerances. Clips per side 8 → 5, screws 2 → 1. Why it works: one tool and one fitting replace two, and a character line is cheaper to control than a gap. Benchmark: general practice; the Lucid Gravity, with up to 112 cu ft of storage, shows how large luxury SUV cargo areas benefit from fewer, larger trim panels.

title: Open beam-mounted dash shelf replaces lockable glovebox on utility trims
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] On the utility trim family the passenger glovebox assembly (bin, door, latch, damper, lamp, lock) is replaced by an open shelf moulded into the IP lower above the exposed beam, with a rubber mat and bungee net; a separate knee-bolster bracket keeps passenger knee protection. Baseline: every vehicle has a lockable glovebox: PP-T20 bin, welded two-piece door, latch with bowden, damper, lamp and switch, lock cylinder, bump stops (≈€26). Proposal: on the utility/adventure trims that use the exposed cross-car beam, the space becomes an open passenger shelf (≈9 l) moulded as part of the IP lower in PP-T20, with a removable TPE anti-slip mat and a fabric bungee net; valuables go to the existing lockable console bin. Passenger knee protection that the glovebox door provided is replaced by a stamped DP600 knee-bolster bracket bolted to the beam, behind a PP-T20 knee panel. Why it works: on outdoor-use trims an open shelf is preferred for quick access, and the deleted mechanism content outweighs the added knee bracket. Benchmark: general practice in utility SUVs; the Defender L663 builds its dashboard around an exposed structural magnesium beam with integrated grab handles, which this shelf sits on.

title: Cargo cover cassette moulded in PP-LGF30 replaces aluminium tube and cast end caps
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The retractable cargo cover cassette’s extruded aluminium tube, two die-cast zinc end caps, separate mounting pins and anodising are replaced by a two-part PP-LGF30 cassette with moulded end caps and mounting spigots, keeping the constant-force spring and fabric. Baseline: retractable cargo cover cassette with a 1.1 m extruded and anodised 6063-T5 aluminium tube, two die-cast Zamak 5 end caps with spring-loaded mounting pins, an internal roller with clock spring, PVC-coated polyester blind and aluminium pull bar. Proposal: a two-piece PP-LGF30 cassette (top and bottom shells, 2.2 mm walls, ribbed) with moulded end caps and spigots, ultrasonic-welded along the length; the spring-loaded pin is a moulded PA6 latch; roller and spring unchanged; pull bar in PP-LGF30 with a steel insert. Why it works: the tube carries only bending from its own weight and occupant lean; long-glass PP achieves the stiffness at lower cost, and the end caps no longer need casting and plating. Benchmark: general practice in cargo management; the Lucid Gravity shows large luxury SUV cargo areas (112 cu ft total) where cover hardware cost scales with length.

title: Twin-sheet thermoformed frunk tub with formed cable caddy replaces injection-moulded tub
description: [800V BEV] The BEV front-trunk tub changes from a large PP-T20 injection moulding with a separate EPP charge-cable insert and drain valve to a twin-sheet thermoformed HDPE tub with formed-in cable caddy and drain lip, cutting tool cost about 80% and piece cost at BEV volume. Baseline: BEV front-trunk tub (≈90 l) injection-moulded in PP-T20 (2.4 kg) on a ≈€0.9M tool, with a separate EPP insert holding the charge cable, a separate rubber drain valve and a needle-felt liner. Proposal: a twin-sheet thermoformed tub in 3.5 mm HDPE (UV-stabilised, black) on aluminium tools (≈€0.18M): the inner sheet forms a stiff double wall with the cable caddy pockets and a lipped drain spout; the needle-felt liner stays as an option. Why it works: at ≈20,000 BEVs per year thermoforming tooling is far cheaper and the twin-sheet double wall gives the stiffness that ribs gave in injection moulding; HDPE is wash-resistant for a wet frunk. Benchmark: the Porsche Macan Electric offers an 84-litre front luggage compartment for bags or charging cables, and the Lucid Gravity frunk is 8.1 cu ft (220 l) with an integrated folding cushion.

title: Single EPP underfloor cargo bin with moulded kit pockets replaces bin plus inserts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The underfloor cargo bin, its separate EPP organiser insert and the tyre-repair-kit holder become one EPP 45 g/l moulding with pockets for the compressor, sealant, tow eye, warning triangle and (BEV) charge cable, deleting two parts and their fixings. Baseline: under the load floor sits an injection-moulded PP-T20 bin (≈1.6 kg) that carries a separate EPP organiser insert and a PP holder for the tyre-repair compressor and sealant, plus a strap for the warning triangle. Proposal: one EPP 45 g/l bin (≈0.55 kg) moulded with pockets for the compressor, sealant bottle, tow eye, jack-free kit, warning triangle and, on BEV, the Mode 2 charge cable; a PP film skin on the floor of the bin resists abrasion. Why it works: EPP tooling is low-cost, the material self-damps rattles so straps disappear, and one part replaces three. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity offers additional storage under its removable rear cargo floor, showing how the underfloor volume of a luxury SUV is used as organised storage.

title: Rear footwell air channels formed in the carpet underlay replace blow-moulded ducts
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The two blow-moulded HDPE rear-footwell ducts and their clips under the carpet are deleted; the moulded PU-foam carpet underlay is formed with two closed air channels skinned by a PE film, so ducting arrives with the carpet and the duct fitting operation disappears. Baseline: two HDPE blow-moulded ducts (≈0.6 kg) run from the console/HVAC rear outlet under the carpet to the rear footwells, fixed by clips to the floor pan or pack lid, with foam pads to prevent rattles, fitted before the carpet (≈1 min). Proposal: the back-foamed PU underlay of the floor carpet (already moulded to the floor shape) is foamed with two 70×25 mm channels; a 150 µm PE film laminated on the underside closes the channels and seals them to the floor; a TPE adapter joins the HVAC rear outlet. On MHEV the channels run beside the tunnel, on BEV across the flat pack lid. Why it works: the underlay is already a 3D moulding at the right place; adding channel geometry to the foam tool costs little and removes a part and an operation. Benchmark: general practice; the Lucid Gravity flat-floor BEV layout shows how carpet systems on a pack floor become the natural carrier for floor-level services.

title: Centre-display carrier co-moulded with centre register housings in PA6-GF30
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The magnesium die-cast centre-display bracket and the two separate centre air-register housings with their screws are replaced by one PA6-GF30 carrier that mounts the display, holds the register vane packs and bolts to the cross-car beam at three points. Baseline: the floating centre display is held by an AM60B die-cast bracket (≈0.45 kg) bolted to the beam; below it two PP register housings are screwed separately to the IP substrate, each needing its own gap-and-flush setting relative to the display. Proposal: one PA6-GF30 carrier (ribbed, 2.8 mm walls; expect ≈0.7-0.9 kg, since its modulus is about a fifth of magnesium's) with the display datum pads, cable channel and the two register housings moulded in; vane packs click into the housings; the carrier bolts to the beam at three M6 points. Why it works: one moulding replaces a casting and two mouldings, and the display-to-register gap is now set by one tool. Display vibration is controlled by rib design (first mode ≥ 45 Hz). Benchmark: general practice; the Genesis GV80 integrated 27-inch display shows the trend of consolidating cockpit display mounts.

title: Integrated-hinge armrest lid with magnetic catch replaces stamped hinge and latch
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The console armrest lid’s stamped steel hinge pair, torsion spring, rivets and push-button latch mechanism are replaced by hinge knuckles moulded into a PA6-GF30 lid substrate on one steel pin with a TPE detent, and a concealed magnetic catch, cutting five parts and two assembly steps. Baseline: the console armrest lid (PP substrate, foam, leather wrap) opens on two stamped and riveted steel hinge arms with a torsion spring, and closes on a push-button latch with a spring, pawl and striker. Proposal: the lid substrate becomes PA6-GF30 with two moulded hinge knuckles running on one 6 mm stainless pin through console-side bosses; a TPE detent cam gives a soft hold-open at 100°; a pair of N42 magnets (one in lid, one steel plate in console) gives ≈25 N closing hold; a finger pocket replaces the push button. Why it works: the lid carries low loads (arm rest 900 N vertical is taken by the console rim), so hinge knuckles in glass-filled PA6 suffice, and magnets avoid latch mechanics and rattle. Benchmark: general practice; the 2025 Tesla Model Y redesigned its centre console and armrest area, showing simplification of console hardware in premium SUVs.

title: Micro-louvre film on a flush cluster lens deletes the wrapped cluster hood
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The wrapped and stitched cluster hood, its substrate and fixings are deleted; an angle-restricting micro-louvre film and anti-reflection coating on the cluster lens control sunlight wash-out and windscreen reflections, so the cluster sits flush in a low brow. Baseline: the 12.3-inch cluster sits under a deep hood – a PP-T20 substrate, foam, cut-and-sew leatherette with stitching – that shades the display from sunlight and stops its image reflecting in the windscreen at night. Proposal: the hood is replaced by a 15 mm low brow moulded in the IP topper; the cluster stack adds a micro-louvre light-control film (vertical cut-off ±30°) between backlight and panel plus an AR/AG coated cover, and a higher-luminance backlight (1,000 nit) for sunlight. Why it works: louvre film blocks upward light paths that cause windscreen reflections, and AR/AG plus brightness handles wash-out; the hood’s cost is almost all decorative wrap. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity places its 34-inch curved OLED Clearview Cockpit floating above the steering wheel without a conventional hood.

title: Laid-thread false stitch on IMG TPO lower IP replaces cut-and-sew wrap
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Lower IP and knee-panel surfaces lose their hand-wrapped, cut-and-sewn leatherette and foam; an in-mould-grained TPO skin with a moulded stitch groove receives a robot-laid real thread, so the stitch look stays while sewing, wrapping and adhesive labour disappear on non-touch surfaces. Baseline: lower IP (knee panels driver/passenger, centre-stack sides) is cut-and-sew PU/PVC leatherette with twin-needle decorative stitching (≈6 m of seam), wrapped by hand over a PP-T20 substrate with 3 mm PU foam and water-based adhesive. Proposal: in-mould grain (IMG) TPO skin (0.9 mm, compact) vacuum-formed directly on the substrate with a 1.2 mm stitch groove; a robot then lays and presses a 0.7 mm polyester thread into the groove with a heat-activated adhesive, giving a real-thread "false stitch" look; the upper IP and touch surfaces keep genuine stitching. Why it works: the lower IP is rarely touched and mostly seen at a distance; a laid thread in a groove is visually indistinguishable at 1 m and needs no sewing or wrapping. Benchmark: the Volvo EX30 shows deliberate de-content of door and dash hardware for cost; our approach keeps the luxury look while removing sewing labour.

title: PA6-GF30 centre-display rear housing with aluminium spreader replaces die-cast shell
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The die-cast aluminium rear housing of the centre display, with its machining and e-coat, is replaced by an injection-moulded PA6-GF30 housing carrying a stamped 0.3 mm aluminium spreader that both shields EMI and spreads heat from the timing controller and backlight driver via a graphite sheet. Baseline: the 14.9-inch centre display uses a 0.62 kg ADC12 high-pressure die-cast rear housing that is trimmed, CNC-faced at the mount bosses and e-coated, acting as heat sink and EMI enclosure. Proposal: a PA6-GF30 (UL94 V-0 not required, FMVSS 302) housing, 2.0 mm walls with ribs, carries a stamped EN AW-1050 0.3 mm spreader that covers the PCB area, grounded at four points to the panel frame; a 25 µm graphite sheet couples the TCON and LED driver (≈4 W) to the spreader, while the backlight LED bars (often 8-12 W at full brightness) keep their own path into the panel frame and spreader; mount bosses carry brass inserts. Why it works: dissipated power is small and spread over a large area, so conduction to a thin aluminium sheet plus natural convection keeps junctions below 95 °C; the stamped sheet closes the EMI cage at a fraction of a casting’s cost. Benchmark: the Genesis GV80 merges cluster and infotainment into a single 27-inch display, illustrating the pressure to cut cost and mass of display housings as screens grow.

title: Hard-coated PMMA cover lens on the non-touch instrument cluster replaces strengthened glass
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The instrument cluster, which is never touched, swaps its 0.7 mm chemically strengthened aluminosilicate cover glass with AG etch and AR coating for a 2.0 mm injection-compression-moulded PMMA lens with siloxane hard-coat and AR coating, keeping optical bonding. Baseline: 12.3-inch cluster with a 0.7 mm chemically strengthened aluminosilicate cover glass, anti-glare etched and AR coated, optically bonded with OCA to the LCD; glass is used because the centre display also uses it, not because the cluster is touched. Proposal: a 2.0 mm optical-grade PMMA lens made by injection-compression moulding with a 3 µm siloxane hard-coat (pencil 3H, Taber ≤ 15% haze after 100 cycles) and a 4-layer AR stack (R ≤ 1%), bonded with LOCA tuned for PMMA expansion; edges radiused to R1.5. Why it works: without touch, scratch exposure is limited to cleaning; PMMA has excellent optics and does not shatter, improving head-impact behaviour; moulding replaces cutting, strengthening and edge grinding. Benchmark: the Xiaomi YU7 HyperVision shows the driver display moving to a non-touch, projected format – the cluster is a viewing surface, not a touch surface.

title: Ribbed PA6-GF50 door-pull core replaces zinc die-cast structural insert
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Each door pull handle’s Zamak 5 die-cast structural insert and its two screws are replaced by a ribbed PA6-GF50 core moulded with integrated screw bosses, carrying the same pull loads at a fraction of the cost and mass. Baseline: four door pull handles, each with a Zamak 5 die-cast insert (≈120 g) inside a PC/ABS cover, wrapped in leather on the visible face, screwed to the door module carrier by two screws plus one to the trim. Proposal: a PA6-GF50 core (≈45 g, 2.5 mm ribs in an I-section, 0.4 mm draft) with moulded screw bosses and brass-free direct screwing (PT screws), overmoulded at the grip with TPE where the leather wraps; the cover and wrap stay. Why it works: a pull handle sees ≈900 N pull and abuse loads that a glass-filled PA6 I-beam handles with safety factor ≥ 2; die-casting, deburring and plating-preparation costs disappear. Benchmark: the BMW iX’s Shy Tech door panels show luxury doors where hidden structure carries functions behind fabric and leather surfaces.

title: Two-shot TPE lip on the door trim carrier deletes PE water shield and butyl
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The polyethylene water-shield film and its butyl bead on each inner door panel are deleted; the door trim carrier is moulded with a second-shot TPE perimeter lip that seals against the door module carrier, so the wet/dry separation is made by parts that are already there. Baseline: each door has a plastic door module carrier holding window regulator and speaker, plus a 0.2 mm LDPE water shield with butyl sealing bead covering the remaining inner-panel openings, applied by hand (≈1.2 min per door). Proposal: the PP-LGF30 door trim carrier gets a 2K TPE (Shore A 45) lip around its lower and rear perimeter, which compresses 3 mm against a flange on the module carrier; remaining access holes in the inner panel are closed by moulded plugs on the module carrier. Why it works: in modern doors the module carrier already forms most of the wet/dry barrier; a compliant lip on the trim closes the residual gap without film or butyl, and removes a messy manual operation. Benchmark: the BMW iX Shy Tech door panels, with speakers concealed in the panel, show how door trims increasingly integrate functions that used to be separate parts.

title: Magnet-retained sun visor on a tabbed headliner base replaces clip-in visor hook
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The sun visor’s free-end clip hook, its wire retention rod and the screwed visor-check bracket are replaced by a ferrite magnet moulded into the visor and a steel-backed check base that snaps into the headliner with two tabs, removing a screw, a bracket and a clip per visor. Baseline: each sun visor has a pivot at the outboard end and a rod at the inboard end that clips into a PA6 visor-check bracket screwed through the headliner into the roof bow; clipping effort and rattles at the clip are recurring quality items. Proposal: a 15×10×4 mm ferrite (or bonded NdFeB) magnet is placed in the visor core at the inboard end; a PP visor-check base with a 0.5 mm steel plate snaps into a headliner aperture with two tabs and is backed by a roof-bow foam pad; the visor simply rests magnetically (≈8 N hold) and swings free. Why it works: the hold force needed is small; a magnet gives silent, tolerance-free retention and removes the screw-in bracket. Benchmark: the Tesla Model Y holds its sun visor with a magnet in the visor gripping a headliner-mounted visor-check base retained by two tabs.

title: Ultrasonic edge-crimp of headliner apertures replaces hot-melt edge folding
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The headliner’s roof-glass, overhead-console and grab-handle aperture edges are no longer folded over with sprayed hot-melt PUR adhesive; an ultrasonic sonotrode crimps the fabric into a moulded groove in the substrate, cutting adhesive, oven time and edge-fold rework. Baseline: ≈4.5 m of aperture edges (panoramic-roof opening, overhead console, grab handles, visors, rear-entertainment pocket) are finished by cutting the fabric with a 15 mm allowance, spraying hot-melt PUR and folding the fabric around the substrate edge with a robot and hand finishing; adhesive cure and edge-lift rework are recurring costs. Proposal: the PET-felt/PU substrate is moulded with a 2.5 mm deep tuck groove 6 mm inside each aperture; a 20 kHz ultrasonic sonotrode pushes and welds the rPET knit fabric (thermoplastic) into the groove, simultaneously trimming it; no adhesive. Why it works: on a PET-felt substrate both fabric and binder are thermoplastic (a PU-glass substrate is thermoset and will not weld, so that construction keeps adhesive or needs a thermoplastic edge strip), so a local weld bonds them in < 2 s per 100 mm; a tuck groove hides the edge as well as a fold. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 uses recycled-PET fabric in its headliner – a thermoplastic face material that suits welding instead of adhesive.

title: Micro-perforated tweeter grille moulded through the A-pillar trim deletes metal grille
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The perforated aluminium tweeter grille and its clip frame on each A-pillar trim are deleted; the grille is moulded through the pillar substrate as a field of 0.8 mm holes and covered by the acoustically open greenhouse fabric, so the tweeter sits hidden behind the trim surface. Baseline: each A-pillar trim has a 60 mm round aperture with a separate perforated, brushed and anodised aluminium grille in a PC clip frame, in front of a 25 mm tweeter. Proposal: the PP-T20 pillar substrate is moulded with an array of 0.8 mm holes at 1.6 mm pitch (≈20-23% open area) over the tweeter zone using a pin insert, and the rPET knit fabric wraps across it; the fabric’s airflow resistance (< 200 Rayl) gives < 1 dB loss above 2 kHz after EQ. Why it works: tweeter output needs only a modest open area, and the fabric hides the holes, so the decorative metal grille is pure cost. Benchmark: the BMW iX conceals its speakers under the cabin surface, behind acoustic fabric, as part of its Shy Tech interior.

title: Needle-punched rPET dilour floor carpet replaces tufted cut-pile, mats stay tufted
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The moulded floor carpet face changes from tufted PA6 cut-pile (850 g/m²) on a primary backing to needle-punched dilour (velour-structured) recycled-PET (550 g/m²) with no separate primary backing; luxury floor mats stay tufted, so the visible feel is unchanged where the occupant touches. Baseline: moulded floor carpet (≈4.5 m²) with tufted PA6 BCF cut-pile at 850 g/m² on a PET spunbond primary, LDPE pre-coat, then moulded with a PU or felt underlay; luxury floor mats sit on top in the footwells. Proposal: a needle-punched dilour face of 100% rPET staple fibre (6.7 dtex, 550 g/m²), whose structured velour surface is formed by fork needles, needs no tufting primary and is directly mouldable with a PE binder; under the mats and in hidden zones a lighter 400 g/m² grade is used; tufted mats stay. Why it works: most of the floor carpet is covered by mats, seats and console; dilour moulds well into deep shapes (no grin-through), is cheaper per m² and keeps a premium velour appearance. Benchmark: the Kia EV9 uses 100% recycled-PET carpets, with recycled fishing-net content as an option.

title: Hot-press densified heel zone replaces the sewn rubber heel pad on driver carpet
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The separate PVC/rubber heel pad that is HF-welded or sewn into the driver-footwell carpet is deleted; the heel zone is densified in the carpet moulding press by a heated insert and sprayed with a thin aliphatic PU wear coat, so the wear resistance is built into the carpet itself. Baseline: a 300×250 mm PVC or rubber heel pad (≈€2.1) is HF-welded or sewn onto the driver-footwell carpet after moulding (≈1 min), and the floor mat covers part of it; its edge often lifts and is a common audit finding. Proposal: in the carpet moulding press a heated (190 °C) shaped insert densifies the fibres in the heel zone to ≈0.6 g/cm³ during the moulding stroke, and an inline robot sprays a 150 g/m² aliphatic PU wear coat in a textured pattern. Why it works: densified fibre with a PU coat reaches the Taber/heel-abrasion targets of a pad without a separate part or seam; it is done inside the existing press stroke. Benchmark: the Kia EV9’s recycled-PET carpets show the move to thermoplastic carpet constructions that can be locally densified with heat.

title: One-way duckbill footwell drains let wading seepage escape, deleting blanking plates
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The four butyl-sealed blanking plates over the footwell e-coat drain holes and the PE moisture-barrier film under the off-road carpet are replaced by four EPDM duckbill valves that seal the drain holes against splash yet let seepage water out after wading, so the carpet underlay no longer needs a moisture barrier. Baseline: the floor pan has four 25 mm e-coat drain holes in the front and rear footwells, closed by butyl-backed steel/PE blanking plates (≈25 s each); because a wading vehicle can take seepage water that then pools under the carpet, the off-road trims add a 2.4 m² PE moisture-barrier film under the underlay to protect it and delay odour. Proposal: four push-fit EPDM duckbill valves (cracking pressure ≈5 mbar, closed against 30 kPa external splash pressure) sit in the existing drain holes at the footwell low points (on BEV only where the hole does not discharge onto the battery-pack lid or into the pack-to-floor gap; drains over the pack keep sealed plates); the PU underlay gets two moulded gutters leading to them; the PE barrier film is deleted. Why it works: with a free drain path, seepage water exits within minutes instead of soaking the underlay, so the barrier film is redundant, and the valves cost little more than plates and are faster to fit. Benchmark: the Land Rover Defender is rated for 900 mm wading on air suspension (850 mm coil), defining the water exposure an off-road luxury SUV cabin floor must tolerate.

title: Two-shot TPE friction collar on register vanes replaces O-rings and spring clips
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Vane-pivot friction in the dash and console air registers is set by a TPE collar moulded on each vane pivot in a second shot, deleting the separate silicone O-rings and steel friction clips and the assembly step that fits them. Baseline: four front and two rear registers, each with 5-6 horizontal/vertical vanes whose pivots get a silicone O-ring or a stamped spring-steel friction clip to hold the set position (≈60 small parts per vehicle), fitted manually or by a dedicated feeder; operating force drifts with O-ring wear. Proposal: vanes moulded in PC/ABS with a second-shot TPE (Shore A 70) collar on each pivot that interferes 0.15 mm in the housing bore, giving 1.5-2.5 N·cm holding torque; the link bar stays. Why it works: the friction element becomes part of the vane, so it cannot be omitted and tolerances are tool-controlled; parts and feeding disappear. title: TPV duckbill moulded on the HVAC condensate spigot deletes drain hose and clamp
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The HVAC evaporator condensate drain loses its EPDM elbow hose, hose clamp and separate body grommet; a TPV duckbill and grommet lip are two-shot moulded onto the case spigot, which passes straight through the dash/floor aperture and seals it. Baseline: the HVAC case drain spigot connects to an EPDM elbow hose with a spring clamp that passes through a rubber grommet in the dash or floor and ends in a check valve; the hose is fitted at marriage of the cockpit (≈30 s, blind). Proposal: the PP-T20 case spigot is lengthened to reach the aperture and is two-shot overmoulded with a TPV (Shore A 60) grommet lip and an integral duckbill check valve; at cockpit marriage the spigot self-seals in the aperture. On BEV the aperture is in the front floor/dash cross-member, on MHEV in the tunnel side wall. Why it works: one moulded feature replaces three parts, removes a blind operation and a leak path (hose-off). Benchmark: general practice in HVAC module design; the Range Rover’s integrated HVAC with air purification shows the luxury module class in which this drain sits.

title: Cut-to-length co-extruded ambient light-guide strip replaces moulded PMMA guides
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Zone-specific injection-moulded PMMA light-guides with separate diffuser films and PC housings are replaced by one continuous co-extruded light-guide strip (clear PMMA core, white diffusing TPU jacket with clip foot) cut to length per zone and clipped into a trim groove, removing a family of guide tools and films. Baseline: ≈4 m of ambient lines (IP, four door uppers, console sides) use injection-moulded PMMA light-guides specific to each zone, each with a diffusing film, a PC holder and an RGB LED at one end; each new trim line needs new guide tools. Proposal: a co-extruded strip – Ø 4 mm clear PMMA core with a 0.6 mm white-pigmented TPU jacket that has a clip foot – cut to length, end-polished and fitted with a moulded LED cap at each end (RGB both ends for uniformity on runs > 0.8 m); it clips into a groove moulded in the trim. Why it works: extrusion has negligible tooling and the diffusing jacket gives uniform side emission without films; the same strip serves every zone and trim facelift. Benchmark: the 2025 Tesla Model Y uses an ambient light strip running across the dashboard and through the door panels.
