title: Fold-flat cargo tie-down: PA6-GF50 overmoulded steel loop replaces chromed forged ring
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The four chromed forged steel tie-down rings with stamped pivot brackets and bolts are replaced by a bent spring-steel wire loop overmoulded in PA6-GF50 with a fold-flat hinge and clip-in base that bolts once to the body, cutting forging, plating and a bracket per anchor. Baseline: four cargo tie-down anchors, each a forged C45 ring, chrome-plated, pivoting in a stamped steel bracket bolted with M8 to a body weld nut, with a trim escutcheon. Proposal: a 6 mm 54SiCr6 spring-steel wire loop overmoulded with a PA6-GF50 body that forms the hinge, the fold-flat detent and the escutcheon; it bolts with the same M8 through a steel sleeve moulded in, and the wire loop wraps that sleeve so the load path is steel-to-steel (the PA6-GF50 does not carry the 3.5 kN). Rated working load 3.5 kN per anchor (above ISO 27955 cargo-securing needs for passenger cars; ISO 27956 covers delivery vans). Why it works: the wire loop carries the tension; the polymer only guides and decorates, so forging, chrome and a separate bracket and escutcheon are eliminated. Benchmark: the Lucid Gravity offers up to 112 cu ft of storage including underfloor space, typical of the large luxury-SUV cargo areas that need multiple tie-down points.

title: Right-hand column stalk takes over drive selection, deleting the console selector module
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The console-mounted shift-by-wire selector module (lever, redundant position sensing, park button, PRND display and its own ECU), its metal finisher, bracket and harness branch are deleted; the right-hand column stalk, which today only carries wiper functions, becomes an ASIL B drive selector inside the existing steering-column control module, and the wiper functions move onto the left combination stalk. Baseline: both powertrains already shift by wire (MHEV 8-speed automatic with electric park lock; BEV EDU park lock), yet the selector is a separate console module: monostable lever with knurled-metal finisher, dual Hall position sensing, P button, illuminated PRND, its own CAN node, bracket and a console cut-out – about €62 piece cost plus €6 finisher, €4.8 of harness and bracket, and a €9 right-hand wiper stalk on the column. Proposal: the right-hand stalk of the steering-column control module becomes the drive selector (up = R, down = D, end push = P, N by a held half-step), with two independent Hall sensors read by two microcontroller channels in the column module (ASIL B), P also applied automatically on door-open/belt-off/ignition-off exactly as the baseline does; wipers move to the left combination stalk (twist ring plus push/pull). The console cut-out becomes a storage tray. Engineering check: no new fail-safe dependency is introduced – park holding is still the mechanical park pawl/park lock commanded by the existing shift-by-wire controller, and loss of the stalk signal defaults to the current selector-fault strategy (hold gear, P at standstill).

ideaData.technicalDescription: Baseline: both powertrains already shift by wire (MHEV 8-speed automatic with electric park lock; BEV EDU park lock), yet the selector is a separate console module: monostable lever with knurled-metal finisher, dual Hall position sensing, P button, illuminated PRND, its own CAN node, bracket and a console cut-out – about €62 piece cost plus €6 finisher, €4.8 of harness and bracket, and a €9 right-hand wiper stalk on the column. Proposal: the right-hand stalk of the steering-column control module becomes the drive selector (up = R, down = D, end push = P, N by a held half-step), with two independent Hall sensors read by two microcontroller channels in the column module (ASIL B), P also applied automatically on door-open/belt-off/ignition-off exactly as the baseline does; wipers move to the left combination stalk (twist ring plus push/pull). The console cut-out becomes a storage tray. Engineering check: no new fail-safe dependency is introduced – park holding is still the mechanical park pawl/park lock commanded by the existing shift-by-wire controller, and loss of the stalk signal defaults to the current selector-fault strategy (hold gear, P at standstill). Reach: the stalk tip sits 60-80 mm behind the rim at 3 o’clock, within the hand envelope without releasing grip. Mass: −0.65 kg module −0.2 kg bracket +0.08 kg stalk electronics = −0.77 kg. The column module moves with the column during the 60-80 mm collapse stroke, so the UN R12 body-block load path is unchanged. Why it works: on a by-wire platform the selector is just a switch, and the column module already has power, a bus connection and a stalk housing. Benchmark: Mercedes places the drive selector on a right-hand column stalk (pressing the end engages Park) on the EQS and on the GLE family.

ideaData.manufacturingImpact: Column module supplier adds a second Hall PCB and a P-button contact to the right stalk; the console line loses one module install (≈1.2 min) and one connector mate. Console moulding tool gets an insert change to close the selector aperture and form the tray. No new plant capex.
ideaData.dfmDfa: One column module part number serves LHD and RHD (stalk handed by side as today); selector and wiper stalks share housing tooling. Console part count falls by four (module, finisher, bracket, harness branch). Column module is EOL-tested with all selector states before shipping.

costSavingPotential.qualitative: High – a whole console module removed on every vehicle
costSavingPotential.calculationBasis: Per vehicle (100% of fleet, both powertrains): console selector module €62 + finisher €6 + harness branch €3.2 + bracket €1.6 + right wiper stalk €9 = €81.8 deleted. Added: selector stalk with dual Hall sensing and P button €24, wiper functions on left stalk €3.5, console storage tray €2.5 = €30. Net piece saving €51.8 (bridge). Low case allows €6.8 for HMI clinic-driven changes (e.g., illuminated PRND ring on the stalk) → €45; high case €55 with second-source column module quote. Net €45-€55 per vehicle × 50,000 vehicles/yr = €2.25M-€2.75M per year (engineering estimate; amortisation over 7 years = 350,000 vehicles where stated).

ideaData.riskNotes: HMI acceptance (customers used to a console selector; inadvertent selection when reaching for wipers) – run an HMI clinic and misuse study. Validate to FMVSS 102 (shift sequence and P display), FMVSS 114 (rollaway/park on exit), UN R121 (control identification and tell-tales), UN R12 column impact with the new stalk mass, ISO 26262 ASIL B for position sensing, and EMC. title: One ebony mould-in-colour finish for all lower hard trims across every interior colourway
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] Lower hard trims stop being colour-keyed: one ebony mould-in-colour finish replaces three, so light-colour compound premiums, high light-colour moulding scrap, colour-change purges, colour-keyed sequencing and plant scuff rework on light sill and kick panels disappear, while colour stays on the upper and touch surfaces. ideaData.dfmDfa: Sensor port keyed to the case so it can only be fitted one way; same sensor part number as today, so no new supplier qualification. One fewer harness branch through the cabin.

title: Venturi-aspirated in-car temperature sensors replace fan-aspirated sensors front and rear
description: [MHEV & 800V BEV] The micro-fan motor, its driver and its noise and bearing failures leave both in-car temperature sensors: a plain NTC housing draws cabin air through an aspirator tube connected to a venturi tap on the HVAC duct, so the blower airflow does the aspirating. Proposal: NTC in a small PP housing behind the same grille, connected by a 6 mm ID PE aspirator tube (≈600 mm) to a venturi tap moulded into the footwell or console duct. Airflow check: at 8 m/s duct speed and a 12 m/s throat the venturi gives Δp ≈ 0.5 × 1.2 × (12² − 8²) ≈ 48 Pa ideal, 20-40 Pa usable at the tap. A 0.5 m/s sample over the NTC needs 0.85 l/min through the tube: Re ≈ 200 (laminar), Δp = 32μLv/d² = 32 × 1.8e-5 × 0.6 × 0.5 / 0.006² ≈ 4.8 Pa, plus ≈5 Pa for grille and entry – about 10 Pa, well inside the 20-40 Pa available. At the lowest blower step (≈3 m/s duct) suction falls with v² to ≈3-6 Pa, the sample speed to ≈0.2-0.3 m/s and the sensor time constant from ≈20 s to ≈40 s, still far shorter than the cabin’s thermal time constant of several minutes. Strength check: UN R17 / FMVSS 202a apply a 373 N·m moment about the R-point and then 890 N to the restraint; at 200 mm lever each tube carries M = 445 N × 200 mm = 89 N·m, I = π/64 (22⁴ − 19⁴) ≈ 5,100 mm⁴, σ = M·c/I = 89,000 × 11 / 5,100 ≈ 192 MPa, below the 420 MPa yield. Mass: −1.6 kg restraint and motor +0.9 kg frame, foam and trim = −0.7 kg per seat. Why it works: a fixed height of 820-840 mm already exceeds the 800 mm front minimum and covers the head centre of gravity of a 95th-percentile male, so most of the restraint’s adjustability is a comfort feature. Benchmark: the BMW iX front seats carry integrated head restraints, and Euro NCAP rated the iX’s front seats and head restraints good for whiplash protection.

ideaData.dfmDfa: Four fewer insertion features and one fewer trimmed sub-part per seat; no headrest that can be fitted reversed or left out at seat build; rear-seat entertainment variants (headrest-post mounted) are routed only to executive seats.
